|  2. Assemble ingredients and equipment. | Staff get ingredients and equipment; residents are not involved. | Use photos of ingredients to support understanding. Show photo and ask resident to get item; wait expectantly. Prompt resident to get target ingredient as required.  |
|  3. Complete steps in the directions. | Staff do each step or provide hand-over-hand assistance to residents to complete task. | Offer choices of tasks to residents using photos or videos. Use photos or videos of each step to demonstrate required actions; wait expectantly for resident to initiate. Prompt resident to complete step only as required; fade prompts. When resident completes task, offer choices of photos of peers to select next participant in activity.  |
|  4. Comment on activity. | Staff talk among themselves; residents have no means to participate (AAC systems are put away to keep them clean). | Ensure that AAC is available at all times; use AAC that can be cleaned easily. Throughout activity, model appropriate comments using speech and AAC (e.g., YUMMY, MESSY, CAKE, STIR). Pause and wait expectantly for resident to comment using AAC; prompt as required. Respond immediately by expanding on the resident's message using speech and AAC.  |

- Beginning communicators who are preintentional
- Those who are intentional but presymbolic
- Those who are at the early stages of symbolic development and are learning their "first words"
- Those who have acquired a corpus of symbols (e.g., spoken words, signs, aided AAC symbols) and are beginning to combine them to communicate more complex messages

These stages of communication development are based on the stages of typical language development; in most cases, they are also applicable to the sequence of communication development for beginning communicators with a wide range of developmental disabilities and complex communication needs (Brady et al., 2018). However, in some cases, it may be necessary to modify this sequence or to set other priorities to accommodate the needs and skills of specific individuals. The sequence is intended to provide general guidelines for goal setting and intervention, not to be applied rigidly. Table 10.2 provides a summary of key goals for beginning communicators at each of the stages of communication development. These goals are discussed in further detail in the rest of this chapter along with intervention procedures.

Intervention to Support Beginning Communicators

Table 10.2. Key goals for beginning communicators at each of the stages of communication development

|  Stage of communication | Key goals for intervention  |
| --- | --- |
|  Beginning communicators who are preintentional | ·Develop intentional communication. ·Identify appropriate signals to indicate acceptance and rejection.  |
|  Beginning communicators who are intentional but presymbolic | ·Use consistent signals to express acceptance and rejection. ·Communicate choices. ·Take turns consistently in social interactions. ·Demonstrate joint attention (shift between the partner and shared activity).  |
|  Beginning communicators who are developing early symbolic communication (i.e., first words) | ·Develop a robust, diverse vocabulary to express a wide range of concepts. ·Initiate requests for objects and activities. ·Make comments/answer simple questions about ongoing activities. ·Ask simple questions.  |
|  Beginning communicators who are learning to combine symbols | ·Continue to develop a robust, diverse vocabulary to express a wide range of early semantic relations. ·Express a greater range of communicative functions. ·Combine symbols to communicate ○More complex comments about ongoing activities ○More detailed responses to questions ○More specific requests for objects or activities ○More explicit protest or rejection ○More complex questions, etc.  |
|  Beginning communicators with challenging behaviors | ·Use socially appropriate alternatives (AAC) to replace the challenging behaviors to ○Request attention ○Request preferred objects and activities ○Reject nonpreferred objects and activities ○Protest or escape from nonpreferred activities ·Use visual schedules to facilitate transitions and increase participation.  |

# INTERVENTION WITH INDIVIDUALS WHO ARE PREINTENTIONAL

At birth, infants with and without disabilities are preintentional; they do not yet understand that they can impact others by communicating. They do not yet understand cause-and-effect relationships; rather, their behaviors are reflexive. For example, they cry reflexively when they are hungry, frightened, or uncomfortable. Infants do not recognize the social consequences of their behaviors, but their caregivers respond to their reflexive behaviors as if they are communicative, and, over time, infants learn the cause-and-effect relationship (e.g., I cry, then Mommy or Daddy feeds me). Once infants recognize the relationship between their behaviors and the effects on caregivers, they begin to use behaviors intentionally to communicate. This transition from preintentional to intentional communication occurs in typical development at approximately 9 months of age.

Not all individuals develop intentionality at this early age; some do not develop intentionality until they are much older. There are numerous factors that may impede the development of intentional communication in individuals with developmental disabilities. Some of these factors may be intrinsic to the beginning communicator;

others may be related to the environment and communication partners. For example, some individuals may have severe cognitive impairments such that they require much longer to make the connection between their behaviors and their caregivers' responses. Some individuals may have motor and sensory impairments that limit the range of behaviors that they can use; their behaviors may be difficult for others to recognize and interpret. As a result, they may not receive consistent responses to their behaviors from their caregivers, making it more difficult for them to learn the causal connection.

The challenges of developing intentionality may be even greater for older beginning communicators. Whereas infants and toddlers with developmental disabilities may have a relatively small group of caregivers, older beginning communicators may interact with many communication partners during the course of a day or week, including family and other caregivers, educational or vocational staff, and many other service providers. Regular staff turnover may increase the number of communication partners even further. Given the large number of communication partners and the difficulty recognizing the behaviors of beginning communicators, there may be significant inconsistencies in how these behaviors are interpreted (Carter & Iacono, 2002). Furthermore, this lack of consistency may persist for many years, creating confusion for the beginning communicator and negatively impacting the acquisition of intentionality.

### Development of Intentionality

Intentionality is defined as purposeful, goal-directed behavior. It is evidenced by 1) persistence of the behavior until the goal is achieved, 2) cessation of the behavior once the goal is achieved, 3) substitution of another behavior or act if the first means is not successful, and 4) a change in the quality of the act if the first attempts are not successful (e.g. increasing the intensity of the behavior—Wetherby & Prizant, 1989). Intentional communication is directed toward the partner and is often marked by eye gaze or body orientation to the partner. Many beginning communicators who require AAC experience significant motor and sensory impairments that may impact the ways in which they are able to demonstrate intentionality (Iacono, Carter, & Hook, 1998; Ogletree, Bartholomew, Wagaman, Genz, & Reisinger, 2012). Table 10.3 provides a summary of potential indicators of intentional communication behaviors that might be demonstrated by individuals with complex communication needs (Iacono et al. 1998; Ogletree et al. 2012). The AAC team should be especially attuned to changes in the magnitude and rate of these behaviors as these are often signs of intentionality (Iacono et al. 1998). If behaviors are intentional, they should occur more frequently within social interactions than in other situations (e.g. Sigafoos et al. 2000).

There may be variation across beginning communicators in the ways that they indicate intentionality (Iacono et al. 1998; Ogletree et al. 2012). Parents and other caregivers are often attuned to their children's signals because they have a long history of interaction together. For this reason, it is important to involve family members and other frequent communication partners in intervention for beginning communicators:

> Parents rely heavily on their own intuition and ability to interpret their child. . . . [This] involves a great degree of guesswork. . . . Parents are often regarded with suspicion about the validity of their interpretations. They often hear from other people that they over-interpret the child and that their comprehension is only an expression of wishful thinking. . . . [However], parents have a unique competence in knowing their children and understanding their children's communication. (Brodin, 1991, p. 237)

Intervention to Support Beginning Communicators

Table 10.3. Potential indicators of intentional communication in individuals with complex communication needs

|  Indicator of intentional communication | Operational definition  |
| --- | --- |
|  Eye gaze | Looking at the partner or object, often accompanied by facial expression or vocalization  |
|  Facial or head orienting | Positioning one's face or head toward (or away from) a partner or object, with or without vocalization  |
|  Vocalization | Producing sound (e.g., grunts, babbling, laughter, crying) directed toward a partner or object  |
|  Facial expressions | Using facial muscles to produce a countenance (e.g., smiling, frowning) directed toward a partner or object  |
|  Physical actions | Producing movements of the upper or lower extremities (e.g., reaching for, pushing away) directed toward a partner or object  |
|  Body posturing | Positioning one's body toward (or away from) a partner or object  |

It is also important to involve an occupational/physical therapist in the assessment to help to distinguish between reflexive behaviors and those that are under volitional control.

The first step in planning intervention for individuals who are preintentional is to conduct an assessment to determine 1) behaviors that are within the individual's repertoire (e.g., turning toward a partner, reaching for an item); 2) antecedents to these behaviors (i.e., situations that precede the behaviors); 3) consequences for these behaviors (i.e., responses of partners to these behaviors); and 4) evidence of intentionality. Individuals at this stage of development are highly context dependent; therefore, this assessment should involve observations of the beginning communicator across a range of typical activities and partners in the natural environment (Ogletree et al., 2012). If geography or service delivery models preclude such observations, then it may be possible for the AAC team to collect valuable information by asking family members or other caregivers to collect videos of the beginning communicator's typical daily activities.

# Intervention to Build Intentionality

The goal of intervention with individuals who are preintentional is to establish intentional communication. Typically intervention includes the following steps:

1. Establish routines focused on motivating activities.
2. Initiate the interaction.
3. Pause and wait expectantly.
4. Watch carefully for a signal.
5. Respond immediately to the signal as if it were intentional.
6. Repeat this sequence.

The example of Linda illustrates what these steps might look like in practice. Linda is an adult with severe speech and motor impairments who lives in a group home with other adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities. The staff in her group home have been working with her to develop intentional communication. She enjoys being fed at

AAC Interventions for Individuals with Developmental Disabilities

mealtimes so this activity was selected as a starting point. The staff start to feed her at mealtime, but after several bites, they stop, focus attention on Linda, and wait for her to signal that she wants to eat. If she turns to them and opens her mouth, they immediately respond by feeding her another bite. She is gradually learning the cause-and-effect relationship between this behavior and the consequence of being fed.

Of course, not all activities are preferred ones. Sometimes individuals reject or protest nonpreferred activities. In this case, communication partners should recognize the intent and respond appropriately to the behavior as a signal of rejection.

The staff in Linda's group home are careful to respond in this way to her intent. When Linda doesn't like a food item, she puts her head down to avoid being fed. The staff are working to develop this behavior into a clear signal of rejection. Each time she puts her head down, the staff respond as if the act is intentional and remove the nonpreferred food. Initially, staff responded to even a slight downward movement of her head, but gradually over time, they have increased the expectations for a clearer signal of rejection through a process of successive approximations.

**Establish Routines Focused on Motivating Activities** Daily routines provide many opportunities for communication, including play and leisure activities as well as activities of daily living (e.g., dressing, bathing, eating). Communication partners should start with simple interactive routines that have a clear structure where the same cues and actions are repeated in a cyclical manner (Light, Parsons, &amp; Drager, 2002). For young children, these activities might include games like tickle games, peek-a-boo, action songs (e.g., "Row, Row, Row Your Boat"), and bye-bye routines that have a regular structure that is repeated each time. For older individuals, these activities might include high-five routines or dancing routines.

Eliza's case illustrates how a communication partner might use routines in this way with a baby to help develop intentionality. Eliza is 7 months old and has Down syndrome. She loves music, especially action songs. Her mom has set up an interactive routine for singing "Row, Row, Row Your Boat" to start to establish the foundations for communication. She sits on the floor facing Eliza and holds her hands. Then she starts to sing the song, rocking back and forth with Eliza. Once the routine has been established and Eliza is enjoying it, her mom stops singing and rocking after every 1–2 lines in the song and waits expectantly for any indication that Eliza wants to continue the game. Eliza is learning that if she starts to rock forward and vocalizes, her mom immediately restarts the action song. Eliza is developing intentionality. Her mom can apply this basic format—action, expectant delay to elicit a communicative signal, respond immediately to the signal—to other interactive games and songs, as well as activities of daily living such as feeding or dressing.

As much as possible, communication partners should perform the steps of these routines in the same sequence and manner each time so that the beginning communicator can begin to anticipate what happens next. Communication partners need to work together to establish consistency in these routines, especially when there are numerous potential partners involved in the same activity.

Intervention to Support Beginning Communicators
331

Once beginning communicators consistently signal within a range of simple repetitive routines, they may be introduced to more complex routines that involve a series of steps, each of which may necessitate a different type of signal response. When learning to participate within these more complex routines, beginning communicators may require more structured opportunities with systematic prompts (e.g., Keen, Sigafoos, &amp; Woodyatt, 2001; Siegel &amp; Wetherby, 2000).

Adam, a young man who is deafblind and has severe physical disabilities, is learning to participate during a changing routine at the swimming pool. His personal care attendant uses short, simple sentences to describe each step and pauses expectantly at each step to mark the opportunity for Adam to participate. Because Adam has severe sensory impairments, his aide provides touch cues to support him in understanding and anticipating the next step. For example, while rubbing Adam's swimsuit against his wrist, the aide says, "Put on your swimsuit." After each step, the aide pauses for at least 10 seconds and observes Adam for a signal. If Adam responds with a signal that can be interpreted as acceptance (e.g., lifts his leg to step into his swimsuit), the aide continues the routine. If Adam responds in a way that signals rejection (e.g., cries, moves away), the aide stops the routine. In a few minutes, the aide initiates the step again, explores an alternative way of proceeding, or terminates the routine altogether. If Adam does not produce any type of signal after the expectant delay, the aide repeats the touch and spoken cue and waits at least 10 seconds for a signal. If Adam still gives no signal, the aide acknowledges this and continues the routine.

**Pause and Wait Expectantly** A key element of the routine is the expectant delay that signals the opportunity for the beginning communicator to signal acceptance or rejection. The length of the pause depends on the individual's level of responsiveness and the extent of motor involvement. Individuals with severe motor and/or cognitive impairments require much longer pauses to have time to plan and produce signals. Those who are learning new routines will require longer pause times than those who are participating in more familiar, established routines. If beginning communicators have significant motor impairments, facilitators may have to assist them in completing all or part of the routine. The goal is to facilitate the individual's development of communicative signaling and foster self-determination within the context of a familiar activity.

**Identify Potential Signals** Building the foundations for communication within these routines depends on identifying potential signals that the individual can use to participate. In typical development, the signals that emerge early on are usually tied directly to the activity. For example, an infant will open his or her mouth to signal the desire for another spoonful at mealtime, start to wiggle to resume playing a tickle game, hold hands up to be picked up, reach for a preferred toy, or push away a nonpreferred item. An infant would not typically open his or her mouth to signal a request for a tickle game since this act is not closely tied to the actual activity. At this early stage of communication development, where possible, the AAC team should focus on encouraging beginning communicators to develop these types of presymbolic signals that are tied closely to the actual activity or event. However, some beginning communicators may have significant motor impairments that limit their repertoire of potential motor acts. They may

need to rely heavily on eye gaze, facial expression, or other subtle behaviors as signals. It is important to work closely with family to determine any signals that have already been established and to build on these routines. It is also important to work closely with an occupational or physical therapist to identify motor acts that are under the individual's volitional control that might be used to establish intentional communication, as well as those that are reflexive unintentional behaviors.

Brian's example illustrates the distinction between these two types of motor acts. Brian had severe cerebral palsy and demonstrated numerous persistent reflexes. His occupational therapist reviewed these reflexes with the other members of the AAC team as well as his family and cautioned that these reflexive behaviors were not under Brian's volitional control. She emphasized that he was not necessarily intending to communicate rejection when he turned his head away; sometimes this behavior was part of an asymmetrical tonic neck reflex (ATNR), in which his head turned away to the side, and the arm and leg on the same side extended and the arm and leg on the opposite side bent. She urged his communication partners to carefully observe his legs and arms when he turned his head away to determine if the behavior was reflexive or intentional.

### Recognize and Respond to Signals

To support beginning communicators in learning the cause-and-effect relationship between their behaviors and the social consequences, it is essential that communication partners recognize their signals and respond to them as if intentional. When a beginning communicator signals, the partner should 1) label the behavior, 2) model the signal, 3) state the meaning, and 4) fulfill the intent.

The group home staff working with Linda, described earlier in this chapter, uses this method to help her learn to signal her desire to eat. An adult with severe multiple disabilities, Linda is learning to signal that she wants something to eat by looking at the group home staff and opening her mouth. The staff have been taught to recognize and respond consistently to her signals to help her develop intentionality. As soon as Linda opens her mouth, the staff member says, “You opened your mouth,” and models opening his mouth. He then says, “You want to eat,” and immediately feeds Linda.

When there are multiple communication partners as in Linda's case, it is important that all partners are “on the same page” and that they consistently 1) distinguish between intentional and unintentional behaviors, 2) interpret the intentional behaviors in the same way, and 3) respond to these behaviors in the same way. Unfortunately, many partners may find it difficult to distinguish intentional from unintentional behaviors of beginning communicators with complex communication needs (Carter & Iacono, 2002; Iacono et al. 1998; Ogletree et al. 2012). They may also find it difficult to determine the specific intent of a behavior (e.g. a signal for acceptance or a signal for rejection). As a result, they often ignore or misinterpret many of the idiosyncratic behaviors exhibited by children and adults with complex communication needs who are beginning communicators (Rowland, 1990). However, these distinctions are important.

The example of Alyse and Frankie illustrates the challenge that occurs when communication partners misinterpret or ignore idiosyncratic behaviors. Alyse and Frankie are middle-school students who have multiple severe disabilities. They have developed a few idiosyncratic signals that they use to express themselves. For example, when Alyse thinks something is funny, she smiles and moves her hand and arm up and down. When Frankie doesn't want something, he extends his hand with his palm facing out and makes a motion to push the object or person away. Both Alyse and Frankie enjoy spending time with the other students at their school, but their peers have significant difficulty recognizing their signals and interpreting them consistently (Holyfield et al. 2018). As a result, they often misinterpret Alyse's and Frankie's intents.

### Develop Signal Dictionaries

To assist communication partners in recognizing and responding consistently to the behaviors of beginning communicators, the AAC team should develop signal dictionaries. Signal dictionaries include three elements: 1) a description of the signal, 2) the meaning of the signal, and 3) the response required of the communication partner. It is often difficult to describe signals precisely so it may be helpful to accompany any explanation with a visual depiction (e.g. photo or video of the individual producing the signal). These dictionaries can then be posted in the rooms (e.g. hospital room, classroom) frequented by the beginning communicator so that they are readily available as references for caregivers and staff. Video dictionaries can also be used to help an individual's peers understand and respond to communication behaviors more successfully.

## INTERVENTION WITH INDIVIDUALS WHO ARE INTENTIONAL BUT PRESYMBOLIC

As beginning communicators develop intentionality, they consistently use signals to communicate, but these signals are not yet symbolic. At this stage, beginning communicators are therefore considered to be presymbolic. In typical development, the presymbolic stage occurs between approximately 8 and 9 months when intentionality develops and 12 months when first words (i.e. first symbols) emerge. During this stage, infants initially learn to communicate for two primary reasons:

1. To express needs and wants and regulate the behavior of others
2. To interact socially and develop social closeness

In the case of behavior regulation for needs and wants, the focus is on the desired object or activity (Light, 1988). In the case of social interaction, the focus is on the communication partner (Light, 1988). Over time, infants gradually learn to coordinate their attention to Holyfield and colleagues (2018) developed a video dictionary that provided multiple examples of the idiosyncratic signals of three middle-school students with severe multiple disabilities. They then used the videos to teach the students' peers to recognize and interpret the signals consistently. Prior to the instruction, the typical peers only recognized and interpreted 33% of the signals of the beginning communicators correctly. After instruction with the video dictionary, the peers in the experimental group recognized and interpreted correctly 86% of the signals. In contrast, the peers in the control group, who did not receive the video training, did not demonstrate any improvement; they recognized and interpreted only 28% of the signals produced by the students with severe multiple disabilities.

AAC Interventions for Individuals with Developmental Disabilities

the shared object/activity and to the partner. They first begin to check their partner's attentional focus between 9 and 12 months, then begin to respond to their partner's pointing between 11 and 14 months, and begin to direct their partner's attention themselves between 13 and 15 months (Carpenter, Nagell, &amp; Tomasello, 1998). This coordination between the shared activity and the partner is known as joint attention. Joint attention is critical to the development of symbolic language because it allows the child to make the association between words and their referents in the environment. During this stage of communication development, infants anticipate routines and participate accordingly. They begin to understand the spoken words for familiar people and objects, but their comprehension is context bound. In other words, they understand the word, mommy, in context, when Mommy is beside them.

Even though beginning communicators at this stage are not yet using words or other symbols, they still communicate a lot. Initially, infants use just a few signals to communicate, but over time, they develop a significant repertoire of signals that they use to communicate their intent. Initially, these presymbolic behaviors are tied to the immediate context. Often they involve contact gestures such as reaching for preferred items and pushing away nonpreferred ones. Gradually, infants learn to point to a preferred item. Unlike contact gestures (e.g., reaching for and pushing away), pointing does not require direct contact with the object or activity. Over time, beginning communicators also learn to use representational gestures such as holding up their arms to be picked up or miming drinking from a cup. These developments mark the transition from presymbolic to symbolic communication.

In general terms, interventions for beginning communicators who are intentional, but presymbolic, focus on the following goals (see Table 10.2):

1. Develop clear signals to express needs and wants and regulate the behavior of others (e.g., signals to express acceptance and rejection, communicate choices, and request objects or activities).
2. Take turns consistently in social interactions and develop social closeness.
3. Demonstrate joint attention (i.e., shift attention between the partner and the shared activity).

## Establish Clear Signals for Acceptance and Rejection

Some of the first signals that beginning communicators learn are ones to express acceptance of preferred items or activities and rejection of nonpreferred items or activities. They learn to use these signals communicatively through consistent interpretation and contingent responsiveness (Sigafoos &amp; Mirenda, 2002; Sigafoos, O'Reilly, Drasgow, &amp; Reichle, 2002). Initially, these signals may be quite subtle; they may be recognized only by familiar partners who are attuned to the beginning communicator. Over time, communication partners should shape these signals into more explicit forms that will be understood by a wider range of partners. This shaping occurs through a process of successive approximations whereby partners initially respond to a subtle signal, but gradually "up the ante" and expect the beginning communicator to produce more explicit signals.

Communication partners can facilitate the use of signals to express acceptance and rejection by providing clear offers of objects or activities throughout the day (e.g., by holding out an iPod with headphones and asking the beginning communicator "Do you want music?" and then waiting for a signal of acceptance or rejection). There

Intervention to Support Beginning Communicators
335

are numerous opportunities throughout the day for partners to offer objects or activities for acceptance or rejection: for example, offering a specific food during a meal, a specific drink for snack, a toy during play, a video during break, or a clothing item during dressing. Each of these represents an opportunity for the beginning communicator to learn to use clear signals for acceptance and rejection. Initially, partners should only offer options one at a time to simplify the communication demands. If the beginning communicator rejects an option, the rejection should be acknowledged and the communication partner should offer an alternative option.

Depending on their capabilities, beginning communicators may use a variety of signals to communicate acceptance (e.g., reaching for, smiling, pointing at) or rejection (e.g., pushing away, turning away, frowning). Communication partners should respond to these signals by labeling the meaning, fulfilling the intent, and then modeling a more conventional AAC symbol. For example, when the beginning communicator pushes away food to signal rejection, the partner might say, "No. No food." and model a head shake (a conventional gesture).

Sometimes practitioners may report that the goal for the beginning communicator is to communicate yes/no responses. However, it is very important to remember that yes and no are linguistic forms that can be used to communicate different intents, some of which emerge early in development and some of which are much more difficult to acquire. For example, young children learn to express these concepts to communicate rejection/protest and acceptance early in communication development (e.g., they learn to respond to questions such as "Do you want ___?"). However, they do not learn to communicate yes to confirm the truth of a statement or no to deny the truth of a statement until later in their communication development (e.g., to answer questions such as "Is this a dog?" or "Is your name ___?"). These are much more difficult communicative functions. When setting goals, AAC teams should be precise and indicate the communicative function (e.g., Sam will use a head shake to communicate no to reject nonpreferred items or protest).

Maxwell's father is helping him learn to use the conventional gestures no and yes to communicate rejection and acceptance. Maxwell's dad tries to help him put on his red t-shirt, but Maxwell turns his head away and starts to whine. His dad recognizes this signal of rejection, says, "No, not the red shirt," shakes his head to model the conventional signal for no, and puts the red shirt away. He then goes to get Maxwell's favorite shirt—one from the Vancouver Canucks, his dad's favorite hockey team. His dad offers this shirt to Maxwell and says, "Do you want your Canucks shirt?" Maxwell smiles and lifts up his arms for his dad to pull it over his head. His dad recognizes this signal of acceptance, models a head nod yes, responds, "Yes, you want your Canucks shirt," and immediately helps Maxwell to put it on.

## Teach How to Communicate Choices

Once beginning communicators are consistently expressing rejection or acceptance when a single object or activity is offered, then they can begin to learn to communicate choices. In designing interventions to support the communication of choices, the AAC team must:

1. Identify opportunities to communicate choices.
2. Determine how to represent the choices.

3. Determine how to present the choices (choice arrays).

4. Select instructional techniques.

### Identify Opportunities to Communicate Choices

The first step in teaching beginning communicators how to communicate choices is to identify when, where, and by whom choices can be offered to the individual throughout the day. Some occasions to communicate choices are obvious: deciding what food to eat or drink, which activity to pursue during free time, which book to read, what music to play, which television show to watch, and which clothes to wear. Other instances may be less obvious, such as choosing a partner for an activity or choosing how to complete an activity. Allowing the individual to choose the order in which to complete a series of tasks may increase compliance when the tasks are ones that are nonpreferred but necessary. For example, an adult who is in the hospital might choose which vital signs to have taken first (e.g. temperature or blood pressure); a child in preschool might choose which toys to clean up first. In this way, beginning communicators are able to exert some level of control in the activity. Learning to communicate choices not only supports the development of communication skills, but also provides important experiences that start to form the foundation for self-determination. Many opportunities to communicate choices can be embedded in high-interest activities.

For example, Zeke is a 15-month-old with Down syndrome who always keeps a number of stuffed animals with him. While Zeke is eating breakfast, his mother asks, “Who is going to eat breakfast with you?” She holds out his teddy bear on her right side and says, “Your bear?” and then holds out his lion on her left side and says, “Or your lion?” She then looks at Zeke and waits. He vocalizes and reaches for the bear. His mom immediately responds by labeling his choice and responding to his request. She says, “Oh you want Teddy to eat breakfast,” and she sits the bear in the chair beside Zeke. She then holds out two different boxes of cereal and asks, “Does Teddy want Cheerios?” as she holds out the box of Cheerios on her right side, and then asks, “Or does he want Rice Krispies?” as she holds out the box of Rice Krispies on her left side. Zeke reaches for the Rice Krispies so his mother acknowledges his choice and gets a bowl and pours a few Rice Krispies into the bowl. She then proceeds to offer Zeke a choice of cereal for his breakfast.

Sometimes, communication partners report that beginning communicators do not seem to have many preferences or interests. In this case, communication partners should gradually introduce some new activities, environments, foods, and people so that the beginning communicator can begin to develop preferences. Sometimes older beginning communicators persist with the interests that they developed when they were younger; they may have limited exposure to age-appropriate activities (e.g. music, magazines, video games). When presented with such unfamiliar options, they may express no interest. However, with sufficient exposure and encouragement, most adolescents and adults with disabilities develop interests in a variety of age-appropriate options.

Chrissy's story illustrates how this can be done. When Chrissy was referred, she was 10 years old. She had a rare genetic disorder that resulted in vision, hearing, and motor

impairments. She was a beginning communicator and was learning to communicate choices. She was primarily interested in Sesame Street, Blue's Clues, and other television programs for young children. So we capitalized on those interests and introduced numerous opportunities for her to communicate choices about these shows and related play activities. However, we also started to introduce her to more age-appropriate options. Within a year, she had developed a strong interest in High School Musical (and a crush on Zac Efron) like many of her peers at school. We modified her communication opportunities and supports to incorporate these new interests and continued to introduce a range of additional age-appropriate activities to expand her interests.

Determine How to Represent Choices At this stage of communication development, beginning communicators are intentional but not yet symbolic, so choices should be presented in a concrete manner using real, meaningful, familiar items (e.g. drinks, foods, toys) rather than abstract symbols of those items. For example, during a dressing routine, a caregiver might offer a woman with complex communication needs the choice between a blue shirt and a red one by holding out the actual shirts. It is not always possible to use the actual object for the choice, however. For example, when providing a child with a choice between going to the gym or listening to music, it is not possible to hold up the gym as a choice. In this case, the partner may need to use an associated object, that is, an object regularly associated with the gym, such as a head band or wrist band that is regularly worn by the child at gym (see Chapter 6 for further discussion of associated objects or tangible symbols). Later, once beginning communicators are transitioning to symbolic communication, the actual objects can be paired (and eventually replaced) with photos, visual scene displays (VSDs), or line drawings.

Beginning communicators can express their choices using a variety of means. Initially, many beginning communicators will simply reach for the item that they want. Over time, as they begin to understand the relationship between their selection and the provision of the item, they may learn to point (either with an isolated finger or an open hand or fist, depending on their motor capabilities). Partners may facilitate the transition from reaching (and grabbing) to pointing by holding the items farther away, just outside the individual's reach. Some beginning communicators have severe motor impairments and are not able to use their hands to reach or point; they may need to use eye pointing to indicate the item they want. Initially, they may simply look at the item that they want, and communication partners should respond to this look as their indication of selection. Over time, partners should encourage the beginning communicator to use three-point eye gaze to make the selection, looking first at the partner, second at the item, and then third at the partner again. This three-point eye gaze communicates the choice more explicitly.

Determine How to Present Choices When providing opportunities, partners must determine how choices will be presented to the individual. Initially, they should offer choices between only two options. Later, the number of items presented may be gradually increased to include three, four, or more items, as the individual learns to visually scan and select from more options. Large choice arrays for individuals with motor impairments may require aids such as an eye-gaze board, scanning device, or another system that displays the options so that they can be selected (see Chapter 7 on alternative access).

When teaching individuals to communicate choices, partners should make the offer as explicit as possible: Sit directly in front of the beginning communicator at eye level.Present the first item and label it (often on the right side).Present the second item and label it (often on the left side).Present both items together (typically shoulder width apart) and ask what the individual wants.Pause and use expectant delay (i.e. make eye contact, use an expectant body posture and facial expression, and wait).

Beginning communicators with visual impairments may need their communication partners to position choices to accommodate field cuts or other difficulties. When individuals have significant visual impairments or are functionally blind, options may need to be presented tactually instead of visually.

Hunter's case illustrates how a paraprofessional might use tactile presentation with a child with visual impairments. Hunter experienced a traumatic brain injury in a motor vehicle accident 3 years ago when he was a toddler. He has significant motor, cognitive, and visual impairments as a result. He attends kindergarten at his local school. His paraprofessional has learned to offer him opportunities to communicate choices throughout the day so that he can participate in class activities. She places the two choices on the tray on his wheelchair, one on the right side (e.g. an iPod with headphones) and the other on the left (e.g. a preferred book). She then puts his right hand at midline in the center of the tray. She helps him to move his right hand across the tray to feel the item on the right; she labels it as a choice while he feels it, asking, “Do you want to listen to music?”; and then she returns his hand back to midline. Next she helps him to move the same hand across the tray to feel the item on the left, and she labels it as a choice while he feels it, asking, “Or do you want me to read a book?” She then helps him move his hand back to midline. She releases Hunter's hand and waits to allow him time to touch the item that he wants. As soon as he touches one of the choices, she responds immediately by labeling his choice and providing the selected item.

### Use Effective Instructional Techniques

Because beginning communicators who are presymbolic are just learning to understand spoken language, it is often very helpful to start by providing beginning communicators with models (or demonstrations) to show them what is expected. In this case, a third party (e.g. a paraprofessional, peer, sibling, or parent) sits beside the beginning communicator, and the instructor provides a choice to the third party. The third party should respond to the choice using the same modality as the beginning communicator (e.g. reaching for the item, pointing with an index finger, eye pointing). As soon as the third party makes the selection, the instructor should label the choice and provide the selected item. These third party models demonstrate how to communicate choices and the effect of doing so.

In addition to third-party models, most beginning communicators will require prompts to help them learn how to communicate choices successfully. These prompts may include time delay or expectant delay, gestures, spoken cues, and/or physical assistance (see Chapter 3 for more discussion of prompts that might be used in instruction). The prompts may be presented in a least-to-most prompting sequence,

Intervention to Support Beginning Communicators
339

starting with those prompts that provide the least support (e.g., time delay or expectant delay) and gradually increasing support only as required until the beginning communicator successfully indicates a choice. Or, the instructor may use a most-to-least prompting hierarchy by providing maximum support initially to ensure success and then gradually fading this support as the beginning communicator learns how to communicate choices.

## Respond with Natural Consequences

When beginning communicators communicate a choice, partners should always respond immediately by labeling the choice and providing the selected item to the individual. Beginning communicators need to experience this natural consequence to learn the link between their behavior (i.e., selection) and the consequence (i.e., the item provided). It is therefore important that communication partners respond immediately by providing the item selected, even if they think that the beginning communicator made a mistake and indicated a nonpreferred item. The communication partner should immediately provide the selected item and let the natural consequence of the selection occur. If the beginning communicator then rejects the item, the communication partner can follow up and offer a new opportunity to communicate a choice. It is important to remember that beginning communicators will require numerous opportunities to make selections with natural consequences before they learn the association between their selection and the provision of the selected item.

Nan lives in a group home. She is learning to communicate choices. Tom, one of the group home staff, offers her a choice of juice or milk at lunch. Nan is not attending; she reaches out and touches the milk.

Tom: You reached for the milk. You want milk. [gives Nan the milk that she chose]

Nan: [pushes the milk away and begins to whine and cry]

Tom: Oh, you don't want milk? Okay, we'll try again in a minute. [removes the milk, pauses for a minute, and presents a new opportunity to choose between milk and juice]

## Teach How to Request Objects and Activities

Once the skills for communicating choices are in place, instruction in the initiation of requests can commence. Often these interventions involve the introduction of AAC symbols (e.g., photos, VSDs, line drawings, switches with spoken output); therefore, they are most appropriate for beginning communicators who are transitioning from presymbolic to symbolic communication. These interventions are discussed in more detail in the next section on beginning communicators who are at the early stages of symbolic development. However, it should be noted that the foundations for these symbolic requests can be established when beginning communicators are presymbolic and still rely on actual objects to communicate their choices. To support self-initiated requests by beginning communicators who are presymbolic, partners need to ensure that the actual objects or items of interest to the beginning communicator are available within the environment, that they carefully observe the beginning communicator for self-initiated requests (e.g., pointing or eye pointing to the item in the environment), and that they then respond immediately by providing the indicated item.

Diane, an adult living in a group home, progressed in this way from communicating choices to making requests. Diane is a 26-year-old woman who has cerebral palsy. She lived most of her life in an institution. When she moved into a group home in her community, the staff learned to provide Diane with choices between objects and activities and Diane rapidly learned to communicate choices by pointing to the desired item. Once she understood the relationship between her pointing and the natural consequences of receiving the item, she started to initiate requests by pointing to preferred objects and activities in the environment. For example, when she wanted to listen to music, she pointed to the radio and vocalized to get the attention of the staff. These opportunities to communicate choices and initiate requests were important steps toward increased communication effectiveness and greater self-determination for Diane.

## Teach How to Take Turns in Social Interactions

Often intervention with beginning communicators focuses primarily on the expression of needs and wants through the communication of choices, requests for preferred objects and activities, and the expression of rejection or protests. To develop communicative competence, beginning communicators must also learn to take turns in more extended social interactions. Many beginning communicators, such as those with ASD, face greater challenges with social interaction than with the expression of needs and wants. Therefore, it is critical that they receive intervention not only to learn to make requests, but also to learn to interact socially. Learning to take turns in social interactions is the foundation for building social closeness and friendships; these relationships are critical to quality of life.

In the words of one parent:

> “There's more to life than cookies.” These words were spoken by the mother of Brian, an 8-year-old child with multiple disabilities as she urged the school team to focus not just on teaching requests, but also on teaching the skills to support social interactions. They illustrate her realization that her son needed to learn how to establish and develop social relationships with others. (Light et al. 2002, p. 187)

In these interactions, the focus is on the communication partner; participants take turns back and forth, extending the interaction.

In the section on developing intentionality, we discussed intervention to establish initial turn taking within social songs and games that have predictable and highly repetitive routines—playing peek-a-boo, participating in bye-bye routines, singing “Row, Row, Row Your Boat,” giving high fives or fist bumps. Over time, as beginning communicators establish basic turn-taking routines, intervention should focus on teaching a wider range of signals to participate in a greater variety of interactive routines. For example, young children with developmental disabilities may learn to participate in songs or shared books that include a range of actions (e.g. “The Wheels on the Bus,” “The Itsy Bitsy Spider,” “I'm a Little Teapot”). Communication partners should initiate the activity and then pause at key junctures in the interaction, marking the opportunity for the child to take a turn by producing the required action. Although there are numerous turn-taking songs and books for young children, there are not as many that are appropriate for older beginning communicators.

Intervention to Support Beginning Communicators
341

However, communication partners can easily create their own action routines with older beginning communicators to foster turn taking.

Hassan was 25 years old when he was referred for services. He had a severe intellectual disability from a near drowning when he was a child. He loved basketball, as did his personal care attendant. To encourage Hassan to take turns in social interactions, his attendant read him an adapted storybook about his favorite basketball player—LeBron James. The attendant gradually established a routine to encourage Hassan's turn taking through repeated readings of the book. Each time, the attendant paused at key places in the story and waited expectantly for Hassan to make the required action (e.g., pretending to dribble the basketball, pass it, or dunk it). Initially, the attendant modeled the required action for Hassan and prompted him to complete the action as well. Over time, the attendant faded the prompts until Hassan was consistently taking turns in the story using a range of representational gestures.

## Develop Joint Attention

Once beginning communicators have learned how to make requests and how to take turns to build social interactions, they need to develop joint attention. Whereas the focus in requesting is typically on the preferred object or activity and the focus in social interaction is on the partner, in developing joint attention, beginning communicators need to coordinate attention between the partner and the shared object or activity. Joint attention is critical to language development, especially vocabulary acquisition. When beginning communicators share the same focus of attention as their partner, they are better able to make the link between a new word (e.g., spoken word, sign, or graphic symbol) and its referent (e.g., the object, action, person to which it refers). Some children with developmental disabilities, such as children with ASD, experience challenges learning joint attention. Therefore, they may require concerted intervention to build these skills. Kasari and colleagues demonstrated that young children with ASD and complex communication needs increase their joint attention significantly when provided with intervention (founded on a combination of developmental and behavioral principles) that provides modeling and direct teaching (e.g., Kasari, Freeman, &amp; Paparella, 2006).

Interventions to build joint attention typically involve familiar partners and activities that are of interest to the beginning communicator. Initially, the communication partner may keep the activity in close proximity to his or her face, thus minimizing the joint attention demands. Over time, as the beginning communicator learns to shift attention from the partner to the shared activity and back, the communication partner may gradually move the activity farther away, increasing the joint attention demands. The partner may use speech, pointing, and other movements to capture the attention of the beginning communicator first to the partner and then to the shared activity. Movement may be particularly effective as a cue since the research on visual processing shows that movement has a strong effect on capturing visual attention (Jagaroo &amp; Wilkinson, 2008). These prompts can then be faded gradually over time.

Marcus's mother used these techniques to begin developing his joint attention. Marcus is 3 years old and has a diagnosis of ASD. His speech-language pathologist and parents are

AAC Interventions for Individuals with Developmental Disabilities

working with him to build joint attention to support language learning. He loves to watch animals on his iPad. His mom holds the iPad close to her face and calls Marcus's name using a surprised look to capture his attention. Once Marcus looks at her, she looks at the iPad, points to the screen, and activates the animal video to attract Marcus's visual attention to their shared activity. As soon as the short animal video stops, Marcus's mom points to the animal and says and signs its name. She then repeats the cycle with a new animal video.

# INTERVENTION WITH INDIVIDUALS WHO ARE DEVELOPING EARLY SYMBOLIC COMMUNICATION

The transition from presymbolic to symbolic communication is highly significant. Symbols allow the expression of a greater range of concepts and ideas, and they support communication about referents that are not immediately present in the environment. In typical development, infants usually make this transition at approximately 12 months of age (range from 10 to 14 months) when they begin to produce their first spoken words (Bloom, 2000). Young children's early interactions are built around objects, people, and events in their immediate environments that are of interest, and these are the words that emerge first in typical development. The first words learned are highly personalized. There is not a common set of core words that emerge among all young children; rather, early vocabularies vary significantly among children depending on their interests, experiences, partners, and environments. Children's first 50 words include multiple parts of speech; however, the majority of children's first words are nouns (60%–65%), followed by action words (14%–19%), and then modifiers (e.g., no, dirty) and person-social words (e.g., please, bye—Fenson et al., 2007; MacWhinney, 2015; Owens, 2005). Often children's first words refer to people and objects that move and/or make noise, thus attracting their attention. The overwhelming majority of early vocabularies are content words; only a very small percentage (0%–4%) are function words (Owens, 2005).

The following account illustrates how variation in first words is apparent even in twins with very similar early experiences and exposure to language.

My twins were never apart as infants so they had virtually identical experiences within their environments and they received virtually identical language input. Yet, their first words were by no means identical. Although there was some overlap, the majority of their first words were unique, no doubt reflecting the intersection of their distinctive interests and personalities with their environment. Their first words were not easily predicted without careful consideration of the objects, people, activities, and social events that were key components of their lives and were highly salient and motivating to each of them individually. Who would have predicted that one of my son's first words would be "lawnmower"? And who would have predicted that one of my daughter's first words would have been the holophrase "sit-down" (a phrase that we used with her frequently when she tried to escape from her highchair)? Watching my twins learn their first words made me realize how personalized early vocabulary selection needs to be for individuals with complex communication needs at the first words stage and how much their early learning of words is tied to their immediate lived experiences. (Janice Light, personal communication, September 2018)

Intervention to Support Beginning Communicators
343

The transition to symbolic communication is a gradual one. Children continue to rely on nonsymbolic modes of communication (e.g., pointing, pushing away), but they gradually learn to use more and more symbols to express themselves. For the most part, children acquire single words first although sometimes they use holophrases (i.e., 2- to 3-word phrases that children use as a single unit such as: all-done, what's-that?, and sit-down). Although these holophrases are actually composed of multiple words, young children use them as a single unit, representing a single specific meaning. They do not yet understand how to break these holophrases down into their component parts and how to recombine the parts to communicate novel messages. Initially, the process of learning new symbols is relatively slow. Gradually, the rate of acquisition increases. By age 5, children with typical development tend to have an expressive vocabulary of more than 2,000 words. From age 6 to 8, the average child acquires 6–7 new words per day and from age 8 to 10, approximately 12 new words per day (Bloom &amp; Markson, 1998)!

Interventions for beginning communicators who are developing early symbolic communication skills should support both semantic and pragmatic development. Specifically, these interventions should target goals to

1. Develop a robust and diverse vocabulary
2. Develop greater competence expressing needs and wants (e.g., initiate requests)
3. Increase turn taking and joint attention in interactions and foster expression of a range of communicative functions, including commenting, answering questions, and asking questions (See Table 10.2.)

## Develop a Robust Vocabulary

Individuals with complex communication needs face a rather formidable challenge learning language. Like their peers who can speak, they must learn the meanings of the spoken words they hear—but then, unlike their peers, they must also learn to express these concepts via unaided and/or aided AAC in order to communicate. They experience an asymmetry between the input they receive (spoken language) and their output (AAC involving multiple modalities) (Light, 1997; Smith &amp; Grove, 2003). Given these challenges, beginning communicators typically require concerted intervention to build their early semantic skills. This intervention involves first choosing which vocabulary concepts to teach, selecting appropriate representations for these concepts, and then teaching the vocabulary in meaningful contexts.

## Choose Vocabulary Concepts

The first step to AAC intervention to teach vocabulary is to determine which concepts to target. In recent years, a "core" vocabulary approach has gained popularity in AAC intervention (e.g., Geist, Erickson, &amp; Hatch, 2015; Van Tatenhove, 2009). However, as Laubscher and Light (2018) point out, this approach is not appropriate for beginning communicators at the early stages of language learning for a number of reasons. Most of the proposed core vocabulary lists are based on the spoken language of older individuals, and they do not reflect the language of beginning communicators at the early stages of semantic development. Although the words on these core lists are intended to represent the most common words that are used the most frequently, in fact, many of the words on core vocabulary lists may not actually occur very frequently (i.e., frequency of 1 in 2,000 words) and they may not be very common across speakers (e.g., used at least once

AAC Interventions for Individuals with Developmental Disabilities

by only 50% or 66% of speakers; Laubscher &amp; Light, 2018). Furthermore, there is not a lot of agreement across lists in determining which words are core words. Finally, and most importantly, the majority of words on these core lists are function words that help to structure phrases and sentences (e.g., a, the, here, to, do, can, that; Yorkston, Dowden, Honsinger, Marriner, &amp; Smith, 1988). These structural words become important in later stages of language development when individuals are learning syntax and should be targeted at that point, but they are not appropriate at the early stages of symbolic development. There is very little correspondence between the words that are included in most core vocabulary lists and the words that are typically acquired early in language development (Laubscher &amp; Light, 2018).

It is important to personalize vocabulary for beginning communicators (Beukelman, McGinnis, &amp; Morrow, 1991; Fallon, Light, &amp; Paige, 2001; Marvin, Beukelman, &amp; Bilyeu, 1994). Initial vocabulary should be selected in response to the needs, interests, experiences, partners, and environments of the individual. Beginning communicators should be actively involved in this process (Holyfield, Drager, Light, &amp; Caron, 2017). This early vocabulary should reflect the people, objects, actions, descriptors, and social words used in the immediate environments (see the MacArthur-Bates Communicative Development Inventories, Fenson et al., 2007, for the types of words that emerge early in young children's communication development).

**Select Appropriate Representations** Once the AAC team determines the underlying vocabulary concepts to target in intervention, the team must determine how to represent these concepts. As described in Chapter 6, there are a wide range of AAC symbols that can be used to represent vocabulary concepts, including unaided ones (e.g., manual signs, conventional gestures) and aided ones (e.g., partial objects or tangible symbols, photos, VSDs of meaningful events with embedded hotspots for vocabulary concepts, video VSDs, line-drawing symbols such as Picture Communication Symbols or SymbolStix). Representations should be selected based on the needs and skills of the beginning communicators. The AAC team should carefully consider the learning demands of the AAC symbols as well as their communication power. Beginning communicators at the early stages of semantic development may be more accurate with symbols that are more transparent, such as photos (e.g., Mirenda &amp; Locke, 1989), and ones that provide contextual support for learning, such as photo VSDs (e.g., Drager, Light, Curran Speltz, Fallon, &amp; Jeffries, 2003; Light, McNaughton, &amp; Caron, 2019).

**Teach Vocabulary in Meaningful Contexts** A variety of instructional techniques can be used to teach vocabulary, ranging from social pragmatic approaches using modeling of AAC and speech within naturally occurring interactions to more structured explicit or direct instruction. In typical development, most children learn underlying concepts and the spoken words that represent these concepts in the context of naturally occurring interactions. They demonstrate interest in people, objects, activities, and other relations; communication partners respond and provide models of relevant words; children choose words of interest to them from the spoken input provided and then try them out immediately in context; and their partners provide feedback, allowing the children to fine-tune their understanding and use of these new vocabulary concepts (Light et al., 2019).

Traditionally, it has been challenging to support this type of language learning in naturally occurring interactions with individuals with complex communication

Intervention to Support Beginning Communicators

needs. It is often time consuming to add new vocabulary to aided AAC systems (both low-tech and high-tech). Although parents and professionals may try to anticipate needs and interests, inevitably beginning communicators encounter situations where they do not have access to the AAC symbols that they need to express themselves in the moment. As a result, it is difficult for parents and other partners to respond spontaneously to the interests of beginning communicators by introducing relevant vocabulary concepts (see Warren &amp; Brady, 2007); yet this responsivity by communication partners is critical to language learning.

Taj's example illustrates the frustration that results when beginning communicators do not have access to the vocabulary that they need. Taj was 22 years old when his mom referred him for services. He had multiple disabilities and relied on AAC to express himself. He had acquired about 30 concepts that reflected people, objects, activities, questions, relational concepts, and social words experienced in his daily life. One day when Taj and his mom were at the rehabilitation center for an appointment, the elevator broke down. Taj was very excited about all of the commotion that ensued as the fire department worked to rescue those that were trapped. No one had anticipated the elevator's breakdown or the arrival of the fire department so Taj had no way to communicate about the experience in the moment. He was very frustrated by the lack of vocabulary. His mom was frustrated that they had missed out on a motivating and meaningful opportunity to support Taj's expressive vocabulary development.

The recent development of AAC technologies that support Just-in-Time (JIT) programming (described in Chapter 6) provides a means to address this challenge. This technology allows communication partners to add vocabulary spontaneously during interactions in response to interests and needs and also allows beginning communicators to be actively involved in the process (Holyfield, Drager, Light et al., 2017). The vocabulary is immediately available to the individual to use, providing opportunities to develop understanding and use within naturally occurring interactions.

Just-in-Time programming was used effectively with Irene in early childhood to support her language learning. Irene has a dual diagnosis of Down syndrome and ASD. Her parents referred her for services when she was 17 months old. She was presymbolic and communicated requests by reaching for the object she wanted or taking her mother to the object. We introduced Irene and her mother to AAC technology that supported Just-in-Time programming and showed them how to snap photos of meaningful events (automatically adding them as VSDs) and how to create hotspots within the VSDs to program speech output to provide Irene with the vocabulary she needed to communicate. Irene had just started therapeutic horseback riding and loved it. Her mom snapped a photo of Irene riding, and they quickly added a hotspot for the horse and programmed the speech output "horse" along with the sound of the horse neighing, all in less than 1 minute. Irene immediately selected the hotspot, listened to the speech output, and then pointed to her horse and tried to make the sound of neighing. A few weeks later, Irene had the chance to help groom her horse by brushing the horse's tail. She selected the VSD for horseback riding, showed it to her mom, and repeatedly touched the tail. Her mom quickly added a hotspot with the vocabulary concept "tail," responding to Irene's interests in the moment and enriching her language learning.

AAC Interventions for Individuals with Developmental Disabilities

The research demonstrates that young children with developmental disabilities and older beginning communicators at the first words stage benefit when communication partners use Just-in-Time programming to provide vocabulary on the fly during interactions in response to their needs and interests; beginning communicators take more communicative turns and communicate a greater range of concepts when they are introduced to AAC technologies that support Just-in-Time programming (e.g., Drager et al., 2019; Holyfield et al., 2019; Light &amp; Drager, 2012; Light et al., 2019).

## Provide Input via Speech and AAC

Young children with typical development learn language by listening to others using spoken language within their daily lives. In a similar way, beginning communicators who rely on AAC benefit when their communication partners provide input using speech and AAC. Such input provides beginning communicators with the opportunity to learn the spoken language(s) of their family and broader community as well as the language code of AAC (i.e., the meaning of the AAC representations). It is important to remember that beginning communicators may need numerous exposures to symbols before they understand their meaning or use them expressively. Too often beginning communicators get only limited exposure to AAC, restricting their rate of language acquisition. Consider that infants hear more than 600 spoken words during each waking hour (Hart &amp; Risley, 1995). They will have heard more than a million spoken words before they say their first word! Yet too often we expect beginning communicators with complex communication needs to understand how to use AAC without ever seeing others use AAC to communicate.

Partners can provide AAC input in the form of unaided AAC and/or aided AAC. When unaided AAC, specifically signs, are used in conjunction with speech, this approach has been labeled "total communication." There are also a number of different interventions that rely on partners providing aided AAC input, including aided language stimulation (Goossens', 1989), augmented input (Romski &amp; Sevcik, 1996), natural aided language (Cafeiro, 2001), aided language modeling (Drager et al., 2006), and aided AAC modeling (Binger &amp; Light, 2007). These interventions vary somewhat in terms of specific characteristics (e.g., number of symbols modeled, timing of aided AAC input in relation to spoken input, and so on). All of the interventions involve, at a minimum, a partner who 1) provides appropriate spoken language input to the beginning communicator, in the context of a motivating, interactive activity; 2) points to aided AAC symbols while speaking; and 3) provides opportunities for the beginning communicator to use AAC during the activity. All of these interventions are based on the premise that, by observing communication partners using aided AAC during motivating and meaningful activities, beginning communicators "can begin to establish a mental template of how symbols can be combined and recombined generatively to mediate communication during the activity" (Goossens', Crain, &amp; Elder, 1992, p. 101).

Owen is 4 years old and has severe developmental apraxia. He is playing with the blocks with a friend, Tyus, and his speech-language pathologist (SLP) in his preschool program. His SLP points to symbols on his AAC display (shown here in small capitals) while she speaks.

SLP: "What [WHAT] do you want to build [BUILD]?"

Owen's friend (Tyus): "We could build a tower [TOWER]. Or a bridge [BRIDGE]."

Intervention to Support Beginning Communicators
347

Owen: TOWER

SLP: "OK. We'll build [BUILD] a tower [TOWER]. Should we make [MAKE] it big [BIG] or little [LITTLE]?"

Owen: BIG BIG

Tyus: "Gigantic [BIG BIG]!"

SLP: "Alright. Let's build [BUILD] a gigantic tower [TOWER]. A big [BIG] big [BIG] tower [TOWER]."

Often AAC input is used in conjunction with other instructional techniques that facilitate language learning:

1. Asking open-ended questions to provide opportunities for communication
2. Providing expectant delay or time delay to allow beginning communicators the opportunity to process the input and take a turn
3. Responding contingently to the turns taken by beginning communicators
4. Expanding on their communication turns
5. Prompting beginning communicators to take turns in the interaction

A number of research studies have investigated the effects of interventions that incorporate aided AAC input (see the meta-analyses by Allen et al., 2017; Biggs et al., 2018; O'Neill et al., 2018, for further details). The research consistently demonstrates that interventions that include aided AAC input/modeling are effective with individuals across a range of ages (from toddlers to adults) and across a range of disabilities (e.g., ASD, cerebral palsy, Down syndrome, intellectual and developmental disability). Moreover, the interventions are effective when implemented by a range of partners (e.g., parents, peers, paraprofessionals, speech-language pathologists) using a range of aided AAC, both low tech and high tech. Interventions with aided AAC input from partners support a range of positive outcomes for beginning communicators. They have large effects on comprehension and very large effects on expressive communication. They positively impact pragmatic skills (e.g., taking turns in interactions), semantic skills (e.g., vocabulary acquisition), and morphosyntactic skills (e.g., acquisition of targeted sentence structures).

**Prompt If Required** Prompting beginning communicators to use targeted language skills also seems to be important to vocabulary acquisition. For example, Romski and colleagues (2010) found that toddlers were more apt to acquire new vocabulary when they were prompted to use the AAC symbols in interactions (the AAC output condition) than when they simply observed others using the symbols (the AAC input condition). As discussed in Chapter 3, prompts may follow a least-to-most or a most-to-least sequence depending on the individual's needs and skills.

**Provide Explicit Instruction as Required** Not all beginning communicators easily learn vocabulary concepts from speech and AAC models within naturally occurring interactions. Some may require more explicit instruction to learn the spoken words and/or the AAC symbols that represent these concepts. An explicit or direct instruction approach is based on the premise that symbol-referent learning is fundamentally a match-to-sample task (Wilkinson &amp; McIlvane, 2002). To teach symbols to beginning communicators, the AAC team arranges structured teaching trials that require a learner to match symbols to their referents. Typically, during initial

AAC Interventions for Individuals with Developmental Disabilities

instruction, the referents are objects. For example, a facilitator might place photographs of a cup and an apple on a table, give the learner a cup, and prompt the learner to place the cup with the photo of the cup (Franklin, Mirenda, &amp; Phillips, 1996). Additional explicit instructional techniques (e.g., stimulus fading and stimulus shaping; Reichle &amp; Drager, 2010) can be combined with this basic approach to teach symbol comprehension and production in a structured format (see Wilkinson, 2005; Wilkinson &amp; Albert, 2001). As beginning communicators learn AAC symbols in structured trials, it is important that they also have numerous opportunities to use these symbols in meaningful activities within their lives to ensure generalized use.

The AAC team should select the instructional approach that fits best with the beginning communicator's needs and skills as well as the target vocabulary and environment. The team should collect data to determine the effectiveness and efficiency of the intervention, and make adjustments as required, knowing that there are other instructional options available as required.

## Teach How to Initiate Requests for Objects and Activities

In addition to supporting semantic development, intervention at the early symbolic stage of communication development should also focus on increasing skills to express a range of communicative functions. As beginning communicators acquire AAC symbols (e.g., signs, photos, VSDs, line drawings), these symbols can be mapped onto existing routines to communicate choices throughout the day. For example, rather than providing a choice using objects, the communication partner can instead offer the choice using photos or other AAC symbols. These interventions follow similar procedures to those described in the prior section for beginning communicators who are presymbolic, but they gradually introduce AAC symbols to replace actual objects.

In addition to communicating choices when provided with the opportunity to do so, it is also important for beginning communicators to learn to initiate requests. The ability to initiate requests supports the development of communication skills and self-determination, and enhances quality of life. Learning to initiate socially appropriate requests for preferred objects and activities (as well as to reject nonpreferred items) also reduces challenging behavior (see the last section of this chapter for further discussion of interventions to reduce challenging behaviors). In this section, we summarize some of the most common techniques used to teach beginning communicators to initiate requests. These methods include the generalized requesting approach (Reichle, York, &amp; Sigafoos, 1991) and the Picture Exchange Communication System (PECS; Bondy &amp; Frost, 2001; Frost &amp; Bondy, 2002), as well as a general case approach that can be combined with both of these. Regardless of the instructional approach used, it is important to remember that the issues related to opportunity, age appropriateness, and other factors discussed earlier are also relevant when teaching requesting.

## Teach Generalized Requesting

One of the most well-established instructional approaches for teaching generalized requesting employs a combination of explicit instruction and incidental teaching (Reichle et al., 1991; Sigafoos &amp; Reichle, 1992). Generalized requesting is accomplished when the individual uses a single symbol (e.g., WANT or PLEASE) to initiate requesting and then makes choices among two or more offered options. Use of a generalized request symbol requires no symbol discrimination skills because only one symbol is used to initiate the request. To initiate generalized requests, individuals are taught to 1) get their partners' attention using

Intervention to Support Beginning Communicators
349

an appropriate signal (e.g., tapping a partner's arm, raising a hand, or activating a recorded message); and 2) indicate the generalized request symbol (e.g., WANT, PLEASE). Generalized requesting should be taught across a variety of activities to promote generalization (e.g., with food items at breakfast, with books at the library, with games during leisure time).
