This approach has been demonstrated to be effective with individuals with a range of developmental disabilities, including those who face significant communication challenges (e.g., individuals with Rett syndrome; Sigafoos, Laurie, &amp; Pennell, 1995, 1996).

## Teach the Picture Exchange Communication System

The Picture Exchange Communication System (PECS; Frost &amp; Bondy, 2002) was designed to encourage spontaneous requests. In this intervention, learners are initially taught to exchange symbols for desired items rather than point to them on a communication display; the communication partner then provides the requested item or activity. This exchange marks explicitly the give and take of the communication process. PECS instructional techniques are similar to (and partially derived from) both verbal prompt-free instructional strategies (Mirenda &amp; Datillo, 1987; Mirenda &amp; Santogrossi, 1985; Mirenda &amp; Schuler, 1988) and expectant delay strategies (Kozleski, 1991).

Instruction in PECS begins with an assessment of preferred objects and activities for the beginning communicator. In phase I of PECS instruction, the individual learns to pick up a single symbol (e.g., photograph, line drawing) and hand it to a partner, who gives the person the associated item (e.g., food, drink, toy). At this early stage, only one symbol is available so the beginning communicator does not need to discriminate between symbols. Initially, a "prompter" sits behind the individual and provides physical and gestural cues to prompt the individual to initiate the exchange; the prompter does not provide spoken cues, such as "What do you want?" or "Give me the picture." Over time, the prompter gradually fades the prompts until the symbol-item exchange is made by the beginning communicator without assistance. In phase II of instruction, the partner gradually moves away so that the person learns to find the symbol, take it to the partner to initiate the request, and then exchange it for the desired item. In phase III, the number of symbols available is increased and the individual is taught to discriminate between the symbols, using a comprehension check procedure. Phase IV targets teaching the individual to use a sentence to express the request by first selecting the symbol I WANT followed by the symbol for the target item or activity (e.g., MUSIC). In phase V, the individual is taught to answer questions, such as "What do you want?" In phase VI, the individual is taught to respond to other types of questions (e.g., "What do you see?" "What do you hear?") using simple sentences (e.g., I SEE . . . , I HEAR . . . ; see Frost &amp; Bondy, 2002, and Bondy &amp; Frost, 2009, for additional information).

PECS has been shown to be effective in teaching beginning communicators across the age range to make requests, including individuals with ASD (Bondy &amp; Frost, 2009), global developmental disabilities (Bock, Stoner, Beck, Hanley, &amp; Prochnow, 2005; Rehfeldt &amp; Root, 2005; Stoner et al., 2006), cerebral palsy (Almeida, Piza, &amp; LaMonica, 2005), and blindness (Lund &amp; Troha, 2008). Meta-analyses of single-case research have shown that PECS has moderate to strong effects on increasing requesting and moderate effects on reducing challenging behaviors (e.g., Ganz, Davis, Lund, Goodwyn, &amp; Simpson, 2012). PECS may be most appropriate to teach basic requests; there is far less evidence of its effectiveness in teaching commenting or other important communicative functions. Beginning communicators may require other interventions to increase these important skills.

AAC Interventions for Individuals with Developmental Disabilities

## Teach Conditional Requesting Using General Case Instruction

General case instruction can be used in conjunction with either generalized requesting or PECS to teach what some authors have referred to as “conditional requesting” (see Reichle &amp; Johnston, 1999; Sigafoos, 1998; Sigafoos &amp; Mirenda, 2002). This approach involves analyzing the relevant stimulus and responses associated with particular tasks or situations and teaching individuals both when to respond and when not to respond under a variety of conditions (Simacek, Pennington, Reichle, &amp; Parker-McGowan, 2018).

Conditional requesting was used effectively with Cay, a young woman with cerebral palsy who uses a wheelchair for mobility and has difficulty with fine motor skills. To teach Cay to request assistance by pointing to a generic HELP, PLEASE symbol on her lap tray, her AAC team first identified a number of diverse situations across relevant environments in which she would be likely to require assistance (e.g., opening tightly closed containers, opening heavy doors, fastening buttons and snaps on her clothes). The team also identified specific situations in which she would not require assistance (e.g., opening loosely closed containers, entering automatic doors, using Velcro fasteners). Next, her team conducted a task analysis to identify the steps involved in the task (e.g., recognizing the need for help or the lack of need, gaining a listener’s attention if help is required, asking for help, waiting while assistance is provided, and saying thank you). Several different members of Cay’s team provided instruction to increase frequency and enhance generalization. All provided spoken prompts and models that they faded quickly to teach Cay to use her HELP, PLEASE symbol in the situations when needed and to refrain from doing so when she did not require assistance.

Although the general case technique to teach conditional requesting requires more time and instructional planning than teaching requests in only one or two restricted contexts, research suggests that it is also more likely to result in spontaneous use and generalization of newly acquired communication skills (Reichle &amp; Johnston, 1999; Sigafoos, 1998; Sigafoos &amp; Mirenda, 2002).

## Teach How to Comment on Activities

As beginning communicators build their symbolic communication, it is important that they learn to express a range of communicative functions to participate in interactions—not just to initiate requests, but also to comment on experiences, express feelings, ask questions, and so on. Communication partners often respond to the communicative attempts of beginning communicators as if they are requests. Beginning communicators need to have opportunities to express a range of communicative functions in their daily interactions, and they need access to the vocabulary to do so. At this stage of communication development, they require contextual support to communicate effectively, so they do best when opportunities to comment are infused into ongoing activities. They have difficulty communicating about past or future events (i.e., participating in displaced talk); these skills develop later. Opportunities to make comments, answer questions, and express feelings can be incorporated into a wide range of daily activities, including shared book reading, watching videos together, participating in play or leisure activities, completing work tasks, or participating in activities of daily living.

#### Reduce Joint Attention Demands

When beginning communicators are learning to make comments about ongoing activities, they must coordinate their attention across the partner, the shared activity, and the AAC system, all while also attending to their own behavior (e.g. monitoring spoken and AAC input, generating an appropriate comment or question, considering how to express it using AAC, and then locating and selecting the required symbols; Smith, McCarthy, & Benigno, 2009). Communication partners can reduce these joint attention demands in two ways. First, they can hold the aided AAC system close to their face so that the attentional shifts are minimized, or they can sign or gesture within the beginning communicator's focus of attention. The research shows that infants demonstrate more frequent and longer coordinated joint attention when the AAC system is aligned with the partner's face than when it is located on a surface (e.g. floor, table) away from the partner's face (Smith et al. 2009). Similarly, research shows that mothers of infants and toddlers who are learning manual signs usually sign within their child's line of regard, rather than off to one side or from another position (Clibbens, Powell, & Atkinson, 2002).

Communication partners can also reduce joint attention demands by incorporating shared activities into AAC technologies (Light & Drager, 2007). For example, books can be programmed into AAC technologies by snapping photos of the pages and incorporating relevant vocabulary to comment about the story. Or favorite videos can be downloaded to AAC technologies with video VSDs; these videos can be paused at favorite points to add relevant vocabulary to support commenting. In these examples, the shared activity (e.g. book, video) is integrated with the AAC supports so that the beginning communicator does not need to shift attention between these two.

#### Provide Instruction to Teach Commenting

Typically intervention to teach commenting follows these steps (Light & Drager, 2019). The communication partner

1. Encourages the beginning communicator to choose a motivating shared activity
2. Sets up an opportunity for the beginning communicator to comment within the activity (e.g. by performing an action, making a comment, asking a question, or simply waiting)
3. Provides models of AAC along with speech
4. Pauses and focuses attention on the beginning communicator, marking the opportunity for the beginning communicator to comment and providing time to do so
5. Responds immediately to the beginning communicator's turns by recognizing the intent and expanding on the message

Prompts can be provided as required using either a least-to-most or most-to-least hierarchy.

Book reading can be used to begin to teach commenting, as in the case of Gavin. Gavin was referred for services when he was 25 months old. He had severe cerebral palsy and had only limited use of his hands. He had a tracheotomy and was not able to use speech to communicate. He loved to read books with his mom. One of his favorite books was But Not the Hippopotamus by Sandra Boynton. We used this book as a way to introduce Gavin to commenting. We programmed the book into Gavin's AAC technology and added a hotspot for the hippopotamus on each page. His mom read the book and paused each

time she came to the line, “But not the hippopotamus.” She waited for Gavin to select the hotspot to speak out the line.

Book reading has been used successfully to promote commenting in one-on-one shared reading interactions or in small groups in school or library programs with children with cerebral palsy (e.g. Trudeau, Cleave, & Woelk, 2003), ASD (e.g. Bedrosian, 1999), Rett syndrome (e.g. Skotko, Koppenhaver, & Erickson, 2004), and multiple disabilities (e.g. Bellon-Harn & Harn, 2008). Shared book reading has also been used successfully to support commenting and social interaction between preschoolers with complex communication needs and their peers (e.g. Therrien & Light, 2016, 2018). Older beginning communicators can also learn to comment using motivating, adapted books and magazines that reflect topics that are age-appropriate (e.g. sports, cooking, popular culture). As beginning communicators learn to make simple comments, communication partners can introduce more complex activities and more varied opportunities for commenting using a range of vocabulary concepts.

Remember the example of Hassan, the 25-year-old man with severe intellectual disability who loved basketball. He initially learned how to make simple comments when his personal care attendant read him an adapted storybook about his favorite basketball player—LeBron James. As Hassan developed competence, his attendant gradually introduced AAC symbols (e.g. lebron, dribble, shoot, pass, dunk, posterize, basketball, chest bump, hooray) to allow Hassan to comment on the book while reading. The attendant paused at the end of each page in the story and waited expectantly for Hassan to comment. The attendant responded to Hassan's comments by expanding on them and talking about the story. Over time, Hassan learned a range of new vocabulary and used it appropriately to comment on the story.

Books are not the only shared activities that can be used to teach commenting. Many beginning communicators enjoy watching videos or television shows, and these can also be used as a context to increase commenting and social engagement (Caron, Laubscher, Light, & McNaughton, 2019).

Hassan's personal care attendant capitalized on his interest in LeBron James and used videos to build commenting. Hassan loved to watch highlights of LeBron's games. His personal care attendant downloaded these videos to the video VSD app on Hassan's tablet. Each time Hassan showed interest in a segment of the video, they paused the video and the app automatically created a VSD to support Hassan's communication. Hassan then indicated where he wanted to add a hotspot (e.g. on the basketball as LeBron made a dunk), and he helped his personal care attendant draw the hotspot. The aide checked with Hassan to determine what vocabulary to add and then recorded the speech output (e.g. “Dunk!”). Each time they played the video, it automatically paused at the VSD, providing Hassan with the opportunity to comment on the video and also the opportunity to add more vocabulary (e.g. a hotspot on the opponent that was dunked on with the speech output “Posterize!”).

Communication partners should build opportunities for beginning communicators to comment into a wide range of daily activities. Depending on their interests,

Intervention to Support Beginning Communicators
353

age, and environments, beginning communicators can participate in situations such as the following:

- During circle time at school, a child selects photos of his or her classmates to greet them.
- During music class, the child selects the appropriate symbols on an AAC app to sing each line in the song.
- When playing cars with a peer, the child selects appropriate sound effects on an AAC app (e.g., vroom, crash).
- At a sports event, the adolescent cheers for a favorite team by selecting the symbol of the team's logo to chant with the crowd.
- When baking, the adult comments on the food by selecting appropriate symbols (e.g., YUM).

These are just a few examples of situations that might be used to promote commenting by beginning communicators. The opportunities for beginning communicators to participate are endless, limited only by the imagination of their communication partners. The opportunities and vocabulary should always reflect the needs and skills of the individual. It is important that the contexts and vocabulary selected are motivating and are understood by the beginning communicator.

## Teach How to Ask Questions

In addition to learning to comment, beginning communicators also need to learn how to ask questions. Too often, learning to ask questions is neglected as a goal for beginning communicators. In typical development, children learn to ask basic questions early in development; it is important that individuals with complex communication needs also have this opportunity. Questions are powerful tools that allow beginning communicators to control their learning, increase their language development, and sustain social interactions. Asking questions allows children to fill in gaps in their knowledge and further their cognitive and language development (Chouinard, 2007). For example, children ask, "What's that?" to learn the names of a wide range of objects, places, and people. They ask "Why?" to understand more complex cause-and-effect relationships. Despite the importance of questions to cognitive and language development, often beginning communicators who rely on AAC do not have access to the vocabulary required to ask questions. It is important to provide beginning communicators with access to the tools to ask early emerging questions and to teach them how to do so.

Early in AAC intervention, when Gavin was 2 years old, we taught him how to ask, "What's that?" He was so curious about the world, and we knew that teaching him to ask this question would allow him a way to build his vocabulary and foster his cognitive development. We wanted to choose a representation that would make sense to Gavin. We knew from the research (Light et al., 2008) that young children typically drew a child pointing at something as a way to represent "What's that?" so we used a photograph of a young child pointing with a quizzical expression as the representation. Gavin was very interested in trucks so we chose a large book of construction vehicles and introduced it to Gavin and his mom. Gavin's mom acted as a third-party model: First she pointed to a picture in the book, and then she selected the representation WHAT'S THAT? from Gavin's

AAC Interventions for Individuals with Developmental Disabilities

AAC technology, producing the speech output "What's that?" with appropriate intonation. I immediately responded by labeling the truck she had indicated and talking about its use. Then we waited expectantly, focusing attention on Gavin. He immediately indicated one of the photos in the book (i.e., a wheeled excavator) and then asked, "What's that?" I labeled the truck and explained its use. Gavin then insisted that we add the new vocabulary to his AAC technology. From then on, he regularly used his AAC technology to ask, "What's that?" His vocabulary exploded as his parents were able to follow his lead and provide access to the concepts that he desired.

# INTERVENTION WITH INDIVIDUALS WHO ARE LEARNING TO COMBINE SYMBOLS

In typical development, by the time toddlers are 18-24 months of age, they have usually acquired approximately 50 words (Owens, 2005) to express a wide range of concepts, including people, actions, objects, places, questions, relational terms, and social words. This breadth of vocabulary is important, because it ensures that children have the tools to communicate about a range of experiences and to begin to express more complex messages. This broad vocabulary also influences cognitive development in positive ways. As children learn new concepts, they are able to think about their world in new ways.

Once children have acquired approximately 50 words, they start to combine these words to communicate more complex messages to express a range of intents (e.g., requesting objects or activities, rejecting, greeting, commenting, asking questions, expressing emotions). They need access to a sufficiently large and diverse vocabulary to develop early two-word combinations. Over time, they learn to express a wide range of semantic relations using two-word combinations such as agent-action (e.g., Mommy go), action-object (throw ball), action-locative (e.g., go pool), recurrence-action (e.g., more tickle), and descriptor-entity (e.g., big cookie). As children develop competence with early semantic relations, they begin to attempt more complex utterances (e.g., agent-action-object, such as "Mommy read book"; agent-action-locative, such as "Daddy go home"). At this early stage of symbolic development, young children do not typically include structural words in sentences (e.g., the, a, and, to).

To support beginning communicators who rely on AAC in expressing more complex messages, it is important that they have the opportunity to continue to develop a robust and diverse vocabulary that represents a wide range of semantic concepts (e.g., agents, actions, objects, locatives, descriptors). Once beginning communicators have acquired a sufficiently large vocabulary and are consistently using single symbols (e.g., spoken words, signs, line drawings, hotspots within VSDs) to make requests, comment, answer questions, and ask questions, then the AAC team may begin to target symbol combinations. Usually intervention first targets use of symbol combinations to express the communicative functions that the individual already expresses using single symbols. For example, beginning communicators may learn to use multisymbol combinations to

- Make more complex comments (e.g., Daddy work; Max fall down)
- Ask more complex questions (e.g., Where Daddy? Who crying?)
- Make more specific requests (e.g., more book, big cookie)
- Provide more explicit rejection or protest (e.g., all done work, no bath)

Intervention to Support Beginning Communicators
355

Later the individual may learn to utilize symbol combinations to express new communicative functions as well. See Table 10.2 for a summary of potential goals for intervention.

As with other skills, interventions to teach the expression of early semantic relations may vary from those that utilize explicit instruction in more structured contexts to those that use more naturalistic strategies in daily interactions. Typically, these interventions involve the following strategies:

1. Setting up motivating opportunities for beginning communicators to use symbol combinations to express a range of functions
2. Modeling the use of two-word messages by using speech and AAC
3. Waiting expectantly for the beginning communicator to express a longer message (specifically continuing to wait when the beginning communicator produces or selects a single symbol)
4. Responding immediately to these messages by fulfilling the intent (e.g., providing the requested item, responding to the question)
5. Expanding on the message and modeling the use of more complex messages via speech and AAC

Depending on the needs and skills of the individual, the AAC team may use either a least-to-most or a most-to-least prompting hierarchy to support learning. Research suggests that interventions in which communication partners (e.g., parent, paraprofessional) provide aided AAC models in conjunction with speech are effective in increasing the frequency of multisymbol messages expressed by children who use AAC, including those with ASD, cerebral palsy, and intellectual and developmental disability (e.g., Binger, Kent-Walsh, Berens, Del Campo, &amp; Rivera, 2008; Binger, Kent-Walsh, Ewing, &amp; Taylor, 2010; Binger &amp; Light, 2007; Tönsing, 2016).

Many beginning communicators who use AAC tend to rely primarily on single-symbol messages to communicate (e.g., Light, Collier, &amp; Parnes, 1985). When they produce or select a single symbol, their communication partners often jump in immediately before they have the opportunity to extend the message, thus preempting opportunities for them to learn to combine symbols. It is important for the AAC team to work with communication partners to teach them to continue to wait expectantly when the beginning communicator produces or selects a single symbol to mark the expectation and provide the time for the individual to express a more complex message. It is also important to recognize that not all situations require multiword messages. We all rely on single-word messages (known as elliptical responses) in some situations (e.g., If someone asks me, "What's your name?", I respond, "Janice," not "My name is Janice."). Intervention to teach beginning communicators to use symbol combinations should target those situations where more complex messages are required to enhance communication effectiveness.

## SUMMARY OF AAC

## INTERVENTIONS FOR BEGINNING COMMUNICATORS

With appropriate AAC intervention, beginning communicators can

- Develop intentional communication
- Learn to express needs and wants and participate in social interactions

Develop joint attentionDevelop symbolic communication using speech, unaided, and/or aided AACAcquire a robust and diverse vocabularyExpress a range of early semantic relationsCommunicate to express a range of communicative functions (e.g. requests for objects or activities, comments, asking questions)

Unfortunately, some beginning communicators do not receive the AAC intervention required to build these skills. They may have limited means to communicate. As a result, they may become frustrated and may develop challenging behaviors as an attempt to impact their environment.

## INTERVENTION WITH INDIVIDUALS WITH CHALLENGING BEHAVIORS

When beginning communicators do not have effective means to communicate and influence their environment, it is not unusual for them to exhibit challenging behaviors, including tantrums, hitting, screaming, pushing, biting, and various forms of self-injurious behavior. In fact, challenging behaviors have been reported in more than 90% of individuals with ASD (Jang, Dixon, Tarbox, & Granpeesheh, 2011). Often these challenging behaviors occur when individuals with complex communication needs are attempting to influence their partners or control their environment but have limited means to do so. In the absence of other means of communication, some beginning communicators may use challenging behaviors to protest, reject, request preferred activities, request attention, or escape nonpreferred situations. Challenging behaviors are almost always communicative in nature and should be treated as such (e.g. Carr et al. 1994; Durand, 1990; Mirenda, 1997; Wacker, Berg, & Harding, 2002; Walker & Snell, 2013).

When challenging behaviors occur, intervention is required to reduce the challenging behavior and replace it with alternative, more appropriate means of communication. This intervention should be guided by three important principles. First is the principle of functional equivalence. According to this principle, intervention should focus on teaching the individual an alternative behavior that serves the same function as the challenging behavior (Carr, 1988). In determining potential communicative replacements, the AAC team should consider the second principle, the principle of efficiency and response effectiveness. This principle states that people communicate in the most efficient and effective manner available to them at any given point in time. Therefore the communication alternative must be at least as easy for the individual to produce as the challenging behavior and it must also be as effective in obtaining the desired outcome (Horner & Day, 1991). If the new communication behavior is more difficult or less effective, the challenging behavior will persist.

Finally, the third principle is the principle of goodness of fit, which states that sometimes the most appropriate response to challenging behaviors is to adapt the environment to create a better fit with the beginning communicator's needs and skills, thus circumventing the challenging behavior. Sometimes only simple adaptations are required to reduce challenging behavior. For example, a paraprofessional might use a timer to let a student with ASD know that the current activity is ending in 5 minutes and a new activity is starting; or a parent might provide a child with cerebral palsy with a preferred stuffed animal to hold while taking seizure medications. However, sometimes

more comprehensive multifaceted changes to the environment are required when the current arrangements are not appropriate given the needs and skills of the individual.

Many beginning communicators live in isolated environments with few opportunities for positive social interactions; are expected to engage in repetitive, nonpreferred tasks; are unable to choose their communication partners and aides; and have limited opportunities to exercise control or choice on a daily basis (Brown, 1991). As Carr, Robinson, and Palumbo (1990) noted, the appropriate response in such situations is to focus on changing the environment or the sequence of events, not the person. As we learn more and more about the relationship between challenging behavior and communication, it has become apparent that it is critical to provide beginning communicators with frequent opportunities for communication and self-determination in the context of meaningful, interactive activities to circumvent the development of challenging behaviors. These opportunities are also their right.

Individuals with intellectual and/or developmental disabilities have the same right to and responsibilities that accompany self-determination as everyone else. They are entitled to opportunities, respectful support, and the authority to exert control in their lives, to direct their services, and to act on their own behalf. (Position statement on self-determination, The Arc, an organization for Individuals with Intellectual/Developmental Disabilities, n.d.)

## Functional Communication Training

Although in some cases environmental adaptations on their own may be sufficient to address challenging behaviors, typically intervention is also required with the beginning communicator to provide more appropriate communication alternatives. Functional communication training (Carr & Durand, 1985) is an intervention that has been used widely to address challenging behaviors. It involves a set of procedures designed to reduce challenging behaviors by teaching functionally equivalent, socially appropriate communication skills. It starts with a thorough assessment to identify the specific behaviors that are occurring, the frequency of their occurrence, the antecedents of the behaviors (i.e. the events that precede them), and the consequences of the behaviors (i.e. the events that immediately follow the behaviors). Three procedures might be used to collect this information to determine the antecedents, the behaviors, and the consequences (A-B-C assessment; Wacker et al. 2002): interviews of parents or other communication partners, daily behavior logs in which communication partners keep track of the occurrence of the behaviors, and observations of the individual during daily activities (especially those that are likely to trigger the challenging behaviors). The assessment will lead to hypotheses about the function(s) of the challenging behavior (e.g. to escape a nonpreferred activity or person; to gain attention).

The team then conducts a functional analysis to test these hypotheses and determine the function(s) of the behavior(s) of concern so that they can design and teach appropriate alternatives (see Crone & Horner, 2003; Dunlap et al. 2010; Sigafoos, Arthur-Kelly, & Butterfield, 2006, for examples of functional behavioral assessment procedures). Once the team identifies the function of the challenging behavior, they must then select an alternative means of communication that will result in this same end goal and is as easy as (or easier than) the challenging behavior, applying the principles of functional equivalence and efficiency and response effectiveness. Essentially,

|  2 | Consider whether environmental adaptations (e.g., visual schedules, augmented input) are necessary. | Evaluate the goodness of fit between the individual's needs and skills and environmental demands.  |
|  3 | Provide a socially acceptable communicative replacement (AAC) for the challenging behavior and teach its use. | Replace the challenging behavior with a functionally equivalent communication alternative (AAC).  |

|  5 | Reduce or eliminate reinforcement of the challenging behavior. | Remove the motivation for the individual to engage in challenging behavior.  |

the individual is taught to produce a socially acceptable communicative act (using AAC) to replace the challenging behavior (Sigafoos, Arthur, &amp; O'Reilly, 2003). Caregivers are taught to respond to the socially acceptable AAC with more reinforcement (e.g., more often, greater amounts, more immediate, longer duration, higher quality reinforcement) than they provide for the challenging behavior. Thus AAC competes with the challenging behavior, eventually replacing it.

A number of meta-analyses have determined the positive impact of functional communication training on the acquisition of communication replacements and the reduction of challenging behavior across disability categories, age ranges, and types of challenging behaviors (e.g., Chezan, Wolfe, &amp; Drasgow, 2017; Gerow, Davis, Radhakrishnan, Gregori, &amp; Rivera, 2018; McComas, Schieltz, Simacek, Berg, &amp; Wacker, 2019; Tiger, Hanley, &amp; Bruzek, 2008). Table 10.4 summarizes the key steps required to plan and implement this training (see Bopp, Brown, &amp; Mirenda, 2004; McComas et al., 2019; Reichle &amp; Wacker, 2017, for further discussion).

Identify the Communicative Function and Provide a Communication Replacement Challenging behaviors may serve various communicative functions. The AAC team needs to identify the communicative function of the challenging behavior and then provide a socially acceptable communication replacement that is functionally equivalent and is as effective and efficient as the challenging behavior. For example, sometimes the communicative function of the challenging behavior is a request for attention (Bopp et al., 2004; Mirenda, 1997); in this case intervention focuses on teaching alternative, socially acceptable attention-getting behaviors. This has been accomplished by teaching AAC, including use of gestures such as tapping or waving a hand or arm (Kennedy, Meyer, Knowles, &amp; Shukla, 2000; Sigafoos &amp; Meikle, 1996), activating a switch with the recorded message PLEASE COME HERE (Northup et al., 1994;

Intervention to Support Beginning Communicators
359

Peck et al., 1996), or activating AAC technology with an attention-getting message such as I WANT TO BE WITH THE GROUP (Durand, 1993).

Often beginning communicators use challenging behaviors to request desired objects or activities. In fact, Mirenda and colleagues found that between one third and one half of published interventions in which AAC was used to reduce challenging behaviors were related to inappropriate requesting behaviors (Bopp et al., 2004; Mirenda, 1997). In these interventions, participants were taught to make generic (e.g., WANT, MORE, PLEASE) and/or specific requests for desired items or activities using a range of AAC supports, including gestures (Wacker et al., 1990), manual signs (e.g., Kennedy et al., 2000), tangible symbols (e.g., Gerra, Dorfman, Plaue, Schlackman, &amp; Workman, 1995), photographs or pictographic symbols (e.g., Frea, Arnold, &amp; Vittemberga, 2001; Peck Peterson, Derby, Harding, Weddle, &amp; Barretto, 2002), single switches with taped messages (Steege et al., 1990; Wacker et al., 1990), and a range of AAC technology (e.g., Durand, 1993).

Some individuals utilize stereotypic behaviors (e.g., spinning, rocking back and forth) and aggressive behaviors (e.g., tantrums, self-injurious behaviors) to signal rejection of nonpreferred to protest nonpreferred activities, or to escape from nonpreferred activities (e.g., Durand &amp; Carr, 1987, 1991; Kennedy et al., 2000). Functional communication training can be used to teach socially acceptable ways to communicate these intents instead, including, for example, learning a head shake to communicate no, producing the sign ALL DONE, or selecting the message NO THANKS from AAC technology. It is critical that the communication replacement is 1) socially acceptable, 2) functionally equivalent to the challenging behavior, and 3) as effective and efficient.

## Work with Communication Partners to Reduce Challenging Behaviors

Typically, challenging behaviors continue in the absence of intervention because they are highly effective and efficient at getting the desired response.

Sal's challenging behaviors functioned in this way. Sal had a genetic disorder and had lived all his life in an institution for individuals with intellectual and developmental disabilities. He was deinstitutionalized when he was in his 20s and moved back into the community to live in a group home with several other men with developmental disabilities. He did not speak and had not been introduced to AAC during his life in the institution. Like many people, Sal had specific food likes and dislikes. When he first moved into his group home, staff reported significant problems at mealtimes. Sal had learned to use challenging behaviors to exert some control over his environment and had a history of screaming, biting, hitting, and throwing furniture. Each time staff offered him a food item that he did not like, Sal began to scream, and his behavior escalated until a staff member removed the item. Unknowingly, the staff were actually reinforcing Sal's use of challenging behaviors. He learned that if he screamed or hit, the staff would remove the nonpreferred item. Moreover, he learned that the more intense his challenging behavior was, the more quickly staff acted to remove the disliked food items.

It is critical to break the cycle and replace challenging behavior with more socially acceptable means of communication. To accomplish this, it is important to work with communication partners (e.g., family, educational or vocational personnel, personal care attendants, group home staff) to teach them to ignore challenging behaviors (to ensure that they are not reinforced) and instead to respond quickly by fulfilling the intent of the message when the individual uses AAC as a communication

AAC Interventions for Individuals with Developmental Disabilities

replacement. For example, Sal learned to press a switch to activate the speech output "no thanks" when presented with a nonpreferred food item. Group home staff were taught to respond immediately when he touched the switch by removing the food but to ignore challenging behaviors should they occur.

**Teach Use of AAC as a Communication Replacement** Beginning communicators, like Sal, will require instruction to learn to use AAC as a communication replacement, especially if they have used challenging behaviors successfully for many years to control their environment. Typically, interventions to reduce challenging behaviors utilize most-to-least prompting hierarchies to interrupt the cycle of challenging behaviors before it starts. In the case of functional communication training, the beginning communicator is closely monitored in situations that typically result in challenging behaviors. In these situations, the interventionist jumps in immediately (before the individual initiates the challenging behavior) and helps the beginning communicator to use AAC as an appropriate communicative replacement. The communication partner then immediately responds to the beginning communicator's socially appropriate message. As the beginning communicator begins to learn to use AAC as a communication replacement, the interventionist gradually fades the instructional prompts until the beginning communicator is spontaneously using AAC rather than challenging behaviors.

Sometimes there are situations in which it is not possible to honor the individual's rejection or request for escape. For example, individuals have to take required medications even if they do not want to. In these situations, it may be possible to reduce the challenging behavior by providing the individuals with some level of control in the situation. For example, they might be able to choose the food or drink with which to take the medications, or choose the sequence in which the medications will be taken, or choose a comfort object (e.g., worry beads, favorite toy) to hold or use while taking the medication. Providing beginning communicators with some level of self-determination or control within the situation typically serves to reduce the challenging behavior.

**Visual Schedules**

Sometimes challenging behaviors result when beginning communicators do not understand expectations and events. Because of difficulties understanding spoken language input, they may not understand what is happening and may have difficulty with transitions to the next activity. Or they may have difficulty understanding how to complete a task and knowing how long it will last. In these cases, it may be beneficial to introduce a visual schedule to support understanding and prevent challenging behaviors.

A visual schedule represents the main activities in a person's day with some form of AAC symbols (e.g., written words, picture symbols, VSDs). A visual schedule may also present the specific steps within a single, multistep activity (e.g., getting dressed, buying groceries). Visual schedules provide an overview of the sequence of activities during a day (or of the steps within a specific activity). They can be used to let beginning communicators know what will happen next and to facilitate transitions from one activity to the next, especially for individuals who have a high need for predictability (Flannery &amp; Horner, 1994). Visual schedules are examples of AAC used to support understanding. They serve to increase participation and independence (van Dijk &amp; Gage, 2019). They have been found to be effective in home, school, and community settings for beginning communicators across a wide range of ages and disabilities (e.g., Bopp et al., 2004; Knight, Sartini, &amp; Spriggs, 2015; Rowland &amp; Schweigert, 1996).

Intervention to Support Beginning Communicators

As with all AAC supports, the team should carefully determine the representation, organization, and layout of the visual schedule based on the needs and skills of the individual. Visual schedules include both low-tech and high-tech options; they can incorporate real objects, tangible symbols, photographs, line drawings, videos, or written words. By definition, visual schedules are intended to represent a sequence of events, tasks, or steps; usually the chronology of events is represented linearly by sequencing representations in a horizontal row or in a vertical column. Some visual schedules are very simple, focusing on a sequence of just two activities (e.g., a "first-then" format); others may include an entire day's or week's activities. Low-tech visual schedules may be displayed separately in a variety of formats, including age-appropriate daily appointment books or wall displays posted in the classroom or work site, or they may be included within communication books used for expressive communication (see Cafiero &amp; Jones-Wohleber, 2019, for examples). Often low-tech visual schedules are designed so that the representations for individual activities or steps are attached by Velcro and can be removed when they are complete, providing beginning communicators with a visual support to understand what tasks have been completed and what remains to be done. Figure 10.1 shows a low-tech visual schedule that uses objects to represent daily activities. Figure 10.2 shows a more complicated low-tech visual schedule that uses picture symbols to represent the sequence of activities at various times during the school day, each day of the week.

Electronic visual schedules can also be created using a range of computer applications, including ones that utilize photos, line drawings, written words, photo VSDs, or video VSDs to represent activities or steps within an activity. Shane (2006) suggested that VSDs may be more appropriate as representations in visual schedules as they provide a more complete representation of the upcoming event (e.g., the people, objects, and actions involved). Video VSDs provide even more explicit demonstrations of upcoming events, tasks, or steps within a task (Spriggs, Knight, &amp; Sherrow, 2015). Research shows the positive effects of video VSDs as a means to teach the appropriate sequence of steps within activities (e.g., Babb, Gormley, McNaughton, &amp; Light, 2019; O'Neill, Light, &amp; McNaughton, 2017). For example, Figure 10.3 is a screen shot of a video VSD used to depict the sequence of steps required for an adolescent with ASD to take the bus to her work placement.

James uses a video VSD to support him in his library job. James is 21 years old and has severe ASD. He has no functional speech and communicates primarily through yes/no responses to partner questions. He participates in a vocational training program and works in the school library. His responsibilities include checking books in and out, reshelving them, and making die-cuts. Despite instruction, he remains very dependent on his job coach to assist him in completing his work tasks, and he rarely communicates. He has difficulty remembering the sequence of tasks that he needs to complete, and he gets distressed when he is uncertain what to do. He was introduced to video VSDs as a visual schedule to remind him of the sequence of steps and task requirements for each job. He watches the video of each step in his work and then completes the step. He is very proud of the independence that he has achieved working in the library (see Babb et al., 2019).

Instruction in the use of a visual schedule is generally conducted during daily routines in naturalistic contexts, with a hierarchy of prompts that are gradually faded.

Initially the individual is prompted to check the visual schedule and select the next symbol in the sequence. When the activity is completed, the individual is then prompted to check the schedule again for the next activity. Over time, these prompts are faded until the individual is using the schedule independently. Table 10.5 describes procedures to create and teach the use of visual schedules with beginning communicators.

Table 10.5. Designing and teaching the use of a visual schedule

|  Design the visual schedule to meet the individual's needs and skills  |
| --- |
|  1. Determine situations where the individual would benefit from a visual schedule that displays the sequence of activities or steps in a multistep activity. ○ Consider visual schedules to (a) promote learning of the daily schedule or the sequence of steps in an activity; and (b) facilitate transitions between activities or steps in an activity thereby reducing uncertainty.  |
|  2. List, in chronological order, the individual's schedule across relevant home, school, and community environments. ○ Include the activities done every day or during a relevant portion of the day; or list all of the steps required in the multistep activity. ○ Decide how many activities (or steps) to display at one time depending on the skills of the individual.  |
|  3. Determine how to represent each of the activities (or steps in a multistep activity). ○ Choose real objects, partial objects, photographs, line drawings, visual scene displays (VSDs), or video VSDs depending on the needs and skills of the individual.  |
|  4. Decide how to organize and display the symbols to fit the individual's needs and skills. ○ Determine if the visual schedule will be low-tech or high-tech. ○ Determine if the sequence of activities (or steps) should be organized horizontally or vertically.  |
|  5. Devise a method for marking finished activities. ○ For real object symbols, use a “finished box” into which the individual can deposit each object after finishing the activity. ○ For low-tech schedules with photographs, VSDs, or other graphic symbols, turn the symbol over or remove it from the visual schedule at the end of each activity. ○ For visual schedules programmed into AAC technologies, scroll through the navigation bar to hide the finished activity and reveal the next one.  |

(continued)

AAC Interventions for Individuals with Developmental Disabilities

Table 10.5. (continued)

|  Teach the individual to use the visual schedule  |
| --- |
|  1. Introduce the individual to the visual schedule during the day's activities or while completing the steps in a target task.  |
|  2. For each activity or step, model use of the visual schedule for the individual. ○ Introduce the representation for each activity (or step) in the context of that activity to ensure that the individual understands the representation.  |
|  3. Before each activity, prompt the individual to review the visual schedule and select the next symbol in the sequence. ○ Prompt the individual to take the symbol to the related activity and complete the activity (or step). ○ Follow a least-to-most or most-to-least prompting sequence depending on the individual's needs and skills.  |
|  4. When the activity is completed, prompt the individual to indicate the completed activity in the manner determined (see Step 5 above). ○ Make sure discarded symbols are readily accessible to the individual at all times to provide the option of using them to ask to do that activity again.  |
|  5. Look for signs that indicate that the individual understands and is making the connection between the visual schedule and the sequence of activities or steps that it represents. ○ Observe whether the individual selects a symbol and then goes to the place where the activity typically occurs, starts to get required materials, and initiates the activity.  |
|  6. Gradually fade the prompts until the individual is able to successfully follow the visual schedule independently.  |

# CONCLUSIONS

In this chapter, we considered AAC interventions to enhance the communication and participation of beginning communicators of all ages at each of the stages of early communication development, including

Beginning communicators who are preintentional
- Those who are intentional but presymbolic
- Those who are at the early stages of symbolic development and are learning their "first words"
- Those who have acquired a corpus of symbols (e.g., spoken words, signs, aided AAC symbols) and are beginning to combine them to communicate more complex messages
- Those who demonstrate challenging behaviors

The chapter described interventions to support individuals with complex communication needs in reducing challenging behaviors and successfully acquiring basic communication skills to express needs and wants, interact socially, comment on shared activities, and ask questions. The next chapter (Chapter 11) considers AAC interventions for individuals who have acquired basic communication skills and are developing more advanced skills to attain communicative competence.

# Intervention to Build Communicative Competence

To participate successfully in a wide range of environments (educational, vocational, health care, and community living), individuals who rely on AAC must develop more advanced skills to build their communicative competence. Communicative competence is not innate; rather it is learned over time (Light &amp; Binger, 1998). Developing beginning communication skills (as described in Chapter 10) is a critical first step in this process, but it is only the first step. Individuals with developmental disabilities who use AAC require effective, evidence-based intervention to extend their skills and maximize their communication. Communicative competence relies on the integration of knowledge, judgment, and skills across four interrelated domains: linguistic, operational, social, and strategic (Light, 1989; Light &amp; McNaughton, 2014). In addition, communicative competence is impacted by psychosocial factors, including motivation, attitude, confidence, and resilience (Light, 2003; Light &amp; McNaughton, 2014). This chapter discusses intervention approaches to build communicative competence with individuals who rely on AAC, including interventions to teach skills in the linguistic, operational, social, and strategic domains and considerations to build motivation, positive attitudes, confidence, and resilience.

This chapter focuses on intervention for individuals who have already acquired basic symbolic communication skills as described in the previous chapter (Chapter 10). This group may include individuals with a range of developmental disabilities, including autism spectrum disorder (ASD), cerebral palsy, Down syndrome, and intellectual disabilities; the group may also represent a range of ages (from young children to adults). Intervention goals should be determined on an individual basis and should build on the individual's strengths. Different skills or psychosocial factors may be targeted as priorities depending on the communication needs, environmental demands, and skill profile of the individual.

There are a range of intervention techniques that can be used to teach linguistic, operational, social, and strategic skills to individuals who use AAC, including explicit instruction, incidental teaching, modeling of AAC use in naturalistic interactions, conversational coaching, and strategy instruction. These approaches are discussed in more detail in Chapter 3. Once basic communication skills are established and interventions target more advanced strategies and skills, often AAC teams make increased use of approaches such as strategy instruction. Strategy

375

instruction includes the following steps (Kent-Walsh & McNaughton, 2005; Light & Binger, 1998):

1. Identify the target strategy or skill to be taught.
2. Explain the strategy to the individual and discuss why it is important.
3. Demonstrate how to use the target strategy.
4. Discuss situations in which the individual should (or should not) use the strategy.
5. Provide numerous opportunities for the individual to use the strategy during naturally occurring interactions (and role plays if appropriate).
6. Provide guided instruction as required (i.e. prompting the individual to use the strategy successfully) and provide feedback on performance.
7. Evaluate progress and adjust intervention as required to improve effectiveness.
8. Check for generalization and long-term maintenance.

It is important to remember that there is no single instructional approach that is universally best for all individuals in all contexts (Gevarter et al. 2013). Ultimately, the AAC team should select instructional approaches based on the needs and skills of the individual who uses AAC and the communication partners, the skills or strategies to be targeted, and the contexts in which they are required.

Of course it is not sufficient to just provide intervention with the individual to build new skills; it is also critical to address environmental barriers and provide instruction for communication partners, as required, to ensure that the individual has meaningful opportunities for communication and the AAC supports required to interact successfully. (See Chapter 4 for further information on working with families and other communication partners to ensure meaningful opportunities for communication, and Chapters 5--8 for discussion of AAC supports.)

## Language Skills

One of the most critical domains in the development of communicative competence for individuals with developmental disabilities is language. Without well-developed language skills, individuals with complex communication needs remain severely restricted in their understanding and expression. The development of language skills is a complex process for individuals who use AAC: They must develop skills in the spoken language of their families and broader social communities; and they must develop skills in the “language code” of their AAC system (Light, 1989; Light & McNaughton, 2014).

Gus Estrella, an expert communicator via AAC, emphasized the importance of language skills as the foundation for communicative competence: “Dig in, get the support of both the school and the social services agencies, get the devices funded, and [then] make us work our little tails off until we master enough language to become competent communicators.” (Estrella, 2000, p. 33)

### Skills in the Spoken Language of the Family and Community

To develop communicative competence, individuals need to learn skills in the spoken language of the family and community, including both comprehension and expressive skills. Some individuals need to develop the skills to participate in bilingual environments.

Intervention to Build Communicative Competence

# Comprehension of Spoken Language

From birth, children with complex communication needs regularly receive spoken input provided by their parents and other caregivers. It is the first language to which they are exposed and forms an important foundation for language learning. Sevcik and Romski (2002) argued that comprehension skills are critical to communication: The individual must be able to fulfill the roles of both listener and communicator in interactions. Smith (2015) noted that comprehension has been described as a "driver of language development" (p. 218). Unfortunately, AAC interventions often focus solely on building expressive communication to the neglect of comprehension:

... a primary focus on production may actually make learning to communicate via AAC systems extremely difficult. In these cases, the individual is asked to produce communications with the assumption that he or she has an adequate foundation of understanding on which to build these AAC productions. (Sevcik &amp; Romski, 2002, p. 453)

Individuals with developmental disabilities are language learners; as such, they will benefit from intervention to enhance their comprehension skills. Goals might include 1) increasing understanding of single-word vocabulary that represents a wide range of concepts, both concrete and abstract; 2) improving comprehension of a range of sentence structures (e.g., understanding wh- questions, responding appropriately to one-, two-, or three-step instructions); and 3) increasing comprehension of morphosyntactic structures (e.g., plural, past tense). Generally, AAC teams may draw on what is known about typical language development to guide their goal setting (Gerber &amp; Kraat, 1992; Savaldi-Harussi, Lustigan, &amp; Soto, 2019; Smith, 2015). For example, the team may start by targeting early emerging wh-questions first (e.g., what, who, where) and target more difficult questions later (e.g., when, how). However, sometimes the team may tamper with the typical developmental sequence to support the individual in meeting specific environmental demands that are priorities (Gerber &amp; Kraat, 1992).

Some individuals with developmental disabilities struggle significantly with comprehension of spoken language due to concomitant hearing impairments, auditory processing difficulties, and/or significant language impairments. They may benefit from the use of augmented input, that is, the use of AAC in conjunction with spoken input to support comprehension (e.g., Romski &amp; Sevcik, 2003). Augmented input provides supplemental input via the visual channel; in the case of aided augmented input, it also provides more permanent input, allowing greater processing time. Research shows that provision of aided AAC input supports comprehension (e.g., Allen, Schlosser, Brock, &amp; Shane, 2017; O'Neill, Light, &amp; Pope, 2018). Unfortunately, educators and peers typically do not provide augmented input to children who rely on AAC (Barker, Akaba, Brady, &amp; Thiemann-Bourque, 2013). If individuals benefit from augmented input, then it is important to provide training in its use for family and other communication partners.

This type of training was provided to Josh's communication partners. Josh was six years old when his parents referred him for services. He had a diagnosis of ASD and was included in a general education kindergarten class with support from a paraprofessional. Although he had the academic skills to be successful in the class, he was struggling and frequently exhibited challenging behaviors that disrupted the class. Observations of the classroom revealed that these behaviors occurred whenever his teacher provided oral instructions to the class. Often these oral instructions were very

complex (e.g. “As soon as you complete your teacher-assigned center, you can either have a snack or you can choose a student-selected center.”). Josh experienced significant challenges with auditory processing and he did not understand multistep instructions presented orally. He was unsure what was expected of him and struggled with the rapid change of activities. He used his challenging behavior to escape the situation. Josh was able to read sentences and was able to follow multistep instructions in writing. We worked with Josh's teacher and taught her how to provide a written daily schedule for Josh and how to augment her oral instructions to the class by writing or typing out the instructions as she spoke them. She naturally simplified the complexity of her instructions when she had to write or type them out, making the directions easier to understand. Josh benefited from the augmented input; he had the time he needed to process the written instructions. His challenging behaviors immediately decreased with this simple adaptation to the environment to create a better fit with his needs and skills. And the entire kindergarten class benefited as they were regularly immersed in meaningful literacy experiences throughout the day. (Light, Roberts, Dimarco, & Greiner, 1998)

### Expressive Skills in the Language of the Family and Community

Beyond the development of comprehension skills, individuals with complex communication needs also need to develop expressive skills. By definition, they are unable to rely on natural speech to meet all of their communication needs, so they will need to develop skills in the language code of their AAC system, but they may also be able to make use of some natural speech to express themselves. Although some individuals with complex communication needs do not produce any speech at all, others use a small repertoire of speech approximations that may be understood by familiar partners; and still others may be able to rely on speech as a primary means of communication with familiar partners, but may require AAC to augment, supplement, or clarify their speech, especially with unfamiliar partners. Thus, most individuals with complex communication needs also need to develop as many expressive communication skills in the spoken languages of their family and community as possible since speech may be one modality that they can draw on as part of their comprehensive communication system. Too often, service providers believe erroneously that they must make an either-or decision: either work on speech production or provide AAC intervention. Rather, many individuals with complex communication needs benefit from interventions that combine a focus on expression using natural speech with a focus on AAC to enhance communication effectiveness (Oommen & McCarthy, 2015).

### Skills to Participate in Bilingual Environments

Given the increasing diversity and globalization of society, many individuals with developmental disabilities are exposed to more than one spoken language in their daily lives. Their families may speak a different language or dialect from that of the broader community. These languages each have different vocabulary, syntax, morphology, and pragmatics, as well as different written forms. Individuals who live in bilingual communities must learn skills in the different spoken (and written) languages in order to develop the communicative competence required to participate in their families and broader communities. They must develop the conditional knowledge to know when to use which language and with whom.

Gus Estrella, introduced earlier in this chapter, grew up in a Hispanic family. He poignantly described the challenges that he faced learning to communicate effectively at home and school:

> Prior to starting preschool, my family and friends all spoke to me in Spanish. That was all I knew. So you can imagine my reaction when I started going to preschool. I was entering uncharted territories. I was about to be left with total strangers, foreigners! It was doubtful that anyone would know any Spanish, so what was the likelihood of somebody understanding my little signs for when I needed something, like lunch! What if I need to go to the little boys' room and they think I'm having a seizure! These were the concerns that a little boy had to deal with and figure out how to cope with his new surroundings. . . . I felt isolated since I couldn't tell anybody what I was thinking or feeling. (Estrella, 2000, p. 33)

In the past, families from different cultural and linguistic backgrounds were often advised to only speak English to their children with developmental disabilities. However, the research demonstrates that there is no disadvantage when children with developmental disabilities are exposed to two spoken languages—the language of their family and that of the broader social community (e.g. Ohashi et al. 2012). In the case of individuals who live in diverse communities, the AAC team should work closely with both the family and the school or broader community to deliver culturally competent services and support the individual in developing competencies in both languages (e.g. Harris, 2015; Soto & Yu, 2014).

### Skills in the Language Code of AAC

Because individuals with complex communication needs are unable to rely on their natural speech to meet all of their communication needs, they must also develop skills in the “language code” of the AAC systems that they utilize, including the representational aspects of AAC symbols (Mineo Mollica, 2003) as well as the semantic, syntactic, and morphological aspects required to express meaning (Blockberger & Sutton, 2003). Acquisition of these skills is complicated by the fact that many AAC systems are not actually true language systems (Light, 1997). They are essentially semantic systems that include sets of graphic symbols to convey concepts, but have no inherent syntax or morphology. Developing competence with the language code of the AAC systems is further complicated because there is an asymmetry (Smith & Grove, 2003) between the language code through which individuals who require AAC receive most of their input (i.e. the spoken language of their families and broader social community) and the language code through which they express themselves (i.e. typically multimodal expression that may include use of speech or speech approximations, gestures or signs, and/or aided AAC). Furthermore, individuals with complex communication needs typically have limited access to models of effective communication via AAC (Ballin, Balandin, Stancliffe, & Togher, 2011). Even when families and professionals are trained to provide aided AAC input, they typically do so for less than 10% of their spoken input (Romski & Sevcik, 2003). This AAC input is often sporadic and focused only on key words; it does not provide a model of competent language expression via AAC. Often adult partners show limited variation in their aided AAC models; they

AAC Interventions for Individuals with Developmental Disabilities

may lack knowledge of the content of AAC displays and may lack fluency in locating vocabulary (von Tetzchner, 2018).

AAC systems that utilize traditional orthography map most closely on to the semantics, syntax, and morphology of spoken language, but these systems still require the individual to learn how to code spoken language into written form (i.e., the development of literacy skills). Literacy skills provide much greater generative capacity than AAC systems that utilize graphic symbols; they may bring greater symmetry to interactions because input and output are provided through the same language system, albeit via spoken and written modalities. These are just some of the reasons why it is critical to teach literacy skills to individuals who use AAC as early as possible to maximize their communication options and their language learning. (See Chapter 12 for discussion of literacy intervention.)

Given the challenges described, individuals who rely on AAC require intervention to develop their comprehension and expression. Building communicative competence requires skills in all aspects of language: semantics, syntax, morphology, and pragmatics. Issues related to the development of semantic, syntactic, and morphological skills are presented in the following sections; those related to pragmatic development are discussed later in this chapter in the section on social competence. Table 11.1 provides examples of language skills that might be targeted in intervention.

# Semantic Skills

The term semantics refers to the meaning of vocabulary concepts (words). Vocabulary knowledge is very important; it is a strong predictor of language and literacy outcomes (McKeown, Beck, &amp; Sandora, 2012). Individuals with robust vocabulary

Table 11.1. Examples of language skills to build communicative competence

|  Domain | Examples of knowledge, judgment, and skills required  |
| --- | --- |
|  Develop skills in the native language(s) spoken and written in the home and broader social community | ·Understand spoken single-word vocabulary that represents a wide range of concepts ·Understand a wide range of simple and complex sentence structures (e.g., wh- questions, directions) ·Understand morphology (e.g., plural, past tense) ·Develop as many expressive skills (content, form, and use) in the spoken language(s) of the home and broader social community as appropriate ·Code switch between different language(s) and cultural norms as required ·Develop literacy skills to understand and use the written language(s) of the home and broader social community; code switch between these written language(s) as required  |
