Intervention to Build Communicative Competence

knowledge can use their existing knowledge to support further word learning (Ambridge &amp; Lieven, 2011); in contrast, those with poorly developed vocabulary knowledge lack the foundation to facilitate ongoing lexical development. Individuals who demonstrate limitations in their vocabulary development are at substantial risk for poor educational and vocational outcomes (Armstrong et al., 2017).

**Challenges Developing Semantic Skills** Language input plays an important role in semantic development. Children develop larger vocabularies when they receive richer language input from adults, especially in the context of mutual, social activities where parents are responsive to children's interests (e.g., Hart &amp; Risley, 1995, 1999). Thus, it is important that individuals who use AAC are exposed to a rich and varied vocabulary that reflects their interests and experiences and is appropriate to their development. To communicate successfully via AAC, they must learn not only spoken words and their meanings, but also the corresponding AAC representations (e.g., signs, written words, graphic symbols, hotspots in visual scene displays). Romski and Sevcik (1996) found that AAC symbol learning was facilitated significantly when individuals with complex communication needs demonstrated understanding of the spoken words that were the symbols' referents. However, they also demonstrated that individuals with severe intellectual disabilities were able to learn the meaning of AAC symbols (i.e., learn the direct association between the symbols and their referents) without necessarily understanding the spoken words.

Developing vocabulary knowledge is complicated because individuals with complex communication needs often do not have the opportunity to select the lexicon for their AAC displays. Whereas children with typical development have the opportunity to hear words in their daily interactions and then try them out expressively, individuals who rely on AAC must rely on communication partners to provide vocabulary for them (e.g., demonstrate a manual sign, add a graphic symbol to their aided display).

Adam's mother describes the challenge in this description of her son, a 9-year-old boy who relies on a wide range of AAC techniques:

Over the years, . . . [Adam] has added some of the structure, rules, and intricacies of language. He added these in the same way he adds to his vocabulary: when he wants and needs them to communicate, when he's given the words with which to do them, and when it isn't too much trouble to use them! Come to think of it, that's just about the way my daughter developed her language, and she doesn't use AAC. The only difference between the kids was that my daughter didn't have to wait for someone to give her a way to express those words. (Gregory &amp; McNaughton, 1993, p. 22)

Because many individuals who require AAC do not have control over the vocabulary in their AAC systems, their external lexicons (i.e., the words on their AAC displays) may not reflect their internal lexicons (i.e., the words that they know; Blockberger &amp; Sutton, 2003; Smith, 2015; Smith &amp; Grove, 2003). Nelson (1992) described the problem as follows:

How can [we] assess what words and structures a young child knows if the only words and structures available [to] the child . . . have been provided by someone else? How can [we] know whether a preliterate child might actually have a variety of words in mind to express a concept or communicate a feeling, but cannot because the words are inaccessible for expression? (p. 4)

AAC Interventions for Individuals with Developmental Disabilities

Learning literacy skills circumvents the problem of vocabulary access as individuals who are literate can express any concept through spelling. For those individuals who are not yet literate, AAC technologies that support just-in-time (JIT) programming may be another way to ensure access to vocabulary in the moment as it is required. These technologies provide quick and easy programming such that vocabulary can be added on the fly by communication partners during daily interactions in response to interests and environmental needs (Schlosser et al., 2016). Individuals who rely on AAC have the opportunity to participate actively in vocabulary selection and programming (Holyfield, Drager, Light, &amp; Caron, 2017). As discussed in Chapter 10, JIT programming may be especially important for early vocabulary development as it directly links new vocabulary concepts to the contexts within which they are learned and used. However, it may also offer a significant advantage in educational environments where students require access to a diverse, rapidly changing academic vocabulary. In this way, individuals who use AAC can try out new concepts immediately and receive feedback from communication partners, allowing them to fine-tune their understanding of both spoken words and the associated AAC symbols. Often individuals who use AAC do not receive feedback from their communication partners on their vocabulary use, particularly if they overextend words. For example, if a child with complex communication needs uses the symbol cow to refer to a horse, a partner might tell her the correct spoken word (No, that's not a cow, that's a horse) but not show her the correct symbol on her communication display, even if it is there (Smith &amp; Grove, 2003; von Tetzchner &amp; Martinsen, 1992). Providing appropriate feedback is important to foster vocabulary development.

The semantic development of individuals who use AAC may be further compromised if they are provided with access to only a limited range of concepts. Most individuals who use AAC have access to fewer than a thousand concepts (unless they are able to spell), and many have access to fewer than a hundred concepts. These limited vocabularies are in stark contrast to the vocabularies of typically developing children which demonstrate rapid growth from 18 months on. Some AAC interventions focus on teaching core vocabulary words (i.e., a small number of words that are used relatively frequently across individuals). These words have value in that they are often useful across a range of contexts. Furthermore, these core vocabulary lists include some of the structural aspects of language that are often neglected in intervention with individuals who use AAC (e.g., parts of speech other than nouns that can be used to construct phrases and sentences such as  $a$ , the, to, did; Geist &amp; Erickson, 2016). However, it is very important to complement this core vocabulary by teaching a large, rich, and varied vocabulary to support language learning, cognitive development, and long-term educational and vocational outcomes (Laubscher &amp; Light, 2018).

## Interventions to Build Semantic Skills

Given the challenges in semantic development for individuals with complex communication needs, it is not surprising to find that many individuals who use AAC demonstrate less robust vocabulary knowledge than their typical peers (e.g., Lund &amp; Light, 2006). As a result, most require intervention to build their vocabulary knowledge. This chapter focuses on intervention to teach vocabulary; see Chapter 5 for discussion of selecting vocabulary and Chapter 6 for discussion of AAC representations of vocabulary concepts. Chapter 10 discussed interventions to teach first words (AAC symbols) to beginning communicators. This chapter focuses on intervention to continue to build a rich and varied vocabulary that

Intervention to Build Communicative Competence

includes a wide range of content words (both concrete and abstract), as well as structural words to support morphosyntactic development and specialized vocabulary to support communication in specific contexts (e.g., vocabulary for academic and work environments, management of activities of daily living, reporting abuse). These interventions range from ones that support fast mapping in naturalistic contexts to ones that provide structured explicit instruction.

## Fast Mapping

Fast mapping refers to the ability to learn a new word or concept with only minimal exposure to it (Carey &amp; Bartlett, 1978). It is the process that accounts for the rapid vocabulary acquisition of children without disabilities. In typical development, fast mapping occurs during daily interactions when children hear new words. Through a process of deduction, using their prior word knowledge as well as the context, they determine the meaning of these new words. For example, a young child might see his older brother kick a soccer ball into the net and yell "goal." Because the child already knows his brother's name and the concepts "ball" and "run," he might deduce that the new word "goal" does not refer to any of these but rather is specifically associated with the main event—the ball going into the net. The initial or fast mapping may not be completely accurate. For example, the child may not understand exactly what does and does not constitute a goal or how a goal relates to the score. However, the initial mapping provides a starting point, and the mapping is then gradually refined through ongoing exposure, use, and feedback in a process of extended mapping.

Can individuals with complex communication needs fast map? Several experimental and intervention studies suggest that the answer is yes (e.g., Drager et al., 2006; Romski et al., 2010; Romski, Sevcik, Robinson, Mervis, &amp; Bertrand, 1996; Wilkinson &amp; Albert, 2001). For at least some individuals with complex communication needs, fast mapping can be used to teach new vocabulary and AAC symbols, and build semantic knowledge.

## Shared Book Reading

Fast mapping may occur across a wide range of naturally occurring daily activities. However, as children grow, books become an increasingly important context for acquiring new vocabulary concepts. There is strong evidence that reading books to children advances vocabulary learning and has the added benefit of also advancing literacy skills (Duursma, Augustyn, &amp; Zuckerman, 2008). Reading to children with complex communication needs provides a rich source of new vocabulary concepts that may not be encountered in daily life (e.g., giraffe, sorcerer, volcano); this new vocabulary helps to build world knowledge and enhance cognitive development. Using book reading as a means to introduce new concepts may be especially important for children with disabilities who may have more limited access to a rich array of world experiences due to health issues, accessibility barriers, attitudinal barriers, financial challenges, and/or behavioral issues. Books provide textual and pictorial supports for introducing new concepts and relating them to the children's prior knowledge and experiences (see Chapter 12 for further discussion of shared book reading). Although shared book reading is most often discussed as an early childhood activity, in fact, the benefits persist throughout life. Reading books is an effective mechanism to introduce older individuals to increasingly advanced vocabulary, sentence structures, and genres to build their linguistic competence. Families and other communication partners should continue to read books to ensure access to this rich language learning opportunity.

Michael Williams has a graduate degree in Library Science and has served as a leader, mentor, and advocate in the field of AAC. He talks about the important role that his family played during his childhood by consistently reading to him. He asserts that it was through listening to books that he developed a rich and diverse vocabulary, strong language skills, and a lifelong love of writing.

### Focused Stimulation

One of the hallmarks of fast mapping is that it occurs with relatively few exposures to the new word. However, some individuals with complex communication needs may benefit from increased exposure. Focused stimulation is an intervention technique whereby parents and other communication partners provide frequent, highly concentrated models of target vocabulary within activities that follow the individual's lead or interest (Weismer, Venker, & Robertson, 2017). Focused stimulation using aided AAC input has been used to build receptive vocabulary of individuals with complex communication needs (e.g. Drager et al. 2006). AAC interventions that focus on teaching core vocabulary often provide focused stimulation. Instructors target a single concept or a small set of preselected target vocabulary each week, providing frequent models (via speech and AAC) of the target concepts (Van Tatenhove, 2009). Despite the importance of AAC models, research by Romski and colleagues found that toddlers with complex communication needs demonstrated greater gains in their expressive vocabularies in interventions when they were prompted to use target vocabulary expressively rather than simply exposed to models of vocabulary use (Romski et al. 2010). Thus the most effective interventions may be ones in which individuals who require AAC receive numerous models of target concepts (via speech and AAC) and are also expected to use these concepts in meaningful activities with feedback on their use.

### Explicit Vocabulary Instruction

Although many individuals benefit from less structured interventions that rely on focused stimulation and fast mapping, some may require more explicit instruction to acquire new vocabulary concepts. They may need repeated opportunities to learn these new concepts, with prompting support to do so. Fast mapping is most effective if individuals are exposed to just a few new concepts at a time so that they can develop hypotheses as to their meanings. Explicit instruction may be advisable when there are numerous new concepts introduced at one time, as when starting a new academic unit at school (e.g. a unit on landforms, or a unit on endangered animals).

Interventions that utilize explicit instruction provide systematic, organized, and direct instruction using a most‐to‐least prompting hierarchy (Archer & Hughes, 2011). This prompting support may include repeated modeling of the target vocabulary (using speech in conjunction with AAC), numerous opportunities for guided (prompted) practice to encourage the individual's successful use of the new vocabulary in meaningful contexts, and multiple opportunities for independent practice using the vocabulary with corrective feedback as required to promote understanding and appropriate use. For example, Yorke, Light, Caron, McNaughton, and Drager (2018) evaluated the effects of explicit instruction infused within book reading to teach academic vocabulary (i.e. the names of endangered animals) to preschoolers with complex communication needs.

### Summary of Interventions to Build Semantic Skills

In summary, it is important that individuals who use AAC acquire a rich and varied vocabulary composed not just of core vocabulary, but also a wide array of content words to support participation

Intervention to Build Communicative Competence

in education, employment, health care, and community activities. Intervention to build semantic skills might include 1) exposure to rich and varied language input within daily activities (including book reading) with opportunities for fast mapping of new vocabulary, 2) focused stimulation for key vocabulary concepts to provide increased exposure via spoken and AAC models, and 3) explicit instruction. When selecting an appropriate intervention approach, the AAC team considers the needs and skills of the individual who uses AAC as well as the number and nature of the words targeted. Regardless of the intervention used, it is critical that individuals who use AAC are exposed to rich and varied language input (using speech and AAC) that builds on their current semantic knowledge and regularly introduces new concepts. Furthermore, it is important that they have numerous opportunities to use these new concepts expressively across a range of meaningful contexts.

Some individuals with developmental disabilities who rely on AAC have mastered the intricacies of language and are able to communicate eloquently as evidenced in their writings. We encourage readers to see the following compilations of writings of individuals who use AAC: Beneath the Surface, edited by Michael Williams and Carole Krezman (2000), and Speaking Up and Spelling It Out compiled by Melanie Fried-Oken and Hank Bersani (2000).

## Syntactic and Morphological Skills

Just knowing word meanings (semantic knowledge) is not sufficient to ensure communicative competence. If individuals who use AAC are to participate actively in society, they need to be able to communicate a wide range of messages to express a wide range of intents. They need to be able to combine concepts to communicate more complex meanings; they need to develop syntactic and morphological skills. Syntax refers to the rules that govern the structure of sentences, including word order. Morphology refers to the structure of words, specifically at the level of morphemes, the smallest units of language that carry meaning (e.g., plural -s, present progressive -ing). Fey (2008) summed up the importance of morphosyntax: "Put very simply . . . syntax is the key to determining who did what to whom" (p. 44).

## Challenges Learning Syntax and Morphology

Some children with developmental disabilities demonstrate rapid learning of a range of semantic-syntactic structures with minimal instruction (Binger, Kent-Walsh, King, Webb, &amp; Buenviaje, 2017), and some adults demonstrate the necessary morphosyntactic skills to successfully communicate complex messages (Lund &amp; Light, 2007). However, in general, many individuals who use AAC demonstrate marked difficulties with both receptive and expressive morphology and syntax (e.g., Blockberger &amp; Sutton, 2003; Smith, 2015). Overall, the research suggests the following patterns of morphosyntactic use in individuals who rely on AAC. Many individuals rely primarily on short one- or two-word messages to express themselves, both in spontaneous and elicited conditions (e.g., Light, Collier, &amp; Parnes, 1985c; Soto, 1999; Sutton &amp; Morford, 1998). When they do use full clauses to communicate, they tend to use simple clauses (e.g., I like cake), with limited use of complex structures such as questions, commands, negatives, and auxiliary verbs (Soto &amp; Toro-Zambrana, 1995; van Balkom &amp; Welle Donker-Gimbrère, 1996). Often messages consist primarily of content words with morphological markers omitted, even when these markers are available on the AAC display (Blockberger &amp; Johnston, 2003; Soto &amp; Toro-Zambrana, 1995; van Balkom &amp; Welle Donker-Gimbrère, 1996).

AAC Interventions for Individuals with Developmental Disabilities

Several researchers have noted that individuals who use AAC may demonstrate constituent word orders that differ from the individual's spoken language, regardless of the AAC modality used (e.g., Smith &amp; Grove, 2003; Trudeau, Morford, &amp; Sutton, 2010). For example, for the sentence The dog eats the bone, a person using graphic symbols might produce a sentence in subject-object-verb order (e.g., DOG BONE EAT) or verb-subject-object order (EAT DOG BONE). Even individuals with more advanced language skills often have difficulty with word order in compound sentences (Smith &amp; Grove, 2003). There are a number of hypotheses that may account for these difficulties with morphosyntax, including ones related to intrinsic factors, extrinsic factors, or some combination.

Syntax and morphology are complex aspects of language; in fact, these are the aspects of language that are especially vulnerable to impairment (Feldman &amp; Messick, 2009). Individuals who use AAC may be even more vulnerable to difficulties with syntax and morphology, as most AAC systems are primarily semantic systems that support the expression of meaning, but may not provide support for the development of syntax and morphology. Some individuals who use AAC primarily have access to nouns within their AAC systems, making it difficult to combine concepts to communicate more complex meanings. This overemphasis on nouns may impede syntactic and morphological development (von Tetzchner &amp; Martinsen, 2000). Some individuals may not have access to morphological markers within their AAC systems (Blockberger &amp; Johnston, 2003). Those who do may only be able to access morphology through a complicated process that requires well-developed metalinguistic skills, whereby they must first analyze the message to identify the type of morphology required and then locate and select the relevant morphological marker on their display (e.g., present progressive, past tense). In addition, learning syntax and morphology may be even more complicated for individuals with complex communication needs. They typically rely heavily on multimodal communication that uses combinations of modes to communicate messages (e.g., gesture + graphic symbol, speech approximation + symbol), none of which share a syntax or morphology (Light, 1997). Furthermore, they seldom see models of competent communicators using appropriate syntax and morphology via AAC (Ballin, Balandin, Togher, &amp; Stancliffe, 2009; Smith, 2015).

Learning syntax and morphology may be particularly complex when individuals use line drawings to represent vocabulary concepts. Smith (1996) provided an example by referring to the Picture Communication Symbol (PCS) for sit, which is a line drawing of a person sitting on a chair. When asked to use AAC symbols to express the sentence The girl is sitting on the chair, one of the participants simply pointed to the symbol for sit, rather than combining the symbols for girl, sit, on, and chair. In fact, this participant was correct—the symbol for sit conveyed the full message and precluded the need to use multiple symbols to construct the message.

The size of the message units made available to individuals who use AAC is another factor that may affect syntactic and morphological (as well as semantic) development. Message units can vary significantly in length: Selection of one symbol may equal one paragraph of output (e.g., selection of a HAMBURGER symbol to retrieve the spoken message, Hi. I'd like a hamburger with tomato and lettuce, no mustard, no ketchup, and extra onions. To go. Thanks), or selection of one symbol may equal one morphological marker (e.g., an arrow pointing to the left that indicates past tense). In between these two extremes are symbols that represent sentences (e.g., a single symbol that

Intervention to Build Communicative Competence

means leave me alone), phrases (e.g., a single symbol that means I want or I don't want), and individual words (e.g., happy, sleep).

Longer, more complete message units speed up the communication process, which is often both slow and cumbersome, especially for individuals who access their AAC systems through alternative access techniques (Blockberger &amp; Sutton, 2003; Paul, 1997). In addition, longer message units may be more easily understood by communication partners. Therefore, longer message units may be advantageous for these circumstances:

- Emergency situations where it is critical that partners understand quickly (e.g., I can't breathe)
- Situations where timing is important (e.g., while watching a sporting event or telling a joke)
- Frequently used messages that are communicated on a regular basis
- Communication with unfamiliar partners who have no experience with AAC (e.g., buying groceries at the store)

On the other hand, longer message units may impede communication accuracy and flexibility and may negatively impact the development of syntax and morphology.

Tim vocalized to get his mother's attention, then looked at his mom, looked at his dinner, looked back at his mom, frowned, then selected the line drawing of the dog from his computer-based AAC system (thus retrieving the preprogrammed message "My dog's name is Skippy"). After numerous attempts, Tim's mother eventually determined that Tim intended to communicate the message "dog," not the extrinsic message produced by the speech synthesizer, and that he was trying to tell her to give his dinner to his dog because he didn't like it. (Light, 1997, p. 65)

For Tim, having only a sentence-level message associated with the symbol dog actually slowed down his communication and created confusion. His mother had to first figure out that the extrinsic message (i.e., My dog's name is Skippy) was not the message Tim intended to communicate, and then she had to play "20 questions" to understand what he really meant. Clearly, the ability to communicate more flexibly is one of the important advantages of shorter message units such as words and morpheme markers. Having opportunities to manipulate word- and morpheme-length units is also important for syntactic and morphological development. Paul (1997) recommended that children with complex communication needs have access to the means to build up and break down sentences within their AAC systems. When vocabulary is provided as single words, the individual has direct control over message components and has the opportunity to combine and recombine concepts to extend generative capacity (Blockberger &amp; Sutton, 2003). These productive experiences putting sentences together to communicate more complex meaning also provide individuals who use AAC with opportunities for feedback to enhance their skills. Correct language structures can be reinforced and expanded (e.g., a child selects the symbols WANT BALL; the father replies, "Oh, you want the red ball" and points to symbols for WANT RED BALL, thus expanding the child's message). Incorrect structures can be corrected through modeling (e.g., a child puts on a hat in the dress-up center and selects the symbols HAT FUNNY; the teacher responds by laughing and modeling the correct sequence of

the message, saying, “That's a funny hat!” while selecting the symbols funny hat). Ultimately, decisions regarding the appropriate length of message units should be made on an individual basis, depending on the needs and skills of the individual, the needs and skills of the communication partners, the environmental demands, and the specific target messages.

The acquisition of syntax and morphology may be further complicated because individuals who use AAC seldom receive instruction in this area (Blockberger & Johnston, 2003); AAC interventions often focus on basic semantic and pragmatic skills. In addition, individuals who rely on AAC may have only limited (if any) opportunities to express complex messages in their daily interactions. As soon as they communicate a single concept (or several concepts), communication partners may jump in and help to co-construct the message, preempting the opportunity for the individual to communicate a more complex message. Sometimes individuals who use AAC (especially those with significant motor impairments) omit morphemes because they choose efficiency over accuracy as a strategy for enhancing the speed and reducing the effort of communication (Blockberger & Sutton, 2003; Light, 1997; Mirenda & Bopp, 2003). They may demonstrate greater morphosyntactic complexity when they believe that their partners lack background information than when they believe their partners share background knowledge (Solomon-Rice, Soto, & Heidenreich, 2017).

### Intervention to Teach Morphosyntactic Skills

Given the challenges of learning syntax and morphology, many individuals who require AAC benefit from intervention to teach these skills. Binger and colleagues emphasize that AAC teams should target semantic growth, but they argue that AAC intervention should also focus on morphosyntactic development for both are fundamental to linguistic competence (Binger et al. 2017). Fey (2008) proposed five general principles to guide grammar interventions (see Table 11.2). A number of specific interventions have been proposed to remediate morphosyntactic difficulties, including ones that rely on focused stimulation with aided AAC modeling and ones that incorporate explicit strategy instruction (see Binger & Light, 2008, for an overview of potential intervention approaches).

### Focused Stimulation and Aided AAC Modeling

Several studies have explored the effects of various AAC modeling techniques, such as the System for Augmenting Language (SAL; Romski & Sevcik, 1996), aided language stimulation (Goossens', Crain, & Elder, 1992), and aided AAC modeling (Binger & Light, 2007), to support the expression of multisymbol messages by individuals with a range of developmental disabilities. In many of these studies, AAC modeling was used in conjunction with focused stimulation that provided repeated exposure to target structures (see Binger & Light, 2007, 2008). Results of these studies demonstrate consistently the benefits of aided AAC modeling (using both low- and high-tech AAC) to increase the length of messages, especially from one-symbol to two- or three-symbol messages. AAC modeling can also be combined with incidental teaching techniques, such as mand-model (Iacono, Mirenda, & Beukelman, 1993; Nigam, Schlosser, & Lloyd, 2006) and time delay procedures (Binger, Kent-Walsh, Berens, del Campo, & Rivera, 2008; Binger, Kent-Walsh, Ewing, & Taylor, 2010).

Intervention to Build Communicative Competence

|  Principle | Example/implication  |

|  1. Consider questions such as “What kinds of meanings does the person produce with single graphic symbols?” and “What kinds of symbol combinations would make the person's messages more complete and more readily interpretable?”  |

From Fey, M. (2008). Thoughts on grammar intervention in AAC. Perspectives on Augmentative and Alternative Communication, 17, 43-49; adapted by permission. Copyright 2008 by American Speech Language Hearing Association. All rights reserved.

A few studies have examined the use of AAC modeling to teach production of basic morphosyntactic structures (e.g., present progressive -ing, possession -'s, regular past tense -ed, third-person singular -s), as well as more complex ones (e.g., auxiliary verb + main verb + ing, inverted yes/no questions; e.g., Binger, Maguire-Marshall, &amp; Kent-Walsh, 2011; Bruno &amp; Trembath, 2006; Kent-Walsh, Binger, &amp; Buchanan, 2015). During the interventions, the instructor typically modeled the target structure repeatedly using aided AAC. If the child produced an incorrect or incomplete structure, the instructor provided a recast by modeling the correct utterance using AAC followed by a complete spoken sentence. Binger and colleagues emphasized the importance of providing contrastive models (i.e., models of other structures) in addition to the target ones to ensure that learners recognize when each marker is required (or not required) (see Binger et al., 2011, for additional discussion of this issue).

AAC Interventions for Individuals with Developmental Disabilities

Conversation-Based Intervention Soto and Clarke (2017, 2018) evaluated the effects of conversation-based intervention on the grammatical skills of children with severe motor speech disorders who used AAC. The intervention focused on supporting the children in their use of a range of morphosyntactic structures (e.g., pronouns, verbs, bound morphemes) in the context of personally relevant scaffolded conversations with trained clinicians. Clarke, Soto, and Nelson (2017) specifically highlighted the pivotal role that recasts (i.e., adult reformulations of children's messages) may play in language learning for individuals who use AAC as recasts respond to, expand on, and provide corrective feedback (Clarke et al., 2017). Although some individuals may benefit from interventions that emphasize AAC modeling, others may require more explicit instruction to learn morphosyntactic structures.

Explicit Instruction Lund and Light (2003) described an intervention program that used explicit strategy instruction to teach adults who used AAC various morphosyntactic structures (e.g., adjective phrases, auxiliary inversion in wh- questions, infinitive constructions). The instruction consisted of three main components:

1. An explanation of the target grammatical rules and the benefits
2. Practice identifying correct and incorrect forms of the constructs in spoken and written forms (e.g., He wore his new shoes versus He wore his shoes new)
3. Practice correcting errors using their AAC technologies, with think-aloud statements provided by the instructor to explain the processes required to correct errors

The instructor provided prompting and corrective feedback as required to support successful use of the target forms. It is important to note that this intervention relied heavily on metalinguistic skills (i.e., the ability to reflect on and talk about language). It was appropriate for the adults who participated, but would not be an appropriate approach for individuals who have not yet developed metalinguistic skills.

## Summary of Interventions to Build Language Skills

Some individuals with developmental disabilities who rely on AAC have well-developed semantic and morphosyntactic skills. However, many individuals with complex communication needs face both receptive and expressive language difficulties that stem, at least in part, from the fact that their language-learning experiences are very different from those of individuals who can speak. It is critical that the individuals who rely on AAC receive effective, evidence-based intervention to maximize their semantic, syntactic, and morphological skills in order to further their communicative competence.

## OPERATIONAL SKILLS

Although language skills are essential to the development of communicative competence, they are not sufficient on their own. Individuals with complex communication needs must also learn the operational skills to access and use AAC (Light, 1989; Light &amp; McNaughton, 2014).

Intervention to Build Communicative Competence

1. They may need to develop the skills to produce unaided AAC (e.g., produce the hand shape, orientation, position, and movement for a range of manual signs or gestures).
2. They may need to learn the skills required to technically operate low-tech or high-tech aided AAC (e.g., locate and select symbols, navigate to additional AAC displays).

# Learning Demands for Using Aided and Unaided AAC

Use of unaided and aided AAC imposes a range of learning demands—motor, sensory perceptual, cognitive, and linguistic. It is important that the designs of AAC supports are driven by the needs and skills of individuals with complex communication needs to minimize these demands (Light &amp; McNaughton, 2013). Key changes to system design can substantially reduce learning demands. For example, McCarthy and colleagues demonstrated how the use of dynamic presentation (animation) to designate the offer of items from a scanning array significantly reduced the learning demands of scanning for young children (McCarthy et al., 2006; McCarthy &amp; Boster, 2018).

To minimize learning demands, the AAC team should select and personalize AAC supports (unaided and aided) so that they are appropriate for the individual's needs and skills (see Chapter 8). Even when AAC supports are selected and personalized based on the individual's needs and skills, there will still be some operational skills that must be learned. Table 11.3 provides some examples of operational skills that might be targeted in intervention. Intervention by a multidisciplinary AAC team is essential.

Table 11.3. Examples of operational skills to build communicative competence

|  Domain | Examples of knowledge, judgment, and skills required  |
| --- | --- |
|  Produce unaided symbols as appropriate | ·Plan and produce the required hand shape, position, orientation, and movement to form manual signs or conventional gestures ·Plan and produce the required body movements to act out messages via pantomime ·Plan and produce the required body movements to produce other unaided codes (e.g., eye-blink codes, looking up to say yes)  |
|  Operate low-tech and high-tech aided AAC accurately and efficiently | ·Open communication book, turn pages, and select target AAC symbol ·Locate target symbol, pick it up, and hand it to partner when using PECS ·Use paper and pencil to draw concept ·Use access technique to select required AAC symbols (e.g., direct selection with finger, fist, toe, or eyes; row-column scanning with a single switch; directed scanning with a joystick) ·Navigate to other AAC displays within aided AAC technology ·Adjust volume of speech output as required  |
|  Operate digital communication apps and other mainstream communication tools | ·Access digital communication tools (e.g., e-mail, Facebook, Twitter, Instagram, SnapChat) ·Capture and upload photos and video to support communication via digital communication media ·Navigate between apps/tools to meet needs  |

Key: PECS, Picture Exchange Communication System.

Intervention to Teach Operational Skills

Before starting intervention, it is important to ensure appropriate seating/positioning and appropriate accommodations for vision and hearing impairments as these all impact operational skills significantly (see Chapters 2 and 3 for further discussion). The overriding goal of instruction in operational skills is to promote accuracy and efficiency, and reduce effort and fatigue as much as possible. Ultimately the goal is to develop sufficient automaticity or fluency with operational skills that the individual does not have to devote conscious cognitive resources to technical operation and can instead devote full attention to the communicative interaction (Light & Lindsay, 1991). It is well recognized that automaticity is built through repeated practice. Treviranus and Roberts (2003) argued that too often intervention to build access skills focuses only on learning the skill; they emphasize the importance of extending intervention long enough to build automaticity of performance.

This is borne out by the experience of Randy Horton. He described the significant demands he encountered learning the operational skills for his AAC technology, requiring approximately 96 hours of learning and practice in his case. He highlighted the lack of intervention provided to support the development of operational skills:

> People without disabilities receive 12 years of writing and language teaching during school. I had next to none. . . . Usually the consumer is given 2 to 6 hours of teaching how to use the [AAC] device. Extensive, intensive teaching during implementation is the key to success. (Horton, Horton, & Meyers, 2001, p. 49)

Typically, interventions to teach operational skills involve demonstration of the skills, opportunities for repeated practice of these skills in structured contexts, prompting to ensure successful use, and feedback on performance. Intervention should also include opportunities to apply the operational skills in meaningful contexts to support communication. Approaches to intervention range from those that utilize explicit instruction in structured trials to those that adopt a cognitive developmental approach to support conceptual understanding of the underlying processes involved in access. For example, automatic linear scanning can be taught via a highly structured approach, using most-to-least prompting to teach the individual to 1) identify the target symbol from an array with the location randomized across opportunities; and 2) activate the switch, but only when the cursor touches the target symbol (Reichle, York, & Sigafoos, 1991). The conditional response is taught using positive teaching examples (i.e. when the cursor touches the target symbol) and negative teaching examples (i.e. when the cursor touches a distractor symbol other than the target).

Alternatively, intervention can utilize a cognitive developmental approach to build the individual's conceptual understanding of the underlying operation. For example, in the case of scanning, the individual needs to understand and coordinate 1) the relationship between the cursor and the target symbol on the display, and 2) the one between the switch and selection. In this case, intervention with a young child might use the analogy of a game of tag (wherein the cursor is “it” and the switch is used to tag the target concept) to teach the coordination of these two important relationships to enhance performance, using an experience that is familiar to the child (Light, 1993). More recently, attention has focused on methods to teach eye gaze as an access method (e.g. Chen & O'Leary, 2018); it is more difficult to demonstrate and prompt this access method.

Intervention to Build Communicative Competence

Regardless of the instructional approach utilized, it is important that decision making in selecting, personalizing, and teaching access techniques is data driven. Koester and Simpson (2014, 2017) demonstrated that data-driven decision making and adjustments resulted in significant improvements in rate of communication for individuals with motor impairments. Ultimately successful acquisition of the operational skills required to utilize AAC depends on four factors (Mumford &amp; Chau, 2016):

1. Personalized design of the access technique based on the individual's needs and skills
2. Instruction in operational skills for the individual
3. Instruction for family and communication partners
4. Integration into meaningful, functional activities

Careful consideration of these factors was necessary to support Li Na in acquiring the operational skills needed to use eye-gaze as an access technique. Li Na was 30 months old when her parents referred her for services. She had severe cerebral palsy and required adaptive seating. She had no functional use of her legs and arms. She was already using eye gaze to indicate objects or activities of interest in her environment. We introduced her to a low-tech eye-gaze system and taught her parents how to read her gaze to allow her to select AAC symbols to request activities, ask questions, and comment on events. This low-tech approach allowed her to communicate immediately, with a partner's support. We also introduced her to AAC technology controlled through eye gaze to enhance her independence. Her occupational therapist started to work with her to teach her the operational skills required to use the technology accurately and efficiently. Once Li Na was comfortable with the new technology, it was integrated into her daily communication. However, she continued to make use of her low-tech system as well, especially when she was tired or when she was in bed or lying on the floor.

As this case illustrates, a single access technique may not meet the needs of many individuals with complex communication needs; rather they may need to learn several access techniques to accommodate changes in positioning, fatigue, or environments (Fager, Fried-Oken, Jakobs, &amp; Beukelman, 2019). AAC intervention should always target immediate needs, but also include plans for the future.

## SOCIAL SKILLS

The development of linguistic and operational skills ensures that individuals who use AAC have the tools that they require to attain communicative competence. However, simply having these tools is not sufficient; they also need to develop the social skills to use these tools effectively in daily interactions. Social competence requires both sociolinguistic and sociorelational skills (Light, 1989; Light &amp; McNaughton, 2014). Sociolinguistic skills refer to the pragmatic aspects of communication, in other words, discourse skills (e.g., taking turns, initiating and terminating interactions, maintaining and developing topics) and skills to express a wide range of communicative functions (e.g., requesting attention, requesting information, providing information, confirming). Sociorelational skills refer to the interpersonal aspects of communication that form the foundation for developing positive relationships, and include skills

AAC Interventions for Individuals with Developmental Disabilities

such as participating actively in interactions, demonstrating interest in partners, and projecting a positive self-image (Light, Arnold, &amp; Clarke, 2003).

Individuals who use AAC face numerous challenges in the development of social skills. Some, such as individuals with ASD, may have disabilities that are associated with specific impairments in social interactions; they may have difficulty developing the other orientation skills to focus on their communication partners. People require numerous opportunities to interact with a wide range of partners to develop their social competence; they need to experience successful interactions, and also to learn from unsuccessful, failed interactions. Unfortunately, many people who use AAC have an extremely limited social circle; they may interact primarily with family or with paid professionals (Blackstone &amp; Hunt Berg, 2012). Due to attitudinal barriers in society, they may have few meaningful opportunities to interact with a diverse range of partners, including adults and peers, to develop their social skills.

This was the case for Mike, who was 23 years old. He had severe cerebral palsy and used AAC technology to support his communication. He had graduated from high school and was involved in AAC intervention to build his social skills. Despite several weeks of intervention, he had made limited progress. Upon reflection, we recognized the problem. In the course of his week, he only had the opportunity to interact with three people—his mother, the next-door neighbor who stopped by every few days, and his speech-language pathologist who saw him once a week for services at an outpatient clinic. How was he supposed to develop social skills if he had so few opportunities to interact with others? We revised the focus of his intervention significantly to ensure that he was involved in his community and had meaningful opportunities to interact with others. He loved music and was very knowledgeable, so we encouraged him to volunteer at the local radio station putting together playlists. In this context, he had the motivation, the need, and the opportunity to develop his social competence.

Given the challenges in developing social skills, individuals who use AAC often require intervention to build competence in the social domain, including sociolinguistic and sociorelational skills. Table 11.4 provides examples of sociolinguistic and sociorelational skills that might be targeted.

## Intervention to Build Sociolinguistic Skills

It is challenging to learn the sociolinguistic skills to participate effectively in communicative interactions, especially when using AAC. When individuals who use AAC interact with partners who use natural speech to communicate, these partners typically dominate and control the interactions; individuals who use AAC have difficulty getting into the conversation, staying in the conversation, or participating in meaningful ways. Numerous studies have indicated that individuals with complex communication needs tend to express a limited range of functions, primarily responses to questions and simple requests for objects or activities (e.g., Carter, 2003a, 2003b; Iacono, 2003; Light et al., 1985b; von Tetzchner &amp; Martinsen, 1992). Many people who rely on AAC tend to occupy a respondent role in interactions; they seldom initiate conversations and respond primarily when obligated to do so (e.g., Calculator &amp; Dollaghan, 1982; Light et al., 1985a; von Tetzchner &amp;

Intervention to Build Communicative Competence

Table 11.4. Examples of sociolinguistic and sociorelational skills to build communicative competence

|  Domain | Examples of knowledge, judgment, and skills required  |
| --- | --- |
|  Develop appropriate sociolinguistic skills for various partners and contexts | ·Express a wide range of communicative functions (e.g., request information, provide information, provide clarification, confirm/deny, request attention) ·Communicate complex needs and wants ○Provide detailed instructions to manage personal care ○Communicate needs effectively and efficiently in interactions with health care professionals ○Develop a plan for emergencies ·Initiate and sustain social interactions ○Use appropriate initiation and topic-setting strategies ○Maintain and develop topics of conversation with adults and peers ○Fulfill obligatory and nonobligatory turns in interaction ○Participate in displaced talk about past or future experiences ○Tell stories ·Exchange more complex information ○Explain concepts; describe procedures ○Prepare conference or class presentations ○Self-advocate; report crime, abuse, or neglect ·Choose appropriate AAC and/or digital communication tools to meet needs as required ·Use appropriate form, content, and conventions as required for the audience and media  |
|  Develop appropriate sociorelational skills | ·Participate actively in interactions (e.g., take nonobligatory turns; make meaningful contributions) ·Be responsive to partners; provide appropriate feedback as a listener ·Demonstrate active listening skills; demonstrate respect; express empathy as appropriate ·Demonstrate interest in partners (e.g., use the partner's name, ask partner-focused questions) ·Put partners at ease ·Project a positive self-image ·Maintain a positive rapport with partners; communicate respect ·Give feedback and handle conflict effectively as required  |

Martinsen, 1992). In contrast, partners who use natural speech tend to control conversational topics, ask many questions (often ones that only require yes/no or single-word responses), and spend a significant amount of time repairing and/or averting breakdowns during interactions with people who use AAC (Basil, 1992; Iacono, 2003; Light et al., 1985b). Given these interaction patterns, many individuals who use AAC benefit from intervention to teach sociolinguistic skills, including the skills to initiate, maintain, and develop topics, and to express a range of communicative functions. In Chapter 10, we discussed intervention for beginning communicators to teach basic pragmatic skills such as simple requests, taking turns in social interactions, and basic commenting during shared activities. This chapter focuses on intervention that targets more advanced sociolinguistic skills in order to communicate more complex needs and wants, develop social interactions, and exchange more complex information.

#### Teach How to Communicate More Complex Needs and Wants

Usually people who require AAC learn effective ways to express their basic needs and wants when they are beginning communicators. They learn to communicate choices, initiate requests for preferred objects and activities, and reject nonpreferred items in socially appropriate ways (see Chapter 10). However, as they grow older and develop more advanced communication skills, they may require intervention to learn how to make more nuanced and detailed requests (e.g. asking a parent permission to go out with friends). These types of requests require diverse vocabulary and more sophisticated sociolinguistic skills. The individual needs to understand the perspective of the communication partner and must compose a convincing argument based on this perspective.

Some individuals with severe motor impairments may require assistance from others for activities of daily living and may need to develop communication skills to provide precise and detailed requests to manage their personal care (Collier & Self, 2010). In addition, individuals who use AAC also need to develop the skills to manage medical care and to deal with emergency situations (e.g. floods, tornados, fire). All these situations require communication of needs and wants in a clear, comprehensive, and organized manner that reflects understanding of the perspective and prior knowledge of the communication partner. (See Chapter 13 for further discussion of these skills.)

One adult who relies on AAC explained the importance of learning to direct his care:

> It's not enough to tell him (my attendant) to lift me from my bed to my wheelchair. I need to tell him how I want to be lifted and positioned. Getting services done in the way I want is all about communicating the details involved in that activity. (A. Shelbourne, personal communication, November 13, 2007; as cited in Collier & Self, 2010, p. 167)

Learning the sociolinguistic skills to communicate complex needs and wants in situations such as these is essential to ensure the health and well-being of individuals who rely on AAC. However, these skills alone are not sufficient to ensure a high quality of life. Individuals who use AAC also need to learn the sociolinguistic skills to initiate and sustain interactions to build social closeness.

#### Teach How to Initiate and Sustain Social Interactions

It is through social interactions that we develop and maintain social closeness with others; these interactions are fundamental to attaining a high quality of life. Once individuals who use AAC have learned basic turn taking and commenting skills (as described in Chapter 10), they have the foundation skills to learn to engage in more extended social interactions.

#### Initiation and Topic-Setting Strategies

People who rely on AAC need ways to start interactions and establish topics of conversation. Initially, they may require visual supports to help them initiate interactions. These supports might include, for example, shared activities, remnants, or collections. These supports provide a concrete way to alert the communication partner to the topic and they also provide something for the dyad to do together or talk about. For example, Therrien and Light (2016, 2018) described an intervention that utilized shared book-reading activities as a concrete

means for children with complex communication needs to initiate and sustain interactions with their typical peers. Laubscher, Light, and McNaughton (2018) described an intervention that taught children with ASD and their typical peers to interact during play activities that served to establish the focus of the interaction.

Collections can also be used to initiate interactions between individuals who rely on AAC and communication partners, especially peers. Many individuals of all ages enjoy collecting various types of favorite objects—stickers, stuffed animals, sports cards, baseball caps—the possibilities are endless! For example, a teenager might wear a different baseball cap to school every day, or a child might bring a toy robot for show and tell at school. The collection provides concrete support for initiating and sustaining interaction.

Trevor was in elementary school when he was referred for AAC intervention. He had cerebral palsy and used a manual wheelchair for mobility. He really wanted to make friends with the other children in his class, but he needed strategies to get them to come over to him to play. His mother had an ingenious idea to help him initiate interactions with his peers. She added the following phrase to his AAC technology: Hey, look what I have. Wanna play? Then she helped him to choose a small toy, a different one each day, to take into school. The message allowed him to initiate interaction with his peers and the toy gave them something to do together.

Remnants saved from activities can also provide a way for individuals who use AAC to initiate topics about motivating events. Remnants include anything associated with the event (e.g. ticket stubs, brochures, maps, party hats). Like collections, remnants provide a concrete way to initiate an interaction, but they support greater diversity of topics. Typically the remnants are paired with appropriate vocabulary about the topic to support communication. Remnants also provide support for communication partners who may find it easier to understand the individual and sustain the interaction when they have contextual support (Light, McNaughton, & Caron, 2019). See Figure 11.1 for an example of a conversation book used to initiate social interaction.

### Conversational Coaching

Although it is important to initiate interactions, individuals who rely on AAC must also learn to sustain these interactions. Hunt and colleagues developed an intervention that used coaching to teach individuals with developmental disabilities to participate in social interactions with their peers (Hunt, Alwell, & Goetz, 1988, 1991a, 1991b). In this intervention, the person who used AAC was coached to initiate a conversation by pointing to a photo, remnant, symbols, or words in a communication book either to ask a question (e.g. do you like basketball?) or make a comment (e.g. i love the warriors). Next, the conversational partner was coached (as required) to respond to the question or comment, make an additional comment about the topic, then ask a question, and wait to allow the individual time to respond. The coach then prompted the person who used AAC (as required) to answer the question, comment as desired, and ask another question. This cycle (depicted in Figure 11.2) was repeated until the conversation reached its natural end point. Similar strategies have also been used to teach adults with developmental disabilities who use AAC to participate in conversational exchanges (Dattilo & Camarata, 1991; O'Keefe & Dattilo, 1992; Spiegel, Benjamin, & Spiegel, 1993).

Intervention to Build Communicative Competence

Coaching strategies can also be taught to family members or peers, with the goal of teaching them to support the communication of individuals who use AAC during natural social routines. For example, Trottier, Kamp, and Mirenda (2011) taught six typically developing classmates to provide coaching to two boys with ASD during social game routines at school. Similar results were also reported for three preschoolers with ASD who were coached by their peers to use AAC during play routines (Trembath, Balandin, Togher, &amp; Stancliffe, 2009). Interventions using coaching have also been implemented successfully by families; for example, Cheslock and colleagues reported positive effects for a 30-year-old woman with moderate intellectual disability who was coached by her mother to use AAC during social exchanges (Cheslock, Barton-Hulsey, Romksi, &amp; Sevcik, 2008). Thus, it appears that service providers, family, and peers can be taught to provide coaching to successfully support both children and adults who rely on AAC in learning the skills to engage in extended social interactions.

Displaced Talk Not all social interactions revolve around ongoing shared activities; many involve displaced talk. Displaced talk is a term used to describe communication about past or future events (as opposed to communication about an ongoing activity). Many individuals with complex communication needs have difficulty participating in displaced talk as these conversations provide less contextual support and rely heavily on language skills alone. Caron and colleagues described an interesting intervention to support individuals who use AAC in learning to participate in displaced talk (Caron, Holyfield, Light, &amp; McNaughton, 2018). They utilized AAC video VSD technology with an 8-year-old boy with severe ASD to capture videos of meaningful events within his day (e.g., feeding the ducks at the local park, crashing his bike); they then added relevant vocabulary to allow him to communicate about the events. The videos provided contextual support to help him learn to engage in displaced talk about past events (see Figure 11.3 for a screen shot of a video VSD used to talk about past experiences).
