AAC Interventions for Individuals with Developmental Disabilities

## Story Telling

Often social conversations revolve around sharing stories of past experiences or events. Therefore, it is important that individuals who use AAC also develop narrative skills that extend beyond the sentence level to the discourse level of communication. Narratives are critical to identity development, social connections, and belonging (Soto, Solomon-Rice, &amp; Caputo, 2009). Because communication partners often control interactions, individuals who use AAC may have limited experience engaging in extended discourse. They may have never had the opportunity to serve as a narrator and tell a story (Waller, 2006). Given this lack of experience, it is not surprising to find that the narratives of children who use AAC are typically shorter, less complete, and less cohesive than those of their peers without disabilities (Smith et al., 2018). Individuals with complex communication needs typically require intervention to teach narrative skills to support social interactions. Waller and colleagues described intervention with a school-aged child that combined the use of AAC technology and instruction to support the development and retrieval of personal narratives (Waller et al., 2001). Soto and colleagues evaluated the effects of intervention to build narrative skills with school-aged children who use AAC (Soto et al., 2009). The intervention utilized photos of personal experiences, a story map, and language elicitation strategies (e.g., open-ended questions, fill-in-the-blank sentences, binary choices), as well as modeling of vocabulary and morphosyntactic structures. In addition to teaching narrative skills in face-to-face interactions, these skills are often targeted in literacy instruction as well (see Chapter 12).

As individuals who use AAC are called upon to participate increasingly in longer social conversations that require displaced talk about past and future events and story telling, they will need to rely more heavily on their language skills, emphasizing the importance of language intervention as described earlier. These skills will not only support extended interactions to build social closeness, but also interactions to exchange more complex information.

## Teach How to Exchange More Complex Information

When individuals who rely on AAC participate in educational placements, work environments, and community activities, they face demands to exchange complex information. For example, they may need to explain concepts to demonstrate their understanding of academic content at school; they may need to describe procedures to others at work; they may need to prepare presentations for classes, conferences, or other speaking engagements. Unlike the narrative skills used in social conversations and displaced talk, these interactions require skills in describing, explaining, and persuading. In this type of information exchange, the individual must be able to clearly establish the main idea and then provide more details to support the main argument. The information must typically be communicated with precision; the focus is on the actual content of the message rather than the social interaction (Light, 1988). The descriptive, explanatory, and persuasive communication skills required for these types of interactions are often learned through reading and may also be targeted expressively in writing instruction (see Chapter 12). Given the linguistic and operational demands of these types of interactions, individuals who use AAC may choose to prepare content in advance to communicate via preprogrammed messages stored in AAC technologies. Sometimes it may be preferable to use other media for this type of information exchange, including written reports, e-mails, or other digital communication media.

Intervention to Build Communicative Competence

As individuals who require AAC participate in a greater range of educational, vocational, and community activities, they inevitably encounter numerous barriers (policy, practice, attitude, knowledge, or skill barriers) that necessitate advocacy. Intervention to develop self-advocacy skills should start early on. Children with complex communication needs can start to learn strategies to stand up for themselves and ensure their rights from a young age. For example, initially, this may be as simple as providing feedback to an educational assistant as to an appropriate pace of feeding (e.g., smiling when the pace is appropriate; vocalizing and turning away when the pace is too fast; McNaughton, Rackensperger, Wehmeyer, &amp; Wright, 2010). Over time, individuals who use AAC may need to develop skills to exchange more complex information to advocate in situations that may involve a range of partners, both familiar and unfamiliar.

Sometimes the negative situations confronted by individuals with complex communication needs are very serious ones. Children and adults with disabilities are highly vulnerable to abuse and neglect. Those who rely on others for personal care are particularly vulnerable, and individuals with complex communication needs are even more likely to be victims due to their severe communication difficulties (Bryen, Carey, &amp; Frantz, 2003). When such maltreatment occurs, it severely compromises personal health, safety, and well-being, as well as overall quality of life. Given the increased risk for maltreatment of children and adults with disabilities, it is essential that AAC teams are cognizant of this risk, comply with mandated reporting responsibilities, and plan AAC intervention so that individuals with complex communication needs have the tools and the skills required to access required services and communicate effectively about maltreatment (e.g., Bornman, Bryen, Kershaw, &amp; Ledwaba, 2011; Collier, McGhie-Richmond, Odette, &amp; Pyne, 2006; White, Bornman, &amp; Johnson, 2018). (See Chapter 13 for further discussion of these important issues.)

In summary, individuals who use AAC require intervention to learn the sociolinguistic skills to 1) express more complex needs and wants, including interactions to manage personal care, patient-provider care, and emergency situations; 2) initiate and sustain social interactions, including ones built around shared activities, displaced talk, and storytelling; and 3) exchange more complex information, including descriptions and explanations at school or work, self-advocacy, and reporting of maltreatment.

## Intervention to Build Sociorelational Skills

Social interactions are tremendously important in developing social closeness with others and these social relationships are in turn critical to quality of life. Many individuals with developmental disabilities who rely on AAC report that they are lonely; a lack of meaningful communication with others contributes significantly to this loneliness (Balandin, Berg, &amp; Waller, 2009; Cooper, Balandin, &amp; Trembath, 2009; Østvik, Ytterhus, &amp; Balandin, 2018).

There are many examples of adults who use AAC who have developed communicative competence and have assumed leadership roles in the field, sharing their experiences and advocating for their rights. Please visit the online AAC Learning Center for a wide range of videos of individuals who use AAC communicating about their use of AAC to support their participation in society.

A parent of a school-aged child who uses AAC described the problem:

> No-one comes. We've invited them but nobody comes. For her birthday this year it did work, two kids actually came. But we asked last year at the end of the school year if any of her classmates would mind just popping over in the summer time, spending an hour with her, or going to the movies with her, and no-one volunteered, so . . . [long pause] . . . now she . . . she likes to be by herself and work on her computer and look up information. (Batorowicz, Campbell, von Tetzchner, King, & Missiuna, 2014, p. 245)

There are numerous factors that contribute to the lack of meaningful social interactions, including policy and practice barriers that result in isolation of individuals who use AAC, as well as attitudinal, knowledge, and skill barriers related to peers. (See Chapter 4 for further discussion of interventions to reduce these barriers.) In addition to these opportunity barriers, often individuals who use AAC demonstrate limitations in their sociorelational skills (Light et al. 2003) that may negatively impact their development of positive social relationships:

1. They may lack access to the vocabulary to support positive reciprocal social interactions.
2. They may lack the social experiences required to develop these skills.
3. They may experience specific deficits in social development that impact the use of sociorelational skills.
4. They may not receive appropriate intervention to support their learning of these skills.

Ironically, AAC intervention may unwittingly teach individuals who use AAC to interact in ways that do not promote social competence. For example, in an effort to provide individuals who use AAC with opportunities to practice their linguistic skills, AAC teams may frequently ask them questions and encourage them to talk about themselves believing that these experiences will be motivating and meaningful. Unintentionally, individuals who use AAC may learn that social interactions are all about them; they may not learn the skills to effectively reach out and demonstrate an interest in others, skills that are critical to social competence.

After high school graduation, Rosa (a young woman with cerebal palsy who relies on AAC) secured a job doing data entry. After her first two weeks, her job coach checked in. Rosa was able to meet the task requirements of the job, but overall things were not going well. Her co-workers were avoiding her at breaks and in the lunch room. They did not like spending time with her. They reported that she was self-focused and self-absorbed. All she did was talk about herself. Throughout high school, Rosa had had lots of opportunities to talk about her experiences with her teacher, her aide, and her speech-language pathologist to build her language skills, but she had never learned how to ask partners about their experiences and show an interest in their lives. She lacked the social skills that she required to be a valued co-worker. With intervention, she quickly learned to ask partner-focused questions and demonstrate an interest in others; doing so allowed her to build more positive, reciprocal relationships with her co-workers.

As this example illustrates, sociorelational skills are not just important in interactions for social closeness, but in any interaction with other people in school, work,

Intervention to Build Communicative Competence

home, or the community. Interactions to express needs and wants, exchange information, and build social closeness are much more successful when individuals who use AAC demonstrate positive sociorelational skills. Sociorelational skills bear special importance for individuals with complex communication needs as they may face significant barriers in forming interpersonal relationships (Anderson, Balandin, &amp; Clendon, 2011; Light et al., 2003).

What sociorelational skills should be targeted in intervention? Take a minute and reflect on the people with whom you enjoy interacting, as well as those with whom you do not. What is the difference between these two sets of people?

The classic book, How to Win Friends and Influence People (Carnegie, 2009), delineates the following key skills to build positive social relationships:

1. Show genuine interest in other people.
2. Smile; be positive.
3. Remember and use the person's name.
4. Be a good listener.
5. Talk in terms of the other person's interests.
6. Make the other person feel important—and do it sincerely.

All of these sociorelational skills depend on individuals demonstrating other-orientation skills. They must understand that different people have different experiences, perspectives, and beliefs (referred to as theory of mind; Baron-Cohen, Leslie, &amp; Frith, 1985). Once they develop this understanding, they are able to consider the social consequences of what they say and do. Tager-Flusberg (1997) explained the importance of these skills: "Much of our everyday use of language involves understanding intentions and related mental states in other people" (p. 155). Some individuals who require AAC may experience deficits in the development of theory of mind, impacting their sociorelational skills. They may have limited access via AAC to the state verbs (e.g., believe, think, know, feel) that are important to the development of theory of mind (Light et al., 2003). Given the challenges that individuals who use AAC face in the development of sociorelational skills, many will require concerted intervention to build knowledge, judgment, and skills in the sociorelational domain. Table 11.4 highlights some key sociorelational skills that may support individuals who use AAC in developing positive social relationships. Several interventions have been proposed to teach sociorelational skills, including ones that target the use of nonobligatory turns/listener feedback, active listening, partner-focused questions, and conflict resolution.

Jim Prentice, an expert communicator via AAC who worked as a statistical record keeper at a large company, poignantly illustrated the importance of developing social competence:

When I started to work, I'm sure that all the employees surrounding my workstation probably thought that I was someone from Mars. I rode in on my motorized wheelchair and had some sort of device attached to my chair. I rode past them and they really didn't know whether I was able to talk. If they did talk to me, they weren't sure I was able to answer them. . . . I stopped them in their tracks, before they were frozen on the spot, and said, "Good morning, my name is Jim. How are all of you doing today?" Big smiles came on their faces, and they seemed to answer in unison, "We are fine, and it's nice to have you working with us." That sure broke the ice. I felt like one of the team then. I made sure I programmed a few jokes into my communicator so that it would make my conversations more friendly and comfortable for them. It worked! (Prentice, 2000, p. 209)

AAC Interventions for Individuals with Developmental Disabilities

## Teach Use of Nonobligatory Turns/Listener Feedback

Communication partners value interactions with people who demonstrate active engagement in the interaction and listen to what is said. Often individuals who use AAC fulfill their obligatory turns (i.e., answer questions) in interactions, but forfeit their nonobligatory turns (i.e., fail to take turns following partners' comments; e.g., Light et al., 1985a). Communication partners dominate and carry the burden of the interaction. Research suggests that people perceive individuals who use AAC to be more competent communicators when they participate actively in the interaction and take nonobligatory turns compared to when they do not (Light, Binger, Bailey, &amp; Millar, 1997). Several interventions have taught individuals to use short nonobligatory turns following a partner's comment or statement to demonstrate their engagement and interest; these nonobligatory turns might include head nods, smiles, simple gestures (e.g., thumbs up), or short interjections communicated via AAC technologies (e.g., awesome, no way, yeah, uh-huh). These brief social interjections place few linguistic demands on the person who relies on AAC, but still provide important social feedback to let a communication partner know that the person who uses AAC is engaged and interested in the interaction. Buzolich, King, and Baroody (1991) reported the successful use of explicit instruction that utilized graduated prompting plus time delay to teach the use of these types of social comments (e.g., this is fun, sounds good, yuck) to three students who relied on AAC technologies. In a related study, Light and colleagues used strategy instruction successfully to teach individuals with a range of developmental disabilities to use nonobligatory turns in their interactions (Light et al., 1997). Following intervention, partners reported greater satisfaction with the interactions and perceived the individuals who used AAC to be more competent communicators. Teaching the use of simple nonobligatory turns to provide partner feedback and demonstrate engagement is an important first step in building sociorelational skills. Once individuals who use AAC develop these skills, they may benefit from intervention to teach more advanced active listening skills.

## Teach Active Listening Skills

McNaughton and Vostal (2010) developed an active listening strategy (known as the LAF, Don't CRY strategy) to support the development of positive social relationships. The LAF strategy targets the following positive sociorelational skills: 1) Listen and communicate respect; 2) Ask appropriate questions to demonstrate interest and find out more; and 3) Focus on what partners are saying and provide positive encouragement (e.g., Light et al., 2007). The strategy also cautions participants, "Don't CRY": 1) Don't criticize communication partners; 2) Don't react hastily without considering the consequences; and 3) Don't "yakkity yak" (i.e., talk excessively) about yourself. The LAF, Don't CRY strategy was taught to adults who used AAC using the strategy instruction model, implemented online. All of the participants successfully acquired the active listening skills and later applied the skills successfully to build positive relationships with adolescents who also used AAC within an online mentoring program. All of the adolescents indicated that they were very satisfied with their mentors and their interactions (Light et al., 2007).

## Teach Use of Partner-Focused Questions

One of the most powerful sociorelational skills is the use of partner-focused questions, that is, asking people about themselves and their interests. Unfortunately, AAC instruction often focuses primarily on teaching people to make requests for objects and activities, answer questions, and

Intervention to Build Communicative Competence

make comments, but not on teaching them to ask questions about their conversational partners' thoughts, feelings, and experiences (Blackstone &amp; Wilkins, 2009; Light et al., 2003). Partner-focused questions demonstrate an interest in the communication partner, encouraging interaction.

Randy Kitch, a disability rights activist who relies on AAC, highlighted the importance of partner-focused questions in this e-mail to an adolescent who also relied on AAC and was having difficulty making friends at school:

So you think you don't have any friends at school? Do you ask other students questions about themselves, about the homework assignments, and school activities? Sometimes you need to focus on them first before they will focus on you. (Light et al., 2003, p. 376)

There are a wide range of potential partner-focused questions, including How was your weekend?, What do you think?, What's up?, What do you have planned for tonight?, and How was your vacation? Light, Binger, Agate, and Ramsay (1999) used strategy instruction successfully to teach the generalized use of partner-focused questions to individuals who relied on AAC who ranged in age from 10 to 44 years. The participants and their communication partners all reported that their interactions were more enjoyable and lasted longer after intervention. Teaching the use of partner-focused questions may be particularly effective with individuals who use AAC who are still developing linguistic competencies. By asking partner-focused questions, they are able to engage actively in social interactions with minimal linguistic demands because they control the topic of the conversation; it is the partners who need to generate responses to questions.

Use of partner-focused questions improved social life for a young man named Chuck once these questions were programmed into his AAC technology. Chuck was 26 years old and had an intellectual disability. He lived in a group home and worked at the local grocery store bagging groceries. He had very limited speech. He was very excited to receive AAC technology with speech output and learned to use it effectively at work to greet customers and ask if they wanted "paper or plastic bags?" His speech-language pathologist programmed vocabulary into his AAC technology so that he could request preferred objects and activities, but she did not include any partner-focused questions. When Chuck came home from work, the group home staff typically put his AAC device away. They saw no need for him to use it as he was able to independently fulfill his needs and wants. Chuck was lonely; he had limited social interactions with others. We worked with Chuck's speech-language pathologist to add a range of partner-focused questions to his technology and taught him how to use them. When he got home from work, Chuck used his AAC technology to ask the group home staff and other residents about their interests and experiences. Everyone enjoyed interacting with Chuck when he asked partner-focused questions; no one put his AAC technology away.

A specific form of a partner-focused question that can be used to extend conversations is the response-recode strategy (Farrier, Yorkston, Marriner, &amp; Beukelman, 1985). When people respond to questions and then ask related questions in return (e.g., I'm going away for spring break. What are you doing?), they are using response-recodes. O'Keefe and Dattilo (1992) used explicit instruction to teach the response-recode

strategy successfully to three adults with developmental disabilities in conversations. Family members and caregivers reported lasting changes in the participants' social interactions and agreed that the skill was “fundamental to true conversational involvement” (O'Keefe & Dattilo, 1992, p. 231).

### Teach How to Give Feedback and Handle Conflict

Unfortunately, not all social relationships are positive all of the time. Sometimes things do not go as expected, and individuals who use AAC need to be able to provide feedback and handle conflict. Failure to handle problem situations effectively may have significant negative impacts, including personal feelings of frustration and anger, as well as poor care, health, and well-being.

Jon Feucht described the frustrations he experienced working with his personal care attendants and the process of learning to provide feedback and resolve conflicts:

> “I had a lot of problems when I first started working with attendants. The biggest problem was communication. I just didn't know how to get my point across without getting mad. Over time, I tried different techniques of getting my point across. I kept ideas that worked and abandoned those that failed.” (Feucht, 2001, p. 30)

Although some individuals learn how to provide feedback through trial and error, many would benefit from intervention to expedite their learning. Collier and Self (2010) suggest the following strategy to support individuals who use AAC in learning how to provide feedback and resolve conflict:

State what happened.Explain the impact using “I statements.”Wait and listen.Describe a concrete step(s) to resolve the problem.

Ariel used this strategy effectively to address an ongoing problem with a personal care attendant that affected her daily life and ability to work. Ariel is an artist; she sells her paintings at a local farmers' market and on Etsy. She has severe cerebral palsy and uses a powered wheelchair for mobility. She lives independently. She has only limited use of her hands and requires support from personal care attendants for all activities of daily living. One of her attendants had repeatedly shown up for work late, leaving Ariel stranded in bed. When her attendant finally showed up, Ariel implemented the strategy that she had learned to provide constructive feedback. First, she used her AAC technology to state what had happened and explain the impact: “You were more than an hour late for work today. When you are late, I feel angry and frustrated. I cannot get out of bed, eat, drink, or go to the bathroom. I cannot paint. If I do not paint, I cannot sell my paintings to earn a living.” She then waited and listened to her attendant's response. Then she presented some concrete steps to solve the problem: “Please make sure that you leave for work at least 20 minutes earlier in the morning. I know that the traffic is bad. That will give you more time for your commute. If something happens and you are going to be late, please phone to let me know right away. If you will be more than one hour late, please phone your agency to arrange a replacement.”

Learning strategies to provide feedback to others may not only improve interpersonal relationships and overall quality of life, but may also empower individuals

Intervention to Build Communicative Competence

who use AAC. These are not just important skills in daily living, but also in employment contexts.

As these interventions suggest, in many ways the development of sociorelational skills is more complex than learning linguistic or operational skills. In the case of sociorelational skills, individuals need to learn to use the target skills themselves while all the time monitoring their communication partners and adjusting skills accordingly based on their partners' responses. As a result, they may require extended practice with a wide range of partners in a variety of situations to develop competence in the sociorelational domain.

# STRATEGIC SKILLS

Despite intervention that targets skills in the linguistic, operational, and social domains, many individuals with complex communication needs still confront limitations in their communicative competence because of motor, sensory, cognitive, and/or linguistic impairments, substantial environmental barriers confronted in society, and the nature of communication via AAC. In these cases, they must develop coping strategies to bypass these limitations and allow them to make the best of what they do know and can do (Light, 1989; Light &amp; McNaughton, 2014). These compensatory strategies may be temporary, used for a time while the individual learns new linguistic, operational, and/or social skills; or the compensatory strategies may be required long term in situations where limitations in the linguistic, operational, and/or social domains cannot be remediated (Light, 1989). Often the most effective strategies grow out of the ingenuity and resourcefulness of individuals who rely on AAC. Mirenda and Bopp (2003) drew on the research and personal experiences of individuals who use AAC and developed a comprehensive review of strategies that might be used to overcome limitations in linguistic, operational, or social competence. Table 11.5

Table 11.5. Examples of strategies to overcome language, operational, and social challenges

|  Domain | Examples of knowledge, judgment, and skills required  |
| --- | --- |
|  Use compensatory strategies to bypass limitations in the linguistic domain | ·Ask partner to write/type or point to symbols to augment spoken input and bypass comprehension difficulties ·Use mementos to bypass vocabulary limitations and establish the topic ·Ask communication partner to provide choices to overcome vocabulary limitations ·Alert the partner that necessary vocabulary is not available ·Ask the partner to guess and provide clues to bypass vocabulary limitations  |
|  Use compensatory strategies to bypass limitations in the operational domain | ·Use telegraphic messages to enhance rate of communication ·Ask partner to predict as message is spelled to reduce fatigue and enhance rate of communication ·Have partner assist in locating appropriate page to help with navigational demands ·Prepare messages in advance to reduce partner waiting time  |
|  Use compensatory strategies to bypass limitations in the social domain | ·Use an introduction strategy to teach the partner what to do ·Use humor to maintain a positive rapport and put the partner at ease ·Use regulatory phrases to manage the interaction ·Use effective repair strategies as required to resolve communication breakdowns ·Utilize digital communication media to bypass demands of face-to-face interactions and increase social network  |

AAC Interventions for Individuals with Developmental Disabilities

provides examples of strategies used by individuals who require AAC to overcome linguistic, operational, and social limitations.

## Intervention to Build Strategic Competence

The research to date has investigated the effects of interventions that target strategic skills, such as introduction strategies, humor, regulatory phrases, and clarification strategies to repair communication breakdowns.

**Teach Introduction Strategies** Most people without disabilities have had no prior experience or training in how to interact with individuals who use AAC. They may be uncertain what to do. It may be important for individuals who rely on AAC to learn to use an introduction strategy when they meet someone new (Light &amp; Binger, 1998). An introduction strategy includes two key components: 1) information about the person's means of communication and 2) information about what the communication partner can do to facilitate the interaction (Light &amp; Binger, 1998). In some situations, the individual may want to also add some information about his or her disability, but this is not always necessary or appropriate. The key is to let the new communication partner know what to expect and how to interact.

Maureen is a 44-year-old woman with cerebral palsy who leads a very active life. She uses AAC technology to communicate and frequently encounters new communication partners in the community (e.g., stores, restaurants, sporting events) as well as at her job. She developed the following introduction strategy that she uses to let these new partners know what to expect and what to do when they interact with her.

HI. I UNDERSTAND WHAT IS SAID TO ME. I USE THIS COMPUTER TO COMMUNICATE; I JUST TYPE IN MY MESSAGE AND THE COMPUTER SPEAKS IT OUT. YOU CAN READ THE SCREEN IF YOU DO NOT UNDERSTAND. PLEASE WAIT PATIENTLY WHILE I AM TYPING ON THE COMPUTER. WHEN I SEND YOU A MESSAGE, CHECK WITH ME TO MAKE SURE YOU UNDERSTOOD CORRECTLY. I NOD MY HEAD TO SAY "YES" AND SHAKE MY HEAD TO SAY "NO." IF YOU DO NOT UNDERSTAND, PLEASE LET ME KNOW. THANKS! (Light &amp; Binger, 1998, p. 104)

Light and Binger (1998) utilized strategy instruction to teach individuals (ages 12–44 years) with a range of disabilities to use an introduction strategy successfully when encountering someone new. People perceived these individuals to be more competent communicators when they used an introduction strategy than when they did not. There may be some specific messages that are especially helpful as introduction strategies. For example, several studies have demonstrated the importance of a brief introductory message, called a *floorholder*, to warn communication partners that message construction may take longer than usual, in both face-to-face and telephone interactions (Bedrosian, Hoag, &amp; McCoy, 2003; Hanson &amp; Sundheimer, 2009).

Collier and Diamanti (2007) recommended that individuals who use AAC develop a personal communication passport or communication access card to explain how they communicate and what their communication partners should do. They provided the following advice for developing communication access cards: 1) Keep the instructions short and simple; 2) Focus on telling people what you want them to do when communicating with you; 3) Keep it real (e.g., a waiter in a restaurant needs to

know how to communicate to take your order; he or she does not need to know how to communicate with you on the phone or in other situations); 4) Have different access cards for different types of situations.

### Teach Use of Humor

Many communication partners feel uncomfortable when first interacting with someone who uses AAC. Some individuals who use AAC have a keen sense of humor, and they may use humor effectively to initiate interactions with others and put them at ease. Laughter decreases stress and also triggers the release of endorphins that make people feel good. Using humor to initiate an interaction may be as simple as sharing a joke card (with the riddle on one side and the answer on the other), or it may involve more complex storytelling using AAC technology with speech output. In planning these interventions, the AAC team should consider the linguistic and operational demands of the humor. Sometimes humor relies on exaggerated physical actions—what we call slapstick humor. In other cases, humor relies on inference and plays on words. Often humor relies on subtle timing that may be difficult for some individuals with disabilities. It is important that individuals who rely on AAC are actively involved in the selection of approaches that utilize humor and that humor is introduced in a way that is developmentally appropriate so that it is understood by the participants. It is also important that humor is introduced in a way that is respectful and is likely to be understood and interpreted positively by communication partners. Finally, it is important to remember that some people are funny and others are more serious. Not every person who uses AAC may want to use humor to initiate interactions. The intervention will be most effective if it is a good fit with the personality of the individual and if it is expected to be well received within the target environment.

Binh, who was attending college as a full-time student, often used humor to put others at ease. Binh was studying horticulture, with a focus on the propagation of orchids. He had cerebral palsy and relied on speech to communicate with familiar partners, but his speech was difficult for unfamiliar people to understand. He was having problems communicating in his classes with his professors and peers. He referred himself to the university clinic for an AAC assessment. The graduate students who were scheduled to conduct the assessment were very nervous as it was their first AAC assessment. Binh had excellent strategic competence. He recognized that they were nervous with him and used humor to put them at ease. He turned to them and said, “Would you like to see my high-tech system?” The graduate students indicated “yes,” eager to see the latest AAC technology. Binh then pulled out a battered old alphabet board and motioned to it: “Ta da!” The graduate students dissolved into laughter, immediately put at ease by Binh's keen sense of humor.

### Teach Use of Regulatory Phrases

Introduction strategies are intended to be used when first meeting unfamiliar partners; however, individuals who require AAC may also need to learn to use regulatory phrases to manage and control aspects of communication with familiar and unfamiliar partners during interactions. Often these regulatory phrases are related to the operation of AAC systems. Such phrases might provide directions to the communication partner with regard to positioning (e.g. can you please come over here where i can see you?); effective use of the AAC system (e.g. please say each letter as i point to it); obtaining and securing

AAC Interventions for Individuals with Developmental Disabilities

conversational turns (e.g., I HAVE SOMETHING TO SAY); or signaling the need to repair a communication breakdown (e.g., WAIT, THAT'S NOT WHAT I MEANT). Buzolich and Lunger (1995) reported on a case study in which an adolescent who relied on AAC was taught to use a variety of regulatory phrases when interacting with her classmates. After the instruction that utilized role playing and conversational coaching with peers, she was able to initiate more topics and use a wider variety of conversational strategies.

## Teach Use of Conversational Repairs

Even when introduction strategies and regulatory phrases are used, individuals may still encounter communication breakdowns. A key element of strategic competence is the use of repair strategies to resolve these breakdowns. Communication breakdowns may occur because of difficulties related to message intelligibility, conversational timing, partners' unfamiliarity with AAC, and numerous other factors (Brady &amp; Halle, 2002; Snell, Chen, Allaire, &amp; Park, 2008). The need for a repair strategy may be signaled explicitly when the communication partner requests clarification (e.g., What?, Pardon me?), or it may be indicated implicitly when the communication partner shows uncertainty, responds in a vague, noncommittal manner (e.g., by changing the topic, feigning understanding), or does not respond at all (Bedrosian et al., 2003; Brady &amp; Halle, 2002).

There are two basic types of repair strategies: repetitions and modifications (Halle, Brady, &amp; Drasgow, 2004). Repetition involves the individual communicating the same message again, using the same modality. Sometimes repetition is effective if the partner truly did not hear or see the initial communication. However, if the partner heard and/or saw the message and did not understand, simply repeating the message is usually not an effective repair strategy. In these cases, it is important for the individual to modify the communication in some way through an addition, reduction, or substitution. Additions involve adding a new element to the original message (e.g., signing JUICE again while also pointing to a glass), whereas reductions involve deleting an element (e.g., pointing emphatically to a single symbol for HELP rather than to the symbols I + WANT + HELP). Substitutions involve using a completely different message than the original one (e.g., activating AAC technology to say LEAVE ME ALONE rather than using speech approximations to say, "Can I please have some time to myself?").

Given the risk for communication breakdowns, many individuals who use AAC benefit from intervention that targets clarification or repair strategies. It can be challenging to teach repair strategies during actual communication breakdowns in naturally occurring interactions because it is difficult for clinicians to prompt appropriate repair strategies if they do not know what the individual is trying to communicate (Light &amp; Binger, 1998). It is not advisable to feign breakdowns in interactions where the communication partner has actually understood the message, as this provides the individual who uses AAC with false feedback about the effectiveness of the communication. Instead intervention may be most effective if it follows procedures such as these:

1. The clinician and the individual who uses AAC share knowledge of the topic (e.g., a movie or TV show they have both seen, a book they have read together, a magazine they have shared).
2. The individual who uses AAC then interacts with a communication partner who does not have the same shared experience.

3. The partner provides honest feedback when he or she does or does not understand the individual who uses AAC.
4. When communication breakdowns occur, the clinician uses coaching or prompting to support the individual who uses AAC in repairing the communication successfully using either repetition or modifications.

Teaching at least two forms of repair strategies is important so that if the first is unsuccessful, the person has another alternative option (Halle et al. 2004). All of the repair strategies targeted should be both socially appropriate and sufficiently transparent to communication partners to communicate the intended message.

Use of introduction strategies, conversational repair strategies, and regulatory phrases are just a few examples of some of the skills in the strategic domain that individuals who use AAC may need to learn to overcome intrinsic limitations in linguistic, operational, or social skills or extrinsic limitations from policy, practice, attitude, knowledge, or skill barriers from communication partners.

## Competence in Digital Communication

So far in this chapter we have focused on the development of communicative competence in face-to-face interactions. These interactions obviously play a critical role in daily life in families, at school, at work, in medical settings, and in the community. However, in today's society, communication extends well beyond face-to-face interactions to written communication and digital communication (e.g. texting, e-mail, social media; McNaughton & Light, 2013; Shane, Blackstone, Vanderheiden, Williams, & DeRuyter, 2012). Chapter 12 discusses intervention to teach literacy skills to individuals with complex communication needs so that they develop communicative competence in written communication. In this section, we briefly consider the need to build communicative competence in digital communication (e.g. e-mail, Facebook, Twitter, SnapChat, Instagram).

Digital communication has taken on an increasingly important role in recent years as media to enrich social interaction, but also for information exchange, education, medical care, employment, e-commerce, and activities of daily living, to name just a few purposes. Digital communication may take on even greater importance for individuals who use AAC given the challenges that they often encounter in face-to-face interactions; these media may increase opportunities for self-determination and self-representation while also enhancing friendships (e.g. Hynan, Goldbart, & Murray, 2015; Hynan, Murray, & Goldbart, 2014).

An adult with cerebral palsy who relies on AAC described the benefits of digital communication media as follows: “Face-to-face conversation is difficult using AAC because we get ignored or walked passed. Social media can help overcome this.” (Caron & Light, 2016, p. 30)

To use digital communication effectively, individuals with complex communication skills need to learn a range of new linguistic, operational, social, and strategic skills. They must have functional literacy skills to send and receive messages on many digital communication platforms. They may need to learn a new set of vocabulary (e.g. acronyms such as LOL -- laughing out loud; YOLO -- you only live once) and new syntactic rules (e.g. the average Tweet is around 25--35 characters with an upper limit

AAC Interventions for Individuals with Developmental Disabilities

of 280 characters), as well as a new set of sociolinguistic norms (e.g., knowing with whom to communicate, about what, when, where, in what form, and for what purposes to use digital communication; Light &amp; McNaughton, 2014). Furthermore, these social norms vary across digital platforms. Because digital communication is often asynchronous, individuals who use AAC must learn the rules for using each of these media without the benefit of immediate, visible, partner feedback.

With increased use of digital communication platforms, individuals with complex communication needs also face increased operational demands (Grace, Rhagavendra, Newman, Wood, &amp; Connell, 2014). Each of the digital communication tools is designed with different representations, organizations, and layouts of information as well as different access techniques; and each of these different designs imposes different learning demands (Light &amp; McNaughton, 2014). Typically these tools are not well integrated, so individuals who use AAC must also learn to navigate between apps or tools as required (Caron &amp; Light, 2016). Interestingly, many digital communication platforms (e.g., FaceBook, SnapChat, Instagram) also support extensive use of visual images (e.g., photos, videos) for expression. The use of visual images to supplement communication is definitely of benefit to many individuals who use AAC because these images can augment communication and reduce the burden on language and literacy skills. However, the use of digital images also increases operational demands, as individuals may need to learn to capture and post photos and videos as well as post comments or captions. Given the importance of digital communication and the constellation of skills required to use these media effectively, it is not surprising that adults with cerebral palsy have recommended that AAC teams prepare individuals who use AAC for effective digital communication (Caron &amp; Light, 2016). Ultimately, AAC teams should provide intervention to maximize the communicative competence of individuals who use AAC across a broad array of media—face-to-face interactions, digital communication, and written communication.

## PSYCHOSOCIAL FACTORS THAT SUPPORT COMMUNICATIVE COMPETENCE

The attainment of communicative competence, in face-to-face, digital, and written communication media, by individuals who rely on AAC is impacted not just by linguistic, operational, social, and strategic competence, but also by a range of psychosocial factors, including motivation, attitude, confidence, and resilience (Light, 2003). Individuals with complex communication needs often face substantial barriers in developing communicative competence. It is these psychosocial factors that determine whether they are motivated to learn the necessary skills, have the positive attitude required to do so, demonstrate the confidence to try (knowing that they may fail sometimes), and apply the resilience to bounce back and try again in the face of challenges (Light &amp; McNaughton, 2014).

## Motivation

Motivation is critical to the development of communicative competence, for it impacts the individual's desire or drive to communicate with others in daily situations (Light, 2003). Communication via AAC is challenging. When individuals are motivated, they are more likely to tackle the demands of communication via AAC; when motivation is low, they may be overwhelmed by these demands and may forfeit communication opportunities (Clarke, McConachie, Price, &amp; Wood, 2001).

Intervention to Build Communicative Competence

Jan Staehely, who uses AAC to support her communication, described the challenge of maintaining motivation when she did not have effective means to communicate:

I had become so used to not being able to say something in depth to a person that I started to believe that I was a person who didn't have much to tell people. . . . I fooled myself into thinking that I didn't have anything to say. (Staehely, 2000, p. 9)

People are most apt to be motivated when they believe that something is worth doing and that it is achievable. To build motivation, AAC intervention should 1) focus on meaningful communication opportunities that are truly valued by the individual and family, and 2) provide effective supports to ensure that the individual experiences success in attaining these goals.

## Attitude

In addition to motivation, communicative competence will also be determined, at least in part, by the attitudes of individuals with complex communication needs (and those of their families). Individuals are more apt to use AAC when they have positive attitudes toward these communication supports. Attitudes may be impacted by the individual's age, personality, skills, needs, prior experiences, and expectations, as well as the prior experiences and expectations of family and communication partners and the demands within the communication environment (Lasker &amp; Bedrosian, 2000). Attitudes are also impacted by factors related to AAC (e.g., learning demands, appearance, functionality). When individuals and their families reject AAC, the first step should always be to examine the relevance and functionality of the AAC system. AAC supports should always reflect the needs and priorities of the individual with complex communication needs and the family.

Rob Rummel-Hudson has a daughter, Schuyler, who requires AAC. He described the effect of different AAC systems on his daughter's attitude toward AAC and, as a result, her willingness or unwillingness to utilize AAC to support her communication:

Her enthusiasm [with her new AAC technology] was perhaps the most significant development, perhaps more important than whether or not she intuitively "got it." She did, but even better, she was fascinated by the device. She used it for everything. . . . We knew that if a speech prosthesis was going to work for her, it was going to be because she took the initiative to make it happen, the same way she came to embrace sign language and, conversely, the way she completely rejected the picture identification system that every one of her schools had tried to get her to use . . . My pity went out to the person who tried to make Schuyler do something she didn't want to do, or who tried to keep her from doing something she liked. (Rummel-Hudson, 2008, p. 223).

The way that the team introduces AAC may impact strongly the attitudes of individuals with complex communication needs and their families. Sometimes, AAC is introduced as a last resort, a method of communication to be used because the individual has "failed" to develop speech. It is more appropriate and effective to introduce AAC as what it is—a means to enhance communication effectiveness and support participation.

## Confidence

Motivation impacts the individual's drive to communicate. Attitudes toward AAC impact willingness to use AAC to communicate. However, it is confidence that actually determines the individual's propensity to use AAC in any given situation

(Light & McNaughton, 2014). Using AAC to meet communication needs requires individuals to try techniques that are new and unfamiliar to them, their communication partners, and society generally. Often they must make this leap without having experienced models of others who successfully communicate using AAC (Ballin et al. 2009). Seeing or interacting with others who use AAC who have attained communicative competence may serve as a critical support in building communicative confidence (Ballin, Balandin, & Stancliffe, 2012).

Rick Creech (1995), who was a pioneer in his use of AAC in both postsecondary settings and the workplace, explained:

> Until we have seen a fluent interactive, augmented speaker who shares our physical circumstances, there may have been little in our personal experience to indicate that we, ourselves, would someday actually ‘talk'. (p. 12)

## Resilience

Confidence may determine the individual's propensity to attempt to communicate, but it is resilience that influences whether or not the individual perseveres despite the many challenges and potential failures that may be encountered. Resilience refers to the individual's capacity to “prevent, minimize, or overcome the damaging effects of adversity” (Grotberg, 1995, p. 7). It is inevitable that individuals with complex communication needs will confront failure at times in their attempts to communicate successfully. Communication failures provide important opportunities for learning and may ultimately fuel subsequent success, but only if the individual is resilient enough to move on and try again. Resilience may be bolstered by protective factors, including both individual resources (e.g. problem-solving skills, self-esteem, optimism, faith) and environmental factors (e.g. encouragement and support from family, mentors, peers, or others; Luthar, Cicchetti, & Becker, 2000; Masten, 2001). Individuals with more protective factors are more likely to demonstrate resilience in the face of communication failures and are more apt to continue to work toward building communicative competence in the face of adversity (Dickerson, Stone, Panchura, & Usiak, 2002; Smith & Murray, 2011).

The following e-mail was sent by an adolescent with cerebral palsy who used AAC who was having trouble making friends at school: “The other kids at school are rude. . . . I mean I don't have any friends in school. They just freak out about my chair. . . . I'm too tired with everyone's reactions. . . . I gave up with my peers.”

An adult mentor who also had cerebral palsy and used AAC responded as follows, encouraging resilience: “You can't give up on your peers because you need to educate them. Get real . . . you're only 16 and they are too . . . They are human. Humans need someone else to teach them that people with disabilities are just like anyone else. I went through the same thing you are going through. . . . Giving up is the easy way out. Of course, it's your decision.” (Light, McNaughton, Krezman, & Williams, 2002)

## Intervention to Build Positive Psychosocial Factors

Given the impact of motivation, attitude, confidence, and resilience on the development of communicative competence, AAC teams should consider interventions to

Intervention to Build Communicative Competence

address these factors. One important intervention goal to target is problem-solving skills. Several studies have evaluated the effects of online instruction utilizing principles of strategy instruction to teach a problem-solving strategy, specifically the DO IT! strategy. The DO IT! strategy includes the following steps to support effective problem solving: 1) Describe the problem, 2) Outline potential ways to solve the problem, 3) Identify the best solution, 4) Take action, and 5) Celebrate success! The adults and adolescents with complex communication needs who participated in the online instruction acquired the problem-solving strategy, generalized use to actual interactions, and reported satisfaction applying the strategy in their daily lives (Light et al., 2007; McCarthy, Light, &amp; McNaughton, 2007).

Not all interventions to address psychosocial factors follow traditional models of service delivery by professionals. Mentor programs may be a powerful way to build motivation, positive attitudes, confidence, and resilience. It has been said that a mentor provides a brain to pick, a shoulder to cry on, and a kick in the pants. There are a number of examples of successful mentoring programs for individuals who rely on AAC (e.g., Ballin et al., 2012; Cohen &amp; Light, 2000; Grace, Rhagavendra, McMillan, &amp; Gunson, 2019; Light et al., 2007). These programs have linked adolescents or younger individuals who rely on AAC with adult mentors who also use AAC, often via digital communication media (e.g., e-mail, FaceBook, Skype). Results suggest that mentoring by adults who are successful using AAC may be effective in easing transitions, solving problems, and building confidence and resilience for younger individuals who require AAC.

Michael Williams (1996), who is himself an expert communicator via AAC, described the importance of mentoring:

Falling in love, starting a new school, starting a new job, changing communities or homes, mastering a skill, learning a new piece of assistive technology—all are easier and more fun if the experience can be shared with and guided by someone who has 'been there'. (p. 1)

Light and colleagues (2007) found that mentors and protégés discussed a wide range of challenges within the mentoring program, including attitude barriers in society, limitations of AAC technologies, funding delays, technology breakdowns, gaps in the service delivery system, lack of knowledgeable service providers, low expectations, lack of meaningful roles, stereotypes, lack of preparation for independence, difficulty finding appropriate personal care attendants or educational assistants, family stresses and supports, challenges making friends and building close relationships, social isolation, and frustrations about their disabilities. Mentoring programs seem to benefit not only the protégés, but also their mentors (Light et al., 2007).

Michael Williams (1996) highlighted the benefits of mentoring, not just for protégés who receive support and encouragement, but also for mentors who have the opportunity to make a positive contribution:

As we master an area of our lives, it is important to go back and find someone else who would like to master the same thing. When you teach someone what you know, there are now two of you blazing the trail rather than you by yourself. (p. 4)

AAC Interventions for Individuals with Developmental Disabilities

# CONCLUSIONS

The development of communicative competence is critically important for individuals who use AAC to ensure their effective participation in all aspects of society, including family life, education, employment, health care, and community activities. The development of communicative competence is a complex process that rests on knowledge, judgment, and skills in four interrelated domains—linguistic, operational, social, and strategic. Furthermore, the development of communicative competence is affected by a range of psychosocial factors, including motivation, attitude, confidence, and resilience.

Individuals with complex communication needs face significant challenges in developing communicative competence due to intrinsic factors (e.g., motor, sensory, cognitive, linguistic skills) as well as environmental barriers (e.g., policy, practice, attitude, knowledge, skill barriers) and AAC system constraints. Despite these challenges, there are numerous examples of individuals with developmental disabilities who use AAC who have developed communicative competence, are self-determined, and are highly successful participants in a wide range of educational, vocational, and community activities (see the videos of individuals who use AAC talking about their experiences at the online AAC Learning Center). Research clearly demonstrates that, with effective intervention, individuals who use AAC are able to build a wide array of linguistic, operational, social, and strategic skills as well as motivation, positive attitude, confidence, and resilience. It is incumbent upon AAC teams to work with individuals who use AAC and their families to set appropriate goals to further communicative competence, design evidence-based intervention to teach these skills, and collect data (both performance data and consumer satisfaction data) on a regular basis to ensure the effectiveness of the intervention. It is also critical for these teams to advocate with individuals who use AAC and their families to reduce policy, practice, attitude, knowledge, and skill barriers to ensure that they have meaningful opportunities to participate fully in society.

11.1. What is communicative competence? Individuals who require AAC need to develop knowledge, judgment, and skills in four interrelated domains to build communicative competence. What are these domains?

11.2. What language skills do individuals who require AAC need to develop? What challenges do they face in developing these skills? What interventions might be used to build semantic skills? What interventions might be used to teach morphosyntactic skills?
