The following account illustrates how a learner might be introduced to a reading comprehension strategy and then given opportunities to practice applying it. Gareth, a 5-year-old boy with severe cerebral palsy, learned to read before he started kindergarten. He was introduced to basic reading comprehension strategies early in his literacy instruction. As he read each page or section of a story independently, he stopped to answer questions to ensure comprehension before he went on to read the next section. We used multiple-choice questions (with carefully selected response options) so that Gareth could

quickly and easily indicate his answer. For example, when reading a book about Clifford the dog, Gareth first read the text independently. Then he answered multiple-choice questions such as the following:

Why will Clifford win?

The dogs will raceClifford is big and fastClifford is redClifford will win

This technique provided a quick check of Gareth's comprehension without making undue demands that would result in fatigue. This question-answering strategy also mirrored the demands that Gareth would face later on in many standardized tests. Questions that required both basic factual comprehension and inference skills could be quickly developed by Gareth's teacher or aide during the reading activity, thus minimizing demands for material preparation. Read more about Gareth and see videos of his use of this strategy in the Reading Comprehension section of the web site, Literacy Instruction for Individuals with Autism, Cerebral Palsy, Down Syndrome and Other Disabilities. (Light & McNaughton, 2019)

### Intervention to Build More Advanced Writing Skills

As individuals progress through school and consider future employment, they face increased writing demands. In third grade and thereafter, writing is the most common method used to communicate information and assess an individual's knowledge and learning. Writing not only allows individuals to convey information to others (e.g. tell stories, explain events, express opinions, persuade others) but also provides a mechanism to support an individual's learning and understanding. As individuals write about a topic, they extend and deepen their knowledge (Graham & Perin, 2007). As the educational and vocational writing demands increase, individuals with complex communication needs must be able to generate increasingly longer texts for a variety of purposes, using more complex vocabulary and sentence structures (Foley & Wolter, 2010). Meeting these writing demands requires well-developed knowledge and skills in 1) the conventions of writing, including spelling, punctuation, capitalization, and text production/keyboarding; and 2) the use of writing strategies to plan, write, and edit texts effectively across genres (e.g. narrative, expository, persuasive; Light & McNaughton, 2009b).

Although there are examples of individuals with complex communication needs who have well-developed writing skills (e.g. Koppenhaver et al. 1991), many individuals who rely on AAC demonstrate difficulties with written communication. For example, Kelford Smith, Thurston, Light, Parnes, and O'Keefe (1989) investigated the written communication skills of six individuals (ages 13--22 years) who had cerebral palsy and relied on AAC. They reported that 1) the participants produced a limited amount of written communication in a one-week period; 2) the participants required significant amounts of time to plan, generate, and revise written texts; 3) the participants demonstrated difficulties with morphology; and 4) all but one participant demonstrated difficulties with sentence structures. Focused intervention is required to build advanced writing skills with individuals with complex communication needs.

Literacy Intervention for Individuals with Complex Communication Needs

This intervention should focus on instruction in the conventions of writing as well as instruction in the use of writing strategies.

## Building Knowledge and Skills in Writing Conventions

To produce competent, intelligible written texts, individuals who rely on AAC need to develop skills in spelling (both regular and irregular words) as well as knowledge of the conventions of writing, such as capitalization, punctuation, and paragraphing. Instruction in these skills should be ongoing, starting in the early stages of learning conventional literacy skills. As individuals acquire basic skills, the focus of instruction turns to the development of more complex spelling skills (e.g., long vowel patterns, multisyllabic words with prefixes and suffixes, homonyms) and word study skills (e.g., derivations of words, word meanings), as well as the acquisition of more advanced writing conventions (e.g., use of punctuation, paragraphs). As noted earlier, spelling skills rely heavily on phonological awareness skills and knowledge of letter-sound correspondences. Some individuals with severe speech impairments have difficulty applying their phonological awareness skills to spell words (Hart, Scherz, Apel, &amp; Hodson, 2007); however, there is evidence that individuals who rely on AAC benefit from explicit instruction in spelling (McNaughton &amp; Tawney, 1993; Schlosser, Blischak, Belfiore, Bartley, &amp; Barnett, 1998). In addition, speech output (auditory feedback) has been found to have a positive effect on the spelling performance of both individuals with autism spectrum disorder (Blischak &amp; Schlosser, 2003) and individuals with cerebral palsy (McCarthy et al., 2015), leading the researchers to conclude that speech output should be considered as a support for writing instruction.

Along with the acquisition of more advanced skills in spelling and writing conventions, instruction should also focus on the development of fluency with writing conventions (e.g., spelling skills, punctuation, handwriting, keyboarding, other operational skills). If these skills remain effortful for individuals with complex communication needs, they will have few cognitive resources available to support the actual writing process (i.e., the planning, drafting, and revising of written texts); instead, all of their attention and cognitive resources will be consumed by the conventions of spelling and selecting/producing letters to create written text. As noted earlier, fluency is built through practice. As these skills become more automatic, individuals who rely on AAC will be able to devote their attention and cognitive resources to the content of the writing process rather than the mechanics. Although all individuals benefit from numerous opportunities to produce written texts, it should be noted that for many individuals with complex communication needs—especially those with significant motor, sensory/perceptual, and/or cognitive impairments—the process of producing written text can be especially challenging. As noted by Foley and Wolter (2010), these writers may fatigue easily and may have difficulty sustaining their attention to the writing task. For individuals who have significant difficulty producing text, assistive technologies may be required to provide scaffolding supports, enhance rate, and/or provide spelling and writing aids (see the section on assistive technologies for further discussion).

## Learning to Use Writing Strategies

Skilled writing extends well beyond the simple mechanics of producing written text. To successfully produce longer, more complex texts, individuals must engage in an iterative writing process that includes reflection, production, and interpretation (Hayes, 2000). First, individuals plan and organize the text by reflecting on their ideas and experiences, as well as their goal or

AAC Interventions for Individuals with Developmental Disabilities

purpose; then they translate their thoughts into written language and produce the text (by handwriting or keyboarding); and, finally, they review what they have written, reflect on their goal, and then revise accordingly. As writing demands increase, learning to make use of writing strategies can result in positive gains in writing skills for middle- and high school students with and without disabilities (Graham &amp; Perin, 2007). Typically, writing strategies provide multistep procedures to support each stage of the writing process—planning, writing the text, and editing (see Table 12.7 for examples of writing strategies at each of the stages). Like reading comprehension strategies, these types of writing strategies can be taught using a cognitive strategy instruction model (Deshler &amp; Schumaker, 2006; Santangelo, Harris, &amp; Graham, 2016).

In addition to writing strategies, research suggests that collaborative writing also benefits individuals both with and without disabilities (Graham &amp; Perin, 2007). Collaborative writing involves the development of "instructional arrangements whereby students work together to plan, draft," and revise their writing (Graham &amp; Perin, 2007, p. 42). Conferencing with peers can serve to encourage individuals to assume greater responsibility for learning, increase learning of cognitive strategies (specifically writing strategies), provide feedback and supports during the writing process, and increase motivation through social interactions with peers (NRP, 2000). Bedrosian et al. (2003) described a writing intervention for an adolescent with ASD who relied on AAC that involved instruction in writing strategies as well as collaborative writing with a speaking peer who had a mild cognitive impairment. Specifically, the intervention included the following components: 1) the provision of assistive technologies to support writing (i.e., an AAC device, story grammar map, storyboards with relevant vocabulary and story starters, and story writing software); 2) explicit instruction in writing strategies; 3) modeling of writing by the instructor and the peer; 4) prompting; and 5) written support provided by peer scaffolding. Results suggested that the intervention had a positive impact on the writing of the adolescent

with complex communication needs; his postintervention story was longer and demonstrated more complete story grammar than his preintervention story. These improvements were noted not only in the writing completed collaboratively but also in writing completed independently. Future research is required to further investigate the effects of intervention with individuals who rely on AAC across a wide range of written genres.

## Building Writing Skills for Social Purposes

It is important to note that, as individuals grow, writing not only assumes increased importance educationally and vocationally but also assumes increased importance socially. For example, people in the United States send and receive five times more texts per day compared to phone calls, and a typical teen sends and receives 30 texts per day (Lenhart, 2015). Using electronic communication media (e.g., texting, social networking sites such as Facebook, Snapchat) to build social relationships offers some unique advantages for individuals with complex communication needs because these media allow them to communicate at their own rate and may free them from the negative social attitudes that often limit face-to-face interactions. Written communication via these social media, although often shorter and less formal than writing for educational and vocational purposes, imposes its own set of demands (e.g., use of an appropriate voice for the audience, use of Internet slang such as LOL [laugh out loud], JK [just kidding], and IDK [I don't know]). If individuals with complex communication needs are to develop and negotiate successful social relationships, they will need to develop the written communication skills as well as the operational skills (e.g., skills to access and create web sites and blogs, skills to upload and download video and images) that allow them to participate effectively via these media as well (Caron &amp; Light, 2016, 2017; Grace, Raghavendra, Newman, Wood, &amp; Connell, 2014).

## ASSISTIVE TECHNOLOGIES TO SUPPORT LITERACY

In addition to requiring empirically based literacy instruction to develop reading and writing skills, individuals with complex communication needs may also require access to a wide range of assistive technologies to support literacy development, including assistive technologies that provide 1) access to communication, 2) access to literacy instruction, and 3) supports to compensate for reading and writing difficulties. Decisions about assistive technologies should be made by the AAC team in conjunction with the individual and family. Assistive technologies should be customized according to the needs and skills of the individual as well as the communication and literacy demands (see Chapter 8).

## Assistive Technologies for Communication

Individuals with complex communication needs require access to unaided and/or aided AAC to allow them to communicate and participate fully within literacy activities and instruction, from the early stage of emergent literacy development through the development of more advanced literacy skills. These AAC systems include those that support written communication (both conventional writing and early emergent writing activities) and telecommunication (e.g., texting, email), as well as systems that support face-to-face communication during literacy activities and instruction (e.g., choosing topics, talking about books, answering

comprehension questions, summarizing or retelling stories, asking questions about books, expressing opinions). AAC systems must include appropriate vocabulary to support communication during literacy activities and instruction. The communication demands of literacy activities and instruction differ from the functional communication demands in daily life. Individuals with complex communication needs require access to AAC systems that incorporate the more formal semantics, syntax, and morphology of written language, as well as the story grammar to structure narratives and build the language foundation that underpins literacy development (e.g. Bedrosian et al. 2003).

In addition to providing a means to support participation and discussion during literacy activities, AAC can also be used as an alternative mode to provide responses during literacy instruction. For example, Johnston et al. (2018) described adaptations that allowed individuals with complex communication needs to use signs or graphic AAC symbols to respond effectively and efficiently during instruction in sound blending, phoneme segmentation, decoding, and/or sight word recognition.

Recent software developments, including the transition to literacy (T2L) feature that is available on a range of AAC technologies, also support the acquisition of new skills—in this case, the transition from the use of graphic symbols to text (Light et al. 2014). The T2L feature can be used with either grid displays or VSDs. When an individual touches a symbol or hotspot programmed with the T2L feature, the associated written word appears dynamically on the screen, pauses for 3 seconds, and then fades away (see Figure 12.5). The T2L approach has been demonstrated to be effective in teaching sight word recognition with literacy learners with a wide range of ages (ages 3--46 years), and with various disabilities, including ASD, cerebral palsy, and Down syndrome (see Light, McNaughton, & Caron, 2019 for a summary of recent research and a list of AAC apps with the T2L feature).

## Assistive Technologies for Instruction

In addition to communication, technologies can also be used to further literacy instruction, either through the provision of instructional supports for literacy learning or in the delivery of computer-assisted instruction. For example, Spooner et al. (2015) investigated the use of an adapted text (Charlotte's Web), presented on a tablet computer, with five children with severe disabilities. The text was programmed to be read aloud using the text-to-speech function of the device, and communication supports (e.g. four pictures) for responding to partner questions were also available to the child. All five children demonstrated gains in their ability to respond to comprehension questions, and all five children reported that they enjoyed the reading activity.

Furthermore, there are numerous software applications for computer and mobile technologies (e.g. iPad) that provide instructional activities or games to supplement instruction in letter--sound correspondences, decoding, and encoding activities. Before implementing these applications, it is critical to ensure that they address appropriate instructional goals, use appropriate instructional methods and materials, and are accessible for individuals with complex communication needs who may have motor and/or sensory/perceptual impairments.

There are now a number of evidence-supported, computer-based instructional programs that include adaptations for people with complex communication needs. See the AAC Learning Center web site (McNaughton & Light, 2019) for more information.

# Assistive Technologies to Provide Support for Reading and Writing Difficulties

Finally, there are a wide range of technologies that provide the means for individuals with complex communication needs to bypass specific literacy demands or compensate for specific skill deficits. For example, spell checkers can be used to compensate for spelling difficulties, on-screen dictionaries can be used to compensate for vocabulary limitations, linguistic prediction can be used to enhance rate or compensate for spelling limitations, screen readers can be used to compensate for reading difficulties, and software applications with graphic organizers and concept maps can provide visual supports for the planning and organization stage of the writing process. E-books and digital texts also offer a number of advantages for individuals with complex communication needs: 1) text can be easily modified to accommodate visual impairments (e.g., larger font size, spacing, color contrast); 2) text can be read aloud as a support to reading skills; 3) definitions and explanations can be provided for new concepts to support vocabulary development; 4) links can be provided to additional support materials to build world knowledge; and 5) electronic coaching that prompts individuals to use reading comprehension strategies can be built into the software (Anderson-Inman &amp; Horney, 2007).

It is important to remember that simply providing assistive technology does not ensure successful literacy opportunities for individuals with complex communication needs. By reducing demands in one skill area, assistive technologies may actually increase demands in another. For example, access to texts through screen readers or other electronic media with speech output does not necessarily ensure successful comprehension of texts (Boone &amp; Higgins, 2007). The provision of these assistive technologies simply shifts the comprehension demands from the visual graphic modality of written text to the auditory modality of spoken text. The challenges of vocabulary knowledge, world knowledge, and comprehension monitoring remain, regardless of the modality of presentation. Depending on the individual, this shift in modality may or may not facilitate comprehension and learning. Thus, it is important to ensure that assistive technologies and electronic texts are designed and implemented in ways that minimize the processing demands and maximize motivation and learning for the individual (Anderson-Inman &amp; Horney, 2007). As with other assistive technologies, applications of reading and writing technologies are most effective if they are implemented along with effective evidence-based instruction to support their successful use by individuals with complex communication needs.

The CAST (formerly Center for Applied Special Technology) Universal Design for Learning (UDL) Book Builder provides free online tools to develop e-books with many features that are appropriate for individuals with complex communication needs.

# CONCLUSIONS

The acquisition of literacy skills is fundamental to participation in today's society. Literacy skills support cognitive development, facilitate participation in education, increase employment opportunities, promote social relationships, enhance access to a wide range of technologies, and provide opportunities to engage in motivating leisure pursuits. Literacy skills provide even greater benefits for individuals with complex communication needs who have limited speech abilities: For these individuals, the

acquisition of literacy skills expands communication options significantly, provides visual supports for language learning, enhances perceptions of competence, elevates expectations, and increases self-esteem.

Research has demonstrated that it is indeed possible to provide effective intervention to maximize literacy outcomes for individuals with complex communication needs, starting by first developing emergent literacy skills, then transitioning to learning early conventional literacy skills, and ultimately building advanced literacy skills to support participation in educational, vocational, health care, and community settings. Light and McNaughton (2009b) argued that there are five key components to effective literacy intervention:Providing sufficient time for literacy instructionTargeting appropriate skills known to improve literacy outcomesUsing proven, effective instructional techniquesProviding appropriate instructional adaptations and supports to accommodate the needs and skills of individuals with complex communication needsBuilding positive rapport and ensuring motivation for learning

The research discussed in this chapter provides the knowledge base that is essential to improve literacy outcomes for individuals with complex communication needs: implementation of evidence-based practices, ongoing data collection, and performance monitoring to ensure the effectiveness of these practices for each individual. However, this science, although essential, is not sufficient on its own to ensure successful outcomes. Tied to this knowledge must be the fundamental belief and commitment to the right of all individuals to have the opportunity to learn and to seek their full potential. Every individual can benefit from participation in literacy activities. Our society has vastly underestimated the learning potential of many individuals with complex communication needs. There is a growing body of research-based evidence demonstrating that individuals who rely on AAC can learn to read and write if they are provided with appropriate instruction. When individuals with complex communication needs can read and write, they have access to a whole new range of educational, vocational, and social opportunities. The acquisition of literacy skills empowers individuals with complex communication needs to meet their life goals.

Bob Williams describes the profound impact that acquiring literacy skills had upon his life: “I am thankful for one ... gift I received early on in life which most people can take for granted: the gift of literacy—of reading and writing, of making sense of the world and having the reciprocal ability of letting the world make sense out of you and come to respect you for all that you have to offer and contribute. This to me is the true gift and power of literacy in each of our lives. (Bob Williams, 2000, p. 247)”

# Intervention to Enhance Participation in Education, Employment, and Community Settings

David B. McNaughton

AAC intervention must address not only an individual's current needs, but also prepare him or her for future environments. For individuals with developmental disabilities, there will be five key domains of participation in their lives: education, employment and volunteer activities, assisted and independent living, heath care, and community participation. Each of these environments creates a need for both environment-specific vocabulary and communication strategies to support successful interaction.

In each of the five domains, there are examples of how access to AAC can support active participation and inclusion for people with complex communication needs. This is not to say that all educational programs, businesses, and service providers are currently fully prepared to provide needed communication supports, or that the transition to providing communication access to needed services for all will be easy. It is clear, however, that people with severe disabilities have an ethical right, and in many cases a legal right, to participate in society in the same manner as persons without disabilities (Americans with Disabilities Act, 1990; Individuals with Disabilities Education Improvement Act, 2004; Mirenda, 2014; United Nations, 2006). There is also a growing body of evidence that we have the knowledge and skills to achieve positive outcomes in education (e.g., Spooner &amp; Browder, 2015); employment and volunteer activities (e.g., McNaughton, Bryen, Blackstone, Williams, &amp; Kennedy, 2012; Trembath, Balandin, Stancliffe, &amp; Togher, 2010); assisted and independent living (e.g., Collier &amp; Self, 2010); health care (e.g., Thunberg, Buchholz, &amp; Nilsson, 2016); and community participation (e.g., Collier, Blackstone, &amp; Taylor, 2012; Solarsh &amp; Johnson, 2017). To achieve these positive outcomes, society must address the critical element that too often is absent—a shared belief that active and meaningful participation for all is both necessary and possible (Mirenda, 2014; McNaughton et al., 2019).

Although each of the five domains presents unique challenges, there are also evidence-based strategies that are common to successful intervention in any setting.

483

This chapter therefore provides both an examination of successful AAC interventions in the five domains (i.e. education, employment and volunteer activities, assisted and independent living, health care, and community participation) and a review of three key supports to successful intervention at any age, and in any environment: promoting self-determination, preparing for transitions, and setting high expectations for valued outcomes.

## EDUCATION

A child's educational program should provide both academic and social preparation for adult life. The right to a free and appropriate public education is affirmed in the law in many countries. In the United States, the Individuals with Disabilities Education Improvement Act of 2004 (PL 108-446) mandates publicly funded education for children and youth with disabilities beginning at age 3. If assistive technology is needed, including AAC, the school must ensure that the technology (and services to learn how to make use of the technology) is provided.

Federal law in many countries also stipulates that decisions regarding the educational needs of a child, and the services to be provided by the educational system, should be made on an individualized basis and documented in an individualized education program (IEP) for each child with disabilities. For example, in the United States, children with disabilities are expected to participate in the general education curriculum, and to receive educational services in the least restrictive environment (i.e. to be educated in the same classroom as their peers without disabilities to the maximum extent appropriate). Children with disabilities are also expected to participate in state accountability measures, although children with the most severe disabilities may participate in alternative assessment activities (Towles-Reeves, Kearns, Kleinert, & Kleinert, 2009). The list shown in the text-box summarizes the steps for developing an appropriate IEP for children with complex communication needs.

### Develop an Appropriate Individualized Education Program

It is important for the AAC team to determine priority goals for each student so that meaningful educational programs can be designed, implemented, and evaluated. Jorgensen (2018) provides a 15-step process for writing standards-based IEPs for individuals with severe disabilities:Involve the parents.Describe the student's and parent's vision for desired outcomes, based on a person-centered planning process.Write a student profile.Report results of the most recent assessments.Describe student's present levels of performance in academic and functional areas.Write inclusive annual goals and short-term objectives.

7. Determine how progress on goals will be measured and how often it will be reported.

8. Describe the supplementary aids and services that will enable the student to achieve the annual goals and short‐term objectives.

9. Describe the supports for school personnel on behalf of the student (e.g. additional training).

10. Detail type, personnel responsible, amount, location, and duration of special education and related services that support the student's inclusion.

11. Indicate the student's placement, percentage of time the student will be in general education, and rationale for time that student will not participate with students without disabilities.

12. Describe student's participation in district and state assessments.

13. Write inclusive transition goals and services.

14. Consider special factors, such as communication needs, limited English proficiency needs, and so on.

15. Write the section of the IEP for inclusive extended school year services.

Careful review of historical outcomes for children who receive special education services has resulted in calls for new approaches to educational programs. Although children with disabilities have had a right to a free and appropriate public education in the United States since 1973, in the past too many children with severe disabilities had educational programs with inappropriate educational goals, inadequate instruction, and limited or no contact with their same‐age peers without disabilities (Jorgensen, 2018). There is a growing recognition of the benefits of an inclusive education—high‐quality educational opportunities, with appropriate supports, in the general education classroom (Jorgensen, 2018; Mirenda, 2014). Indeed, many states require written justification in the IEP of how a child's educational program addresses state standards for learning, and why a child is receiving educational services in any setting (e.g. a self‐contained classroom, an isolated clinic room) other than the general education classroom.

As support for the legal mandate for participation in the general education curriculum, there is growing evidence that an inclusive education can support the acquisition of valued academic and social skills. With appropriate instructional support, children with complex communication needs can make meaningful academic progress in literacy (Ahlgrim‐Delzell et al. 2016; Mandak, Light, & Boyle, 2018), math (Spooner, Root, Saunders, & Browder, 2018), and science and other academic skills (Spooner & Browder, 2015). Equally important to the academic benefits is the opportunity to interact with same‐aged peers—to develop friendships and social skills that will be important not only during the school years but beyond. Again, recent systematic reviews provide evidence that appropriate interventions can increase peer interactions for children with complex communication needs across the school‐aged

years, from preschool to adolescence (Chapin, McNaughton, Boyle, & Babb, 2018; Chung & Carter, 2013; Therrien, Light, & Pope, 2016).

Providing an inclusive education is not just an issue of where a child receives instruction, but how the student is supported in learning and participating. There are five key elements in providing a high-quality inclusive learning experience: collaborative teaming, comprehensive and individualized planning, high-quality instruction, fostering of membership and relationships, and individual communication supports (Carter & Draper, 2010; Hunt et al. 2009; Soto, 2009).

John Draper is an adult with cerebral palsy who uses AAC, and who received an inclusive education during his middle- and high school program. After graduation from college, he established a business (Together We Rock!) to provide educational programs to promote accessible and inclusive communities (Carter & Draper, 2010; Draper, 2018). Additional information is available at the Together We Rock web site.

## Collaborative Teaming

For students with complex communication needs, the development and implementation of successful academic programming requires collaboration by the members of the AAC team.

John Draper described his school experiences in the following way:

> As a student with a physical disability and as an augmentative communication user, I experienced both successes and challenges in my academic pursuits. My successes were aided by the presence in my life of visionary parents, open-minded educators, dedicated paraprofessionals, and an exemplary team of education professionals who were committed to working together to explore possibilities and find solutions . . . My success in meeting the rigors of the school curriculum depended in part on the extent to which my educational team worked collaboratively. It was not uncommon for more than 30 professionals to be involved in my life at any one time. It was a constant struggle to get everyone to work together effectively and not to become distracted by their individual mandates, policies, and turfs. It took time for everyone to realize that true collaboration could only be achieved when the team understood everyone's individual roles, clarified expectations in writing, and established communication guidelines. (Carter & Draper, 2010, p. 73)

The development and delivery of effective inclusive educational programs requires collaboration between education professionals, the parents, and the student (Hunt, Soto, Maier, Müller, & Goetz, 2002). For AAC team members working in schools, collaborative teamwork is especially important (Binger et al. 2012). The speech-language pathologist will typically be the member of the educational team with the greatest knowledge and experience in AAC and language development. However, the parent will have critical information on the child's current skills and needs (and future goals); the general education teacher will have the best understanding of the grade-level curriculum; the special education teacher will bring expertise on curriculum modification; the occupational therapist will be knowledgeable of adaptations to tasks to lessen physical demands and enhance performance; and additional team members will also have important knowledge to contribute. It is critical that there is consensus among team members as to the goals that will be addressed, and the strategies that will be used to support communication and educational participation in a range of environments (e.g. the classroom, home, the community). Working as a team allows

Participation in Education, Employment, and Community Settings
487

appropriate education and communication opportunities to be provided throughout the day to support the achievement of both immediate and long-term goals; for example, the parent can help the special education teacher understand the future living environments anticipated for the child, and what community participation skills will be needed; the general education teacher can help the speech-language pathologist learn what vocabulary will be needed in upcoming educational activities; the special education teacher can model and implement specialized instructional techniques to promote learning.

## Comprehensive and Individualized Planning

Planning for educational programs should reflect the knowledge gained from the experiences of others, but also be driven by the interests and ambitions of the individual student.

John describes how his educational planning process was individualized to address his interests and goals:

As I entered high school, I began a dialogue with family, friends and professionals regarding my future. Basically, I wanted an immediate answer to the question "What am I going to do with the rest of my life?" But I was only really able to answer that question after participating in various learning opportunities that helped me begin to understand my strengths, limitations, and interests. For example, I took optional subjects, such as entrepreneurial studies—and an independent class project that focused on creating a business—that provided valuable information relevant to my future as an entrepreneur. There was also a work-based learning opportunity at a local community newspaper that proved to be a win-win situation for both my employer and me. My assignments enable me to improve my writing skills, and my employer learned firsthand about the need and requirement to have a workplace that is accessible and inclusive of people who have a disability. (Carter &amp; Draper, 2010, p. 78)

Careful planning is needed to ensure that educational goals reflect the strengths, challenges, and interests of the individual. To support communication and a focus on desired outcomes, it is important to develop an annual strengths-based student profile that can be used to guide decision making and goal setting. This profile can be developed through informal interviews with family members and others who know the student well, as well as through person-centered planning processes such as the Making Action Plans (MAPS) process (Forest, Pearpoint, &amp; O'Brien, 1996). Whatever process is used, the following key questions should be addressed (Jorgensen, 2018):

- What is the student's history?
- What are the family's and student's dreams?
- What is the nightmare? What are the fears?
- Who is this student? What are his or her interests, talents, strengths, and personality?
- What does the student need in this school year to put him or her on the path to achieving the dream?
- What steps need to be taken, and who will put the plan into action? What is the time frame for completing the action steps? How will the team know that the action plan has been successful?

AAC Interventions for Individuals with Developmental Disabilities

The creation of a comprehensive outcomes-focused plan based on the skills, needs, and interests of the student is the first step in identifying the instructional goals that may be addressed within a general education curriculum (e.g., literacy). Additionally, educational planning for the student with complex communication needs may include the identification of goals (and the development of instructional activities) related to functional skills needed for participation in school (e.g., participating in group discussions) and the community (e.g., arranging public transportation, managing personal care attendant services).

## Designing High-Quality Instruction

Once goals have been identified for a student, the educational team should design instruction to maximize learning and participation (Browder, Wood, Thompson, &amp; Ribuffo, 2014). There are four key instructional strategies and supports: universal design for learning, curriculum accommodations, systematic instruction, and assistive technology.

**Universal Design for Learning** Given the heterogeneity of today's classroom, educational materials and instructional activities should be designed from the beginning to address the needs of a wide variety of learners, with additional modifications for the student with complex communication needs as required. A universal design for learning approach suggests the consideration of three principles, as follows:

1. Use multiple, flexible methods of presentation in delivering instruction to students.
2. Support multiple, flexible methods of expression for student responses.
3. Provide multiple, flexible options for engagement by students.

When teachers use the three universal design for learning principles to set goals and design instruction, all students—including but not limited to those with complex communication needs—are likely to benefit (Rose &amp; Meyer, 2006). For example, Bedrosian, Lasker, Speidel, and Politsch (2003) described how the use of story grammar maps (a commonly used instructional tool) can benefit not only typically developing children, but also an adolescent with complex communication needs (in this case, a 14-year-old student with autism spectrum disorder [ASD]). Following the implementation of a multicomponent intervention that included story grammar maps and working with a peer, the student with ASD wrote stories that contained more words and demonstrated a better understanding of the elements of an effective story. Additionally, both the student with ASD and the peer communicated that they enjoyed the writing activity, and that they would like to interact with the other student in social contexts outside the writing project.

**Curriculum Accommodations** Even when teachers have given careful consideration to supports for comprehension and participation using the principles of universal design for learning, there may still be a need for individualized accommodations (Soto, 2009). The Participation Model (see Chapter 2) can serve as a guide. The educational team should 1) review expectations for students without disabilities in the classroom, 2) determine the individual's current level of performance, and 3) identify instructional accommodations that will support understanding and participation for the individual with complex communication needs. In some cases, it may be necessary to select an alternative objective or substantially modify the class objective (Soto, 2009). Ruppar, Afacan, and Pickett (2017) described how evidence-based practices such as

Participation in Education, Employment, and Community Settings
489

curriculum accommodations and systematic instruction were used to support literacy instruction for Caitlyn, a student with complex communication needs in a ninth-grade general education English/language arts class. The educational team developed an adapted version of the class text (The Odyssey), and then made use of a shared reading activity during 23 intervention sessions, all of which occurred in the general education classroom. As a result of the intervention, Caitlyn learned to make appropriate use of new vocabulary items (e.g., trip, brave, hero), and to answer questions about the text (e.g., "Who went on a trip?"). Caitlyn demonstrated learning for all of the targeted skills, and the educational team (including special education teachers, the general education teacher, parents, administrators, and paraprofessionals with whom the student worked) agreed that the intervention had improved Caitlyn's knowledge and skills in key areas of the curriculum. They also reported that they would support the use of similar activities in the future. Table 13.1 describes six commonly used curriculum adaptations (which can be used singly or in combination), as well as examples of their use with students with complex communication needs.

Table 13.1. Educational accommodations

|  Type | Definition | Example  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  Size | Adjust the number of items a student is expected to learn or complete | Seamus types using eye tracking and an onscreen keyboard to write. To accommodate his slow rate of text entry, his math test consists of 5 problems rather than 10.  |
|  Time | Adjust the amount of time allotted for learning, task completion, or testing | Stacy writes quite slowly when she uses her head mouse to compose text via her AAC device. To provide sufficient time for text composition, her social studies teacher asks her a question at the end of every class period. Stacy then prepares the answer at home in the evening and stores it in her AAC device. The next day when her teacher asks her the question, Stacy is able to quickly provide the answer in class.  |
|  Level of support | Adjust the amount of personal assistance provided by peers or adults | During the Romeo and Juliet unit, a paraprofessional programs the lines spoken by the apothecary into Mitchell's AAC device and helps him practice activating them on cue.  |
|  Input | Adjust how instruction is delivered | Mr. Hashman uses an interactive whiteboard to write key words and draw simple pictures during a whole-class discussion of Tom Sawyer.  |
|  Output | Adjust how the student is expected to demonstrate learning | In Foods class, Terry cuts out magazine pictures of the four food groups and places them in a concept map to show what he has learned.  |
|  Difficulty | Adjust the skill level, problem type, or rules about how the learner approaches the activity | Mitchell reads a computer-based version of To Kill a Mockingbird that allows him to both read and listen to selected words spoken aloud, as needed.  |

Key: AAC, augmentative and alternative communication.
Source: Cole et al., (2000).

Systematic Instruction

The use of systematic instruction has been demonstrated to provide successful outcomes for a wide variety of academic skills (Browder et al. 2014) for people with severe disabilities. In a systematic instruction approach, the teacher first breaks a target skill into smaller pieces, and then teaches components of the skill through the use of techniques such as modeling, prompting, feedback, and reinforcement. Data are collected on student performance and used to make decisions about instruction. Spooner, Ahlgrim-Delzell, Kemp-Inman, and Wood (2014) provide a description of how systematic instruction was used to teach four elementary school--aged students with ASD and complex communication needs to participate in a shared reading activity on an iPad. Following intervention, all students demonstrated increased participation in storybook-reading activities (e.g. turning the pages in the digital book, touching the repeated story line on the iPad).

Assistive Technology Many students with complex communication needs require assistive technology such as AAC to support expression; however, assistive technology can also play an important role in helping them learn new skills. For example, in a video modeling approach, a video is made of the target behavior (e.g. playing appropriately with peers, completing a math worksheet); the student then watches the video and imitates the observed behavior. Video modeling has been demonstrated to be a valuable learning tool for a wide range of academic and social skills (Wong et al. 2015). Also, digital books (i.e. books presented on tablet computers), as described in Spooner et al. (2014), have also provided increased accessibility and supported engagement for students with severe disabilities (Mandak, Light, & McNaughton, 2019; Therrien & Light, 2016, 2018).

## Fostering Membership and Relationships

An educational program should address not only academic goals, but social goals as well. Interaction with peers makes school a more positive experience and provides opportunities to learn valuable social skills. Without intervention, most children with complex communication needs typically interact with teachers and other support personnel, and not with their same-age peers (Chung, Carter, & Sisco, 2012a). With appropriate supports, children with complex communication needs can enjoy the academic, social, and emotional benefits of peer interaction (Chung, Carter, & Sisco, 2012b; Therrien et al. 2016).

Intervention to foster inclusive membership and relationships should change according to the age and needs of the child (Hunt et al. 2009). In a review of the effects of peer support interventions on the communication of preschoolers with ASD, Chapin et al. (2018) described the use of friendship training/ability awareness groups, the selection of play materials based on the interests of the child with ASD, and the provision of AAC as key components to supporting interaction in inclusive early childhood classrooms. At the grade school level, Chung and Carter (2013) described the positive impact of a multicomponent intervention package for children with complex communication needs (including paraprofessional support, peer initiation, and access to the child's AAC device). Both use of AAC and peer interactions increased for the children who participated in the intervention.

## Providing Individual Communication Support

One goal of education for students with complex communication needs is meaningful academic and social engagement in all aspects of the school day. To accomplish

Participation in Education, Employment, and Community Settings
491

this, students must have access to appropriate AAC systems that not only support quick access to frequently used vocabulary, but also enable participation in a range of communication activities. It is especially important that students learn the meaning of words, and develop access to a wide range of expressive vocabulary, to support participation in educational and social settings (Bryen, 2008; Lee, Kim, &amp; Park, 2005). Indeed, language performance appears to be one of the strongest predictors of academic performance (Pace, Alper, Burchinal, Golinkoff, &amp; Hirsh-Pasek, 2019), and it has been suggested that language acts as a cognitive tool kit to help children reason about and discuss the world that surrounds them (Gentner, 2016).

Too often, however, students who use AAC are provided with communication systems that have a severely restricted vocabulary that is primarily designed to address needs and wants, or they are expected to use a small number of words to fulfill a wide range of communication functions (Binger &amp; Light, 2008; Johnson, Bornman, &amp; Tönsing, 2017; Light, Parsons, &amp; Drager, 2002). If this happens, students who require AAC are often forced to be passive learners: They cannot ask or answer specific questions in class, provide specific information describing their understanding of a topic, or participate in the vocabulary-rich interactions that support language growth and the development of critical thinking skills (Light &amp; McNaughton, 2014). As adults, they are unprepared to participate in the workplace or volunteer activities (Creech, 1993; McNaughton, Light, &amp; Arnold, 2002), or to communicate in ways that support personal safety and health care (Bryen, 2008; Lever, 2003).

It is often challenging to keep vocabulary in a student's AAC system current because the content needed to participate in general education classrooms changes rapidly. This is one of the reasons that literacy skills are especially critical for individuals with complex communication needs—it is only once individuals are able to spell that they have real access to the wide range of vocabulary needed for successful participation in the general education curriculum (see Chapter 12).

The Participation Model (see Figure 2.2) provides a useful framework for vocabulary planning for students who rely on AAC in general education classrooms. The model begins with identification of participation patterns and communication needs, which, in this case, requires an assessment of the needed vocabulary and the general education teacher's expectations with regard to student engagement in the classroom. It also requires examination of the strategies teachers use to support student understanding and responding (e.g., small group discussions, working with peers, class presentations) so that any barriers to participation (including the lack of needed vocabulary) can be identified and remediated.

There is growing evidence of the positive impact of high-quality inclusive learning experiences that incorporate collaborative teaming, comprehensive and individualized planning, high-quality instruction, fostering of membership and relationships, and individual communication supports (Browder et al., 2014; Hunt et al., 2002). Furthermore, it is clear that educational programs can play a key role in preparing individuals with complex communication needs for active and meaningful participation in adult society, including employment and volunteer activities (Carter, Austin, &amp; Trainor, 2012; Rossetti, Lehr, Pelerin, Huang, &amp; Lederer, 2016).

## EMPLOYMENT AND VOLUNTEER ACTIVITIES

Some individuals who use AAC are active in a wide variety of employment and volunteer activities, including as educators, technology consultants, policy analysts, customer service providers, writers, artists, and cleaning service providers

AAC Interventions for Individuals with Developmental Disabilities

(McNaughton et al., 2012; Rossetti et al., 2016). These successful outcomes in work and volunteer settings are reported for people with a wide range of disabilities, including cerebral palsy (McNaughton et al., 2002; McNaughton, Symons, Light, &amp; Parsons, 2006), ASD (Richardson, McCoy, &amp; McNaughton, 2019), and multiple disabilities (Heller et al., 1996; Light, Stoltz, &amp; McNaughton, 1996). However, despite these success stories, numerous barriers to employment and volunteer participation remain for adults with complex communication needs, including attitudinal barriers, inadequate educational preparation, and a lack of appropriate community supports.

The greater an individual's cognitive and physical challenges, the greater the need for the AAC team to identify a variety of employment and volunteer opportunities, to work with employers and organizations to modify job activities, and to ensure the ongoing provision of needed supports. Three key elements should be considered in preparing for successful employment and volunteer activities (McNaughton, Arnold, Sennott, &amp; Serpentine, 2010):

1. Developing knowledge and skills that are valued in the community
2. Identifying jobs and volunteer activities that are a good match for the skills and interests of the individual who uses AAC
3. Ensuring that needed supports are available to maintain success

## Developing Knowledge and Skills That Are Valued in the Community

Careful planning and preparation during the school years increase the probability of positive employment and volunteer outcomes as adolescents and adults. Key areas of preparation include the development of personal areas of expertise and communication skills.

## Personal Areas of Expertise

Successful participation requires the ability to perform the work or volunteer activity, as well as key communication and social interaction skills (Bryen, Potts, &amp; Carey, 2007). It is not necessary that the individual can perform a job before beginning work or volunteer activities—many aspects of a job are best learned on the site. A wide variety of approaches have been demonstrated to be effective in supporting workplace instruction, including systematic instruction, self-monitoring, and video modeling (Cannella-Malone &amp; Schaefer, 2017). The use of video visual scene displays (VSDs) is an important enhancement of video modeling and provides integrated supports not only for learning new skills, but also for communication (Light, McNaughton, &amp; Jakobs, 2015). As described in Chapter 6, specialized software supports the creation of videos (to support learning a new skill) that contain VSDs (to support communication). The VSDs, which contain hotspots to support communication, are programmed to appear at key moments in the video; these pauses at key junctures mark the appropriate opportunity for participation and communication, and the VSD provides the necessary vocabulary for the learner with complex communication needs to fulfill the communication demands at that point in time. Babb, Gormley, McNaughton, and Light (2019) provide evidence that the use of AAC technology with video VSDs supported both the learning of new skills and increased communication for a young man with ASD and complex communication needs in a vocational setting (i.e., working in a library).

Although many skills are best learned in the workplace setting, it is helpful if an individual has acquired job-related knowledge and skills that are common to many

work settings (e.g. following a work schedule, requesting assistance as needed). Part-time jobs or employment-related volunteer activities while in middle- and high school help to prepare individuals for adult work activities (Carter et al. 2012).

Anthony Arnold is an adult with complex communication needs who teleworks from his home and provides both product testing and customer support for the Prentke-Romich Company, a manufacturer of AAC technology. As an individual who uses AAC to communicate, Anthony has specialized expertise and a special interest in helping others to use the technology effectively. Some customers who require technical support make a special effort to contact Anthony for assistance because of the respect they have for his skills with AAC technology. Anthony credits his expert use of AAC technology and his high school work experiences for his employment success today. He explained as follows:

> I have a brother who is 4 years younger, and John attained a newspaper route at the age of 11. He was earning a paycheck to buy extra things his allowance wouldn't, and I think that is when I first began wanting a job so I could buy stuff I couldn't afford on just my allowance. So that following summer I asked my parents to drop me off at Job Services. My parents let me do my own speaking to express what I wanted, and I was then placed in youth job training for a month. They then placed me at a computer store where I did data entry during my junior and senior years of high school. I credit working at this computer store for my current success working in technical service at the Prentke-Romich Company because I learned a great deal about software, hardware, and operating systems during those 2 years. These are the same skills I have to use today when I troubleshoot a person's device.

You can read more about Anthony's story at the AAC Learning Center web site, including his presentation on 30 years of AAC: Stories from the past, and ideas for the future (Arnold, 2018).

### Communication Skills

Workplace skills are not the only ones needed for employment success. Both individuals who use AAC and their employers have emphasized the importance of being able to communicate effectively in the workplace (Bryen et al. 2007). This should not be interpreted as meaning that individuals with limited communication skills cannot be employed—there is increasing evidence that individuals with a wide variety of skills can obtain and maintain employment (Richardson et al. 2019). Although there is no threshold set of communication skills required for employment, individuals with limited communication skills are more dependent on the availability of skilled communication partners and are more limited in their job options (Light et al. 1996).

Some vocabulary and communication demands can be anticipated (and addressed in school programs), but some are job specific. As Rick Creech (an individual who relies on AAC and who worked for the Pennsylvania Department of Education) noted, “The workplace requires an expanded vocabulary because in the workplace employees use words they do not use anywhere else” (Creech, 1993, p. 105). It is important not only that people who use AAC have access to a broad vocabulary, but also that they have additional strategies to ensure that their views are heard in fast-moving conversations. Strategies such as preprogramming of frequently used words and phrases, and increased use of written communication (including e-mail) can help to address the challenges of face-to-face communication (McNaughton & Chapple, 2013).

Communication in the workplace is about more than discussing work activities; individuals who use AAC also need to participate in the social interactions

AAC Interventions for Individuals with Developmental Disabilities

that maintain a positive work environment. Storey and Provost (1996) reported the positive impact of the introduction of communication skills instruction and communication books featuring social vocabulary (e.g., sports, hobbies) on the social interactions of three workers with complex communication needs. Based on a study of workplace conversations, Balandin and Iacono (1999) highlighted the importance of considering the specific work environment and typical conversation topics of employees when identifying needed vocabulary. Although some core vocabulary items are common to many workplaces, some unique vocabulary will be specific to a particular type of interaction. For example, Balandin and Iacono reported that expletives were an important part of social mealtime discussions for some of the conversations they observed, but clearly this vocabulary is not appropriate to all workplaces and settings!

Literacy skills are closely related to communication skills. Once individuals are able to spell, they have access to any desired vocabulary item. Certainly there is evidence that people who use AAC can obtain employment with limited literacy skills; Light et al. (1996) reported that 48% of the employed individuals who used AAC were considered to have limited reading and writing skills (e.g., were unable to read a newspaper). However, those individuals who had stronger literacy skills typically reported higher levels of satisfaction with their jobs, received better pay, and had greater opportunities for advancement (Light et al., 1996).

## Identifying Activities That Are a Good Match for the Person Who Uses AAC

The development of a good match between employee skills and interests and employer needs is key to a positive work or volunteer experience. For individuals with strong literacy skills, there are often a number of options for work or volunteer activities (see Anthony's story related earlier in the chapter). For those individuals whose educational programs emphasized the acquisition of life skills, creative and individualized employment solutions may be needed. It is important to identify an activity that is a good match for the skills and interests of the individual.

Paul is an example of someone who found work that suits his interests and skills. Paul is an adult with ASD who communicates using a small portable AAC device. During the school years, he prepared for employment by working in the cafeteria at his school. During that experience, the AAC team learned that Paul did best in activities that were predictable but not repetitive. For example, Paul learned routines for cleaning and tidying the cafeteria and classrooms, which included a series of activities (wiping tables, stacking chairs, sweeping the floor) that were completed in a consistent order, but could be performed in different parts of the cafeteria and school. Upon graduation, with the support of his speech-language pathologist, his family, and a parent advocacy group, Paul obtained a job at a local supermarket bagging groceries. At first, Paul's employer was reluctant to hire an individual with ASD. During a trial employment period, however, Paul was able to demonstrate that bagging groceries was a good match for his preference for activities that were predictable but not repetitive. Paul not only completed the essential work requirements for the activity (i.e., bagging groceries, thanking customers for shopping at the store by using his AAC device), but he also had the best work attendance record of any of the check-out clerks!

Obtaining Needed Supports

Like all individuals, people with complex communication needs require supports in order to be successful in the workplace. Some individuals with physical disabilities may require specialized transportation and ongoing personal care assistance at the job site, while others may require the development of a workplace support network to assist with day-to-day challenges. Job carving provides one useful approach to supporting workplace participation. In this approach, the employment team first determines an individual's skills and interests, and then identifies a portion of duties in an existing job that is a good match for those capabilities.

Larry is an adult diagnosed with ASD who has benefited from a job carving approach to workplace participation. He can read and write short sentences, and also communicates using sign language. While in school, Larry participated in job placements in government offices, where he used his literacy skills to assist with mail delivery and to file documents. As Larry approached graduation, his family and teachers made use of their social networks to identify possible job opportunities. Larry's teacher contacted her brother-in-law, who worked for a television cable company; the two of them then worked with the company to job carve a unique employment position for Larry. The employment team identified a number of activities that were good matches for Larry's existing skills or involved skills that could be acquired at the workplace. Larry learned to deliver office mail at the company and to fulfill photocopying work requests. He also began to learn basic typing skills in anticipation of taking on new office responsibilities. Once Larry began work, the office supervisor took a special interest in ensuring that Larry had a positive work experience. It is interesting to note that as an individual who speaks English as a second language, the office manager was very aware of the challenges of communication in the workplace, and she played a special role in supporting Larry's successful workplace participation.

## Preparing for Employment and Vocational Activities

In today's economy, employment activities change quickly, and it is unrealistic to think that a person will perform the same task throughout his or her work life. It is ineffective, therefore, for an individual to invest an inordinate amount of time in prevocational training for a specific task. Although there are many important skills that should be addressed within school programs (e.g. communication skills, literacy skills), the best place to learn many specific job skills is in the workplace, where the individual learns to deal with the wide range of work activities (and make use of needed supports) that exist in the real world. Indeed, it is ideal if job and volunteer placements begin while the individual is still in school (Carter et al. 2012). In this way, the educational team can address key skills for employment and volunteer success, including developing knowledge and skills that are valued in the community, identifying jobs and volunteer activities that are a good match for the skills and interests of the individual who uses AAC, and ensuring that needed supports are available to maintain success (Bumble, Carter, McMillan, Manikas, & Bethune, 2018; McNaughton, Rackensperger, Wehmeyer, & Wright, 2010).

Additional information on the employment and volunteer experiences of people who use AAC is available at the AAC Learning Center web site.

AAC Interventions for Individuals with Developmental Disabilities

# ASSISTED AND INDEPENDENT LIVING

It was the best of highs. It was the worst of terrors. I was elated. I was depressed. I smiled with joy. I cried with sorrow. I knew everything. I knew nothing. What caused these swings of emotion? Moving out on my own. (Williams, 2001, p. 3)

This passage is how Michael Williams, an adult with cerebral palsy and complex communication needs, describes his experiences in living independently in the community for the first time (you can read more about Michael's story at the AAC Learning Center web site, including his presentation of How far we've come, how far we've got to go: Tales from the trenches [Williams, 2017]).

During the past 40 years there have been dramatic changes in where people with severe disabilities live. Although some people with severe disabilities live at home with family members, many receive residential services from a local or state organization. As recently as 1977, more than 85% of individuals with intellectual and developmental disabilities who received residential services in the United States lived in nursing homes or state institutions (Lakin &amp; Stancliffe, 2007). In 2017, more than 70% of individuals with intellectual and developmental disabilities who received residential services in the United States lived in community group homes (National Association of State Directors of Developmental Disabilities Services and Human Services Research Institute, 2017). In all living situations, however, there are three key areas of concern for individuals with severe disabilities: directing personal care services, supporting personal safety, and preparing for emergency situations.

## Directing Personal Care Services

No matter where individuals with severe disabilities live, quality of life will be strongly affected by the ability to direct one's care and enjoy a positive relationship with personal care attendants. As Anne Abbott (a woman with cerebral palsy who lives in her own apartment) describes:

A good personal assistant or attendant can be my arms and legs for certain daily activities. That frees me up to get on with my work and my life without having to worry about how I'll get to the bathroom or have a cup of coffee. When an assistant is good, life is so much easier. When an assistant is bad, it can be devastating. (Collier &amp; Self, 2010, p. 163)

For persons with complex communication needs to receive appropriate personal care services, they must be able to describe desired procedures (e.g., how they prefer to be assisted in eating, drinking, and bathing), and to give feedback on the provision of services. This can often pose significant challenges. People with severe disabilities may be used to receiving services from people who are very familiar with their preferences (e.g., parents), and have little familiarity with effectively and efficiently describing their needs. People providing personal care services, such as group home workers, often have limited experience working with people with complex communication needs and receive limited training.

Successful communication with personal care assistants requires skills on both sides. Collier and Self (2010) describe a multistep process for developing service plans (see the textbox "Developing and Using Service Plans").

By documenting and then practicing the use of preferred routines, people with severe disabilities can take steps toward improving their care. In the first step, the AAC team works with the individual with complex communication needs to identify

contexts (e.g. drinking, bathing, toileting) for which individualized routines are important to the individual. Next, the individual and AAC team review performance of the current communication routine; for example, when observed, it may be seen that the attendant provided a glass of water when the individual used the phrase “I am thirsty,” but he did not cover the individual's shirt, and the shirt got wet. By observing the impact of current communication strategies, and discussing with the individual what should have happened, the AAC team has the information needed to develop AAC supports for desired care routines. The needed words and phrases can then be made available as appropriate—for example, vocabulary related to meal preparation preferences can be programmed into AAC technologies, bathing routines can be written on communication boards and posted next to the bathtub, computer access setup can be illustrated with photographs placed next to the computer workstation. Collier and Self (2010) further suggest that the individual with complex communication needs practice the use of the service plan routine in role-play scenarios with familiar partners. This provides both an opportunity to make additional modifications to the service plans as needed, and to practice strategies when breakdowns occur: What can the individual do if the attendant skips a step? How can the individual provide positive feedback if the steps have been carried out correctly?

Developing detailed service plans may take a considerable period of time; however, the results can be impactful. As one young man with severe disabilities wrote:

> I spent a year writing up my service plans for different situations. I put them in a binder. I have instructions on how I want people to talk to me; how I can communicate with them; what I want done every morning; how to assist me when I am eating; how to lift me out of my wheelchair, etc. This is one of the best things I have ever done ... I wish I had done it when I was younger. (Collier & Self, 2010, p. 172)

### Supporting Personal Safety

In addition to managing personal care services, people who use AAC must have strategies to ensure their personal safety, no matter where they live. For example, people with disabilities are five times more likely to be victims of sexual violence than people without disabilities (Nixon, Thomas, Daffern, & Ogloff, 2017). Bryen, Carey, and

AAC Interventions for Individuals with Developmental Disabilities

Frantz (2003) surveyed 40 adults who used AAC, and reported that 45% had experienced crime or abuse, but only 28% had reported their experiences to the police. The living situation of many people with complex communication needs—reliance upon support services, limited financial resources, and social isolation—places them at high risk for abuse, and at special risk for continued victimization (Collier &amp; Self, 2010).

Individual advocacy and societal change are required to ensure a comprehensive solution to this problem; however, the AAC team can assist by providing needed information and communication supports. Collier and Self (2010) describe the use of a series of educational sessions to teach 18 adults with complex communication needs strategies for handling conflicts with personal care attendants, safeguarding their privacy, and reporting abuse.

## Preparing for Emergency Situations

During times of emergency (weather, power outages) people with complex communication needs are especially vulnerable. They may be separated from communication partners who are familiar with their AAC system, their AAC technology may not be charged, they may not have access to their wheelchair or other positioning systems needed to access their AAC supports. The AAC community (including the United States Society for Augmentative and Alternative Communication [USSAAC]) has worked to develop resources for emergency communication situations, including materials for people with complex communication needs, emergency response personnel, and AAC advocates. Especially important for people with complex communication needs is a Go Bag—a prepared bag containing contact information for an individual's communication support team, laminated communication displays, medication, and other essential items needed during evacuation to a shelter. Additional information on emergency preparation and disaster relief is available at the USSAAC website (USSAAC, 2018).

## HEALTH CARE

Although people who use AAC may live in a wide variety of housing situations, and may face a wide variety of living challenges, one constant for all individuals is the need for access to high-quality health care (Blackstone, Beukelman, &amp; Yorkston, 2015; Blackstone &amp; Pressman, 2016). Chapter 18 contains a detailed discussion of strategies to support patient-provider communication in medical settings, especially as related to adults with acquired conditions. People with developmental disabilities (e.g., cerebral palsy, Down syndrome, ASD) may experience many of the same challenges in accessing health care services, and they may benefit from some of the same intervention strategies described in Chapter 18. However, many individuals with developmental disabilities also present with unique needs and skills and require individualized supports for communicating in medical settings. Adults with developmental disabilities are living longer and are more likely to be living independently (or in small community-based facilities) than in the past (Balandin &amp; Morgan, 2001; Lakin &amp; Stancliffe, 2007). They also are more likely to have chronic health conditions that will require regular medical attention, and to make use of government-supported health care services (Phillips, Houtenville, &amp; Reichard, 2019).

For people with complex communication needs, the transition from child to adult services may cause special challenges. During childhood, for example, people with

Participation in Education, Employment, and Community Settings
499

developmental disabilities typically depend on three kinds of supports (McNaughton, Balandin, Kennedy, &amp; Sandmel, 2010). Table 13.2 contrasts these supports with the ways adults typically access services.

The ability to establish effective patient-provider communication is essential to successful outcomes. The successful exchange of information helps to equalize the patient-provider relationship, increases patient satisfaction, and improves health outcomes (Blackstone et al., 2015). The patient who is actively involved in identifying problems and setting priorities for treatment is far more likely to follow through on health care recommendations, adhere to medication regimens, and participate in follow-up appointments (Gilmartin, 2004). Too often, health care personnel receive only limited preparation in strategies and supports for interacting with people with complex communication needs, which can slow the rate of communication and result in misunderstandings and communication breakdowns, even exclusion from medical decisions. Without access to effective communication, individuals with complex communication needs are three times more likely to experience preventable adverse medical events, such as medication errors (Hurtig, Alper, &amp; Berkowitz, 2018).

There are three key communication skills that individuals with complex communication needs can use to support more successful patient-provider communication (McNaughton et al., 2010). These include 1) introducing oneself and one's communication system; 2) making use of appropriate communication strategies, including the use of pre-prepared messages; 3) making use of appropriate vocabulary and language to communicate concerns and needs, so as to ensure that previous health care and current health concerns are understood by the health professional.

## Using an Introduction Strategy

Individuals with developmental disabilities will frequently encounter health care professionals who have limited training and experience in working with people with complex communication needs. To prepare for these encounters, people who use AAC need to learn how to introduce themselves and their communication system.

An effective introduction statement should 1) describe how the individual uses his or her communication system and 2) provide instructions on how the new partner
