AAC Interventions for Individuals with Developmental Disabilities

can most effectively communicate with the individual with complex communication needs (Light &amp; Binger, 1998). For example, there may be a message on the individual's wheelchair tray that reads "I point to words in a communication book with my right index finger. Please read them aloud as I point. I will shake my head for 'no' if you have not said the correct word." The statement may also include information about the individual's communication skills and preferences. For example, "I understand everything you say. Please SPEAK TO ME, not to my attendant/family member."

Children with complex communication needs in hospital settings are especially vulnerable to communication problems. Communication challenges often result in their having limited opportunities to communicate, playing a passive role in medical interactions, and experiencing frequent communication breakdowns (Gormley &amp; Light, 2019; Hemsley, Kuek, Bastock, Scarinci, &amp; Davidson, 2013). AAC intervention in these settings should address both the staff's recognition of a patient's individual AAC system and the staff's provision of general communication supports (e.g., offering choices) with children regardless of age or disability level (Gormley &amp; Light, 2019).

Some people who use AAC may take a friend, family member, or support worker with them when dealing with health care professionals. This person can act as a communication assistant and support the interaction with service providers (see Chapter 18). For example, the assistant may read aloud the words that the individual points to on an AAC display (and interpret speech approximations) or take primary responsibility for providing background on the reason for the visit. If individuals who use AAC decide to take a communication assistant with them, they should set clear guidelines both with their support person and health care professionals about how they wish the appointment to proceed (Collier, McGhie-Richmond, &amp; Self, 2010). Regardless of whether individuals plan to speak for themselves or make use of a communication assistant, it is important that people who use AAC are encouraged to prepare well in advance for doctor's appointments and health consultations.

## Making Use of Appropriate Communication Strategies

Interactions with health care professionals can be challenging for anyone. Most medical encounters are time limited, involve people who don't know each other very well (or at all), and take place under stressful conditions (Blackstone, 2016). Typically, the patient makes a brief opening statement, and then the health care professional asks questions. Patients are expected to be able to describe their own health status and current medications, present an organized description of their symptoms, and demonstrate personal attitudes of ownership and honesty about their medical condition (Bryen, 2008).

The use of AAC requires that both the individual who relies on AAC and the health care professional adjust their communication behaviors to achieve a common understanding. For example, individuals who rely on AAC may need to recognize that their gestures and speech approximations will not be understood by health care professionals and prepare their messages in advance. They need to use easily understood communication systems like alphabet and word boards and speech-generating technologies when communicating with health care professionals. The health care professionals may need to allow for a slower pace of interaction and accept the individual's use of preferred communication modes. In these situations, Blackstone and Pressman (2016) recommend the development and use of a health passport, an individualized document that contains relevant medical history (e.g., age, current medications, past

medical procedures). The information in the health passport can be used to respond to common intake questions, and thereby ensure that the health care history is communicated accurately and that the interview time can focus on current health concerns.

In addition, individuals who rely on AAC may want to prepare a message that presents an organized list of their concerns so that the appointment time can focus on asking (and answering) questions and achieving desired outcomes (Burns, Baylor, & Yorkston, 2016).

Laura used the strategy of preparing a message clearly detailing her concerns to ensure a medical appointment would be focused and productive. Laura was an active teenager who had severe cerebral palsy and used a powered wheelchair with a customized insert for mobility. She had grown over the past year and was experiencing significant discomfort in her wheelchair. She had an upcoming seating appointment at the rehabilitation center, but she was worried that she would not get the opportunity to communicate her concerns at the appointment. So, she prepared an e-mail and sent it to the team prior to the appointment along with photos of her current positioning. Her e-mail read:

Please fix my wheelchair.

The headrest is too far over to the right.

My right hip is red.

My left hip hurts when I'm in the chair.

The belt cuts into my chest at the front.

The laptray is resting on my legs.

My right hip falls asleep.

My left hip falls asleep too.

The lower parts of my legs hurt because of the way they hang.

My bum feels OK.

My left shoulder hurts because it is being pushed forward.

My neck gets stiff.

Thanks for fixing my chair.

From Laura

## Making Use of Appropriate Vocabulary and Language

To successfully communicate health concerns, people who use AAC will need access to appropriate vocabulary and the sociolinguistic skills to advocate for their needs (see Chapter 11). Research by Bryen (2008) demonstrated that few words related to health care, body parts, and sexuality are typically available in the preprogrammed vocabulary of AAC devices. A lack of access to needed vocabulary has serious implications, as Sarah Lever, a woman with cerebral palsy who relies on AAC, described:

> Sometimes even when we want to speak out, we don't have the right words to do so. Most communication aids don't come with vocabulary necessary to end the silence about crime and abuse. Many of us don't have easy access to the right vocabulary in our communication devices. Not having adequate vocabulary raises the risk of people who rely on AAC being victimized because we are identified as unable to tell anyone when crime or abuse occurs. It allows those who would commit crimes against us to continue undeterred.

We need adequate vocabulary to talk about crime and abuse, and we need to know how to use that vocabulary. (Lever, 2003, p. 4)”

Caregivers and family members need to work with individuals who use AAC to prepare questions and other information in advance of appointments, and to support them in describing their health status, medications, and so on. This should include careful review of the availability of needed vocabulary, and the addition of words and phrases to support active and meaningful participation in interactions with health care professionals as required (Beukelman, Schrunk, Thiessen, Fager, & Ullman, 2012; Bryen, 2008).

As a result of new standards of practice for hospital accreditation (The Joint Commission, 2010), an increasing number of health care facilities offer their patients picture and alphabet boards to support their communication in emergency situations or during hospitalization. The standards make clear the expectation that “the hospital effectively communicate with patients when providing care, treatment, and services” (Standard PC.02.01.OX) and that appropriate supports, including interpreters and communication boards, be made available and used appropriately.

David Chapple, an adult with cerebral palsy who relies on AAC technology, described his reflections on a visit to the emergency room at a local hospital:

> I wasn't very surprised that none of the nurses and doctors had ever seen an AAC system. They had a lot of questions. Sometimes I felt like they were more interested in my ECO (a communication device) rather than my health . . . It was a little overwhelming because I was in a lot of pain and I didn't feel like giving a lecture about how to use the ECO. I know that seems sarcastic since the nurses needed to know everything, but that was my mind at the time. Once I had a little rest and been given something for the pain, I realized I needed to make people understand me so they could give me the best care. (Chapple, in McNaughton et al. 2012, p. 49)

Interacting with health care professionals is just one example of a situation in which people who use AAC need to interact with people who have limited experience with AAC. Increased expectations for community participation will result in more frequent interactions with people who are unfamiliar with AAC technologies.

## COMMUNITY PARTICIPATION

Community participation can take many forms for people who use AAC. Collier et al. (2012) describe the results of a survey of 61 adults with complex communication needs, including their experiences and expectations for accessing stores, professional services, and restaurants. Dattilo et al. (2008) and Hajjar, McCarthy, Benigno, and Chabot (2016) describe the community recreation experiences of adults who use AAC, and their participation in a wide range of activities, such as attending sporting events, going to movies, skiing, and horseback riding. In these settings, people who use AAC often interact with unfamiliar individuals (e.g. store employees, café workers) who may have had limited (if any) interactions with people who make use of AAC, and who may experience difficulty with the interaction (Collier et al. 2012). To support

successful communication at these times, it is important to consider preparation both for individuals who use AAC and their communication partners.

## Supporting the Skills of the Person Who Uses AAC

People who use AAC may need instruction to learn new strategies (e.g. introduction strategies; Light & Binger, 1998) for use in the community, so as to supplement communication strategies that may only be effective with familiar partners. People who use AAC also describe the importance of selecting modes of communication appropriate to the needs of the partner when interacting in the community. Michael Williams, who makes use of many different AAC techniques, describes himself as a “multi-modal man”: ready to make use of preprogrammed vocabulary on AAC technology with unfamiliar partners, while also able to rapidly construct messages on an alphabet board with more familiar partners (Williams, 2004).

For some individuals, consideration of community communication partners leads to the identification of new needs for AAC intervention. Mechling and Cronin (2006) describe how AAC technology was introduced to three young adults with complex communication needs to support community participation (e.g. ordering desired items in a fast-food restaurant). Prior to the intervention, the students typically pointed to items in the restaurant or waited to be asked yes/no questions to obtain desired items, strategies that were not always successful. After learning to use the AAC technology, all three students demonstrated the ability to request preferred items, and these requests were responded to appropriately by the restaurant staff at high levels (more than 97%).

In addition to participation in local stores, restaurants, and recreational activities, consideration must also be given to participation in the virtual community. Individuals who use AAC have described the important role that digital communication platforms such as Facebook play in connecting with others to maintain social closeness, enjoy greater participation in social interactions, and overcome some of the challenges experienced in face-to-face communication (Caron & Light, 2016; Raghavendra, Newman, Grace, & Wood, 2013).

As an adult with cerebral palsy who uses AAC noted in Caron and Light (2016), Social media gives me a chance to share things that I might not have had the opportunity to otherwise . . . Often in group conversations I am just a listener because I don't want to stop the conversation to make everyone figure out what I am saying [when using speech] or wait for me to type it out [when using AAC] . . . As an AAC user it provides me a good way to communicate and be included . . . without feeling like I am holding up everyone else. (p. 30)

## Supporting Community Partners

There is increasing recognition that there are many individuals who would benefit from communication supports to enhance community participation, including not only people who use AAC, but also people with limited literacy skills, people who are deaf/hard of hearing, and people with cultural and linguistically diverse needs. The creation of communication-accessible environments can lead to improved interactions for many people who experience communication challenges in the community.

Many communities around the world are examining how to create more inclusive environments for people with disabilities (Bumble et al. 2018; Collier et al. 2012). Solarsh and Johnson (2017) describe how people with complex communication needs, AAC communication teams, and community members in Victoria, Australia, have worked to develop standards for communication-accessible environments, as well as procedures for teaching and monitoring the use of standards by customer service providers in business and government organizations. Standards for communication access include, for example, clear signage that multiple methods of communication will be accepted and supported, and training for staff in accepting an individual's chosen method of communication. As of 2017, more than 160 businesses and organizations in Victoria, Australia, had met the standards and earned the right to describe themselves as communication accessible.

Collier et al. (2010) described an innovative approach to the challenge of community participation: Communication assistants were taught to assist in communication exchanges between people with complex communication needs and the staff at community businesses (e.g. shopkeepers, waitresses), who had limited experience with people with severe disabilities. Nine people with complex communication needs participated in the project and made use of the service in a wide variety of settings, including stores, restaurants, banks, and government offices. All nine persons with complex communication needs reported a high degree of satisfaction with the project, and the service providers (e.g. shopkeepers, bank clerks) provided very positive feedback as well.

People who use AAC have new expectations for participation in society (McNaughton & Kennedy, 2010). Providing appropriate supports for both people who use AAC and their communication partners will support active participation in a wide variety of community activities (Arnold, 2018; Dattilo et al. 2008; Hajjar et al. 2016; Rackensperger, 2018).

## SKILLS AND SUPPORTS FOR PARTICIPATION ACROSS THE FIVE DOMAINS

Each of the five domains described here poses unique communication challenges. At the same time, there are three key areas of support that are important across all five domains, and across the life span: the promotion of self-determination, preparation for transitions, and the pursuit of ambitious goals.

### Self-Determination

The term self-determination is used to describe a wide range of behaviors that enable a person to act as the primary causal agent in his or her own life, and to act in ways that maintain or improve that person's quality of life (McNaughton et al. 2010). Self-determination should not be regarded as a set of isolated skills. Although there are specific behaviors that assist an individual in acting in a self-determined manner, it is

Participation in Education, Employment, and Community Settings
505

the integrated and functional use of these component behaviors in acting as primary causal agent in one's own life that is important (Wehmeyer, 1996).

Randy Horton is a young adult who uses speech-generating technology as part of his AAC system. As one form of self-determination, Randy has learned to advocate for his personal safety while riding on public transportation:

I tell the driver politely, at first, what needs to be done. If the driver does not heed my directions, I say "Company rules say that it is your responsibility." Then, if there is still no compliance, I say, "You need to call your supervisor," followed by, "All right I will call them myself." And, "Please send a supervisor," if the driver refused to tie my chair down. (Horton, Horton, &amp; Meyers, 2005, p. 85)

To act in a self-determined manner, people who use AAC must enjoy a strong sense of personal identity. However, it can be difficult for individuals with severe disabilities to establish and maintain a clear sense of their strengths and needs when faced with the labels and low expectations imposed by society.

Jamila, a 17-year-old young woman with cerebral palsy and multiple, complex medical conditions, described the challenge of low expectations faced by many people with severe disabilities:

Most people assume that just because my muscles and lungs and stomach do not work the way theirs do, that my brain and heart and soul are disabled too . . . I am a real and whole human being . . . I want them to know that it is not OK to treat me like I am invisible, or talk about me like I do not exist . . . I am not the puppet of my [speech-generating device]. I am the puppeteer. (Teachman, McDonough, MacArthur, &amp; Gibson, 2018, p. 40)

The acquisition of personal identity and self-confidence is best supported by the opportunity to participate in a wide range of activities, with a wide range of communication partners. In addition, opportunities for making decisions should be a regular part of the daily experience of people with complex communication needs. Children and adults with severe disabilities have demonstrated the ability to exercise control over their environment when provided with structured choice-making opportunities by caregivers (King et al., 2014; McNaughton &amp; Light, 1989). Beyond making choices, people with complex communication needs benefit from opportunities to learn and make use of decision-making strategies (Cohen &amp; Light, 2000; Light et al., 2007). McCarthy, Light, and McNaughton (2007) described the benefit of organized instruction in a collaborative problem-solving strategy (DOIT!) for five young adults who used AAC. Following an average of 8 hours of instruction, all five participants demonstrated the ability to make use of the collaborative problem-solving strategy, and they reported that they would recommend similar instruction to other adolescents who used AAC.

Although self-determination is strongly associated with a high quality of life for people who use AAC (Lund &amp; Light, 2006), and is of high importance to individuals who use AAC (Rackensperger, 2018), it is typically viewed as a low priority by education personnel (Wehmeyer, 2005). This may reflect a misconception that self-determination means independent control over large decisions, which may be viewed as an inappropriate and unachievable goal. As Wehmeyer (2005) noted, however, the goal of education is "not to teach students to control their lives. It is to enable students with severe disabilities to become more self-determined, even if it is just a little more" (p. 119). Individuals with complex communication needs can be

AAC Interventions for Individuals with Developmental Disabilities

assisted in exercising self-determination in a wide variety of situations. For example, for some individuals, at some times of their lives, support for self-determination may include developing AAC displays with special vocabulary to discuss transition options (Cameron &amp; Murphy, 2002). For other individuals, at other times in their lives, it may mean ensuring that the individual has regular opportunities to make choices among preferred meal items and to have those decisions respected (Hingsburger, 2010).

Like communication, self-determination is not one more skill to be learned in isolation, but a critical part of every activity. Too often, young adults who use AAC have come to accept society's reduced view of their skills and interests, and they will need regular meaningful opportunities to exercise self-determination to develop a sense of self and a belief in their own abilities. However, although every life involves unique decisions and choices, the need to exercise control over one's life, to act in a self-determined manner, is common to all. As Light and Gulens (2000) described,

Communicative competence and self-determination are at the core of our existence as human beings. Together, they allow us to define who we are, what dreams we have, how these dreams are realized (or not), and what connections and relationships we build with others. (p. 38)

## Preparation for Transitions

Across the life span, people with complex communication needs will experience many transitions in their lives. For example, as children they will face changes across school grades, and as adults they will experience different employment and volunteer settings, and new living arrangements. The AAC team members can prepare for future environments by sampling the next environment—for example, visiting a future classroom or living situation and considering the communication demands of this new environment, and considering the implications for intervention. At these times, it is valuable to identify key professionals in this future environment and, if possible, arrange for them to visit the individual with complex communication needs in the person's current environment, so they can see current supports and communication performance. It may also be valuable to create videos of current accessing techniques and positioning so that effective approaches can be replicated in future settings. By anticipating future needs (and preparing and practicing needed communication strategies in advance), the AAC team can avoid making big changes in settings and communication systems at the same time. Some changes are always needed in new settings, but ideally the individual with complex communication needs is not dealing with both changes in the environment and large changes in the AAC system at the same time (Beukelman &amp; Mirenda, 2013).

Insight into future environments can also be gained by speaking with individuals who have already negotiated the transition and are successfully participating in the new setting. A series of both face-to-face (Ballin, Balandin, &amp; Stancliffe, 2012) and e-mail-supported (Cohen &amp; Light, 2000; Light et al., 2007) mentor projects, in which older individuals who use AAC share experiences and strategies for addressing challenges with

Additional information on the life experiences of people who use AAC and their family members (i.e., consumer perspectives) is available at the AAC Learning Center web site.

younger individuals who use AAC, have demonstrated the benefits of shared life lessons across the generations. There is also a growing literature of print publications, video presentations, and online blogs by people who use AAC (and their family members) that can be of benefit in planning for life changes.

## Pursuit of Ambitious Goals

Providing effective supports is not just a question of knowledge and skills, but also of attitude—a belief that the individual with complex communication needs has the right to pursue ambitious goals.

In this passage, Tracy Rackensperger (an adult with cerebral palsy who uses AAC) describes the importance of high expectations for team members. Since Tracy wrote these words, she has successfully earned her doctorate, obtained employment in a university setting, and organized the supports needed to live independently.

> Being able to be independent and having the freedom to control my own destiny are the most important things to me. I am a very ambitious individual with lots of goals for my life . . . I, and others who use augmentative communication, want good jobs, good places to live, and individuals who care about us and love us. It is important for the individuals who work with people who use augmentative communication to believe they can succeed at high levels. (Rackensperger, 2006)

You can read more about Tracy at the AAC Learning Center web site, including her presentation on “I go everywhere independently”: AAC supports for a VERY active life (Rackensperger, 2018).

As Tracy's story makes clear, AAC intervention must be a collaborative effort guided by the needs, skills, and interests of the individual with complex communication needs and the individual's family. The use of a person‐ and family‐centered approach is essential for achieving meaningful outcomes (see Chapter 4). Successful intervention also requires that team members not only have knowledge and skills in their areas of expertise, but also possess and demonstrate high expectations for positive outcomes for people with disabilities.

## CONCLUSIONS

The field of AAC has witnessed dramatic changes in recent years. As a result of individual and group advocacy, legislation, and research, there have been dramatic changes in societal participation for children and adults with developmental disabilities who require AAC (Light & McNaughton, 2012). Now, many individuals who use AAC expect to be active and meaningful participants in a wide range of environments—family, school, work, and community. Children with ASD, cerebral palsy, Down syndrome, and other developmental disabilities are using AAC to participate in general education classrooms, to learn literacy skills, to prepare for active and meaningful participation in adult society, and to interact with friends and family members (e.g. Babb et al. 2019; Brock, Biggs, Carter, Cattey, & Raley, 2016; Chung & Carter, 2013; O'Neill, Light, & McNaughton, 2017; Therrien et al. 2016). Adults with severe disabilities are living in the community and using AAC to participate in employment, to volunteer, and to take part in recreational activities (e.g. Caron & Light, 2016; Richardson et al. 2019; Solarsh & Johnson, 2017; Trembath et al. 2010).

Chris Klein is an individual with severe cerebral palsy. As a child, Chris had limited access to AAC supports and was frequently frustrated by breakdowns in communication at school and at home. He is now an expert user of AAC technologies and, with the use of his AAC devices, teaches in college classes and interacts with preservice communication and education professionals across the United States. He wrote the following to describe the impact of AAC in his life:

> AAC is my bridge to the world, and a window for the world to see the real me. It supported me in moving from frustration to communication, and from isolation to relationships with others. AAC has given me the tools to live independently, to participate in society, and to contribute to the lives of others as a husband, teacher, and friend. (McNaughton et al. 2019, p. 56)

Continued progress will require a willingness for all to reconsider past assumptions, and to embrace ambitious new goals (Bumble et al. 2018). There is clear evidence of the positive outcomes that are possible when appropriate supports and interventions are provided—the challenge for the future is to make the possible the probable for all (Light & McNaughton, 2012).

IV

Augmentative and Alternative Communication Interventions for Individuals with Acquired Disabilities

.

14

# Individuals with Acquired Physical Conditions

Laura J. Ball, Amy S. Nordness, and David R. Beukelman

Sam had amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) for 6 years. For 4 of those years, he used mechanical, invasive ventilation and nutritional support. He was diagnosed with ALS after he noticed weakness in his arms and decided to see a neurologist. After about a year, his speaking rate began to slow. Even though his speech was still completely intelligible, a speech-language pathologist from the ALS clinic monitored his speech performance for change. This strategy provided time and opportunity to complete voice/message banking (audio recording of messages to eventually be stored in his augmentative and alternative communication [AAC] technology) and choose, obtain funding for, acquire, and learn to operate AAC technology before his speech intelligibility deteriorated. When Sam's assessment indicated slowed rate (i.e., approached 125 words per minute compared with 190 words per minute of typical adult speakers, or approximately 70% of the typical rate) on the Speech Intelligibility Test–Sentence Version (Yorkston, Beukelman, Hakel, &amp; Dorsey, 2007), he completed an AAC assessment and began to bank a few preferred messages. Within a couple of months after completing the AAC assessment, Sam began to notice that communication partners were straining to understand him in some situations. Soon thereafter, his speech deteriorated very rapidly, and he was no longer understandable (even by family members) within 3 more months. Because an AAC assessment had been completed in a timely manner, his AAC technology arrived prior to the rapid deterioration, and he had time to learn how to operate and communicate effectively with it before he became completely unable to speak intelligibly. He used the system with gradually more frequency, particularly in situations where his communication broke down. Because of weakness and paralysis, he controlled tablet computer-based AAC technology using eye tracking to produce messages through spelling, word prediction, and message retrieval. He maintained an active social life by e-mailing and texting colleagues, friends, and family members. He used the telephone to communicate by pairing his AAC technology voice with a speakerphone. He also used his technology to access the Internet and read online newspapers and electronic books. In addition to his high-tech AAC system, Sam used eye-linking, low-tech techniques (see Chapter 7) when his eye-tracking technology was not available or convenient. He accessed his AAC system with eye-tracking technology until a couple of weeks before his death. At that point he used low-tech eye linking to communicate with those around him.

519

This chapter summarizes assessment and intervention approaches to a number of acquired physical impairments that result from neurological conditions and cause motor speech disorders, including ALS, multiple sclerosis, Guillain-Barré syndrome, Parkinson's disease, brainstem stroke, and others. Subsequent chapters discuss information related to the acquired disabilities of traumatic brain injury, aphasia, and dementia secondary to stroke.

## AMYOTROPHIC LATERAL SCLEROSIS

ALS is a progressive, degenerative disease of unknown etiology involving the motor neurons of the brain and spinal cord (Mitchell & Borasio, 2007). It attacks nerve cells controlling voluntary muscles but does not affect sensation. There are two types of ALS, sporadic and familial, with 90% to 95% of individuals exhibiting the sporadic form and 5% to 10% the familial form (ALS Association, 2018). Prevalence data on ALS from 2013 reported 5.0 cases per 100,000 people in the United States. Additionally, males had a higher overall prevalence (6.4) compared to females (3.7; Mehta et al. 2016). Yorkston, Miller, Strand, and Britton (2012) report the mean age of onset for ALS as 56 years of age. The most common early symptom is weakness (Wijesekera & Leigh, 2009), with approximately one third of those affected reporting initial upper-extremity (arm and hand) weakness, one third reporting leg weakness, one quarter presenting with bulbar (brainstem) weakness manifested by dysarthria and dysphagia, and 5% presenting with initial respiratory weakness. Extraocular muscles that control eye movements are usually unaffected, as is sphincter control. As the disease progresses, motor weakness may become pervasive, such that the individual requires assistance for personal care, mobility, and feeding, as well as respiratory support. Research in Japan identified neck weakness as the primary prognostic factor of loss of speech, loss of swallowing function, and end of life (Nakamura et al. 2013). The median survival rates are 32 months from onset of symptoms and 19 months from diagnosis (Yorkston et al. 2012). Because respiratory failure is typically the cause of death, forced vital capacity is closely monitored throughout the entire disease process. However, life expectancy can be significantly extended if those with ALS, supported by their families, choose a tracheostomy and mechanical ventilation for respiratory support. Because approximately 80% (Saunders, Walsh, & Smith, 1981) to 95% (Ball, Beukelman, & Pattee, 2003) of people with ALS are unable to speak by the time of their deaths, they commonly require AAC support to meet their communication needs.

## Communication Symptoms

Dysarthria, a motor speech disorder, results from the weakness and spasticity inherent in ALS. Dysarthria of the mixed flaccid-spastic type is almost universally present at some point (Duffy, 2004; Yorkston, Beukelman, Strand, & Hakel, 2010). People with predominantly bulbar (brainstem) involvement experience this speech disorder early in the disease process, and their speech and swallowing functions may deteriorate rapidly. Makkonen, Ruottinen, Puhto, Helminen, For further discussion of AAC for people with ALS, see the webcast AAC: A User's Perspective by Colin Portnuff. For a personal discussion of his AAC use after years with ALS, see the webcast by Godfrey Nazareth, The sky is only the beginning: Living life without limits. Both webcasts are available at https://aac-learning-center.psu.edu.

Individuals with Acquired Physical Conditions

and Palmio (2018) reported 60% of individuals with ALS had lost their speech by 18 months after the onset of their first bulbar symptom. Such individuals may be able to walk and even drive; yet they are unable to speak. Individuals with predominantly spinal involvement, however, may retain normal or mildly dysarthric speech of the same mixed flaccid-spastic type for a considerable period of time even as they experience extensive motor impairments in their extremities.

Although the progression of speech symptoms differs from individual to individual, nearly all people with ALS experience a severe communication disorder during the latter portion of their lives. Laura Ball, Amy Nordness, David Beukelman, and Gary Pattee collaborated to develop and maintain the Nebraska ALS Database, in which they recorded data from participants in ALS clinics sponsored by the Muscular Dystrophy Association and the ALS Association. Of the 300 people with ALS in that group, only 7% communicated by using natural speech at the time of their deaths, and 93% relied on AAC.

In addition to speech, AAC interventionists must also be aware that cognitive and behavioral changes do occur among some people with ALS. Research indicates that although only 6.5% of people with ALS exhibit a frontotemporal dementia, 4% exhibit a mild cognitive impairment. Additionally, 16.5% exhibit a severe and 14% exhibit a mild behavioral impairment (Murphy et al., 2016). The greatest behavioral impairment associated with ALS is apathy, with other characteristics noted to be irritability, inflexibility, poor frustration tolerance, and emotional indifference (Murphy et al., 2016). Although mild impairments rarely prevent successful implementation of AAC systems, it is important to screen for both cognitive and behavioral impairments, as these issues may impact individuals' acceptance of and ability to learn to use AAC systems.

Finally, aphasia may occasionally be associated with ALS (Bak &amp; Hodges, 2001; Mitsuyama, Kogoh, &amp; Ata, 1985; Tsuchiya et al., 2000). In a few rare cases, primary progressive aphasia appears to evolve into ALS. For example, Caselli et al. (1993) reported on seven individuals in whom articulatory and language impairment proceeded to rapidly progressive ALS. Duffy, Peach, and Strand (2007) described a series of cases in which progressive apraxia of speech was ultimately diagnosed as ALS. Researchers have also described a frontotemporal lobar dementia syndrome that has three categories: frontotemporal dementia (primarily involving personality changes), semantic dementia (e.g., fluent aphasia, which is characterized by fluent but often meaningless speech, often with limited understanding of spoken or written words), and primary progressive aphasia (e.g., nonfluent aphasia with loss of spoken or written word meaning; Lomen-Hoerth, 2004; Lomen-Hoerth et al., 2003). Frontotemporal lobar dementia syndrome has been reported to be more common among people with ALS who have bulbar symptoms, are somewhat older (M = 65 years), and have decreased functional vital capacity (M = 66% of predicted respiratory capacity).

## A Model for AAC Intervention

AAC interventionists typically employ some version of the three-phase intervention model described by Ball, Beukelman, and Bardach (2007). The Early Phase (Monitor, Prepare, and Support) occurs during the period from initial diagnosis through referral for an AAC assessment. Speech-language pathologists monitor speech for changes, screen for cognitive and behavioral changes, support voice banking/message banking, and educate the people with ALS, as well as other decision makers, about possible

AAC Interventions for Individuals with Acquired Disabilities

changes in speech performance, as well as other factors, such as respiratory intervention options, that will potentially influence future decisions about communication supports. The Middle Phase (Assess, Recommend, and Implement) refers to the time from the referral for AAC assessment until AAC supports are selected and purchased and initial instruction is completed. The Late Phase (Adapt and Accommodate) involves the time after initial AAC intervention until the individual's death, as modifications in AAC supports are needed to deal with changing communication needs and physical capabilities.

**Early Phase: Monitor, Prepare, and Support** The Early Phase begins at the time of the diagnosis, when the person with ALS often has natural speech that is functional to meet daily communication needs. If the person has spinal-onset ALS, changes in speech performance may not yet have begun. If the person has bulbar-onset ALS, mild changes in speaking rate may have begun, in which case this phase may be quite brief.

**Monitor Speech Performance** An important activity in the Early Phase is to monitor speech performance on a systematic schedule to detect changes that signal the need for a timely referral for an AAC assessment. In the past, reduction in speech intelligibility (understandability) was used as the standard for determining when an AAC assessment should occur. However, once reductions in speech intelligibility are observed, such precipitous drops in intelligibility commonly occur that there is usually insufficient time to initiate and execute AAC assessment and intervention before the individual is unable to meet his or her communication needs through natural speech alone. Research has demonstrated that a progressive reduction in speaking rate precedes reduction in speech intelligibility (Ball, Beukelman, &amp; Pattee, 2002; Yorkston, Klasner, et al., 2003).

Appropriate timing of AAC intervention requires systematic monitoring of speaking rate and intelligibility. Objective, rather than subjective, measures are essential because subjective estimates of intelligibility are often inaccurate. The authors use the Speech Intelligibility Test-Sentence Version (Yorkston et al., 2007) because it provides an objective measure of speaking rate and intelligibility. The speaking rate can be measured when the test is administered in the clinical setting so that the clinician can immediately provide rate information to the medical staff, the individual with ALS, and those who accompany the individual. This test produces a set of 11 sentences that are read aloud by the person with ALS. Speaking rate is calculated immediately, and the utterances are later transcribed to obtain measures of speech intelligibility and efficiency.

Additional measures in all speech subsystems (i.e., respiratory, phonatory, articulatory, and resonatory) are being studied to identify even earlier predictors of bulbar decline. Rong, Yunusova, Wang, and Green (2015) reported that articulatory and phonatory predictors may be a sensitive indicator of early decline. Although some measures, such as alternating motion rates (e.g., "puhpuhpuh") and sequential motion rates (e.g., "puhtuhkuh"), can be obtained in a multidisciplinary clinic setting, many other measures require extensive equipment to capture voice and kinematic measures that may not be available in many clinics, and therefore these measures are difficult to complete except in a specialized clinical setting.

Ball et al. (2002) reported that people with ALS gradually reduce their speaking rate as ALS progresses. The relationship between speaking rate and speech

523

intelligibility is illustrated in Figure 14.1. These authors recommend that an AAC assessment be recommended when the speaking rate approaches 125 words per minute. When speaking rate reaches approximately 125 words per minute, a rather dramatic decrease in speech intelligibility is expected (i.e., within the next 2 months for some individuals and within 4 to 6 months for others). For a limited number of individuals, dysarthria of such severity that it reduces speech intelligibility occurs prior to significant rate reduction; in such cases, an AAC assessment is recommended when sentence intelligibility drops below 90%, regardless of speaking rate (Ball et al., 2007). Speaking rate can be accurately monitored via conventional analog or digital telephone technology if an individual with ALS is unable to travel to a clinic due to distance, weather, health, or transportation difficulties. Measures of speaking rate are essentially identical for face-to-face and telephone monitoring (Ball, Beukelman, Ullman, Maassen, &amp; Pattee, 2005). Of course, speech intelligibility scores are affected by telephone transmission and should not be evaluated at a distance over a telephone.

Screen Cognition and Behavioral Function A second activity in the Early Phase is to screen cognition and behavioral function. Because cognitive and behavioral impairments can affect communication, decision making, and use of AAC systems, it is important to identify individuals with cognitive and behavioral impairments early in the course of the disease. The Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis Cognitive Behavioral Scale (ALS-CBS) is an effective screening tool that can assess both cognition and behavior (Woolley et al., 2010). If individuals score below a cut-off for frontotemporal dementia, clinicians can consider referring for a more comprehensive neuropsychological assessment and trial compensatory supports (Merrilees, Klapper, Murphy, Lomen-Hoerth, &amp; Miller, 2010), or begin a simplified communication system early to allow for time for the individual to habituate to the technique.

Figure 14.1. Speaking rate and intelligibility decline for people with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). (Key: WPM, words per minute.)

Support AAC Options

A third activity in the Early Phase is to support people with ALS if they choose voice banking and/or message banking as AAC options. It is important to inform people with ALS and their families about the option to voice bank and/or message bank early, as the best time to record their voice is before speech changes occur. Voice banking refers to the process of recording the individual's speech to create a synthetic voice that approximates their natural voice. This allows a speech synthesizer to use the voice of a person with ALS to generate novel messages and to generate messages via spelling words. The process can take 4--6 hours of recording time, and individuals with ALS frequently need to break this up into smaller increments due to fatigue. There are currently several commercial companies that use a range of different methods to support voice banking.

Message banking refers to recording some personally chosen messages in your own voice and inflection as a .wav file that can be uploaded to an AAC technology and played at a later date when you want to say one of those messages. Some individuals with ALS opt for message banking, while others choose none and rely solely on the synthetic voices available in their AAC technology.

### Refer to an AAC Team

A fourth activity in the Early Phase is to make a timely referral to an AAC team, so that there is sufficient time to complete the assessment, select AAC options, purchase the AAC technology, and instruct the person who will rely on AAC and his or her facilitators.

### Assist in Implementation of AAC Supports

A fifth activity in the Early Phase is to assist the speaker with ALS to implement AAC supports that will preserve communication effectiveness of their natural speech for as long as possible. By reducing speech effort and fatigue but amplifying residual speech, and by allocating speaking time for important social or informational exchanges during the day, the individual can conserve energy to communicate effectively, even though dysarthria might be apparent to communication partners. Some individuals benefit from utilizing a voice amplification system to support their communication and reduce the overall effort required to speak. For a limited number of individuals with specific velopharyngeal weakness that interferes with speech or oral breathing and without hyperactive reflexes or spasticity, a palatal lift may be recommended (E. Hanson, Yorkston, & Britton, 2011; Yorkston et al. 2010). Some individuals with bulbar ALS who experience loss of effective communication or considerable fatigue while speaking may choose to use an AAC application on a mobile tablet or smart phone to support effective communication in situations where communication is particularly difficult, or to reduce fatigue. It is also important to educate persons with ALS and their caregivers about arranging their environment for successful communication (e.g. turn off background television/music when talking, light on speaker's face, and so on), as well as maximizing the hearing of communication partners.

Toward the end of the Early Phase, some people with ALS use their remaining natural speech to prepare video or audio recordings for their loved ones. As Tom neared the time when he needed AAC to communicate, he arranged to prepare video-recorded messages for his wife, each of his children, and his children's spouses. He talked to each of them individually as he recalled important memories and shared experiences. He told them how

much he appreciated and loved them. He talked about his disease and how much their care and respect meant to him. After completing the recordings, he selected pictures and had them incorporated into the video.

### Educate People About AAC-Related Decisions

A sixth activity in the Early Phase is to educate the person with ALS and decision makers about AAC-related decisions. This education includes information about natural speech deterioration, timing of AAC assessment, low- and high-tech AAC options, and technology purchases, as well as funding. The goal of this education is to prepare them to efficiently make AAC-related decisions at the appropriate time. We have observed that some people are very interested in this information and actually seek out additional information, whereas others express little or no interest and indicate that they will rely extensively on professionals to guide their decision making. Some choose early adoption of a mobile tablet (e.g. iPad, Android tablet) with a communication application. It may be helpful to consider the targeted AAC system if/when arm and hand function no longer allows the individual to access a touchscreen; transition will be easier if the timing of implementing the new system is identified and the communication app remains generally consistent across the technologies.

A 55-year-old male developed bulbar symptoms while he was actively engaged in his career and family. He desired to continue working as long as possible, even though his work relied heavily on his speech to conduct trainings in-person and via video connection from a distance. He banked his voice early to prepare for future changes. He worked closely with his employer for support to continue giving his trainings by scheduling them to allow for vocal rest between presentations. He integrated more visual materials throughout his presentations to support comprehension and supplement his speech in the context of changes. He utilized handwriting to resolve quick communication breakdowns in person, but this was not effective for group presentations or speaking over the phone. He downloaded an AAC application to his smart phone and tablet to support communication breakdown in large group settings, over the phone, and throughout work presentations. This application supported a way to upload his banked voice messages. He also found these tools to be extremely helpful to manage his medical care at the ALS multidisciplinary clinic, as the hospital system wanted him to utilize digital communication media to access his medical records, make appointments, and communicate with his care team through the patient portal of his electronical medical record. This proved to be an efficient way to take charge of his medical care as his speech declined. It also allowed him to utilize other digital communication media outlets, such as e-mail and texting, to prepare his clients in advance of presentations, resolve unanswered questions, and make a personal connection with his clients. When his speaking rate reached 125 words per minute, he participated in an AAC evaluation to explore a system that could meet a greater number of communication needs. He was starting to lose function in his hands and was struggling to access his smart phone and tablet. With AAC technology, he was able to regain effective access to a high-technology device and was able to connect to the communication media outlets that he already had been using to stay in control of his medical care and work. Although he was still able to use one hand to access his techology via direct selection, he selected technology that could also support eye gaze access as needed in the future.

Overall, he effectively accessed multiple communication supports, low-tech and high-tech tools, and various communication media outlets as his muscle function changed over time. In addition, he was confidently prepared to make decisions that would support his lifelong communication.

### Middle Phase: Assess, Recommend, Implement

During the middle phase, the person with ALS participates in an AAC evaluation, in which four activities are stressed: 1) identifying participation patterns and associated communication needs; 2) assessing current and anticipated capabilities—motor (physical), cognitive, speech and language, visual, and hearing; 3) assessing potential constraints affecting AAC decisions, as well as social and personal care supports; and 4) selecting low- and high-tech AAC options to meet current and future needs.

### Identify Participation Patterns and Communication Needs

Individuals who experience acquired physical disabilities that affect their ability to communicate often also experience other dramatic changes in their lives. Depending on the progression of the specific condition or disease, these changes may occur gradually (as with a degenerative disease such as ALS) or more abruptly (as with an acute impairment such as trauma or stroke). Individuals' physical disabilities, along with personal lifestyle preferences, determine their communication needs and their participation roles and contexts. For example, some people with severe degenerative disabilities such as ALS prefer to center their lives within their home environment. Sam, described at the start of this chapter, was such an individual. These individuals find that it is more efficient and less demanding on their families to establish their homes as their primary work, social, and care setting rather than to continue to participate extensively in the larger community. Thus, they may work at home if they are active vocationally. Friends and family visit them at home, and they travel only for special events. Some use the Internet to maintain contact with their social and support networks. Eventually, they may go through numerous transitions involving their living situation (e.g. private home, assisted living, nursing home, hospice), which will have an impact on the available funding for AAC as well as necessitate changes to their AAC systems.

Continued employment plays an important role in the lives of some individuals with ALS (McNaughton, Light, & Groszyk, 2001). Jamie wished to continue working after she was diagnosed with bulbar ALS. She continued to work in her position as a data-entry specialist, using multimodal technologies for her daily communication supports. She used her computer with the keyboard to enter data, access the Internet, and send e-mail. She used her cell phone to send text messages to family and friends. Although she identified a more complex AAC technology to fully meet her communication needs, she purchased mobile technology with an AAC application for communicating with people in meetings, socially, and on the telephone. She selected this as a temporary measure, knowing that she would require AAC technology with additional options in the future. Although she was experiencing hand weakness and atrophy, she made the decision because she retained the ability to access touchscreen technology with her hands. Interventions for people with ALS who wish to continue to work should include computer literacy and Internet training to provide options for continuing employment by accessing a range of supports. Expanded electronic communication options such as e-mail, the Internet, electronic conferencing, and

cellular technology have resulted in expanded opportunities for employment, volunteering, distance learning, financial transactions, and commercial activity. Participation in virtual activity is of little interest to some people who use AAC technology; however, others participate regularly, both socially and vocationally, using the Internet.

Other individuals adopt a different participation strategy and attempt to stay active in the community as long as they possibly can. These individuals may continue to work outside the home, travel, and attend recreational activities, religious services, and social events with friends and family. The following case study provides an example of this strategy.

Tom and his family maintained a very externally focused lifestyle even after he was diagnosed with ALS. During the first 18 months following his diagnosis, Tom and his wife traveled extensively, at times with their children, at times with Tom's siblings, and often with friends. When he began to use a wheelchair and eventually rely on AAC technology, they scheduled “Time with Tom” at a local restaurant every Monday during the dinner hour. Friends, former colleagues, church members, neighbors, and relatives stopped by to participate at their convenience. Tom continued to attend athletic events and concerts. He telephoned family and friends to celebrate birthdays and anniversaries. Needless to say, Tom received considerable support and developed comprehensive AAC skills in order to participate in these extensive social interactions (Rutz, 2005).

Decisions about patterns of participation substantially affect an individual's communication needs and corresponding AAC supports. For example, an individual who communicates primarily at home or in a long-term acute care hospital may need AAC technology that can easily be moved to various rooms on a cart or on a computer stand with wheels, rather than an AAC technology that attaches directly to a wheelchair. Individuals who participate actively in the community need communication systems that are self-contained, compact, and fully portable. Many prefer efficient Internet access via their AAC technology. Most require a means to use the telephone and e-mail. All individuals with ALS require a way to access a call system to reach out for support and to call 911 in case of an emergency. During assessment and intervention, it is important to consider the individual opinions and preferences of adults with acquired disabilities regarding their participation and lifestyle patterns.

A clinician who provides AAC services in a regional ALS clinic reported the following: Of those with ALS who access their AAC technology using eye gaze during the past year, all used this technology to support face-to-face communication, and more than 90% also used this technology for text entry to communicate using e-mail or texting with the medical providers, caregivers, or family members. About 80% accessed the Internet to obtain information about their medical condition, AAC options, or other information of interest to them. Sixty percent accessed their environmental control technology using their eye-gaze AAC technology. Three quarters of these individuals and their communication partners used partner-dependent eye gaze to communicate urgent or immediate needs to interact when the eye-gaze AAC technology was not available to them while they were in bed, in the restroom, or traveling in a vehicle. (K. Rodgers, personal communication, 2018)

Yorkston, Baylor, and Mach (2017) found that the more communicatively active persons with ALS remain, the more positively they rate their communicative participation. In general, Yorkston and colleagues reported speech severity, swallowing severity, and speech usage accounted for 55% of the variance associated with communicative participation. Caron and Light (2015) reported that individuals with ALS reported continued strong communication participation after speech declined, using multiple communication media options.

Developing consensus among the person who uses AAC and the individuals who support him or her is essential to creating a profile of the individual's communication needs and participation. One way to build consensus is to identify potential communication needs and assign each a level of importance. Fried-Oken et al. (2006) reported the importance of expressing certain communication purposes for a group of persons with ALS, and identified calling for help, getting needs met, clarifying needs with caregivers, giving instructions, discussing important issues or concerns, conversing about health care, staying connected, chatting, and expressing feelings as mandatory. Others found being polite, flirting or being romantic, being funny, having casual conversations, chatting, telling stories, talking about religion, conversing about work, and comforting others to be mandatory communication purposes. A review of the information provided previously about Jamie and Tom reveals that many of their communication needs were similar; however, their lifestyle choices dictated different communication solutions.

A detailed needs assessment has advantages for both the person with the disability and the members of his or her family and support networks. For example, it is not uncommon for adults with acquired communication disorders to insist that their AAC systems provide (or maintain) all of the functions of natural speech. This insistence is natural because many people struggle to accept their disabilities and are often frustrated by their inability to communicate in the same way that was possible with natural speech. In the process of completing a communication needs inventory, these individuals are forced to go beyond the generic expectation of “being able to do everything that I could do before this happened” to identify specific communication needs and assign them priorities. In a study examining the purposes of AAC technology use for people with ALS as reported by their caregivers, Rau et al. (2004) found that the two most frequent and highly valued purposes involved regulating the behavior of others (for basic wants and needs) and staying connected (social closeness).

### Assess Current and Anticipated Future Capabilities

As discussed in Chapter 2, AAC teams usually conduct assessments of cognitive, motor, speech and language, and sensory capabilities with people who have acquired physical disabilities. One particularly important aspect of the assessment process for individuals with ALS involves predicting the natural course of abilities. People with degenerative diseases will gradually lose some capabilities while other capabilities remain stable. Subsequent sections of this chapter discuss these issues in more detail with regard to specific disabilities.

Individual patterns of motor control greatly affect the selection of AAC systems for individuals with ALS. It is therefore essential to assess motor capabilities and to consider the impact of fatigue throughout each day. Motor capabilities generally differ markedly, depending on whether the person first experiences bulbar or spinal

symptoms. Typically, a physical and/or occupational therapist will be involved in the motor assessment.

People with predominantly bulbar (brainstem, speech) symptoms are initially able to control AAC technology that they can carry and operate via direct selection using their hands or fingers. However, in time, they are often unable to access their AAC technology with their hands or fingers and must shift to a head- or eye-tracking, direct-selection access technique. Of course, this is essentially always the case if they choose to use invasive ventilation for respiratory support, as this usually will extend their life expectancy and increase the time that they will need to access their AAC technology with head- or eye-tracking strategies. It is imperative that they select a device that can transition with them as their motor capabilities change.

People with ALS who exhibit predominantly spinal symptoms usually experience extensive trunk- and limb-related motor impairments before they become unable to meet their communication needs through speech. For individuals with spinal ALS, the need for an augmented writing system often precedes the need for an augmented conversational system. Individuals with severe impairments related to limb control usually require a mounted system with either head- or eye tracking for direct-selection access, because the time will come when they cannot access their AAC technology with arm or hand movements.

### Assess Constraints and Select High- and Low-Tech AAC Options

A variety of external constraints may affect AAC decisions in general, and some of these constraints are especially common for people with acquired communication disorders. As noted previously, the attitudes of family members and friends about the communication disorder in general and the acceptance of AAC technology in particular may influence decisions. Typically, families of people with ALS accept AAC options because they realize that ALS is a degenerative disease.

Another constraint involves the availability of communication facilitators to learn about the operation and use of AAC technology in order to assist the person who relies on AAC to learn and maintain it. In some locations, facilitators may not have access to adequate support for certain types of communication options. Another important external constraint involves the availability of funding for equipment and instruction. Funding patterns for AAC systems vary dramatically in different parts of the world. Some countries, provinces, or states fund AAC systems for children who participate in educational It is impossible to outline such funding constraints in detail in this book because funding policies change frequently. A web site on AAC funding maintained by the Assistive Technology Law Center, Duke University Medical Center Division of Speech Pathology and Audiology, and AACRERC (Rehabilitation Engineering Research Center on Communication Enhancement) is available at http://aacfundinghelp.com; it provides AAC funding information for the United States. Successful AAC interventions require that the AAC team assess constraints and focus on the remediation of these limitations as vigorously as they focus on the individual's communication needs and capabilities.

programs but provide little financial support for adults. In the United States, Medicare, Medicaid, Tricare, and many insurance plans now fund AAC technology and instruction to support face-to-face communication was well as typed messages.

In addition, it is not uncommon for family members and friends to have differences of opinion regarding the person's communication needs as well as the use of assistive technologies. There is no way to predict what these differences will be, but it is important to try to achieve some degree of consensus among these people about the individual's communication needs or, if that is impossible, to at least clarify their differences of opinion and facilitate decision making. We discuss this issue with regard to specific disorders in subsequent sections of this chapter.

### Understand Acceptance and Use of AAC by People with Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis and Their Families

Usually, individuals with ALS demonstrate relatively high acceptance of AAC technology. As AAC technology improves and is more common in society, acceptance rates continue to increase. Mathy, Yorkston, and Gutmann (2000) reviewed AAC use by people with ALS from numerous sources. They referred to data by Gutmann and Gryfe (1996), who evaluated trends in the use of AAC systems for 126 people seen at an assistive technology clinic in Toronto. Among these participants, 27% elected not to pursue AAC interventions. Gutmann, analyzing the same data, reported that “women preferred voice output systems twice as often as men (49% for women, 26% for men)” (1999, p. 211). In addition, “almost an equivalent number of men (27.8%) and women (26%) did not wish any AAC intervention” (Gutmann, 1999, p. 211).

### Help Develop Operational Competence

People with ALS, like most people who rely on AAC, require time and instruction to gain communicative competence with their AAC systems. Linse, Aust, Joos, and Herman (2018) report that families should receive at least five hours of training, in addition to ongoing support, troubleshooting, and customizing over time. Because ALS is predictably degenerative, these individuals are in the unique position of being able to select their AAC systems and learn to operate them while they can still use natural speech to meet at least their most basic communication needs. In fact, if an AAC system is selected and implemented after an individual is no longer able to speak, the AAC experience often becomes extremely frustrating.

Although rapid decline of speech function in ALS is certainly not inevitable, it occurs frequently enough that sound clinical management dictates early preparedness. In our experience, exploration of AAC options should begin when speech has slowed to about 125 words per minute and/or intelligibility is inconsistent in adverse listening situations.

### Provide Facilitator Support

People with ALS require ongoing support from AAC facilitators to use their AAC systems. This support may include instruction in technical or other skills that enable individuals to operate the technology efficiently and accurately. They may also need facilitator support to select and modify messages stored in their systems. In addition, as an individual's capabilities change with ALS progression, facilitators may need to change motor control options and the system position. Facilitators may also have to provide instruction in the social use of the AAC system. Ball, Schardt, and Beukelman (2005) surveyed 68 individuals with ALS who relied on AAC technology, and all reported the presence of a primary AAC facilitator.

Nearly all facilitators (96%) were family members, most of them had nontechnical backgrounds, and 4% were professionals.

### Late Phase: Adapt and Accommodate

The Late Phase begins after the implementation of AAC recommended in the Middle Phase and continues until the individual's death. The objective of this phase is to provide effective communication options in response to changing communication needs, capabilities, and living situations. This enables them to maintain proficiency with the technology while making slight changes to messages and access techniques as their communication needs and capabilities change.

In 2004, Ball, Beukelman, and Pattee reported on the AAC acceptance patterns of 50 individuals who were referred to an ALS clinic. Of the individuals with ALS in this study, 96% accepted AAC technology either immediately (90%) or after some delay (6%). Only 4% (i.e. two individuals) rejected AAC technology completely. In 2007, Ball, Anderson et al. documented the duration of AAC use by people with ALS and reported average durations of 23.1 months for those with bulbar (brainstem) onset and 25.9 months for those with spinal onset. It should be noted that this sample included individuals with ALS who did and did not choose invasive mechanical ventilation support. Acceptance of mechanical ventilation (respirator or ventilator) extends the length of the individual's life and the duration of AAC use. Of course, invasive ventilation also extends the length of time that people with ALS must access their AAC options with minimal movement. None of the people with ALS in this study discontinued use of their AAC technology more than 2 months before their deaths. Families often report that within the last few weeks of life, people with ALS depend more and more on low-tech options, such as eye linking, eye gaze, or partner-assisted scanning (see Chapter 7 for descriptions of these access techniques) to support the co-construction of messages with people who are very familiar with them. Roman, Quach, Coggiola, and Moore (2010) reported that people with ALS find eye linking to be faster and more preferred than an eye-pointing (e-tran) board or partner-assisted scanning. However, some individuals with ALS continue to have the strength and desire to use AAC technology during the last days of their lives.

In 2015, Ball, Pattee, and Beukelman reported on the AAC technology use of 64 people with ALS who were unable to speak. Approximately half of the participants were prescribed eye gaze to access their AAC technologies. Ninety-one percent of these participants used multiple communication supports, including their AAC technology accessed by eye gaze and partner-dependent eye gaze, for urgent or immediate needs or to interact when the AAC was not available because of their location or physical position, such as riding in a vehicle.

It is vital to ensure individuals with ALS are able to continue to make decisions and communicate independently throughout the Late Phase to ensure quality of life and the continued ability to make important end-of-life decisions. Research has shown that quality of life measures are not always aligned between individuals with ALS and their caregivers; as a result, individuals with ALS may need to self-advocate if their wishes change (Linse et al. 2018; Linse et al. 2017).

It is also important to consider positioning adaptations and multiple communication options in the final stage, as individuals with ALS may spend more time lying down versus upright in a wheelchair (Makkonen et al. 2018). Positioning of AAC technology will need to be adjusted to ensure continued access regardless of location

around the home. A continued focus on meeting changing communication needs and preparing families in advance of each step will help individuals with ALS to stay in charge of their care and to be independent communicators throughout the course of the disease.

## Evaluate Intervention Outcomes

There are three primary reasons for measuring the outcomes of interventions with adults who have acquired physical disabilities. The first is to identify the communication needs that have and have not been met. When an intervention approach succeeds in meeting certain communication needs, the AAC team should document the success for the individual and his or her family. If an initial intervention does not meet certain communication needs, the team should refine the approach and intervene accordingly. The second reason for measuring intervention outcomes is to document the effectiveness of the AAC agency providing the service. Agencies that provide funding for AAC interventions with adults usually demand this documentation for continued funding. The third reason for measuring intervention effectiveness is to document the overall AAC efforts of a particular center or agency, which may result in increased administrative support for AAC efforts over time.

## MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS

Multiple sclerosis is the most common neurological condition of young and middle-aged adults. Although rare, pediatric (under age 18) multiple sclerosis occurs with an estimated incidence of 0.2--0.6 per 100,000 individuals (Langer-Gould et al. 2011). The cause of multiple sclerosis is unknown. It is an acquired, inflammatory, demyelinating disease of the central nervous system (Yorkston et al. 2012). Lesions are scattered in the central nervous system, and locations vary from person to person; therefore, symptom patterns also vary and must be considered when making AAC intervention decisions.

In the northern United States, the prevalence of multiple sclerosis is about 1 in 1,000; and in the southern states, the prevalence is about one third to one half of this figure. Approximately 95% of all cases begin between the ages of 10 and 50 years, with a median onset age of 27 years. Although multiple sclerosis is considered to be a disease of young people, it is not uncommon for an initial diagnosis to occur between 50 and 60 years of age. The female-to-male ratio of occurrence is 3:2 (Yorkston et al. 2012). People with multiple sclerosis are more likely to be White than African American and more likely to be African American than Asian.

The natural course of multiple sclerosis differs greatly from person to person. However, the typical relapsing-remitting pattern begins initially, and the progressive form of the disease occurs later. The relapse rate in pediatric-onset multiple sclerosis is higher than in adult-onset, occurring with significantly greater frequency (Gorman, Healy, Polgar-Turcsanyi, & Chitnis, 2009). The average life expectancy of young males with multiple sclerosis is about 35 years following the onset of the disease. The prognosis is worse 1) in males than in females; 2) if the age at onset is greater than 35 years; or 3) if a chronic, progressive pattern appears at onset (Yorkston et al. 2012). Symptoms experienced by people with multiple sclerosis vary considerably; however, visual, motor, and cognitive impairments may occur as the disease progresses.
