initial assessment, as well as the individual's demonstrated potential to learn additional strategies with teaching and cues.

Garrett and Beukelman's (1992) AAC-Aphasia Categories of Communicators Checklist, revised by Garrett and Lasker in 2005 (available at http://word.emerson.edu/jlasker/past-research), provides clinicians with a checklist of present or emerging communication competencies. This observational checklist is designed to help clinicians match AAC support options with a person's capabilities. The AAC team can document competencies and challenges observed within conversational contexts, during unsupported interactions, and during AAC trials with trained conversational partners. When the majority of communication behaviors appear within a single category (e.g., contextual-choice AAC communicator), it is likely that the person is functioning primarily within that category. It is also important to determine if capabilities in the next category seem to be emerging; therapeutic goals can then be developed to move the individual along the continuum from partner-supported to independent AAC communicator.

## Baseline Modality Assessment

A modified PACE (Promoting Aphasics' Communicative Effectiveness) procedure (Davis &amp; Wilcox, 1985) can be used to elicit a communication exchange between a message sender with aphasia and a receiving communication partner; the AAC team can explore the tendencies of the person with aphasia to use different modalities or whether it appears that the person can be taught to use them. The clinician selects an action picture from a commercially available set of picture cards or any other informal source such as magazines or photographs. Pictures can depict a person completing a simple action (e.g., a woman cutting a cake) or represent a story or scene. Using a barrier task format, the person with aphasia is asked to communicate ideas about the picture to a partner who cannot see the picture. The clinician documents the overall success of the communication (i.e., does the partner eventually understand what is happening in the picture?) and also the methods used by the person with aphasia to communicate. Does the person with aphasia attempt to communicate primarily with speech? When speech is not effective at communicating the message to the partner, does the person with aphasia attempt to use other unaided communication strategies, such as gesture, drawing, or writing? If not, when the clinician cues or models the use of these strategies, can the person with aphasia implement them successfully to convey the information to the partner?

This semistructured exercise allows the clinician to document how the person with aphasia utilizes residual speech abilities, how natural it is for him or her to use strategies other than speech, how well gesture or pantomime is used, and how he or she makes use of retained writing abilities (i.e., using air writing, initial letters, word fragments, alphabet boards).

## Conversational Strategy Trials

The AAC team should also assess expressive and receptive linguistic capabilities in a conversational context, both with and without AAC or contextual supports. This may include a general "getting to know you" conversation. In this portion of evaluation, the clinician selects a personally relevant conversational topic (e.g., past work, hometown memories, a hobby or pastime, family, growing up, courting, getting into trouble in school) and introduces it to the person with aphasia while simultaneously modeling

AAC Interventions for Individuals with Acquired Disabilities

partner-supported communication strategies. In particular, the clinician may wish to explore the following partner-supported conversation strategies: written-choice conversation, augmented input, cued question asking, photo or visual scene referencing, and tagged yes/no responses. These techniques are described in greater detail in previous sections of this chapter. As part of the assessment process, the clinician should record data on the accuracy of the responses. For example, when using written-choice conversation or tagged yes/no responses, the AAC team should confirm accuracy with family members or significant others. In addition, the clinician should document how much prompting (e.g., none, minimal, moderate, maximal) was necessary to teach the strategy to the person with aphasia. Finally, it is important to tally whether a topic or message was communicated successfully to the partner.

## Multimodal Communication Screening Task for Persons with Aphasia

Multimodal Communication Screening Task for Persons with Aphasia (MCST-A; Garrett &amp; Lasker, 2005; Lasker &amp; Garrett, 2006) is an informal assessment tool that reveals how a communicator answers situational questions (i.e., "How would you tell me you went to California in July?") by gesturing, spelling, pointing to locations on a map, or locating pictorial symbols throughout the eight-page booklet used in the screening. It also provides information on the person's ability to categorize and to point referentially when telling a story. The MCST-A stimulus book contains the following pages:

1. Concrete concepts represented with pictures, photos, and words (e.g., eat, lamp)
2. Three categories represented with an incomplete series of visual symbols—the person with aphasia chooses from a row of six additional symbols to complete the categories
3. Graphic symbols representing descriptors (e.g., open, cold)
4. Slightly more abstract concepts that can be combined with other items to represent complex meanings (e.g., grandchildren, money, monthly calendar)
5. Two sets of written words and phrases, one for communicating in a pharmacy and another for conversing with grandchildren
6. A set of photographs representing a story sequence for a storytelling/retelling task
7. An outline map of the United States to represent locations of children's homes or favorite vacations
8. An alphabet board to communicate highly specific names (e.g., towns, restaurants) by spelling or pointing to the first letter

The scoring form documents the accuracy of message transmission via use of the symbols in the stimulus book, as well as the types of cues that the clinician uses to help the communicator achieve communication success.

Research suggests that the MCST-A effectively distinguishes between communicators who require partner support to indicate choices and stored-message AAC communicators who can independently search through the booklet to locate symbols (Lasker &amp; Garrett, 2006). Data on the amount and type of cuing can help determine whether the communicator falls into the category of partner-supported (i.e., consistently requires cues to locate symbols to communicate a message) or independent (i.e., needs no cues or minimal cues to locate symbols to convey a message). It is also relatively easy to identify generative AAC communicators. Clinicians can ask the person with aphasia to communicate a complex message (e.g., "How would you communicate that your grandchildren

AAC Supports for Adults with Severe Aphasia and/or Apraxia of Speech

are going to Disney World next month if they have enough money?”) and then observe if the person can successfully communicate this idea by pointing to a logical sequence of pictures, words, letters, or locations on the map. In addition, observing this diagnostic activity may assist some family members to better understand why a clinician may suggest low-tech instead of high-tech options for an individual with aphasia.

## AAC Trials: Transactional Role Play

To evaluate how effectively a communicator can access stored messages on a speech-output system in an actual communication situation, the AAC team can develop scripted scenarios representing a community transaction and program the communicator's AAC technology with relevant messages. AAC technology with digitized speech for stored messages or synthesized speech output systems (for those people with aphasia who have potential spelling capability) may be used. VSDs may also be used to conduct these scenarios. When selecting a sample conversational scenario, the AAC team should consider such factors as time constraints (how quickly the information must be delivered), information specificity, length and complexity of response, predictability (whether messages can be stored in advance and retrieved), communication functions expressed (social closeness versus basic needs), familiarity (with the conversation content and with the partner), and personal relevance (how important the information is to the individual). For example, a consumer-based transaction in which the communicator orders a cup of coffee from a vendor may be considered an easier conversation than one in which the communicator discusses the nature of his or her disability with a medical practitioner.

After a situation has been scripted, the clinician prepares representative types of speech output AAC technologies. Basing the choices on preliminary estimates, the clinician selects technologies with the most appropriate size and arrangement of messages and number of messages per page. In general, a sequence of four to eight pre-stored messages on AAC technology may be used. Then, the clinician should program necessary vocabulary. For example, a coffee-ordering scenario might be scripted to combine speech, gesture (shown in brackets), and technology use as follows:

|  Clinician (in the role of a coffee vendor): | Hi, how are you today?  |
| --- | --- |
|  Person with aphasia: | Fine/good/okay.  |
|  Clinician: | What can I get you?  |
|  Person with aphasia: | I'D LIKE A CUP OF COFFEE.  |
|  Clinician: Okay. | For here or to go?  |
|  Person with aphasia: | [To go].  |
|  Clinician: | What size?  |
|  Person with aphasia: | MEDIUM.  |
|  Clinician: | How do you take it?  |
|  Person with aphasia: | CREAM AND SUGAR.  |
|  Clinician: | Here you go. That will be $1.25.  |
|  Person with aphasia: | Okay. [hands over money]  |
|  Clinician: | Have a good day.  |
|  Person with aphasia: | [Bye].  |

Each communication attempt during the role play is scored based on response adequacy, mode of response (gesture, speech, AAC), timing, and amount of clinician cuing. Clinicians can use a cuing hierarchy described by Light and Binger (1998) for teaching AAC technology. The clinician first waits and creates an expectation that a message will be generated, points to the individual or the AAC tool, and then models the communication behavior.

## Advanced Systems Trials: Combining Stored and Generative Messages

People with aphasia and limited spoken language may benefit from a generative AAC system if they spontaneously use combinations of two or three symbols on the MCST-A, score highly on reading and writing subtests on standardized tests, or write to convey information during PACE picture description tasks. In this situation, a more demanding role play that requires the communicator to use a combination of generative and stored-message strategies can be implemented. Prior research has demonstrated that people with aphasia identify symbols within an AAC device most readily when fewer symbols per screen are displayed and when minimal navigation is required (Petroi, Koul, & Corwin, 2014). To determine whether a person with aphasia can use multiple displays to accomplish a task, we recommend conducting a trial that requires him or her to navigate displays. In a process similar to the basic trials, the clinician creates a scenario that requires the person with aphasia to demonstrate both message retrieval and message formulation. In addition, the clinician notes whether the person with aphasia can repair communication breakdowns with unaided modalities (gestures, speech, spelling/writing), can combine unaided strategies with aided AAC, and can initiate messages.

For dynamic-display AAC, the clinician may choose to program a situation related to planning a trip, buying a car, or having a “getting to know you” conversation on at least two to three displays of the technology. A trip-planning scenario could be introduced as follows: You are going to plan a vacation trip with a travel agent who will book all of the arrangements. You will use anything you can to communicate with the travel agent. You will need to arrange all of the details—where you are going, how you will get there, where you will stay. For this scenario, the clinician can create a main page with some phrase or sentence messages and links to a second page that contains days of the week, money topics, and preferred vacation activities. After the clinician briefly introduces the AAC technology and available messages, the trials proceed at first without extensive instruction regarding AAC approaches. After the initial trial is completed, the communication behaviors are scored, and then instruction and modeling occurs. Following instruction, the role play is then repeated and scored again. The clinician also should note the degree of cueing required for the person with aphasia to perform various operational functions of the technology, such as attending to several screens of information, locating messages successfully, navigating among pages, changing various output features of the technology, turning the technology on and off, utilizing rate enhancement strategies such as word prediction, and storing new messages.

It is also important to consider the nature of the message retrieval formulation techniques employed by different AAC technologies. Some AAC technologies may offer a combination of spelling, picture symbol message access, and word prediction. Others require communicators to locate and string together symbols or icons

AAC Supports for Adults with Severe Aphasia and/or Apraxia of Speech

to create messages. Symbols and images may be contained in folders, on grids, on hidden levels, or on paper pages. Still other AAC technologies enable people with aphasia to access elements of visual scenes to communicate specific messages (Beukelman et al., 2015; Dietz, McKelvey, &amp; Beukelman, 2006). These choices should be considered in light of the communicator's preferences and ability to retrieve messages in these formats.

## Assessing Other Capabilities

Traditional assessment procedures for aphasia typically identify the cognitive, linguistic, and perceptual abilities of an individual with aphasia.

**Residual Language Capabilities** Often, language testing has been conducted prior to AAC assessment, and selected information from these tools can contribute to the selection of AAC supports. First, a standard aphasia battery such as the Western Aphasia Battery-Revised (Kertesz, 2006), the short form of the Boston Diagnostic Aphasia Exam-Revised (Goodglass, Kaplan, &amp; Barresi, 2000), or the Boston Assessment of Severe Aphasia (Helm-Estabrooks, Ramsberger, Morgan, &amp; Nicholas, 1989) will measure the extent of the receptive and expressive language impairment when no external AAC or partner support is available. Communicators with nonfluent aphasia typically exhibit difficulties with syntactic encoding. Therefore, AAC supports that require using symbol combinations to communicate a single message may frustrate these individuals. Even spelling is a type of encoding that requires sequential selection and sequencing of arbitrary symbols to represent sounds and meanings. Because successful spelling requires many repetitions of this procedure, it is often extremely difficult for people with aphasia. Therefore, providing people with aphasia with a typewriter or computer keyboard may be frustrating. People with aphasia may benefit when clinicians consider how the language demands imposed by particular AAC approaches mesh with the capabilities of communicators (Garrett &amp; Kimelman, 2000; Lasker, 2008).

**Cognition** There are numerous factors (both intrinsic and extrinsic), including the individual's cognition, that should be used to determine which AAC supports will work best for which individuals and in which situations. Some researchers in the field of aphasia have offered ideas of how to analyze cognitive capabilities of people with aphasia who use AAC. The Cognitive Linguistic Quick Test Plus (Helm-Estabrooks, 2017) contains several subtests that assess attention, memory, and reasoning without taxing linguistic ability. Helm-Estabrooks (2002) suggested that several nonverbal reasoning tasks (e.g., trail making) may be useful in identifying individuals with cognitive ability to use high-tech, symbol-based AAC. Other research has explored how attention, cognitive flexibility, and executive function may play a role in the use of high-tech devices by people with aphasia (Helm-Estabrooks, 2002; Nicholas &amp; Connor, 2017; Nicholas, Sinotte, &amp; Helm-Estabrooks, 2005; Purdy &amp; Koch, 2006). Ultimately, more research is needed to correlate specific cognitive abilities with the ability of individuals who rely on AAC.

Arranging messages in AAC systems with multiple displays (in low-tech and high-tech devices) may impose significant processing challenges for many people with aphasia who demonstrate problems recalling the location of stored messages and symbols. They must demonstrate sufficient working memory to complete the

AAC Interventions for Individuals with Acquired Disabilities

steps involved in accessing the messages before forgetting their intent or losing their partner's interest. Some people are more independent with low-technology AAC if they have difficulty navigating through the hidden pages of high-technology AAC because messages stored within a simple paper binder or on a single display may be more readily visible and accessible. Wallace and Hux (2013) explored the effect of two different high-tech layouts for navigation—one with multiple displays and static home page and back buttons compared with a navigation ring layout, which included a central photo surrounded by smaller thumbnail photos that could be used to navigate to other displays. The researcher asked people with aphasia to access target sentences on each AAC device. Although participants learned to use both interfaces to navigate the devices, they demonstrated improved efficiency of access and accuracy of learning when provided with a navigation ring.

Individuals with aphasia should also be observed to determine their awareness of their own communicative ability. Are they able to explain their novel communication strategies to unfamiliar partners? Do they know when their language is not adequate for a particular situation? Can they use their strategies in a dynamic manner, for example, using speech and writing when able to do so and then shifting to an AAC support when they experience communication breakdowns? In addition, the clinician should informally observe the individual's initiative and tenacity to convey a message to a partner despite frequent communication breakdowns. Marvin, described earlier in this chapter, initially spent almost half of his communication efforts on resolving breakdowns. However, after he was instructed to shift to a different strategy (e.g., rewording, locating information in his communication notebook) instead of simply repeating the words over and over, the percentage of communication turns used to resolve communication breakdowns decreased from 46% to 11% (Garrett et al., 1989).

Representational Capabilities People with aphasia often understand many of the visual images that are used to represent the world. For example, they recognize various icons of geography, such as maps, and icons of events, such as logos and signs. They also usually retain the ability to identify photographs and drawings that relate to people and places. Many people with aphasia retain knowledge about the relative relationships of size, shape, goodness, and importance among objects and experiences. For example, an individual with aphasia may refer to another adult by gesturing to indicate his or her taller height as compared with a child. However, these abilities should be probed. Asking an individual to tell about his or her family or childhood during a reminiscing conversation in which a scrapbook is used will allow the clinician to informally observe these abilities.

Motor Capabilities Individuals with aphasia following a stroke usually retain the ability to control their limbs on at least one side of the body (usually the left). Therefore, they can typically gesture, turn pages, or point to communication choices in a direct selection mode. However, they may experience difficulties when asked to complete a complex sequence of motor movements (e.g., locating words on multiple pages of a book or multiple levels of an electronic communication technology) because of limb apraxia or cognitive deficits. They may also experience some difficulty physically carrying or manipulating heavy AAC technology, walking (often with a cane or other assistance) and standing while also communicating or using the on/off buttons of those technologies. Consultation with an occupational or physical therapist may be appropriate when deciding on portable AAC technology.

Hearing and Vision

Standard hearing and vision screening procedures can be used to identify sensory impairments (either the communicator's or the partner's) that may interfere with successful communication. Given the average age of people with aphasia and some of their family members, hearing and vision impairments are a risk to effective communication.

### Operational Skills

If they use AAC to augment their communication, communicators may have to learn new operational skills such as turning the technology on and off, comprehending synthesized or digitized speech, locating messages stored on invisible levels, using flowchart operational menus, keyboarding, and charging the equipment.

### Life Experiences and Vocabulary

The experiences and life history of an individual are particularly relevant as clinicians co-construct AAC interventions with them. Most individuals with aphasia have lived for a considerable period of time and have experienced relatively typical, routine lifestyles, so their knowledge about the world is extensive. To gather fuel for upcoming AAC interactions, it may be helpful to informally assess interests, topics, and autobiographical information through interviews with family members prior to beginning an AAC intervention.

### Partner Skills

Because communication partners are so important in communication interactions with people who have severe aphasia, it is useful to assess their capabilities as well. Hinckley et al. (2013) describe steps and measures used to select people for communication partner training. This assessment about the communication skills of partners is obtained from conducting a semistructured interview and observing their interactions with the individual with aphasia. It is also important to determine if the partner is able to learn or is interested in learning new ways of communicating with the person with severe aphasia. The clinician can also evaluate the potential communication partner's speaking style and understandability, handwriting legibility, reading skills, hearing, and vision. Simmons-Mackie et al. (2016) conducted a systematic review of communication partner training related to people who interact with individuals with aphasia. They found that positive changes in skill levels resulted from partner training, which improved the level of participation in communication activities as well as the quality of communicative interactions for people with aphasia. Examples of skills that may be included in communication partner training include the use of techniques described earlier in this chapter (e.g. augmented input, written-choice conversation strategy). See Hinckley et al. (2013) and Figure 15.8 for specific suggestions for how to incorporate communication partner training into an intervention plan in various health care settings and with a variety of communication partners.

## Assessing Communication Needs and Participation in Real-Life Contexts

Guidelines for developing the content of AAC systems generally start with a discussion of the individual's needs, by which we mean the environments and activities in which the person wishes to participate, as well as the specific messages required to communicate in those contexts. Families and friends of people with severe aphasia often play a vital role in identifying these communication needs. For clinicians who are conducting an assessment with an individual who has severe aphasia, the following procedures may be helpful.

Needs Assessment Interview

First, during an initial interview to assess an individual's needs, the clinician can simply ask the communicator, the communicator's family, and significant others to list communication situations that are particularly challenging or difficult for the individual with aphasia. Next, the clinician should ask the interviewees to imagine situations in which they foresee opportunities for meaningful communication. Initially, families may often list situations in which physical needs are communicated (e.g. seeing the doctor, getting dressed). Additional urging to think of situations in which the individual had an important life role prior to stroke may be necessary; providing the family with examples such as betting at the racetrack, saying the dinner prayer at Thanksgiving, attending sports events of grandchildren, and having coffee with a friend also may be helpful. The Aphasia Needs Assessment (Garrett & Lasker, 2004; available at http://word.emerson.edu/jlasker/past-research) may also assist clinicians to obtain some of this information in a systematic manner. For communicators who cannot use their speech to answer these questions without supports, the written-choice conversation strategy described previously may be useful. Providing the communicator with written word choices (representing situations) and scales for rating the relative importance of the activity can provide a window onto the communicator's perceptions of important communication needs.

Fox, Ginley, and Poulsen (2004) described how real-life communication needs were elicited from a group of people with aphasia and their significant others who attended a weeklong communication camp experience. She asked these individuals to describe communication situations that had specifically challenged them and to share strategies that had been particularly effective in those situations. For example, one man told about the difficulties he encountered when trying to order menu items in a fast-food restaurant. He developed an ingenious strategy—shining a red light from a laser pointer on the menu items posted behind the counter—to communicate his food order. Fox and colleagues encouraged participants to develop and incorporate strategies such as the laser pointing technique in their own communication strategy toolkit. This “toolkit” suggestion is an excellent example of how clinicians can assist communicators with aphasia to identify potential solutions to important communication needs in a variety of life situations.

### Topic Sorting

Fox, Sohlberg, and Fried-Oken (2001) encouraged research participants with aphasia to sort topics into preferred and nonpreferred categories prior to engaging in conversational training. They learned that one individual, of the three that participated in their study, communicated much more extensively about topics that he had selected than those that had been chosen for him. This topic-sorting task may be a useful means of identifying important topics and situations, particularly for individuals who cannot express them with their speech (Murphy & Boa, 2012).

### Social Networks

In addition to communication topics and situations, it can be helpful to identify specific communication partners with whom the individual wishes to communicate. With one client, we used the assessment tool known as Social Networks: A Communication Inventory for Individuals with Complex Communication Needs and Their Communication Partners (Blackstone & Hunt Berg, 2003). This tool diagrams the social network of the communicator by using a series of concentric circles to denote level of involvement. For example, the individual communicator is at the center of the circles, those who are identified as life partners are included in the

AAC Supports for Adults with Severe Aphasia and/or Apraxia of Speech

![img-0060.jpeg](../img/beukelman-2020-aac/img-0060.jpeg)

Figure 15.18. Chart showing circles of communication partners as part of the Social Networks Inventory (Blackstone &amp; Hunt Berg, 2003) to assess a client with aphasia. (Copyright © 2019 K. L. Garrett, J. P. Lasker, &amp; J. Fischer.)

first circle, those identified as close friends are in the second circle, and so forth. The authors of this chapter have modified the tool by creating a large visual diagram to interview communicators about their social networks before and after onset of aphasia (see Figure 15.18). We also use partner-supported communication strategies and photos to facilitate the individual's participation in the interview. Communication partners and social networks from before the onset of aphasia were compared with currently available partners. Intervention goals were then designed to improve interactions with the partners who were currently most important to the communicator.

Peer Participation Patterns If it is not possible to conduct a face-to-face interview to identify social networks and communication needs, clinicians can indirectly estimate communication needs by assessing peer participation patterns. Peers can be individuals of the same age or culture as the person with aphasia or can be individuals who have similar interests. For example, if a person with aphasia used to socialize at a veterans' club in town, the clinician could observe or ask others about the types of messages or communication needs that would arise in that situation. It may be helpful to ask the communicator to envision the sequence of communication events within each of these situations so that a comprehensive message inventory also can be created.

# INTERVENTION ISSUES

People with aphasia need varying levels of communication support during their recovery to meet their communication needs and participate in desired life activities. This chapter described types of AAC and partner supports that may be helpful across a continuum of communicators with severe aphasia and apraxia of speech. Even when clinicians successfully match strategies to a person's cognitive-linguistic

capabilities and needs, there are a number of additional issues that may need to be considered.

To promote acceptance of AAC support, clinicians may find it helpful to acknowledge communicators' and partners' hesitations about communicating using these somewhat unusual alternative modalities. Many of the spouses of communicators in the authors' clinics have gradually accepted some level of AAC after several months of simultaneously working on recovery of speech and gradually incorporating AAC into intervention. Group therapy is another positive means of illustrating how AAC and unaided communication modalities can blend. Watching other, more experienced participants converse about old movies or introduce themselves in a simulated social club may be more convincing than academic explanations about the benefits of AAC.

It is also essential that the content of an AAC system and the types of AAC support that are available remain dynamic during the chronic stage and throughout the course of the person's recovery, and that he or she receives training when necessary. As changes occur in the situations and contexts of an individual's life, the AAC system must reflect these changes; otherwise, motivation and interest in using the system will quickly diminish. Continual modification of the content of an AAC system requires that one or more communication partners, usually family members or caregivers, be trained to monitor and adjust the AAC system. Communication partners must also be able to train new people who enter the life of the person with aphasia (e.g. a new son- or daughter-in-law or a new neighbor) so that they, too, can become effective communication partners. Failure to identify and adequately prepare communication partners is a common reason for unsuccessful AAC intervention among people with severe aphasia.

Incorporating AAC use into everyday life can be challenging for individuals with aphasia and their communication partners. As one family member comments, “The most difficult thing for us is actually thinking of when to use the [AAC system]—including it in our daily routines.” (wife of a communicator with aphasia, personal communication, October 25, 2004)

Other issues may impact the success of AAC intervention for individuals with aphasia. They include factors related to the person with aphasia (i.e. capabilities, attitudes), features of the environment in which the person communicates (i.e. partner's attitudes and skills, limited communication opportunities, lack of real life practice), and aspects of AAC technology itself (i.e. inappropriate matches of system features to capabilities; Garrett & Kimelman, 2000; Purdy & Dietz, 2010; Scherer, Sax, Vanbiervliet, Cushman, & Scherer, 2005; Taylor, Wallace, & Wallace, 2019).

The following interaction with the spouse of a contextual-choice AAC communicator reflects some of the barriers that family members may initially project when implementing AAC options at home.

Clinician:So how has it been going at home? Spouse:Oh, it's much easier to communicate with Ken now. He really seems to know what's going on. Clinician:Are you and your sons comfortable with talking more slowly, making sure he understands? Can he clearly tell you “yes” and “no”? Spouse:Yes, although sometimes he laughs if we go too slowly . . . he'll even make fun of us. But we're doing well there. He really thinks about how

he's nodding his head. And he points to what he wants now . . . that really helps.Clinician:Have you been able to talk about more complicated topics? Like what to get the kids for the holidays . . . or opinions on what's happening in the news?Spouse:No, not really . . . mostly we just talk about what he needs and wants.Clinician:Have you tried to use the written-choice technique we practiced?Spouse:No, not much. We need to work harder on that.

Clearly, the success of an AAC intervention depends on flexibility and continuity of service delivery as the individual with aphasia transitions from setting to setting. Professionals, family members, and people with aphasia may wish to work as a team to create better solutions for management of long-term aphasia. Options could include increasing the emphasis on training partners to use immediate communication supports early in the individual's recovery, with more intensive involvement of the speech-language pathologist later in the rehabilitation process. It may be useful to schedule clients with aphasia for routine follow-up visits each year. Some people with aphasia may benefit from weekly group therapy sessions rather than individual intervention sessions only. Still others may benefit from home visits by the speech-language pathologist as well as other health care professionals because some communication challenges may be visible only in the individual's home environment. With careful planning and extended clinical support, AAC interventions can enrich the communication options for individuals and their communication partners at all stages of adjustment to life with aphasia. Therefore, it is important to provide ongoing monitoring of their communication effectiveness to accommodate change in their communication needs and capabilities.

## CONCLUSIONS

Aphasia is an impairment of the ability to interpret and formulate language that can cause communication breakdowns. These breakdowns can affect how a person with aphasia participates in desired life activities. Individuals with apraxia of speech may also experience limitations when communicating with other people. An AAC intervention approach includes supports that ensure each person with aphasia and/or apraxia has a means of communicating at all stages of recovery and in all environments. AAC supports include multiple modalities as well as strategies that may be described as high-, low- or no-technology. AAC strategies serve many functions. They can be used to enhance auditory comprehension and reading comprehension, augment the expression of spoken and written language, and function as additional modalities and sources of context during communication exchanges. An AAC intervention approach also includes communication partner training. This training facilitates effective and efficient communication exchanges between the person with aphasia and his or her partners. While some people with severe aphasia are dependent on communication partners for some aspects of communication interactions, others learn to augment natural modes of communication with AAC supports to become independent communicators. Recommendations for partner-supported AAC strategies can be implemented immediately. A multimodal AAC system will take time to develop based on the individual's communication needs. People with aphasia benefit from an AAC intervention approach that includes communication support during all

phases of their recovery. This chapter described types of AAC and partner supports that may be helpful across a continuum of communicators with severe aphasia and/or apraxia of speech.

# Adults with Degenerative Cognitive and Linguistic Conditions

Elizabeth K. Hanson and David R. Beukelman

Doc lived with his wife in their farm home for 12 years after being diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease. Despite providers were hired to spend time with him at home while his wife went to work. It was sometimes comforting to be able to talk to his wife on the phone when he became anxious, and so her picture with the label "Call Ruth" was placed next to it. During periods of anxiety, his caregivers would take him to the phone, point to the picture, and say something like "Let's call Ruth." Then they would dial her number, tell her that Doc wanted to talk to her when she answered, and handed him the phone. This helped him calm down and alleviated his distress. If the caregiver had simply walked away from him to make the call, he might have misinterpreted it as ignoring him and his distress.

The insidious onset and gradual deterioration of communication effectiveness is a commonly reported symptom of various types of degenerative, cognitive-linguistic conditions. The exact pattern of communication deterioration varies in that some people experience cognitive symptoms such as memory loss with accompanying impaired judgment, reduced problem solving, or impaired visuospatial orientation before changes in their language are observed. Others demonstrate a gradual deterioration of language as an early symptom. Despite the heterogeneity of many symptoms, people with dementia usually retain emotions, such as fear, frustration, anger, happiness, and contentment. The evidence base of effective augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) interventions for degenerative cognitive-linguistic disorders is steadily growing as new technologies evolve in the mainstream and are integrated into supports and strategies for people with these conditions. Specifically, intervention research shows promising impacts for persons with primary progressive aphasia (Mooney, Bedrick, Noethe, Spaulding, &amp; Fried-Oken, 2018), dementia (Hickey &amp; Bourgeois, 2017; Lanzi, Burshnic, &amp; Bourgeois, 2017), Huntington's disease (Yorkston &amp; Beukelman, 2007), and Alzheimer's disease (Jamieson, Cullen, McGee-Lennon, Brewster, &amp; Evans, 2014).

605

AAC Interventions for Individuals with Acquired Disabilities

# DEGENERATIVE CONDITIONS THAT AFFECT COGNITION AND LANGUAGE

The sections that follow discuss several degenerative conditions that may affect cognition and language: Alzheimer's disease, frontotemporal dementia, Lewy body dementia, primary progressive aphasia, and Huntington's disease.

# Alzheimer's Disease

Probably the most commonly recognized dementia, Alzheimer's disease begins with short-term memory loss, becoming confused about time or locations, social withdrawal, mood changes, and difficulty with executive function capabilities such as following directions, managing simple finances, or completing familiar tasks, among others (Alzheimer's Association, n.d.). The etiology of late-onset Alzheimer's disease, the most common form, is elusive. However, the National Institute on Aging (a division of the National Institutes of Health in the United States) suggests a combination of genetic, lifestyle, and environmental components that trigger the condition. Diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease is a process of elimination to rule out other conditions such as anemia, thyroid disease, or vitamin  $\mathrm{B}_{12}$  deficiency (Gazes, Soldan, &amp; Stern, 2012).

The National Institute on Aging estimates that one third of people 85 years or older may have Alzheimer's disease, with the first indications occurring during the sixth decade of life. Early-onset Alzheimer's disease is much less common and has a genetic component that is better understood. It may manifest as early as the third decade of life. Alzheimer's disease begins in the brain's hippocampus (which is where memory consolidation from short term to long term occurs) and entorhinal cortex (which is in the medial temporal lobe and serves as an axis for neural networks dealing with memory).

# Frontotemporal Dementia

As its name suggests, frontotemporal dementia begins in frontal and temporal lobes of the brain. Depending on the origin of the lesion, a frontotemporal dementia will manifest in different ways. For example, executive functions related to planning, prioritizing, or multitasking may be impaired initially, or deficits in language or emotion may appear first (National Institute on Aging, n.d.), "What causes Alzheimer's disease?"). The term frontotemporal dementia is actually a catch-all category for several conditions (National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke, n.d.) such as 1) Pick's disease, for which inappropriate behavior is an early sign followed by memory and language difficulties similar to Alzheimer's disease; 2) frontotemporal dementia with motor neuron disease, which may be concomitant with the progressive loss of motor function in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis; and, 3) progressive supranuclear palsy, which impacts control of eye movements and other motor actions in addition to cognitive function and language, in ways that sometimes make it look like Parkinson's disease. The National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (n.d.) provides a comprehensive list of different dementia types, etiologies, neuropathologies, signs, symptoms, and treatments.

# Lewy Body Dementia

Lewy body dementia shares with Alzheimer's disease the distinction of being one of the most common causes of dementia (National Institute on Aging, "Diagnoses of

Adults with Degenerative Cognitive and Linguistic Conditions

Lewy body dementia", n.d.). Early on, it manifests in one of three ways: 1) with memory impairment, which may lead to a misdiagnosis of Alzheimer's disease; 2) with motor impairment, which may lead to a misdiagnosis of Parkinson's disease; or 3) with hallucinations and behavioral issues, which may lead to a misdiagnosis of schizophrenia (Lewy Body Dementia Association, n.d.). The diagnosis is actually two related subcategories: dementia with Lewy bodies or Parkinson's disease dementia (National Institute on Aging, "Diagnoses of Lewy Body dementia, n.d."). They share underlying physiologic changes in the brain (i.e., the growing collection of Lewy bodies) and are differentiated by the timing of which impairment occurs first; earlier cognitive symptoms within 12 months of motoric impairment associated with parkinsonism and cognitive symptoms that occur 12 months or more after motoric impairment.

## Primary Progressive Aphasia

Primary progressive aphasia is identified as a form of frontotemporal dementia that primarily impacts language and causes difficulty in daily living activities (Gorno-Tempini et al., 2011; Mesulam, 2013). Primary progressive aphasia was originally identified as a single, unique condition. However, now three variants have been identified and may be diagnosed through clinical observation, imaging studies, or histopathologic evidence. The three variants are 1) non-fluent/agrammatic, characterized by difficulty in production or comprehension of grammatically correct utterances as well as motor speech impairment; 2) semantic, characterized by impaired naming, difficulty understanding single words, and possibly by dyslexia or dysgraphia; and 3) logopenic, characterized by difficulty with single-word retrieval and recognition of sentences and phrases, and possibly by phonologic errors in speech but spared motor speech capability (see Gorono-Tempini et al., 2011, for helpful lists of characteristics that are impaired or spared for each type).

## Huntington's Disease

Dementia related to Huntington's disease is often diagnosed using criteria for Alzheimer's disease (Peavy et al., 2010). The communication limitations associated with Huntington's disease are challenging because they reflect a complex interaction of impaired motor function resulting in slurred speech (dysarthria) and difficulty swallowing, chorea (involuntary, irregular spasmodic movements of the limbs or facial muscles), emotional disturbance, hyperkinetic dysarthria, and disruptive change in cognitive-linguistic capabilities (Klasner &amp; Yorkston, 2000). Early cognitive changes include impaired attention, memory, and cognitive functions, with full dementia developing in some patients in later stages (Murray, 2000). The communication impairments associated with Huntington's disease vary considerably from person to person. Language comprehension deficits associated with Huntington's disease include high-level processing difficulties with metaphoric or ambiguous sentences or sentences containing implied information or complex grammar. Expressive language deficits include use of shorter, less complex, and less grammatical utterances (Murray, 2000). For some, abnormal movements may be restricted primarily to the lower extremities without obvious speech disorder. For others, speech is so impaired that AAC strategies are required (Klasner &amp; Yorkston, 2000).

Huntington's disease is an inherited autosomal dominant degenerative disease, which means that people who have one parent with the disease have a 50% chance

AAC Interventions for Individuals with Acquired Disabilities

of inheriting it. The symptoms of Huntington's disease typically appear in the fourth decade of life, with death occurring 15–17 years after onset. A systematic review of the literature (Pringsheim et al., 2012) calculated the worldwide incidence of Huntington's disease as 0.38 per 100,000 per year. The worldwide prevalence is estimated as 5.70 per 100,000. Asian countries have a significantly lower prevalence of the disease compared to North America, Europe, and Australia. People with Huntington's disease are often unable to speak functionally by the end stages of the disease (Folstein, 1990).

## MEMORY STRENGTHS AND DEFICITS

Dementia involves the impairment of the ability to transfer information from working or short-term memory to long-term memory, which interferes with learning and communication. The impairment progresses and becomes more severe over time. Deficits in dementia affect various memory domains in different ways.

## Memory Domains

Following is a brief review of memory domains.

### Episodic Memory

Episodic memory refers to memory about autobiographical events, that is, the recollection of prior experiences and their contexts (Radvansky &amp; Tamplin, 2012). Although episodic memory encompasses events from throughout a person's life, it is the episodic memory of recent events that is often impaired quite early in dementia (Gazes et al., 2012). Thus, memory loss in the early stages of dementia includes an inability to recall recent information, such as who has visited, where items were left, what was eaten for breakfast, and so forth. Bourgeois and Hickey (2009) suggest that recent episodic memory limitations reflect a reduced ability to transfer information from short-term (working) to long-term memory.

### Semantic Memory

Semantic memory is not autobiographical. It involves factual information and general, organized knowledge and includes the capacity to recall words, concepts, and numbers (Radvansky &amp; Tamplin, 2012). Deficits may be evidenced by an inability to remember facts, such as the name of the leader of one's country, that bananas are yellow, or that both cats and dogs are animals, as well as difficulties recalling words or concepts. Semantic memory impairments are typically observed later in the course of dementia than deficits in episodic memories.

### Procedural Memory

Often the best preserved of the memory domains is procedural memory. This type of memory is used to complete common routines, such as shaving, dressing, driving, and so forth.

## Memory and Communication

Memory plays an important role in human communication. It helps to maintain the thread of a conversation, it ensures that topics are fully discussed, and it allows new topics to be introduced at appropriate times. Impaired transfer from working or short-term to long-term memory can therefore have a severe impact on a person's conversations, resulting in topics being repeatedly introduced, and giving the appearance that the person is not listening. This can be disturbing and frustrating for the conversation partner and can, in turn, have a negative effect on the person as

Adults with Degenerative Cognitive and Linguistic Conditions
609

he or she becomes aware of a partner's negative emotions but does not understand how they have come about.

# INTERVENTION FOCUS: COMMUNICATION STRENGTHS

Nancy and her husband Jim arrived at her outpatient appointment with the speech-language pathologist feeling anxious and confused. Nancy had recently received a diagnosis of primary progressive aphasia from her neurologist and the couple had done some online research that was not entirely helpful or comforting. While Nancy was completing some paperwork, Jim met with the speech-language pathologist in another room. There, he shared his fear of the unknown future. He asked if Nancy would not be able to talk at some point, and how he was supposed to take care of her if that happened. The couple needed better information about the course of the condition and, even more urgently, a plan to prepare for Nancy's expected communication decline. Their story illustrates the need for person-centered assessment and intervention that builds upon the communication strengths the person still has.

Person-centered assessment and intervention for people with dementia focuses on the person, not just the disease, and involves people with dementia and their caregivers (Lanzi et al., 2017). What a person with dementia talks about is not as important as the fact that the person has a conversation with someone (Hydén, 2011). Kitwood (1997) maintains that a specific set of psychological needs must be addressed in the person to sustain mental health. These include needs for comfort, identity, inclusion, occupation, and attachment.

Although strength and deficit profiles differ widely among people with dementia, there are overall patterns of strengths and deficits that occur with each stage of the condition. Person-centered intervention enhances residual strengths at each stage rather than attempting to remediate their communication deficits. Communication strengths and deficits by stage are summarized in Table 16.1. Building on communication strengths and addressing psychological needs is the foundation of interventions for people with dementia throughout the course of the disease;

For example, if a person with dementia experiences deficits in recent episodic memory (i.e., remembering what happened yesterday), communication partners or caregivers could be taught to provide the person with a concrete reminder, such as a memento of a recent event in the form of a remnant or a photograph, rather than admonishing the person.

# INTERVENTION FOCUS: STAGING

Some cognitive-linguistic interventions for some of the conditions described above have a growing evidence base (see Swan et al., 2018, for a systematic review), while other conditions have yet to be addressed in intervention studies. Because all of these conditions have a progressive and devastating impact on cognitive-linguistic capabilities, in the absence of intervention research for a specific condition, clinicians may choose to incorporate AAC interventions shown to be effective for a different type of dementia. In such a case, it is important to monitor the person's response carefully to ensure the intervention is effective.

Considering the stage or phase of the progressive condition may assist clinicians in planning intervention for immediate communication intervention while also planning for future needs as the degenerative cognitive-linguistic condition progresses. King, Alarcon, and Rogers (2007) recommend a proactive intervention plan, given the degenerative neuropathology of most dementias. In anticipation of future declines in language function, these experts recommend intervention that focuses on early incorporation of AAC strategies into everyday communication.

# Early-Stage AAC Intervention

In the early stage of dementia, caregivers and communication partners need to learn how to support communication interaction by reducing the challenge for individuals to remember specific words or events by redirecting conversation as needed and

Adults with Degenerative Cognitive and Linguistic Conditions

providing compensatory strategies for information that needs to be remembered. During this stage, individuals with dementia are aware of memory limitations, and the focus of this stage is to maintain their dignity and self-respect. This stage is also an opportunity for proactive involvement of the person with dementia in designing memory tools that they will use later on. There is an assumption that early involvement in the process will increase the likelihood that people will accept technology supports (Lehoux &amp; Blume, 2000). For example, during the early stages of primary progressive aphasia, affected individuals continue to use speech to interact with others. However, to maintain independence in communication, they need assistance to manage communication breakdowns and to develop strategies that they may need in the future, such as help in word finding (i.e., recall of specific words) with drawing, writing, print, and picture support for commonly used but difficult words. This ability level is consistent with specific-need communicators described in Chapter 15 (severe aphasia). These individuals may benefit from booklets or cards with specific information, prepared questions for difficult situations, and gestures (yes, no, left, right, past, and future) to resolve communication breakdowns. The techniques should be introduced gradually and early so that people with primary progressive aphasia and their communication partners can become familiar with them and accept this type of communication support.

The use of external supports has shown some potential to assist those with Huntington's disease to maintain communication by participating in conversations in early stages (Klasner &amp; Yorkston, 2000). Index cards may be used to rehearse these scripts with the topic and utterance on one side and the key word on the other side. Some with Huntington's disease can generate the utterance simply by looking at the key word (Klasner &amp; Yorkston, 2000). Those with moderate dysarthria need support to resolve communication breakdowns. These strategies must be developed on an individual basis depending on the residual capability of the individual and the willingness of regular communication partners to provide this support. Lanzi et al. (2017) also describe providing scripted information for interactions that are predictable and repeated, such as phone conversations or scheduling appointments.

## Middle-Stage AAC Intervention

By the middle phase of intervention, cognitive problems typically prevent full participation in the activities and interactions that make up a person's life. The person has difficulty remembering to initiate an activity and completing all the steps in it. Klasner and Yorkston (2000), in their case study of a person with Huntington's disease, describe "cognitive supplementation" (p. 158) options to break tasks into manageable steps needed to complete a task such as feeding the cat. For example, this may be done with a sequence of photos with brief descriptive text to show each step of the task printed on paper that may be laminated. The sequence could also be displayed on a tablet device or smart phone or assembled as a short video showing each step of the task.

In the middle stages, people with dementia lose awareness of their cognitive and communication problems. Communication partners need to support interaction that maintains social closeness. To do this, caregivers and other communication partners will need to take more control or leadership of interactions to provide comfort and familiarity in later stages (Bourgeois &amp; Hickey, 2007). Technology such as multimedia memory biographies may become important tools to provide comfort and a sense

AAC Interventions for Individuals with Acquired Disabilities

of personhood through the guided reminiscences that they offer. Multimedia biographies consist of short videos or photo-movies depicting scenes and information—sometimes including music or other audio—that are personally relevant to the individual. These are described later in this chapter.

People with primary progressive aphasia in the middle stage are considered to be generative message or transitional communicators (see Chapter 15) in that they need AAC support in most communication contexts. In addition to communication notebooks and cards, these individuals often benefit from visual scene displays (VSDs) that are familiar (Fried-Oken, Rowland, &amp; Gibbons, 2010). Some may also benefit from drawing pictures to communicate or clarify messages in the same way as people with acute aphasia (Sacchett, 2002). For others, spatial representations such as maps, calendars, family trees, and floor plans are helpful to communicate specific content (Cress &amp; King, 1999). Individuals in this stage often need augmented input strategies to enhance their comprehension of spoken information as well. Such strategies may include the communication partners' use of key words (printed), photos, gestures, drawings, or line drawings in conjunction with spoken input.

## Late-Stage AAC Intervention

By the late stage, individuals with more advanced dementia need much more support to communicate; the communication partner must assume a greater and greater role in interactions. For example, the communication limitations associated with late-stage forms of primary progressive aphasia are often quite similar to the needs of contextual-choice communicators described in Chapter 15. These individuals need help both to communicate and to comprehend information about basic needs and routines. As they enter the late stage, they may continue to use the materials developed in the early and middle stages. However, as they progress further into the late stage, they need to be presented with very limited choices—in the form of key words written on paper or a dry-erase board or objects—to communicate about their needs, preferences, and routines. In this stage, they need increasing support from their communication partners; therefore, partner education is essential to ensure that the person receives effective communication support (King et al., 2007). In the case of individuals who are completely non-speaking and not obviously responsive to speech or visual communication supports, touch and proximity may provide social closeness and comfort where words fail.

## IMPLEMENTING AAC INTERVENTIONS

AAC interventions were helpful for Jerry, a 55-year-old man with Down syndrome who lives independently in his own apartment with support from a community service provider. His direct service providers noticed that he started forgetting his weekly work schedule and so would not be dressed appropriately on days he was scheduled to work his long-standing job at a local fast-food restaurant. His developing forgetfulness was consistent with the early stages of Alzheimer's disease. People with Down syndrome have an extra copy of chromosome 21—referred to as trisomy 21. That means they carry the gene that creates the amyloid precursor protein (APP gene), known to cause the beta-amyloid plaques that clump in the brain along with tau tangles that can lead to Alzheimer's disease. Not all individuals with beta-amyloid plaques and tau tangles develop Alzheimer's. The National Institute on Aging (National Institute on Aging, "Alzheimer's disease in people with Down

Adults with Degenerative Cognitive and Linguistic Conditions
613

syndrome," n.d.) reports that about 50% of people with Down syndrome will develop Alzheimer's disease because of their trisomy 21.

In Jerry's case, a speech-language pathologist recommended a large visual schedule on the wall of his bedroom to help him keep track of his work schedule. Spaced-retrieval therapy helped him learn the procedure to check the schedule during his morning routine, and his morning direct service providers learned to refer to the schedule to remind him about work days if he was not dressed for work when they arrived in the morning.

Many communication interventions are effective for persons with degenerative cognitive-linguistic conditions (Swan et al., 2018). Sometimes a combination of restorative therapy with compensatory strategies is successful (Beukelman, Fager, Ball, &amp; Dietz, 2007). Although a return to premorbid function is not the prognosis for those with degenerative conditions, some learning techniques show positive outcomes that can buy time, so to speak, by building on residual strengths of those experiencing irreversible deterioration.

## Using Spaced Retrieval

Bourgeois et al. (2003) examined the effectiveness of two training approaches, spaced retrieval and a modified cueing hierarchy, to teach strategies to 25 individuals with dementia to remember to use external aids such as memory books and memory wallets. Spaced retrieval involves learning to remember information by recalling it over increasingly longer durations of time. For example, a goal of looking in the memory book to remind oneself when lunch is scheduled would be addressed by talking about the need to remember and cueing the person to look in the book. After the person does so, the clinician would engage in small talk or some other distracting activity for 30 seconds, and then ask the person how to know what time lunch is served. If the person responds by looking in or showing the memory book, the distracting activity would continue, this time for 60 seconds, doubling each time the person correctly remembers the procedure. At the point when the person forgets, the clinician shows the person what to do, and reduces the retrieval time to the last successful duration. A modified cueing hierarchy decreases the strength of a cue to elicit a response based on performance with the previous cue strength. Bourgeois and colleagues (2003) demonstrated that teaching the participants with dementia to check their memory books using a spaced-retrieval teaching strategy resulted in new learning that generally lasted for 4 months after the intervention, and yielded better performance than the modified cueing hierarchy approach, overall. This research demonstrates that, contrary to the view that those with dementia cannot learn, new learning that targets procedural and recognition memory is possible for some, when appropriate intervention is provided.

## Representing and Organizing Language

With regard to AAC strategies and options, Fried-Oken, Rau, and Oken (2000) direct clinicians to address both language representation and organization. Messages communicated to and by a person with dementia can be represented visually using several approaches to symbolization, depending on the person's capabilities. Simple print can be read by many individuals with mild, moderate, and (occasionally) severe dementia. Printed words can be used to label the locations of items, provide memory support, clarify spoken messages, and act as reminders of tasks to be completed. As dementia

AAC Interventions for Individuals with Acquired Disabilities

progresses, printed words can be accompanied by photographs and pictures. If printed words become ineffective, line drawings or photographs may be used to represent language concepts. For some, objects eventually become the most effective way to represent information. Once the language symbolization capabilities of a person with dementia are determined, the range of language content to be represented needs to be identified. Usually, this is a team effort by the person with dementia, caregivers, family members, and others. The content will depend on the person's lifestyle, the settings in which he or she participates, and the supports that are available.

The incorporation of AAC supports into the lives of people with dementia and the members of their social networks (e.g., caregivers, family, friends, members of the public) can be managed using a number of organizational strategies. For example, written choice techniques, originally developed for people with aphasia (Chapter 15), can be used with print or pictures to provide communication choices that represent the preferences and needs of people with dementia. The person with aphasia or dementia can point to the text or picture to communicate a choice. Communication notebooks or small wallets or cards may include information represented using digital photography techniques that allow editing, enhancement, sizing, and manipulation of images to support communication.

Figure 16.1 shows a single communication card from a set developed for a man with Alzheimer's disease. Even after moving to a long-term care facility, he and his wife celebrated their wedding anniversaries with a party at the facility. This was a positive conversation topic for him and was depicted with a digital photo and autobiographical information on a small, laminated card attached to his wheelchair. Caregivers could use it to start a communication topic by showing it to him and commenting about the personal information. This served as a catalyst for meaningful

Figure 16.1. Communication card depicting autobiographic information for caregivers/ communication partners to use in setting a topic of conversation for a man with Alzheimer's disease living in long-term care.

Adults with Degenerative Cognitive and Linguistic Conditions

social communication. This type of information can emphasize the personhood (Kitwood, 1997) of individuals who have to leave so much behind to maintain their health and safety in the care of others when they can no longer live at home.

Communication cards and labels throughout a home may support the person in identifying various rooms of the house, the contents behind closed cupboard doors, or the steps to take to complete an activity such as flushing the toilet after use, hand washing, or taking medicine.

As noted previously, memory books have probably been the most investigated AAC intervention for people with dementia (Lanzi et al., 2017). Bourgeois and colleagues (Bourgeois, 1990, 1992, 1993; Bourgeois, Dikjstra, Burgio, &amp; Allen-Burge, 2001) reported that the quality of conversational interactions for people with mild and moderate dementia improved significantly when they used personalized memory wallets or books. Improvements included increases in the overall number of utterances as well as the number of positive statements and informative utterances from the person with dementia in conversations. In addition, the nursing aides in the study used more supportive comments when talking to the residents.

An external memory aid that builds on the autobiographical focus of memory books while taking advantage of the burgeoning affordability and availability of digital images and audio can provide multimedia biographies (mentioned earlier in this chapter) in the form of digitally edited picture-videos complete with music and narration (Alm et al., 2004; Cohen, 2000; Smith, Crete-Nishihata, Damianakis, Baecker, &amp; Marziali, 2009; Yasuda, Kuwabara, Kuwahara, Abe, &amp; Tetsutani, 2009). Cohen (2000) developed such a tool using digitized photos with slow movement and transitions between pictures, music from the appropriate era, and well-told story narratives to support photos in the biography. Old home movies and videos may also be digitally converted and incorporated. Cohen found such multimedia presentations increased positive engagement and decreased agitation in the persons with dementia for whom the displays were developed and also provided caregivers and visitors with a focus for interactions. Yasuda and colleagues (2009) measured the attention of participants to personalized reminiscence photo videos compared to a popular TV variety show and a news program. Eighty percent of the participants showed greater attention to their personalized photo videos. Alm and colleagues (2004) measured increased attention in participants with dementia and increased enjoyment of the interactions in their communicative partners when using a multimedia reminiscence presentation.

The technologies to produce such multimedia biographies evolve too rapidly to realistically try to provide a list of software or hardware here. However, most computers and tablets now come with easy-to-use photo and video-editing programs, and newer digitized photo picture frames found in the rooms of many nursing home residents now support audio as well as remote uploads of photos via Internet connections.

## IMPLEMENTING AAC SUPPORTS

A variety of AAC supports are currently used to enhance the communication of individuals with degenerative cognitive-linguistic conditions. Some of these are low-technology materials, while some high-technology options are being developed for these individuals as well.

## Communication Notebooks

Communication notebooks are usually small, easy-to-carry binders that contain information that supports the communication efforts of people with complex communication needs. The content and form of the notebooks is personalized. For example, these notebooks may contain photographs or line drawings for an individual who is unable to read or may contain considerable printed information if the individual can read but has difficulty remembering the names of people, places, and activities. The person who will use the notebook or display should be involved early on to participate in selecting content and in organizing the notebook. King et al. (2007) present an excellent discussion of the preparation and maintenance of communication notebooks for people with primary progressive aphasia. Their guidelines enhance the long-term usefulness of such books and are applicable to communication notebook preparation for a person with any form of dementia. Guidelines are as follows:

1. The communication notebook must reflect the person; it must be personalized.
2. The person who will use it must take a lead role in determining its content early in the course of the disease.
3. The communication notebook and opportunities to use it must be available consistently throughout the course of the condition.
4. The communication notebook is never finished; it must be dynamic so that it reflects the changing needs and experiences of the person who uses it and his or her social network.

The person with dementia may initiate use of a communication notebook to repair communication breakdowns in early stages, but caregivers and other communication partners need to assume the responsibility for communicating with it as a form of augmented input or to offer visual responses during communication in later stages.

## Visual Scene Displays

Weissling and Beukelman (2006) offered a low-tech version of VSDs that can be contained in a communication binder for people with aphasia (Chapter 15). These may also be useful for people with primary progressive aphasia or other dementias. VSDs use contextually rich, personally relevant photographs of activities and events to inspire conversational exchanges between the person with a communication impairment and a communication partner. The photos are rich in context, showing people involved in activities, interactions, and events, rather than portrait-type

AAC Interventions for Individuals with Acquired Disabilities

pictures or landscapes. Personally relevant photos are helpful in that they depict people and activities that are related to the person's life and are recognizable. Rather than programmed links for navigation or buttons to provide speech output found on high-tech devices (Beukelman, Hux, Dietz, McKelvey, &amp; Weissling, 2015), a low-tech VSD features a brief section of appropriate instructions for questions related to each photo and a section of text-based information that the person with dementia could use for comments. Figure 16.2 shows how a page of a low-tech VSD could be organized.

# Memory Books

Memory books are another form of visually represented information to support communication for people with dementia and have been studied for years with persons with Alzheimer's disease (Fried-Oken, Mooney, &amp; Peters, 2015; Hopper et al., 2013; Murphy &amp; Boa, 2012). The thinking is that memory books that incorporate photos,

(2001) described a memory book with pages that each contained one sentence or item, such as an illustration, to provide graphic information. Memory books typically include autobiographical information, daily schedules, and problem resolution information, such as instructions about daily tasks or events. For example, while he was still living at home and was confused about his wife's whereabouts, Doc, described earlier in this chapter, could turn to the page with his wife's picture in his memory book. The text with the picture stated the time when she would come home from work. His caregiver during the day could direct him to look in his "book" if he became agitated when he couldn't find his wife. Sometimes he would page through the book on his own and, find that page, read it aloud to himself, and say "okay," suggesting that he understood her absence. Providing information in the form of memory books builds on recognition memory, which takes less effort than recall tasks (Bayles &amp; Kim, 2003).

# Talking Mats

Talking Mats is a low-tech communication system developed by researchers in Europe (Murphy, Gray, van Achterberg, Wyke, &amp; Cox, 2010; Murphy, Tester, Hubbard, Downs, &amp; MacDonald, 2005) to help nursing home residents communicate about their likes and dislikes, and it is effective for people with dementia (Murphy, Alexander, &amp; McLinton, 2016; Stewart, Bradshaw, &amp; Beadle-Brown, 2018). Figure 16.3 shows how an elderly woman placing picture symbols representing activities and events on a visual scale (i.e., under like and dislike) to communicate general feelings and preferences about activities and topics. A digital photo of the display serves as documentation in the
