person's chart. Over time, consistency of responses may validate the communicative intent of the symbol choices. Since it was first introduced (Murphy et al. 2005), Talking Mats has been used with many different populations, including people with Huntington disease (Ferm, Sahlin, Sundin, & Hartelius, 2010), people with intellectual/developmental disabilities (Bunning, Alder, Proudman, & Wyborn, 2016), and those receiving palliative care (Boa, Duncan, Haraldsdottir, & Wyke, 2014).

### VoiceMyChoice

Bourgeois, Camp, Antenucci, and Fox (2016) developed a similar visual system, VoiceMyChoice, to help people with dementia communicate preferences. The visual categories are depicted with the words sometimes, always, and never on cards placed at the top of a mat on a table; the caregiver/communication partner hands the person with dementia labeled picture cards showing activities, personal care activities, and food under those labels. He or she is asked to sort the cards by placing each under one of the three categories. This results in a measure of the person's preference for each of the activities or food shown on the cards. The researchers reported consistent, reliable results based on their Preference Assessment Questionnaire used with 37 residents in a long‐term care facility and 33 caregivers (i.e. communication partners) who worked at the facility. Of note in this study is that nearly half the caregivers did not speak the same language (i.e. English) as the residents they worked with; yet the results demonstrated that participants were effective in communicating preferences.

### Mobile Technology Visual Scene Display App

Mooney et al. (2018) harnessed the power of digital social communication media to develop an experimental app to allow their participants with primary progressive aphasia to take digital photos using an iPad and allowed friends in a controlled social network to submit appropriate words for the participants to select from to describe the photo. The photo appears in a visual scene‐type display (described in Chapters 6 and 15) surrounded by textboxes that populate with messages selected by a natural language processing engine (i.e. a specialized code in an app that predicts appropriate words or phrases to populate text windows on a display). The messages were used by the person with primary progressive aphasia during a retell task. Five of the six participants produced more target words in the condition using the experimental app as compared to control conditions.

### Cognitive Prosthetic Technology

Jamieson and colleagues (2014) reviewed and compared 43 studies focused on what they termed cognitive prosthetic technology to support prospective memory, that is, remembering tasks or procedures, for persons with degenerative or static memory impairment. They describe this technology as portable electronic or digitized versions of memory books or lists. Such devices may offer prospective support in the form of step‐by‐step instructions to complete tasks with audio and visual support. They may also provide reminders to cue new tasks or help an individual transition among tasks. Overall, the authors found consistent evidence that such technology can provide meaningful support for those with memory loss.

Adults with Degenerative Cognitive and Linguistic Conditions

# IMPLEMENTING AAC STRATEGIES AND PARTNER TRAINING

AAC strategies are identified in different ways by different practitioners and researchers. Here, the word strategies identifies behaviors or practices that caregivers and other communication partners can learn to use to support effective communication with a person with dementia, such as paraphrasing information, asking simple yes/no questions, or providing augmented input. As described earlier, AAC supports describes the physical, external, high-tech and low-tech systems or tools used to support effective communication, such as displays, books, and devices.

Intervention should target both the person and his or her communication partners (Andrews-Salvia, Roy, &amp; Cameron, 2003; Bourgeois et al., 2001; Hopper, 2003). As cognitive-linguistic capabilities decline, the responsibility usually shared between two communication partners will increasingly fall to the partner without impairment (Swan et al., 2018). Caregivers, family members, professionals, and friends make up the social networks of most people with dementia, and most of these individuals are used to communicating primarily through speech. Therefore, ongoing training must teach them new and more effective ways to communicate with the individual with dementia by shifting their communication patterns to include accommodating communication strategies and AAC systems such as memory aids (Swan et al., 2018). Table 16.3 lists evidence-based communication strategies identified in the research described in this chapter.

Table 16.3. Evidence-based communication strategies recommended for caregivers and other communication partners of people with dementia discussed in this chapter

|  Authors | Strategy  |
| --- | --- |
|  Lanzi, Burshnic, & Bourgeois (2017) | ·Written cueing strategy to offer key words in text as well as speech (i.e., augmented input) ·Intermittent prompting ·Completion marks (i.e., crossing off items on a calendar or list) ·Wait time for processing and expression ·Give instructions one at a time ·Use cueing phrases such as “Tell me more about that” (e.g., with primary progressive aphasia) ·Augmented input with gestures, writing, and drawing to accompany speech ·Take the lead role in conversations ·Touch and facial expressions without speech ·Modify the environment to reduce visual and auditory distractions  |
|  Savundranayagam & Orange (2014) | ·Repeat information ·Offer choices ·Redirect person to a new topic to address anxiety ·Use gestures with speech (i.e., augmented input)  |
|  Small, Gutman, Makela, & Hillhouse (2003) | ·Eliminate distractions ·Use simple yes/no questions rather than open-ended questions ·Use short, simple sentences  |
|  Wilson, Rochon, Mihailidis, & Leonard (2012) | ·When giving directions, provide one step at a time ·Ask closed-ended questions ·Paraphrase repetitions  |

Lanzi et al. (2017) summarize evidence-based communication strategy use and partner training from a person-centered care approach that focuses on meaningful interactons and involving the person with dementia as much as possible in developing strategies. The authors describe the evidence that supports external strategies (i.e. outside the person) that build upon residual strengths such as processing visual information and reducing cognitive demands. Many of the strategies described are in the form of AAC supports described earlier, such as written information and other graphical representations in various types of books, binders, or wallets, as well as calendars or planners.

Savundranayagam and Orange (2014) investigated effective and ineffective communication strategies used by 15 family members and their loved ones with dementia during meal times. Effective strategies were first identified by reviewing previous research that documented practices found to help people with Alzheimer's disease to communicate and participate in interactions. The researchers video-recorded the 15 couples to capture their conversations during meals and then reviewed the recordings to identify communication breakdowns and repair attempts. They also asked the family members to rate how effective each communication strategy was. They found that family members used effective strategies such as repeating, rephrasing, asking questions, simplifying, giving choices, redirecting, and using gestures and the family members also identified those strategies as being effective. However, other evidence-based strategies, such as writing information down or asking for more information, were not supported by family members, which suggested a need for more caregiver education as the person's communication capabilities and memory degenerated.

Small et al. (2003) studied communication strategies used by 18 married couples that included one spouse with Alzheimer's disease, as the dyads communicated about various activities of daily living. The researchers observed the couples and documented the effectiveness or ineffectiveness of 10 strategies that are commonly recommended to increase communicative success for people with dementia. The researchers also asked the spouses, who did not have impairment, to rate how much they used the strategies and the effectiveness of the resulting interactions. Some of the results were quite surprising. Of the 10 strategies documented, only 3 were found to decrease communication breakdowns: eliminating distractions, speaking in simple sentences, and using yes/no questions. One strategy, using slower speech, appeared to be related to increased communication breakdowns; however, the investigators found that some spouses were not slowing their speaking rate even when they thought they were. In other cases where the rate was slower but still not effective, the researchers postulated that the longer duration of the message increased the burden on the already limited working memory capacities of the spouses with Alzheimer's disease, consistent with previous research (Bayles & Kim, 2003; Tomoeda, Bayles, Boone, Kaszniak, & Slauson, 1990). Overall, the spouses reported a higher level of communicative effectiveness than was supported by the objective data on communication breakdowns. This study emphasizes the critical need for interventions that target the communication partners of people with dementia.

Another study (Wilson et al. 2012), investigated communication among caregivers and residents with Alzheimer's disease living in a long-term care setting. They anticipated the most beneficial strategies would be offering a direction or idea, asking closed-ended questions, and repeating utternaces, based on their literature review. The researchers video-recorded 15 dyads during a hand-washing task and transcribed

Adults with Degenerative Cognitive and Linguistic Conditions

and coded the communication strategies that occurred. The strategies that resulted in the most successful completion of the hand-washing activities were consistent with their hypotheses: giving one direction or idea at a time, asking closed-ended questions, and paraphrased repetition. The investigators pointed out that many commonly recommended strategies, such as slowed speaking rate or simplified syntax are not evidence-based and in some cases are not helpful.

Together, the evidence demonstrates the importance of communication partner training to support communication for people with dementia and the need for speech-language pathologists to provide that instruction as part of the intervention plan. The importance of treating the communication dyad by providing training for communication partners is crucial to the success of interventions for people with degenerative conditions such as dementia.

# CONCLUSIONS

In summary, dementia is a degenerative cognitive-linguistic condition characterized by progressive memory impairment that affects memory, communication, and other cognitive domains. Distinct communicative strengths, as well as weaknesses, exist at each stage of decline. Speech-language pathologists offer a range of evidence-based AAC strategies that support and enhance communication strengths. Such interventions provide meaningful, person-centered AAC supports that are grounded in research, enhance the person's agency in his or her own care, and improve quality of life. In addition, speech-language pathologists are vigilant about sensory deficits, such as hearing and vision impairment that influence communication effectiveness, and can identify and refer to appropriate disciplines. Speech-language pathologists are pivotal to dementia care given the number and variety of degenerative cognitive-linguistic conditions that lead to memory and communication deficits and the growing base of evidence supporting AAC interventions for those conditions.

# Individuals with Traumatic Brain Injury

Susan Koch Fager and David R. Beukelman

Augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) interventions for people who have experienced traumatic brain injury (TBI) have changed dramatically through the years. Until the mid-1990s, AAC interventions occurred primarily with individuals who experienced severe, persistent anarchia or dysarthria following TBI. It was not uncommon for teams to delay AAC interventions until the individual's associated communication disorders stabilized; consequently, many people with TBI were unable to communicate functionally for months or even years after their accidents, putting them at significant risk for negative consequences (e.g., medical errors, frustration, stress, anxiety, lack of information, ineffective patient-provider communication). In the past, AAC teams erroneously thought that cognitive limitations during early stages of recovery would make it difficult for many people with TBI to use AAC; that it would be difficult to select appropriate AAC because the cognitive and motor performance of a person with TBI changes over time; and that some individuals with TBI would recover functional speech and therefore would not require AAC support. With this view, AAC teams often felt that the most conservative approach was the safest when recommending an intervention, but this conservative approach left many individuals without access to a means to communicate and participate in their medical care.

The goal of the AAC team is to provide patient-provider communication assistance as soon as possible (see Chapter 18) so that people with TBI can participate effectively in their medical care and rehabilitation program and are able to communicate their ongoing needs. Thus, the focus of intervention has shifted from providing a single AAC technology for long-term use to providing a series of AAC supports designed to meet short-term communication needs while continuing efforts to reestablish natural speech. For example, intervention might begin with understandable yes/no responses, provide a communication board for immediate wants and needs, develop a way to call for attention, develop communication supports to share information, support written communication, focus on the development of natural speech, and provide instruction in the use of multimodal communication that integrates residual natural speech and AAC supports (Light, Beesley, &amp; Collier, 1988).

This chapter outlines the general approaches to AAC intervention for individuals with TBI. However, because individuals with brain injuries recover over an extended period of time, it is beyond the scope of this book to detail the extensive

627

AAC intervention concepts, techniques, and strategies developed for these individuals. Readers are referred to several papers by Fager and colleagues for more in-depth information (Fager, Doyle, & Karantounis, 2011).

## PREVALENCE AND ETIOLOGY

Injuries to the head that result in temporary or permanent brain damage are quite common. It is difficult to estimate the number of these injuries that occur each year because many go unreported. Individuals who do not lose consciousness or do so only briefly are rarely admitted to the hospital and may not even go to an emergency room. For those with severe injury, immediate medical treatment has changed considerably during the past couple of decades. Advances in medical management at the scene of the accident (e.g. pre-hospital intubation, management of hypotension/hypertension), as well as surgical procedures to lessen the further damage to the brain due to swelling via decompressive craniotomies, have increased the survival rates and improved outcomes for individuals with TBIs (Chowdhury, Kowalski, Arabi, & Dash, 2014; Sahuquillo, 2006).

According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (2019), approximately 2.5 million emergency room visits due to TBI occurred in the United States. Nearly 56,000 died and 288,000 were hospitalized. Between 2006 and 2014, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported an increase of TBI-related emergency room visits of 53%, whereas hospitalizations decreased by 8% and death rates decreased by 6%. Individuals with TBI do not represent a random sample of the total population: more than twice as many males as females are injured. Male children between the ages of 0 and 4 years have the highest rates of emergency room visits, hospitalizations, and deaths related to TBI (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2019).

The causes of TBI are varied. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (2019) reported that of all TBI-related emergency room visits, hospitalizations, and deaths, 47.9% occurred as a result of falls (primarily in the younger and older age groups), 17% were from being struck by or against objects (with 1 in 5 cases occurring in children under the age of 15 years), and 13.2% were attributed to motor vehicle accidents.

Other causes of TBI can be attributed to blast injuries during combat. Blast injuries can result in primary trauma due to overpressurization that can impact the brain, as well as secondary injuries due to flying objects and debris propelled by the blast. The United States Department of Veterans Affairs reported a database study of 1,388 soldiers hospitalized for TBI due to blast injury that found that 55% were graded as Type 1 or most severe, 39% were Type 2, and 6% were Type 3 (least severe—Greer, Sayer, Kramer, Koeller, & Velasquez 2016).

As people with TBI recover, they usually progress through a continuum of care that begins in a trauma unit and may include time in a variety of different living situations. Fager (2003) described the experience of a 36-year-old man who relied on AAC technology to communicate all messages except a few greetings. In the 15 years since his TBI, he had lived in 11 different settings, including an acute care hospital, a rehabilitation center, an assisted living center, his parents' home, and an independent living situation with attendant care. He has successfully used AAC in each of these settings. However, not all individuals with TBI have adequate support to use AAC technologies consistently. Fager, Hux, Beukelman, and Karantounis (2004) documented long-term AAC use patterns by 25 people with TBI and reported that 2 of these individuals discontinued use of their AAC because they did not receive adequate support and/or

Individuals with Traumatic Brain Injury

did not have AAC facilitators to support effective communication in their living situations. The facilitator support received by people with TBI who successfully use AAC is often extensive. Thus, intervention efforts must focus on facilitator preparation as individuals with TBI transition through the multiple living situations that they are likely to experience.

# Cognitive-Linguistic and Communication Disorders

Several categorical scales have been developed in an effort to describe people with severe TBI. The Rancho Levels of Cognitive Functioning Scale (Hagen, 1984), which describes cognitive and associated language behaviors that occur during recovery, is presented in Table 17.1. AAC teams use scales such as this to guide the design of AAC and other interventions appropriate to each stage.

In general, the communication disorders associated with TBI are the result of impairments in three areas. First, some of the language characteristics of people with TBI are a consequence of cognitive impairments, as summarized in Table 17.1. The level of linguistic performance can vary depending on the individual's cognitive level. Second, language disorders may occur because of damage to specific language processing areas of the brain. Sarno, Buonaguro, and Levita (1986) evaluated 125 individuals with TBI by using the Battery of Language Test and reported that 29% of these individuals exhibited classic symptoms associated with acquired aphasia. An additional 36% exhibited subclinical aphasia, which the researchers defined as "linguistic processing deficits on testing in the absence of clinical manifestations of linguistic impairment" (p. 404).

Third, some communication disorders in TBI are caused by damage to the motor control networks and pathways of the brain that occurred at the time of injury. Dysarthria has often been reported as one of the long-term sequelae of TBI. Olver, Ponsford, and Curran (1996) reported that motor speech disorders were present in 34% of their sample 5 years after injury. Yorkston, Honsinger, Mitsuda, and Hammen (1989) surveyed 151 people following TBI and found that prevalence changed as a function of time after onset. Of those in acute rehabilitation, 45% were reported as having mild to moderate dysarthria and 20% were reported as having severe dysarthria. In outpatient settings, 12% demonstrated mild to moderate dysarthria and 10% demonstrated severe dysarthria. Ylvisaker (1986) reported that 10% of children and 8% of adolescents continued to produce unintelligible speech during follow-up studies. Several different types of dysarthria have been observed following TBI, including ataxic, flaccid, spastic, and combinations (Yorkston, Beukelman, Strand, &amp; Bell, 1999).

One mother recounts the first few days in the hospital after her daughter's severe TBI:

[Judy] tried to talk several times during the day. Much of it sounded unintelligible, but occasionally we heard "Where am I?" or other words we could understand. We could not tell if she knew us or understood anything we said. Then a few days later . . . Judy started trying to answer. . . . We spent the rest of the day hanging over her bed admiring her, as you might hang over the crib of a newborn baby. . . . The next day she responded less. This turned out to be a pattern. Nearly every day on which she showed definite improvement was followed by one of passivity or even apparent regression. It kept us on an emotional roller coaster. (D. Thatch, in Weiss, Thatch, &amp; Thatch, 1987, p. 17)

Recovery From Severe Communication Disorders

Communication disorders of individuals with TBI can change dramatically over the course of their recovery. Research has primarily focused on the long-term recovery of individuals with mild TBI. There is limited longitudinal research that describes the patterns of communication changes of individuals with severe TBI who rely on AAC; however, some authors have provided some insight about the course of recovery.

Ladtkow and Culp (1992) followed 138 people with TBI over an 18-month period. They reported that 29 of these individuals (21%) were judged unable to speak at some point in their recovery. Of these 29, 16 individuals (55%) regained functional speech during the middle stage of recovery (i.e. Rancho Levels of Cognitive Functioning IV and V in Table 17.1). Thirteen individuals (45%) did not regain functional speech; unfortunately, the description of the cognitive recovery of those who did not regain functional speech is incomplete. The authors merely indicated that only three people (10%) reached the late stage of recovery, corresponding to Levels VI, VII, and VIII of the Rancho scale.

In a similar study, Dongilli, Hakel, and Beukelman (1992) investigated the recovery of 27 people who were unable to speak on admission to inpatient rehabilitation following TBI. Of these, 16 individuals (59%) became functional natural speakers during inpatient rehabilitation, whereas the other 11 (41%) did not. All individuals who became functional speakers did so at Rancho Level of Cognitive Functioning V or VI (see Table 17.1). Of the 11 individuals who left inpatient rehabilitation unable to speak, one achieved functional natural speech almost 24 months postinjury, and another was making substantial progress toward becoming a functional speaker 48 months postinjury.

As the Dongilli et al. (1992) study shows, people with TBI may experience severe communication disorders for cognitive as well as motor-related reasons. Jordan and Murdoch (1990) described a 7-year-old girl who was mute for 10 months subsequent to coma. Following her mutism, the girl demonstrated rapid and unexpected recovery of functional communication skills, although she continued to experience higher-level language impairments. In a 4-year follow-up report, her speech intelligibility was within normal limits, and she exhibited improvements in her cognitive-linguistic abilities (Jordan & Murdoch, 1994).

Adding to this limited information base regarding recovery from communication disorders are two interesting case studies. In one, Workinger and Netsell (1988) described a man who recovered intelligible speech 13 years after injury and used various AAC technologies during the intervening years. In addition, Light et al. (1988) described the transitions of an adolescent girl with TBI through approximately 3 years of multiple AAC supports before she became a functional natural speaker. Enderby and Crow (1990), who followed four people with severe bulbar dysfunction due to TBI, reported similar outcomes. They reported that although the individuals made few gains within the first 18 months after injury, they made substantial improvements as much as 48 months postinjury.

During the past decade the medical treatment for TBI has changed considerably. Swelling of the brain and pressure on the brain from being enclosed in the skull have been reduced through medications and opening of the skull to relieve pressure. For example, removing sections of the skull (decompressive craniectomy or bone flap surgery) soon after TBI allows the brain to swell outside of the confines of the skull.

Individuals with Traumatic Brain Injury

Once swelling has subsided and the individual is medically stable, the bone flap is typically replaced. In our experience, it seems that there are fewer and fewer individuals with TBI who, while retaining or regaining considerable cognitive function, experience severe speech limitations because of damage to the brainstem due to the interruption of blood flow in the brainstem. Rather, many TBI patients with sustained inability to communicate using their natural speech often also experience considerable cognitive limitations. The multiple capability limitations of these individuals must be considered when selecting AAC options for them.

# NATURAL-ABILITY INTERVENTIONS RELATED TO SPEECH

As noted in the previous discussion, some individuals with TBI recover natural speech following injury, whereas others do not. Predicting the path of natural speech recovery for individuals with TBI is difficult. Therefore, individuals who experience TBI, their families, and their rehabilitation teams must address natural speech recovery on an individual basis.

Some individuals may be able to produce a number of intelligible words, although they may not recover completely functional speech in all situations. Family members, friends, and team members should encourage the use and improvement of these spoken words if they allow the individuals to manage certain aspects of communication interactions. Others with dysarthria following TBI can say many words, but their words are unintelligible because of impaired motor control. They may use AAC techniques to augment the intelligibility of their natural speech. In fact, most individuals with TBI use multiple modes of communication at every stage of recovery. Rehabilitation that emphasizes reestablishing natural speech only or using AAC only may not meet all the communication needs of a person with TBI.

# Topic Supplementation

If a person's speech is marginally intelligible, his or her message can often be understood if the communication partner is aware of the semantic context or topic. This semantic context can be displayed in communication boards containing lists of frequently occurring topics or through photographic images. Hanson and colleagues (2004, 2013) reviewed the literature on topic supplementation for speakers with various types of dysarthria. They reported that topic supplementation increased word intelligibility by an average of 28% and sentence intelligibility by 10.7%. Use of topic supplementation should be considered when dynamic assessment with the technique documents that 1) the individual with TBI can learn to implement it in conversational interactions and 2) the technique has a positive impact on speech intelligibility. In a study involving only individuals with TBI, Beukelman, Fager, Ullman, Hanson, and Logemann (2002) reported intelligibility gains of more than 50% for some speakers and as low as 2.4% for others. With the ubiquity of mobile technologies, the use of photographic images has become a prevalent form of information transfer (Van Dijck, 2008) in the general population. Given the fact that many computerized communication technologies now incorporate on-board cameras and easy transfer of photographic content into AAC software to support communication, the use of photographic topic supplementation may be an effective and desirable method for individuals who have used this method of communication support via digital communication media prior to their injury.

AAC Interventions for Individuals with Acquired Disabilities

# Alphabet Supplementation

Beukelman and Yorkston (1977) reported that a supplemented speech strategy substantially improved the speech intelligibility of speakers with dysarthria. In alphabet supplementation, the speaker identifies the first letter of each word on an alphabet board or other type of AAC display while saying the word. This procedure provides communication partners with information that allows them to restrict their word retrieval to words that begin with the letter indicated. Alphabet supplementation also causes most speakers to pause briefly between spoken words, thereby segmenting individual spoken words. In the same study, Beukelman and Yorkston described the impact of alphabet supplementation on the speech of a young man who had sustained TBI. His habitual sentence intelligibility was 33%, compared with 66% when he used alphabet supplementation. Hanson et al. (2004) reported that, across speakers with various types of dysarthria, alphabet supplementation increased sentence intelligibility by 25.5% and single-word intelligibility by 10%. Use of alphabet supplementation should be considered if an assessment confirms that 1) the individual with TBI can learn to implement it in conversational interactions and 2) the technique has a positive impact on speech intelligibility. In a study involving only people with TBI, Beukelman et al. (2002) reported intelligibility gains of up to 69% for some speakers with severe dysarthria and lesser intelligibility gains for those with less severe dysarthria (see Figure 17.1).

# Portable Voice Amplification

Some people with dysarthria following TBI speak so quietly that their speech is difficult to hear, especially in groups of people or in noisy environments. These individuals may find it useful to increase the loudness of their speech with a portable speech amplifier, provided that their speech is sufficiently intelligible to communicate effectively (see Chapter 14 for a more extensive discussion of this approach).

# AAC ACCEPTANCE AND USE PATTERNS

Outcome studies have described AAC recommendations for individuals with TBI. Fager et al. (2004) described the AAC acceptance and use patterns of 25 individuals with TBI. Following AAC assessment, 17 high-tech and 8 low-tech AAC supports were recommended. Fifteen of the 17 individuals for whom high-tech AAC was recommended received AAC technology. One individual rejected the recommendation, and one did not receive AAC technology due to funding constraints. Thirteen of the 15 individuals who received high-tech AAC continued to use their technology for an extended period of time, for an overall acceptance rate of 87%. Two individuals discontinued use of their high-tech AAC due to loss of ongoing communication facilitator support as they transferred from setting to setting or as staff members changed. All individuals for whom low-tech AAC was recommended accepted the recommendation. Three of these individuals discontinued use of their AAC due to recovery of natural speech. These individuals formulated their messages primarily through letter-by-letter spelling, unless they experienced a preexisting language disorder.

# ASSESSMENT AND INTERVENTION

In general, AAC teams should guide their intervention approaches with people who have TBI on individual levels of cognitive recovery (DeRuyter &amp; Kennedy, 1991; Fager et al., 2007; Fager &amp; Karantounis, 2011; Ladtkow &amp; Culp, 1992). AAC approaches have been described for three general stages of recovery: 1) the early stage, which involves Rancho Levels of Cognitive Functioning I, II, and III (see Table 17.1); 2) the middle stage, which includes Levels IV and V; and 3) the late stage, which includes Levels VI, VII, and VIII.

# Early Stage (Rancho Levels of Cognitive Functioning I, II, and III)

For people who have TBI and are in the early stage of cognitive recovery, assessment is extremely difficult, as explained below; AAC techniques used in intervention will vary.

**Early Stage Assessment** It is almost impossible in the early stage of recovery to assess cognitive, language, or motor control capabilities because the individual may be unable to stay awake or pay attention for any significant amount of time. Thus, at this stage, AAC teams attempt very little formal assessment. Instead, team members document systematic observations to identify changes in the individual's response patterns and to identify functional movements that the individual may use in a subsequent AAC program. Family members, friends, and other communication partners can also observe and chart such information if they spend a large amount of time with the individual. Also, they begin to provide autobiographic information in preparation for vocabulary selection and message management. Because they know the person well, they are in a good position to document changes and responses. Form 5.1 in Beukelman, Garrett, and Yorkston (2007) provides a strategy to document response modes and consistency (Fager et al., 2007).

As individuals with TBI become more alert, they gradually become able to differentiate between two or more people or objects, giving them the opportunity to communicate choices. This is a positive sign because it is often a precursor to the development of a yes/no response. The response mode for differentiation varies from person to person and may include eye pointing, moving a body part, or activating a beeper. The stimuli to which people recovering from TBI are able to respond must be presented in a careful and controlled manner. Family members and communication partners can usually be trained in this approach. They can also provide information about the interests and preinjury activities of the individual with TBI so that medical and rehabilitation personnel can provide the person with interesting and meaningful stimulation.

**Early Stage AAC Intervention** During the early stages of recovery, people with TBI are unable to speak functionally because of cognitive impairments. Some people

may have language or motor control impairments that further contribute to their communication disorder. Fager et al. (2007) suggest that the goals of AAC in the early stages of recovery are to increase the consistency of responses and to shape these responses into meaningful communication.

AAC techniques used at this point vary considerably depending on the individual's overall neurologic involvement. For example, consider the individual who is functioning in the range of Rancho Levels of Cognitive Functioning I to III and who also has considerable motor control impairment. This individual might be unable to respond to stimuli consistently not only because of cognitive problems but also because of motor weakness, spasticity, or lack of coordination. An AAC intervention for such a person might provide an alternative access mode, such as a single switch (Garrett, Schutz-Muehling, & Morrow, 1990). Then, as the individual begins to respond to various stimuli by making purposeful movements, communication facilitators, who support communication effectiveness, can encourage contingency awareness or cause and effect (Lancioni et al. 2014; Lancioni et al. 2011). For example, facilitators might encourage the individual to operate a CD/DVD player or an mp3 player with a single switch to play favorite music, listen to recorded messages from family members or friends, or play short video clips of personal relevance. In addition, a single switch with a control unit can be used to activate electrical appliances such as fans, radios, and lamps. As individuals become more purposeful, they may activate single-message communication technology containing basic greetings and other social phrases with a single switch (see Chapter 5 for additional suggestions). Then, if motor control permits, facilitators can connect two or more switches to different audio devices so that the individual can choose among different musical selections, messages, or videos. During the early stage of recovery, a limited number of symbols (e.g. one to four) might represent choices. Symbols should be brightly colored or exaggerated (Fried-Oken & Doyle, 1992). AAC teams should take care to understand the visual capabilities of individuals following TBI because impairments can range from double vision to cortical blindness. Stimuli (e.g. music, voices, video, pictures) should be motivating and personally relevant. Family members and friends can provide guidance in the development of these stimulus options.

Keenan and Barnhart (1993) documented the return of yes/no responses in 82 individuals with severe TBI: 49% signaled yes/no with head nods, 26% with motor responses of upper and lower extremities, 15% with eye gaze, and 9% with speech. Individuals with primarily cognitive or hemiplegic impairments developed yes/no responses earlier than those with high or low muscle tone. Twenty-nine percent of the individuals regained yes/no responses within 3 months of onset; 66%, within 6 months; and 84%, within 9 months.

### Middle Stage (Rancho Levels of Cognitive Functioning IV and V)

In the middle stage of recovery, the individual may respond consistently to stimuli while still showing evidence of considerable performance and communication impairments due to attention and memory impairments. Individuals who do not have specific language impairments or severe motor control impairments usually begin to speak functionally during these stages, although they may produce somewhat confused messages (Dongilli et al. 1992; Ladtkow & Culp, 1992). AAC materials or strategies to establish communication topics, to represent episodic experiences, or to

identify specific names for people, locations, or events are often useful to support the communication of these individuals. In addition, people with TBI generally begin to indicate their basic needs at this point. These may include comfort messages related to being hot, cold, hurt, or hungry. Individuals may also be able to communicate messages related to their location, the time of day, and other personal information. Family members and friends can assist with the selection of topics that are particularly important to people in the middle stage of recovery.

Early in the middle stage of recovery, people with TBI often experience agitation and poor awareness of their communication deficits. Therefore, they may initially have difficulty accepting AAC interventions. This may be reflected in limited willingness to participate in some aspects of AAC assessment.

### Middle Stage Assessment

The aim of assessment in the middle stage is to identify residual capabilities that the individual with TBI can utilize to achieve the specific communication goals mentioned previously. Examples are provided by Fager et al. (2007); see Form 5.6 in Beukelman et al. (2007). Most of the procedures for this assessment are criterion referenced. The initial assessment often focuses on seating and postural issues, which team members should coordinate with AAC concerns. Proper seating and positioning help to minimize reflex activity, excessive tone, and other movements that may interfere with speech or AAC usage (DeRuyter & Kennedy, 1991). Specifically, “the overall seating and positioning goals during [this] stage should be to provide for a structurally appropriate and functional position in which minimal or no pain is encountered” (DeRuyter & Kennedy, 1991, p. 342).

The RERC on AAC (Rehabilitation Engineering Research Center on Augmentative and Alternative Communication) webcast “Seating and Positioning for Individuals Who Use AT” by Aileen Costigan discusses seating and positioning for individuals who use AAC. Visit the AAC Learning Center to see the webcast.

Assessment of motor control capability is important to determine the individual's direct selection or scanning options. As discussed in Chapter 7, service providers should consider various access sites in terms of accuracy, efficiency, reliability, and endurance. This assessment may be difficult in some cases because people with TBI may require orthopedic surgical procedures that interfere, either temporarily or permanently, with their ability to use specific motor access sites (DeRuyter & Kennedy, 1991). Thus, it is important for AAC specialists to coordinate communication interventions with medical procedures by working closely with the medical team responsible for the individual's overall care. Assessment should also focus on the memory and attention capabilities of people with TBI. Complex scanning patterns (row--column or group--item) may be too demanding, so AAC teams should limit the individual's early scanning experiences to circular or linear scanning.

People with TBI often experience visual-perceptual and visual acuity disturbances, and these should also be considered in AAC assessment (Ciuffreda et al. 2007). At lower cognitive levels, service providers can usually determine visual functioning by observing the individual's ocular response to threat, gross focus movements of the eyes, and ability to follow a bright object or familiar face (DeRuyter & Kennedy, 1991). At higher cognitive levels, many visual disturbances can be noted during trials with AAC displays and input (when available) from other team members who

have training and expertise in vision assessment and treatment (e.g. occupational therapists). Because TBI often results in diffuse axonal injury, the visual impairments demonstrated can vary. Some may demonstrate cortical blindness where they are unable to process any visual information. For these individuals, auditory and tactile feedback are often needed for them to be able to use AAC.

Fager and Spellman (2010) described AAC intervention for an adolescent with cortical blindness and TBI. Using auditory scanning, during which communication options were presented auditorily, she was able to communicate yes/no early in recovery. As her memory and attention improved, she was able to communicate using pre-stored messages. However, because of the added visual challenges, she required cuing and support from her communication partners to locate content on her AAC technology. Communication partners would navigate to the appropriate communication page on her technology and she could select messages during contextualized tasks (e.g. telling a joke to a friend, choosing activities during therapy). Over time, her ability to find and retrieve messages on her technology using auditory scanning improved and she eventually began constructing short, novel messages via spelling.

For others, vision impairments may consist of field cuts (the inability to see content in a particular field of vision), visual neglect, or diplopia (double vision) to name a few. Combinations of these visual impairments can be present as well.

Jim sustained a severe right field cut and double vision after his injury. To maximize Jim's ability to communicate, messages on his communication technology were arranged on the left-hand side of the screen. At first, Jim could only see and access two columns of messages. Because of his double vision, the message buttons were limited to four per column and he managed large print text more accurately than icons or pictures. As Jim progressed, a blank column of red buttons was added to give Jim a visual cue to look to the right. Using this visual guide, Jim was able to progress to five columns of buttons. Jim learned that once he found the visual anchor (blank column of red buttons) he had scanned far enough to search for the appropriate communication content.

The type and severity of visual impairment can be detected through examination from a neuro-optometrist. A member of the AAC team should accompany the individual to such assessments to assist the communication process during the assessment and encourage the examiner to consider AAC-related issues, such as the optimal size for symbols and the array and the optimal distance between the individual and the display. Note that as social support for health care and rehabilitation decreases in some countries, people with TBI are spending less and less time in intensive rehabilitation programs in which AAC services may be available. It is important that people with TBI and their families educate themselves early in the recovery process about available AAC services and how to gain access to such services when they are needed.

### Middle Stage AAC Intervention

Depending on the nature of the brain injury, AAC teams should choose one or two major communication goals for the middle stage of recovery. The goal may be to help the person compensate for attention and memory impairments. This is particularly relevant for individuals with TBI who

AAC Interventions for Individuals with Acquired Disabilities

begin to speak during this stage because they often need communication techniques to help them remember, for example, the names of important people and their schedule of activities. A second goal of intervention in the middle stage applies specifically to individuals who have sustained damage to language or motor control areas of the brain. These individuals probably will not develop natural speech at this point in their recovery. Thus, AAC interventions should seek to provide these individuals with techniques that support conversational interaction. In Levels IV and V, messages that relate to wants, needs, and information sharing are more important to most individuals than messages that support social closeness and social etiquette (DeRuyter &amp; Kennedy, 1991; Fager et al., 2007; Fager &amp; Karantounis, 2011).

Most AAC interventions during the middle stage of recovery are either with nonelectronic means (i.e., alphabet boards, pictures, word boards, yes/no techniques, and partner-assisted scanning) or with a single or limited number of simple displays using AAC technology that generates speech. In an effort to reduce the complexity of communication, AAC teams may elect to use context-specific activity displays at this stage. For example, specific boards might facilitate participation in cognitive rehabilitation activities, recreational events, or daily living routines. Depending on the linguistic capabilities of the individual, photographs, line drawings, or printed words and phrases may be used to represent the messages on the activity displays. For some, icon-only displays (line drawings) versus text-only and text plus icon displays may lead to more efficient navigation of content in AAC technology (Brown, Thiessen, Beukelman, &amp; Hux, 2015). Research has also demonstrated that some individuals with TBI selected decontextualized photographic images more frequently than icons and contextualized photographic images (Thiessen, Brown, Beukelman, Hux, &amp; Myers, 2017). Interventionists should remember that people in this stage of recovery may experience difficulty visually discriminating among similar symbols or symbols with several elements. Individuals might use alphabetic displays, but encoding is almost always too difficult at this stage of recovery (Fried-Oken &amp; Doyle, 1992).

To control the complexity of the AAC supports, teams may choose small activity displays with specific content, rather than large, complex communication boards containing multiple areas of content. The organization of content in communication displays needs to be assessed because some with severe injury can display inconsistent patterns of organization (Brown, Hux, Kenny, &amp; Funk, 2014). For individuals with extensive attention and memory limitations, interventionists might consider written-choice strategies (see Chapter 15). During the middle stage, the individual might also use single switches to activate call buzzers or appliances or to run CD/DVD or mp3 players. Depending on the motor capabilities of the individual, such switch control activities may serve as training for the operation of a long-term environmental control technology.

Communication partners play an important role in structuring communication interactions during the middle stage. For example, partners may need to introduce topics for conversation, suggest the augmentative mode that can be used most productively at a particular time, assist with resolving communication breakdowns, and create motivating communication opportunities. Communication partners should actively help to structure interactions, but they should also be very patient and allow ample time for people with TBI to prepare, clarify, and repair their messages. Perhaps one of the most common partner errors is to rush or offer excessive encouragement during this stage by making multiple suggestions of how to formulate or complete a

message. This can be very distracting and frustrating to the individual with TBI, who must concentrate very hard to think, plan, compose, and finally produce a communicative utterance. At times, partners will also need to learn to provide systematic cuing to enable the person in the middle stage to use his or her communication supports effectively. In time, individuals with TBI should attempt to phase out partner cuing.

DeRuyter and Donoghue (1989) described in detail the AAC interventions over a 28-week period for a man who was unable to speak functionally due to TBI. During the first weeks of intervention (8 months postinjury), he established a reliable yes/no response by nodding his head, and he began to learn the visual-perceptual and upper-extremity skills necessary for eventual use of a communication board. In addition, his AAC team-initiated interventions to encourage the development of natural speech during this time. By the 10th week of intervention, he was able to use a simple alphabet board with approximately 2-inch letters. Initially, he exhibited “extreme frustration” (p. 52) with the board because of his motor planning deficits. By the 26th week of intervention, however, this man exhibited “no hesitation in using his alphabet board when he was unable to communicate effectively verbally or gesturally” (p. 53). His team introduced electronic AAC technology with speech output. With very little training on the technology, he was able to communicate at a rate of up to eight words per minute. At the time of his discharge from the inpatient rehabilitation facility, he communicated via limited speech, sophisticated gesturing, an alphabet board, and AAC technology with an expanded keyboard.

### Late Stage (Rancho Levels of Cognitive Functioning VI, VII, and VIII)

By the late stage of recovery, most individuals have regained the cognitive capability to become natural speakers, and those who remain unable to speak usually experience severe specific language or motor control disorders. Mobile technologies (e.g. smart phones, tablets) might be integrated as communication support if individuals have the ability to access these kinds of technologies. Because these technologies are commonly used by peers and colleagues, the appearance of them may be more acceptable to some (Brunner, Hemsley, Togher, & Palmer, 2017; Paterson & Carpenter, 2015).

Using a smart phone for communication support was a desirable option for Jeremy. Jeremy sustained a severe TBI when he was 12 years old. Following extensive inpatient and outpatient rehabilitation, he recovered his ability to walk. However, his speech remained severely dysarthric, he was unable to use his right hand, and he had limited control over his left (nondominant) hand. Because Jeremy was returning to school, he used text-to-speech communication technology with a large keyboard to accommodate the limited access capabilities he had with his left hand. As Jeremy's ability to use his left hand improved, he transitioned to a large smart phone using a text-to-speech app and a stylus. Jeremy was excited about this transition to the smart phone as it looked much like the phones his peers used.

Additionally, mobile devices may also assist in supporting some of the cognitive challenges that might remain for these individuals as they go about their daily lives (e.g. use reminder apps with tactile or auditory cuing; Lee et al. 2015).

AAC Interventions for Individuals with Acquired Disabilities

Late Stage Assessment AAC teams can use the Participation Model (see Figure 2.2) to guide effective assessment and intervention planning in the late stage of recovery. Analysis of the participation patterns of individuals with TBI and their families forms a particularly important part of this process. When people with TBI move from acute rehabilitation to outpatient rehabilitation, to independent living, and to employment, their patterns and expectations for participation change dramatically. These expectations greatly affect the nature and extent of their communication needs. It is also important to assess opportunity barriers, in much the same manner as is discussed in Chapter 2. For people with TBI in late stage recovery, AAC teams often identify communication needs, assess specific capabilities and constraints, and use these to personalize AAC interventions for the individual who relies on AAC (DeRuyter &amp; Kennedy, 1991; Fager et al., 2007; Ladtkow &amp; Culp, 1992).

Late Stage AAC Intervention In the late stage of recovery, individuals with TBI are generally oriented and able to demonstrate goal-directed, socially appropriate behavior. However, they may still have difficulties learning new information due to residual cognitive impairments. Some individuals may become natural speakers during Level VI. By Levels VII and VIII, most individuals who are likely to become natural speakers without extensive intervention have already done so (Dongilli et al., 1992). Thus, by the late stage of recovery, many people with TBI can interact and converse with their families and friends through natural speech. Nevertheless, even those individuals who regain speech may require AAC for writing support for an extended period. In addition, people with residual language and motor control impairments will continue to require long-term communication support to meet their specific interaction needs. Individuals have many interaction needs at this point, including those related to communicating wants and needs, sharing information, achieving social closeness, and participating in social etiquette routines (DeRuyter &amp; Kennedy, 1991).

During the late stage of cognitive recovery, traditional AAC techniques that resemble those used with other individuals who experience motor and cognitive impairments are often appropriate. Although people with TBI who cannot speak usually experience a high incidence of motor problems, one study found that approximately 78% were able to successfully utilize direct-selection AAC techniques (DeRuyter &amp; Lafontaine, 1987). Almost 75% of the individuals who used direct selection in DeRuyter and Lafontaine's database operated their technology with their fingers or hands, whereas the remainder used eye pointing, headlight pointing, or chin pointing; 16% utilized partner-assisted and unassisted scanning, and the remainder used other or no AAC techniques.

It might be assumed that because of the cognitive impairments associated with TBI, individuals will require AAC that contains pictorial or other nonorthographic symbols. However, this is often not the case. It is important to remember that even late in the recovery process, cognitive impairments may mask considerable residual capabilities. One of the most important capabilities that many people with TBI retain is the ability to read and spell. Thus, many individuals with TBI can utilize AAC supports that employ orthography, including letters, words, and sentences (Fager et al., 2004; Fried-Oken, Beukelman, &amp; Hux, 2011; Fried-Oken &amp; Doyle, 1992). In fact, in one review, Doyle, Kennedy, Jausalaitis, and Phillips (2000) reported that the majority of adults with TBI eventually were candidates for spelling-based access strategies. If

Individuals with Traumatic Brain Injury

coding strategies are used, they need to be relatively concrete rather than abstract (Doyle et al., 2000). These authors provided a summary of the impact of cognitive limitations on AAC interventions with TBI survivors.

Those who assist people with TBI during the recovery process may be well aware that new learning can be difficult and require considerable time and practice. This is an important consideration for individuals who require long-term communication support because some AAC approaches require extensive training for operation. Examples of such methods are those that are technically complex to operate or that require the individual to learn a large number of messages using sequences of alphabetic or iconic codes. The AAC team should exercise caution when introducing such techniques and should be careful not to make frequent changes in a system once the individual has learned it.

# CONCLUSIONS

AAC interventions for people with TBI have changed considerably during the past decade. Rather than waiting until it is determined whether or not an individual with TBI would eventually regain functional speech, the current approach is to provide patient-provider communication assistance so those with TBI can communicate as accurately as possible in their medical care and their rehabilitation programs, and to provide AAC support throughout the various transitions that they and their families face related to personal care, medical care, residential living, and community participation depending on their cognitive and physical capabilities and their life choices.

# Patient-Provider Communication in Medical Settings

In 2010, in the United States, the Joint Commission published *Advancing Effective Communication, Cultural Competence, and Patient- and Family-Centered Care: A Roadmap for Hospitals*, which states the following:

No longer considered to be simply a patient’s right, effective communication is now accepted as an essential component of quality care and patient safety. . . . Effective communication is the successful joint establishment of meaning wherein patients and health care providers exchange information, enabling patients to participate actively in their care from admission through discharge, and ensuring that the responsibilities of both patients and providers are understood. To be truly effective, communication requires a two-way process (expressive and receptive) in which messages are negotiated until the information is correctly understood by both parties. Successful communication takes place only when providers understand and integrate the information gleaned from patients, and when patients comprehend accurate, timely, complete, and unambiguous messages from providers in a way that enables them to participate responsibly in their care. (2010, p. 1)

Accurate, effective communication for patients in medical settings and situations is essential to appropriate, quality care. Medical errors are now the third leading cause of death in the United States (Makary &amp; Daniel, 2016). Such errors may be precipitated by communication failures between patients and providers during medical care (Blackstone, Beukelman, &amp; Yorkston, 2015). Communication breakdowns can occur during any medical care activity, but they are obviously more prevalent with patients who are communication vulnerable, such as those with complex communication needs.

For many of us, knowledge of medical experiences is based on our own medical appointments, on visits with friends or family in hospital or residential care settings, such as nursing homes, or on television documentaries. As a result, we realize that medical communication is often fast paced, involving a range of different medical providers and caregivers. We often think that communication in these settings focuses primarily on health and personal care and that patients are quite passive, having things done to and for them. This perception logically leads to the belief that, because acutely ill patients are so ill and so passive, they do not need to communicate beyond indicating “yes” or “no.” This is not at all the case. Most people in medical and care settings need to communicate regularly with hospital staff, including nurses, assistants, doctors, respiratory therapists, and so forth, to

647

participate in their own medical and personal care. Patients also report an urgent need to communicate with family members at these uncertain and frightening times in their lives. Depending on the length of stay, it may also be necessary for patients to communicate about finances, the operation of a family business, the care of dependent children, and other personal or legal matters.

Hurtig and Downey (2006) surveyed 135 nurses, and 100% of them reported that they were serving patients for whom communication was difficult. They further reported that 95% of the nurses were currently serving patients who would benefit from AAC support, and 99% of them reported that they had used AAC supports with their patients. When one considers the range of different patients served in medical units, the need for AAC support for a wide range of communication needs becomes apparent. This chapter is an introduction to communication supports for these patients.

Professionals who provide regular communication support in these medical environments are referred to 1) Blackstone et al. (2015), Patient-Provider Communication: Roles for Speech-Language Pathologists and Other Health Care Professionals and 2) Hurtig and Downey (2009), Augmentative and Alternative Communication in Acute and Critical Care Settings. Hurtig and Downey provide CD-ROMs containing electronic files of low-tech AAC supports designed for use in acute medical settings. Examples of these communication support materials are provided in Figures 18.1 to 18.5. Sarah Blackstone maintains a web site (http://www.patientprovidercommunication.org/communication_tools.htm) from which a range of patient-provider communication tools and materials can be downloaded.

## Causes of Communication Vulnerability in Medical Settings

Because the individuals whom we describe in this chapter are under direct medical care, we will refer to them as patients, rather than individuals, students, learners, clients, or residents. Patients who are communication vulnerable require communication support in a variety of medical settings, such as

1. During medical visits in an outpatient medical office
2. In acute care medical units in hospitals where patients receive medical care while they recover from illness or surgery
3. In intensive care units (ICUs) where patients who are critically ill receive continuous monitoring by critical care staff while a range of life-sustaining treatments are delivered
4. In long-term acute care hospitals for patients with persistent medical challenges, such as intubation for respiratory support
5. In long-term residential facilities (assisted living and nursing homes)
6. In hospice situations supporting individuals for whom death is ultimately expected

Patient-provider communication strategies are utilized with a wide range of individuals who are unable to communicate accurately and effectively using natural speech or hearing either temporarily or permanently. In these medical settings, communication vulnerability may occur for several different conditions (Blackstone et al. 2015).

# Recent-Onset Medical Conditions

Some patients experience recent-onset communication conditions associated with their current hospitalization or care placement. Recent-onset communication conditions may result from a variety of different medical conditions, including

1. Motor speech, language, or cognitive disorders resulting from traumatic brain injuries (TBIs) (see Chapter 17)
2. Motor speech impairment resulting from myasthenia gravis
3. Language disorders (aphasia) resulting from cerebral vascular conditions (strokes) (see Chapter 15)
4. Loss of respiratory support for speech due to high-level spinal cord injury

Patients with these recent-onset conditions experience admission to intensive care, acute care, or a long-term acute care hospital with severe communication limitations for which they have not received previous AAC interventions. They, and their families, often are unaware of the patient-provider communication options available

# Side Effects of Medical Interventions

Some patients experience communication conditions that result from medical interventions such as

1. Surgery to treat laryngeal, oral, or respiratory cancer
2. Surgery to remove cancerous tumors in areas of the brain that control cognitive, language, or motor function
3. Intubation or tracheostomy to support respiratory function following traumatic injury to the spinal cord or speech structures that interferes with voicing (phonation) for speech

These patients experience complex communication needs due to medical procedures; they may or may not have received communication preparation prior to these medical procedures, depending on the patient-provider communication policies and

Some medical units have standing orders for patients who are scheduled for medical interventions that will likely result in complex communication needs; unfortunately, others do not have such orders. Instead, they only issue specific orders for patient-provider communication after communication breakdowns occur.

Mike S., a 46-year-old man who had Guillain-Barré syndrome, describes what a patient might experience when he or she is unable to communicate with the people providing medical care:

When they put the tubes in, you get to the point of being helpless and you feel a need to communicate and talk to someone. You can't move. And you can't talk. And you want to say things. And you think, "Now I'd like to ask some more questions. You explained to me what's going on. But no, I want to know more now. What's going to happen?" And all you can really do is just lay there. That's when you really, really get spooked the most. (in Fried-Oken, Howard, &amp; Stewart, 1991, p. 43)

# Preexisting Communication Conditions

Some patients enter medical situations with preexisting communication conditions, such as those with speech or language disorders resulting from any of the following:

1. Developmental conditions such as cerebral palsy, autism spectrum disorder, Down syndrome, and Rett syndrome (see Chapter 13)
2. Acquired medical conditions such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), Parkinson's disease, multiple sclerosis, a previous stroke resulting in aphasia, or dysarthria from a previous traumatic brain injury (see Chapters 14-17)
3. Associated congenital or progressive hearing loss resulting in communication vulnerability in medical situations and settings when patients are attempting to interact with medical and care staff who are unfamiliar with them

Finally, some patients have difficulty communicating effectively in medical settings because of their native language, the complexity of their medical situation, or

2. Those who are unfamiliar with medical information related to a medical emergency or recent medical conditions, and therefore are unfamiliar with the vocabulary and terminology used by medical staff to communicate about their medical condition and related interventions
3. Those who need to communicate about legal issues, such as a will, end-of-life document(s), or testimony to law enforcement about an accident or an assault related to their medical condition

For patients with complex medical and/or legal issues, communication can be difficult. The patient-provider communication program for the medical facility or unit should have individuals who serve as communication and legal intermediaries
