# PATIENT-PROVIDER PERSONNEL ROLES

When people with complex communication needs are in medical settings, they interact with a range of different medical and care providers. During an outpatient medical visit, they may communicate with a receptionist, nurse, and physician (or physician's assistant). However, in inpatient hospital settings, it is not unusual for them to communicate with a physician, numerous different nurses, a physical therapist, an occupational therapist, a speech-language pathologist, medical technicians, dietary staff, social workers, pastoral care providers, housekeeping staff, and volunteers, many of whom are unfamiliar with the patient (Hurtig, Nilen, Happ, &amp; Blackstone, 2015). Gormley and Light (2018) reported on the experiences of children with complex communication needs in inpatient rehabilitation settings and found that a child typically interacted with more than 26 different health care providers in a 2-day period.

Family members of children and adults with complex communication needs may be actively involved in communication support roles in medical situations. They may

be involved during outpatient medical visits, the early days of hospitalization, team planning meetings, discharge planning meetings, as well as financial, legal, and end-of-life decision-making discussions. During long-term hospitalization or residence in long-term care units, family members typically cannot be available on a daily basis. During these medically related encounters, medical staff typically interact with patients and their family members.

## Medical Staff

Physicians or physician assistants are responsible for evaluating patients and issuing appropriate medical orders for all areas of care. Therefore, it is essential that these medical personnel be aware of the patient-provider communication resources and services that are available in the medical settings that they serve. A hospitalist is a physician who works exclusively in a hospital and specializes in the care of hospitalized patients. Hospitalists are usually involved in the range of care orders that support patient-provider communication interventions. Other hospitals have specialty wards or units for neurology, otolaryngology, and rehabilitation that are served by physicians or medical residents who specialize in these specific medical areas. Finally, in small hospitals and long-term care facilities, the patient's personal physician is usually responsible for ordering services, including patient-provider communication.

Because nursing personnel are generally responsible for supervising or carrying out many day-to-day activities in the medical care plan, they have extensive contact with both individuals with complex communication needs and their family members. Thus, nurses are in an excellent position to assist the AAC team by monitoring an individual's status, coordinating AAC interventions with the medical care plan, documenting the individual's communication needs, and keeping family members informed of changes in the communication plan. The nursing coordinator often assumes the role of patient advocate during communication intervention and actively encourages physicians to request AAC services.

Respiratory therapists deal with a high proportion of the people in acute care units. These therapists are generally responsible for day-to-day management of individuals' respiratory status, including that of people with endotracheal or tracheostomy tubes. The patient-provider communication team must cooperate closely with respiratory therapists for successful intervention. Ongoing staff education is important, especially in training hospitals in which the staff consists of interns and residents as well as senior medical personnel. The AAC team members may be invited to present their plan directly to the medical team. Instruction about specific patient-provider communication services, however, usually occurs in the context of ongoing service delivery.

## Patient-Provider Communication Team Roles

The patient-provider communication effort for a medical agency, facility, or unit usually involves several participants who fulfill specific roles and assignments (Beukelman & Nordness, 2017). Patient-provider communication coordinators have overall responsibility for the patient-provider communication effort in a unit or facility, as they oversee the program, acquire communication materials and tools, and train medical providers in patient-provider communication strategies. Daily communication facilitators support the communication of specific patients on a daily basis by ensuring that appropriate messages are represented in communication materials; that AAC

Patient-Provider Communication in Medical Settings
655

materials and technology are cleaned, charged, and maintained; and that unfamiliar communication partners are appropriately instructed, when necessary. A legal communication intermediary is an individual who supports accurate communication between a communication-vulnerable patient and legal personnel. When the legal communication involves the medical or care provider, the intermediary is an individual who is not an employee of the medical or care facility or the legal firm involved in the investigation of legal proceedings.

In acute care and rehabilitation settings, paid staff usually assume these communication support roles. However, in long-term residential settings, a range of different staff, volunteers, and family members support communication depending on the policies and practices of the facility as well as the unique communication needs of individual patients.

# MEDICAL ORDERS (REFERRALS) FOR PATIENT-PROVIDER COMMUNICATION SERVICES

Several different types of medical orders can be used to initiate patient-provider communication intervention for patients in medical settings (Beukelman &amp; Nordness, 2017). In many medical settings, physicians or physician assistants only initiate patient-provider communication services with specific referrals. However, some medical agencies have established patient-provider communication policies and strategies that utilize several different medical order types, which are briefly described in the following section.

# Specific Order (Referral)

Specific orders (referrals) specify the transfer of care for a patient from one professional to another. Specific orders may also be requests for a second opinion, to evaluate or manage a particular problem, or to authorize care by a specialist or agency. Typically, a specific referral is ordered by a physician to address the need of specific patients at specific times in their treatment. For example, such a referral would order the assessment of patients for communication disorders and perhaps also initiate an intervention program. Often, a patient-provider communication intervention is not ordered until communication breakdowns occur.

Consider the following case described by Beukelman and Nordness (2017) where a specific order did not result in appropriate management. A 54-year-old woman was diagnosed with Guillain-Barré syndrome. She had lost the ability to use her arms and legs, to breathe, to swallow, and to talk and was intubated. In time, a tracheostomy was inserted, and she remained on the ventilator support. Because the facility did not routinely order speaking valves when patients are on ventilators, a specific order was not entered in the electronic medical record system for a speaking valve evaluation until after she was weaned from the ventilator. Then, a speech-language pathologist evaluated her for a speaking valve, but her anatomy was too small to tolerate it. Orders for patient-provider communication services were requested, but it took nearly a week to obtain another specific order for the patient-provider communication evaluation to be done. Eventually, she was provided with a low-tech laser pointer mounted on her glasses, so she could point to messages on a wall-mounted communication board.

For patients with preexisting severe dysarthria, the need for patient-provider communication in care and medical settings is common. However, specific orders are often not made until there are communication breakdowns. For patients with recent-onset conditions, assessment and diagnostic procedures are ordered with specific referrals by the medical staff. For patients facing treatments or procedures that might further impact communication effectiveness, specific referrals for patient-provider communication support depend on a physician, nurse, or speech-language pathology advocate. In our clinical experience, specific orders are usually not issued until there is a communication breakdown, unless a specific policy is in place.

### Medical Order for Scope of Treatment

A medical referral for scope of treatment can be used to order patient-provider communication support for a patient that will be activated when the communication-vulnerable individual is admitted for medical care or admitted into a medical facility. These orders are issued by a physician following consultation with a patient who has independent legal standing, or family member if the patient does not have independent legal standing. The order usually identifies the type(s) of patient-provider communication support needed, such as AAC or hearing devices. These orders must be reviewed annually by the physician for people with preexisting medical conditions so that the order can be provided to medical providers in unexpected or unpredicted medical situations. Scope of treatment orders are increasingly used for specific people who rely on AAC and live away from their families on a college campus, in an independent living situation, or in an assisted-living facility. A scope of treatment order is issued so that if the individual needs emergency or acute medical care by the campus health center or a local hospital, patient-provider communication support would be ordered upon the admission of the patient into the medical center.

### Standing Order

A standing order prescribes the action(s) and support to be implemented for a patient with a specific medical condition. For example, appropriate patient-provider communication interventions can be specified in a standing order for patients who will be intubated during a surgical procedure or will undergo a laryngectomy for laryngeal cancer or oral surgery for oral cancer. Rehabilitation facilities often issue standing orders for individuals who are admitted following a stroke (CVA), so a specific communication assessment will be completed to determine if patient-provider communication support or further communication intervention is needed, whether or not these services had been provided in the acute medical setting from which the patient was transferred.

### Care Map

A care map or clinical pathway contains a series of orders that designate the patient journey for a special medical condition in a particular medical setting. Care maps are often used by rehabilitation hospitals to treat patients with spinal cord injury, stroke, or traumatic brain injury. These maps order patient-provider communication interventions if needed to support communication effectiveness during medical care or rehabilitation.

AAC Service Delivery in Medical Settings

Melanie Fried‐Oken (2001), writing about her husband's use of AAC in an ICU following a severe bicycling accident, describes it as follows: “[His] messages were short but effective. . . . I remember some of them clearly: Where am I, When, What happened, Move me up/down, Bedpan, More pillow, Get Nurse. . . . It was clear that the perceptions of others were influenced by his communication performance. . . . The portable typewriter [Lightwriter] with voice output was essential in changing the way people talked to Barry and asked him questions. (p. 139)”

Because medical settings are so organizationally complex, onsite professionals, rather than external consultants, usually provide the most effective ongoing AAC services. It is much more difficult for a consultant to come intermittently to a hospital to provide AAC services because the individual who requires the services may be unavailable, too ill, resting, or receiving other medical treatments that take priority at the time of the consultant's visit.

The delivery of AAC services in acute medical settings is structured differently from delivery of AAC services in typical rehabilitation or educational settings. In acute care settings, patients with complex communication needs are typically interacting with providers who are unfamiliar with them personally and unfamiliar with their communication support options. Also, at times, their communication capabilities have recently changed due to the current medical condition. For those with complex communication needs in rehabilitation hospital settings, a speech‐language pathologist and other therapy team members are assigned to a specific patient, so they become familiar with the patient's communication needs and supports. However, the nursing staff may be quite diverse as they serve the patient 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. It is not uncommon for 20 different nursing staff members to interact with the patient during a given week. Of course, AAC services in an educational setting involve much more consistent staffing than in medical settings. Usually, one speech‐language pathologist is assigned to provide AAC support for a student during elementary school, along with one or two teachers and perhaps an aide. In middle and high school, additional teachers will interact with the student depending on the student's educational placement; however, these individuals are consistent throughout the school year. A successful AAC program in any given setting must accommodate factors specific to the setting in order to be accepted and used by patients and medical personnel.

### Establishing a Patient‐Provider Communication Program

It is beyond the scope of this chapter to provide an extensive discussion regarding how to develop an AAC program in an intensive or acute care medical setting (see Costello, 2000; Garrett, Happ, Costello, & Fried‐Oken, 2007; Hurtig & Downey, 2009, for detailed descriptions of this process). Garrett et al. (2007) noted that AAC teams should pay careful attention to individuals' equipment needs in acute care settings, as well as to administrative, organizational, and personnel training issues. They suggested that the following equipment and materials form the basis for many AAC interventions in acute medical settings: 1) a lightweight neck‐type electrolarynx (i.e. one that is positioned against the neck and vibrates the air column within the vocal tract);

AAC Interventions for Individuals with Acquired Disabilities

2) an oral-type electrolarynx (i.e., one that delivers sound into the oral cavity through a tube); 3) materials to construct alphabet boards, word boards, and picture boards; 4) several whiteboards or magic slates (these are generally sold as toys and consist of a sheet of plastic over a piece of coated board that can be written on; when the plastic is lifted, written messages disappear); 5) at times, AAC technology with speech output (tablet or smart phone) for some individuals in long-term acute care units; and 6) a portable mounting system on wheels to hold cardboard message boards or eye-pointing displays. These minimal equipment needs reflect the previously stated philosophy of simplifying AAC interventions in this area and are echoed by Dowden, Beukelman, and Lossing, 1986:

Clinicians with very few AAC systems can nonetheless serve ICU patients quite well . . . The majority of our patients were served with electrolarynges or . . . modified natural speech approaches. With additional access to the least expensive communication systems (Plexiglas boards for eye-gaze, . . . paper and pencil, and a few small text-to-speech typing systems), we were able to serve all but a few of our patients. This means that even the smallest clinical program should consider serving patients in intensive care units. (p. 43)

It is quite common for the AAC team to prepare a set of AAC materials for the intensive care unit or acute care unit in the hospital so that the staff has access to these materials as needed. More extensive AAC technology may be necessary for people who remain in long-term acute care or residential settings. Typically, this technology is purchased or rented by the patient depending on financial support options, life expectancy, and anticipated course of the medical condition.

## PATIENT-PROVIDER COMMUNICATION OPTIONS FOR PATIENTS WITH COMPLEX COMMUNICATION NEEDS DUE TO SPEECH AND LANGUAGE LIMITATIONS

The sections that follow describe options for patients with complex communication needs due to speech and language limitations. Topics addressed include understanding patient issues related to their medical needs and care; use of the Participation Model to identify their communication participation patterns and communication needs; and the assessment of opportunity barriers and supports, access barriers and patient capabilities, specific capabilities and competencies, and constraints affecting communication options.

## Understand Patient Issues

Individuals in medical settings have serious medical needs that are critical to their survival. The delivery of AAC services simply cannot interfere with the delivery of medical care. Communication support services must be integrated into the overall care plan for the individual.

The intensity of medical care affects the AAC program in a variety of ways. Medical staff are responsible for establishing and delivering an overall medical plan in which communication intervention plays an integral role. Thus, the AAC staff cannot provide services without a request or referral from the medical team. The AAC team members must clearly communicate the types of services they can deliver. They must consult with the medical team before and during AAC interventions to ensure that efforts coordinate well with and support the overall medical plan. If communication specialists do not follow these guidelines, they may fail to meet individuals' AAC needs.

Patient-Provider Communication in Medical Settings
659

Because patients in medical settings receive such extensive medical support, it is common for many different professionals as well as visiting family members and friends to have contact with each person during a 24-hour period. Thus, a variety of individuals must be able to understand AAC interventions. Signs on the walls, written messages, or oral instructions must provide instructions for all these people. AAC interventions must be minimally complex and require minimal training and learning to be successful.

## Identify Communication

### Participation Patterns and Communication Needs

The Participation Model (see Figure 2.2) supports the overall delivery of AAC services to people in care and medical environments. Interventionists can expect restricted participation patterns because individuals in acute care, intensive care, and inpatient rehabilitation are essentially in one communication environment, have limited face-to-face contact with people in their social networks, and are not working; however, for some patients, communication over a telephone and over digital networks remains an option. Internet communication is supported in an increasing number of long-term acute care and long-term residential care units (including electronic face-to-face communication at a distance).

Olinda uses a ventilator to breathe as a result of ALS (Fager, Beukelman, &amp; Jakobs, 2009). She communicates, reads, and controls her environment with eye-tracking AAC technology. She e-mailed the AAC clinic and asked for help in learning how to use her technology to communicate using Skype (a face-to-face video-calling application) so that she could communicate in a new way with her son and daughter-in-law who live across the country from her. Her daughter-in-law was pregnant, and Olinda wanted to be ready to see and interact with her first grandchild (S. Fager, personal communication, 2010).

John experienced chronic Guillain-Barré syndrome. Because of his respiratory needs, we assisted him while he was in the long-term acute care hospital unit. His communication was limited in several ways. Using head-tracking AAC technology, John was able to interact with staff and family. To communicate at a distance, he used his AAC technology to speak on the telephone, but most distance communication with his family, friends, and a long-term, personal physician was by e-mail. He also used his head-tracking skills to access information from the Internet and to access electronic games (S. Fager, personal communication, 2012).

### Assess Opportunity Barriers and Supports

Individuals in medical settings deserve to have access to patient-provider communication services to meet their communication needs, and the lack of availability of such services can be considered to be an opportunity barrier. Few hospitals appear to have actual policies against AAC and patient-provider communication services; even so, AAC teams must deal with a number of practice or knowledge barriers to ensure effective patient-provider communication. These barriers may include 1) medical teams that do not refer individuals for AAC services; 2) personnel who prefer not to be burdened with additional work in an already busy (and, perhaps, understaffed) workplace; 3) speech-language pathologists and other professionals

who are not familiar with conducting AAC interventions in these settings; or 4) staffing patterns that result in the speech-language pathologists working in acute and intensive care settings having little or no AAC experience while AAC specialists serve the inpatient and outpatient rehabilitation programs.

### Assess Access Barriers and Patient Capabilities

As with other AAC assessments, those that occur in care settings require considerations of specific access barriers and capabilities.

### Assess Specific Capabilities/Competences: Preliminary Screening

Many individuals in medical settings are unable to participate in extensive assessment procedures. The AAC team should conduct a preliminary screening as the first step of an assessment to determine what capabilities are available to support communication. Garrett et al. (2007) identified a series of communicative tasks that might be considered.

Natural communication signals should be identified and evaluated to determine if the medical staff can accurately interpret them. These signals might include licking the lips to signal the need for lip moisturizer, wrinkling the face to signal pain or itchiness, protruding the tongue to signal the need for a urinal, or closing the eyes to signal the desire to be left alone. Yes/no signals are essential to early communication in ICU settings. Affirmation or negation can be signaled with hand squeezes, eye movement (up for yes and down for no), or thumb movement (up for yes and down or sideways for no). Of course, these codes should be noted on a sign (or whiteboard) posted on a wall in the room, recorded in the medical chart, and shared at team meetings. The AAC team should accommodate the individual's hearing and vision by making sure that the need for glasses and hearing aids is identified and that these aids are routinely provided.

Comprehension and attention strategies that are effective for each patient should be identified. After all, medical and care environments are unfamiliar environments for most individuals. It is typically noisy, with a range of technology and alarm systems in operation, and it is busy, with many different staff coming and going. At times, two or more staff members may be in the room at once, with multiple people attempting to communicate with the patient. Therefore, it is important to identify strategies that effectively get the attention of the patient before questions are asked or instructions are given. Also, Garrett et al. recommended a strategy in which staff “establish and maintain eye gaze with the patient when trying to communicate with [him or her]” (2007, p. 32). Comprehension of information is often assisted by providing visual information in the form of print, drawings, or pictures in addition to the spoken message, a technique known as augmented input. Finally, communication is typically improved if the patient is given a description, involving photographs or videos, of more complex procedures before the procedure is begun, rather than not describing the procedure at all or trying to describe it as the procedure is being implemented.

### Individuals with Insufficient Motor Control for Speech

Some people have insufficient motor control for speech. If this is the case, individuals may require communication systems that use writing, direct selection, and/or scanning, as discussed in the following sections.

Writing Options

Handwriting can serve as an effective communication mode because many people are comfortable and familiar with this mode of communication. Some individuals prefer to use a pencil and tablet so that, as they write and save messages, they can begin to construct their own communication book. Then, rather than writing the same message again and again, they can simply refer to a question or a comment they communicated previously. Others prefer to use a magic slate or Boogie Board, which display messages written with a stylus that can be erased to maintain privacy.

Alec K. a 35-year-old man who had Guillain-Barré syndrome, describes his use of a magic slate:

> I think that board [a magic slate] was my preference over everything. You could communicate quickly and say what you wanted to say. You can write your letters and separate your words, like in normal writing. And it was much quicker and easier to understand by other people. I think they probably like it the best, too. So, the magic board was the best one, once I could start using my hands again. When I was unable to use my hands, of course the alphabet board [for partner-assisted scanning] was the best, assuming that the other person understood how to use it, which many didn't. (in Fried-Oken et al. 1991, p. 47)

### Options for People Who Cannot Write

Some individuals are unable to write by hand, but they can point accurately with their hands, eyes, or head. AAC teams generally encourage these individuals to use direct selection to access AAC. The direct-selection system can be as simple as an alphabet board with some words or phrases on it. Other individuals may prefer a small typing system. Usually, individuals in acute medical settings do not have the time or motivation to learn to use an encoding strategy. Therefore, some prefer to type their messages with word prediction options if available on the technology.

If available, voice output may be preferred by some individuals. Costello, Santiago, and Blackstone (2015) described the use of voice banking for children scheduled in advance for major surgical procedures such as facial reconstruction. Prior to their surgeries, the children recorded messages that were later transferred to simple AAC technologies that they used in the ICU. Thus, the children were able to use their own voices to “talk” during this difficult and stressful time. Small, portable, digitized devices that contain 30--60 easily accessible messages are convenient for this purpose. If individuals have insufficient hand or arm control to use these options, they may use a headlight pointer to indicate words or letters on a wall- or ceiling-mounted chart or on a communication board placed on a mounting stand.

George was unable to communicate, except to move his head slightly side to side to signal “No” and to point with his eyes. With a diagnosis of severe myasthenia gravis (characterized by weakness and rapid fatigue of muscles), he faced an extended hospital stay. An observant nurse informed us that he could move his right foot a bit, so we mounted a laser pointer on his big toe and a communication device at the foot of his bed. With his head propped up slightly so that he could see the device, George spelled his messages by moving his foot. Six weeks later, he recovered sufficiently to return home, speaking once again.

AAC Interventions for Individuals with Acquired Disabilities

Some individuals may be limited to eye pointing in one of two forms. The first form is conventional eye pointing, in which the individual selects and gazes at a message on a display that is mounted on a transparent plastic board. The communication partner then interprets the direction of the individual's eye gaze and reads the related message. The second form, a technique known as eye linking (see Chapter 7), may also be used. In eye linking, the individual looks at the desired message, and the partner (who is positioned opposite the individual on the other side of the transparent communication board) moves the board until his or her eyes are linked directly across from the individual's. At that point, the message that the individual wants to convey lies between the two people. Many individuals find this strategy to be easier than eye pointing.

**Options for People Who Cannot Use Direct Selection** Some individuals do not have the motor capability to engage in direct selection communication. If they have other reliable, consistent motor responses, these individuals may be able to successfully use a scanning communication option. Many families can learn to use partner-assisted scanning, in which an array of letters or messages is displayed on a communication board, and the communication partner points to or speaks aloud various message options. Alternatively, the communication partner speaks the message options, such as reciting rows of the alphabet orally (divided by the vowels, e.g., *a* row, *e* row, *i* row, *o* row, *u* row) and then offering individual letters in the row selected (e.g., *o p q r s t*). During these visual or auditory options, the individual signals when a desired message is reached by making a gesture, blinking the eyes, or activating a beeper with a switch.

## Assess Constraints

A common constraint that affects AAC interventions is related to instruction of communication partners. The short-term acute medical environment imposes extensive learning constraints. First, individuals are very ill and under a considerable amount of stress. Many individuals in these settings demonstrate little ability or tolerance for learning new technologies. Second, many professionals and others interact with these individuals over the course of their stay. Thus, the most effective AAC interventions are those that require minimal communication partner training. As noted previously, individuals and their medical teams tend not to use complicated AAC systems in short-term acute medical environments, unless they have a preexisting communication condition and have been using AAC prior to their current medical admission.

## MEDICAL CULTURES ARE GUIDED BY POLICIES

In many medical and care facilities, patient-provider communication services are initiated, guided, and directed by professionals who are strong advocates for these services; unfortunately, many of these facilities do not have formalized patient-provider communication policies (Beukelman &amp; Nordness, 2017; Blackstone et al., 2015). Often this personal advocacy strategy is only effective for a facility or situation as long as the advocate is employed in that role.

Fortunately, many facilities are beginning to develop patient-provider communication policies and programs that are summarized for outpatient medical clinic visits

Patient-Provider Communication in Medical Settings
663

(Burns, Baylor, Dudgeon, Starks, &amp; Yorkston, 2017), adult intensive and acute care (Hurtig et al., 2015), pediatric acute and intensive care (Costello et al., 2015), rehabilitation settings (Beukelman &amp; Nordness, 2015), residential long-term care (Beukelman, 2015), and hospice care (Bardach, 2015). (See the book by Blackstone et al., 2015, for more detailed discussion of these issues.)

Beukelman and Nordness (2017) provide two checklists (accessible with the Online Companion Materials for this book) related to patient-provider communication services that can be used by care managers and speech-language pathologists to evaluate practices in their medical settings. The Patient-Provider Communication Checklist for Medical/Care Identification of Medical Setting (Appendix 18.1) documents patient-provider communication personnel, medical orders, communication procedures, communication tools/materials, and personnel training. The Evaluation of Patient-Provider Communication Support for Communication-Vulnerable Patients/Residents (Appendix 18.2) documents the patient-provider communication experiences of communication-vulnerable patients in specific medical/care settings.

## FUTURE DIRECTIONS

At the time this textbook was written, advances in patient-provider communication support across medical settings was receiving considerable attention with the publication of research articles and books. However, on a daily basis, these services are still provided very inconsistently. Accurate and efficient communication between patients and their medical and care providers in medical settings requires the ongoing consideration of the AAC and medical fields. This effort will require ongoing research, development of appropriate communication support technologies and materials, preparation of AAC and medical provider staff, and the implementation of patient-provider care policies and practice across medical settings.

# The Importance of Advocacy

In 2006, the United Nations ratified an international convention to uphold the dignity and rights of persons with disabilities. A key component of this international convention is the recognition of the fundamental right of communication for all individuals. Many people who have easy access to speech, writing, and typing take this essential human right for granted. Yet for an estimated 5 million Americans and more than 97 million people worldwide, this basic human right is by no means a given. These individuals have complex communication needs and have limited or no access to conventional channels of communication—speech, writing, and typing. The group of individuals with complex communication needs has no boundaries in terms of age, race, ethnicity, gender, sexual orientation, religion, socioeconomic status, or nationality. It includes children and adults across the life span; it encompasses those with developmental disabilities, acquired conditions, degenerative disorders, and temporary conditions. It is a group to which any of us may one day belong. Without access to speech, writing, and typing, individuals with complex communication needs are severely limited in their ability to express needs and wants, exchange information, develop social relationships, and establish their identities. They are severely restricted in their participation in education, employment, health care, family, and community. But it does not need to be that way.

We hope that this book has shown how AAC intervention can fundamentally change the equation, by providing individuals with complex communication needs with the tools and supports to communicate successfully and to participate within society as they choose. Providing effective, evidence-based AAC intervention requires significant knowledge and skills on the part of the AAC team, including the individual with complex communication needs, family, and professionals from a wide range of disciplines. This book has described the knowledge base underlying AAC intervention. This knowledge base is essential to improve the lives of individuals who rely on AAC.

However, knowledge alone is by no means sufficient. Also required is a deep commitment on the part of professionals and society to the right of communication for all—including those with the most complex needs. The research has clearly demonstrated the positive impact of AAC on outcomes for children and adults across age and disability groups. This research has demonstrated what is possible. Unfortunately, what is possible is still not what is available for many children and adults with complex communication needs in the United States and worldwide. Many fail to receive the high-quality AAC services they require to realize the basic human right of communication. Bob Williams, former Deputy Commissioner of the Administration

667

AAC Interventions for Individuals with Acquired Disabilities

on Disabilities and former Director of the Independent Living Administration of the United States Department of Health and Human Services, and an expert communicator via AAC, summed up the problem as follows:

Why are so many people consigned to lead lives of needless dependence and silence? Not because we lack the funds, nor because we lack the federal policy mandates needed to gain access to those funds. Rather, many people lead lives of silence because many others still find it difficult to believe that people with speech disabilities like my own have anything to say or contributions to make. (p. 250)

Many individuals who require AAC face substantial policy, practice, attitude, knowledge, skill, and service delivery barriers that preclude their access to communication. Concerted advocacy is required to overcome these barriers to ensure access to AAC and meaningful opportunities for communication for all, including those with the most complex needs. There are numerous examples of effective advocacy efforts in the field to improve outcomes for individuals who require AAC, including 1) efforts to enhance early intervention, literacy instruction, community participation, and patient-provider communication; 2) efforts to effect systemic change to continue to improve funding of AAC supports and continue to improve preservice preparation; and 3) the hard work of specific AAC teams to provide opportunities for individual children and adults and their families. Each of us can play a role in these advocacy efforts. We urge each of you to pause as you finish this book, reflect on at least one way in which you can make a positive difference in the lives of individuals with complex communication needs and their families, and commit to that effort. As single individuals, we may not be able to change the world, but as an AAC community we can effect significant positive change.

Perhaps Schuyler Hudson, a young woman who uses AAC, and her father, Rob Rummel-Hudson, said it best when they wrote:

My point . . . for every educator and every employer and policy maker and citizen, is that the only way the world will work for people with disabilities like Schuyler is if it becomes a place defined by opportunity. Inclusion can't be a policy or a goal; the time for that is long behind us now. Meaningful inclusion has to reside in our DNA as a society. . . . We need to create a just and inclusive society with opportunities and authentic relationships and real equity. (Rummel-Hudson &amp; Hudson, 2018)

Bob Williams concluded,

Access to assistive technology and other effective means of expression is vital. Having the power to speak one's heart and mind changes the disability equation dramatically. In fact, it is the only thing I know that can take a sledgehammer to the age-old walls of myths and stereotypes and begin to shatter the silence that looms so large in many people's lives. (Williams, 2000, p. 249)
